artigo.texto: Dubai, United Arab Emirates – Trina Storage, a global leader in energy storage solutions, has once again been recognized on the BloombergNEF (BNEF) Energy Storage Tier 1 List for Q4 2026, marking its 12th consecutive inclusion on the prestigious ranking and completing three consecutive years of Tier 1 recognition. This achievement further reinforces the company's position as a trusted and bankable partner for utility-scale energy storage projects worldwide. The latest BNEF Tier 1 Energy Storage ranking reflects the growing maturity of the global energy storage market and introduces updated assessment criteria with a stronger focus on project financing and bankability. Under the revised methodology, manufacturers are required to demonstrate successful deployment and financing track records through independently financed utility-scale projects. Trina Storage's continued presence on the list highlights the company's proven capability to deliver high-quality, financeable energy storage solutions at scale. "We are honored to be recognized by BloombergNEF for the 12th consecutive quarter," said Mr. Yang Bao, President of Energy Storage Division at Trinasolar. “The evolution of BNEF’s methodology reflects the increasing maturity of the energy storage industry. As customers place greater emphasis on project execution, financing readiness and long-term performance, we remain focused on delivering solutions that create lasting value throughout the project lifecycle.” As solar generation expands across the Middle East and Africa, battery storage can help utilities maintain grid stability and make solar power available after sunset. In Aswan, Egypt, Trina Storage supplied its Elementa 2 system as the exclusive energy storage partner for AMEA Power’s 300 MWh Abydos battery energy storage project, part of Egypt’s first utility-scale solar-plus-storage facility. Trina Storage completed installation and grid connection in 60 days, ahead of schedule. “The next phase of energy storage in the Middle East and Africa will be defined by the ability to deploy at scale while meeting increasingly demanding technical and operational requirements,” said Jack Chen, Head of Energy Storage, MEA Region at Trinasolar. “At Trina Storage, we continue to expand our portfolio with advanced, integrated solutions designed for a range of applications. Our focus is on giving utilities and developers the performance, reliability and flexibility they need for their projects.” The company’s Elementa battery energy storage system incorporates liquid-cooling architecture and advanced battery management technologies designed to support reliable operation across a range of utility-scale applications. Meanwhile, the recently introduced Elementa + Electra integrated DC+AC solution combines high-density battery storage with advanced power conversion technology, simplifying deployment while enhancing system performance and project value. The solution supports demanding utility-scale applications with features including grid-forming capability, black-start functionality, and flexible power control. As the global energy storage industry enters a new phase of growth, Trina Storage will continue to work closely with utilities and developers across the Middle East and Africa to deliver safe, reliable and high-performance solutions that maximize project value and support a more sustainable energy future. About Trina Storage Trina Storage, a business unit of Trinasolar established in 2015, is a global leader in energy storage products and solutions, dedicated to transforming the way we provide energy. Our mission is to lead the renewable energy transition through cost-competitive storage and to provide Solar for Everyone by expanding solar generation at scale. Leveraging decades of expertise in solar manufacturing, we offer cost-effective and flexible storage solutions to meet the diverse needs of our global customers. artigo.texto: TOWN OF MOHAWK — The town of Mohawk has extended its moratorium on battery energy storage systems for another six months to update laws regulating the devices. Town Supervisor Janet DePalma said the town board is expected to review proposed zoning updates next month with a public hearing likely to be scheduled for February to avoid overloading the January organizational meeting. “We just didn't have the time to get everything done before the end of this current moratorium,” DePalma said. The town enacted a six-month moratorium on battery systems earlier this year to give officials time to develop regulations for them. The town board last week extended the pause that would have otherwise expired on Saturday. Officials tasked the planning board with studying the issues and developing recommended zoning regulations for the town board’s consideration. Tighter regulations are expected, but not an outright ban. “We don't want to be unwelcome to what is obviously the state's direction that they want everybody to take. We just want to really set the parameters around how it's done in our town to protect our citizens and to protect our community,” DePalma said. By contrast, other communities are increasingly prohibiting battery systems citing growing safety concerns following fires at lithium-ion battery facilities in Jefferson, Orange and Suffolk counties in summer 2023. Fire broke out at a facility in Warwick in Orange County for a second time in December 2025. The state has since updated its fire code; stricter safety standards took effect this year. Battery bans have been enacted by the city and town of Amsterdam, Florida and Glen in Montgomery County. In Fulton County, the towns of Johnstown, Northampton and Perth have either enacted or extended battery moratoriums this year, as did the city of Johnstown while Gloversville banned them outright. Meanwhile, DePalma said Mohawk is seeking to strike a balance that protects the community while allowing development that aligns with the town’s rural character. It’s the same direction Mohawk has previously taken to more tightly regulate solar development to protect against overdevelopment without barring it completely. “People do want new energy options, but they also want the rural character. So that's what we're really trying to do — is give them that balance of the new options,” DePalma said. As the battery updates are finalized, officials will turn their attention to developing zoning regulations governing data centers. The town adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers in August running through Feb. 13. DePalma said that will likely need to be extended to give the town time to prepare and adopt updated laws. Mohawk enacted its own moratorium after officials found the state’s one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers that would consume 50 megawatts of energy or more didn’t go far enough. State Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order in July enacting the partial pause so state agencies and officials can assess the effect of data center development and come up with standards for future projects to protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities. However, DePalma has argued the state’s moratorium didn’t give municipalities time to enact local zoning rules applying to data centers of all sizes to fit the needs and wants of their communities. Mohawk officials have acknowledged data centers pose a concern due to their size and their significant demand on resources, including electricity and water. Those worries are shared by other rural communities, which led the town of Perth in Fulton County to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers in June. Yet DePalma expects officials will again look to strike a balance that protects the town and its residents while allowing new development. “I'm hearing both sides of it,” DePalma said. “So, we really are not saying ‘no, we don't want it.’ We're just saying we want to control the narrative. We want to know where they're going, how many there's going to be, how big they're going to be. We want to protect what our community wants protected … They want the new options, but they also want the rural character.”

artigo.texto: A chinesa CATL, apontada como a maior fabricante mundial de baterias, abriu um escritório comercial na Argentina para apoiar sua expansão no mercado local de armazenamento de energia, segundo relatos da imprensa argentina citados pelo South China Morning Post. A empresa pretende partir de projetos de baterias para a rede elétrica em Buenos Aires e alcançar aplicações em minas, centros de dados e parques eólicos da Patagônia. A CATL já fornece equipamentos ao maior projeto de armazenamento do país. Também apresentou seus sistemas a 35 companhias interessadas em uma licitação governamental para armazenamento. Na semana anterior à publicação, a fabricante conversou com geradoras de energia e bancos em Buenos Aires, embora não tenham sido informados valores de investimentos, contratos ou metas comerciais. Principais fatos e números - A CATL abriu um escritório comercial na Argentina. - A unidade servirá de base para a expansão no mercado argentino de armazenamento de energia. - A empresa já fornece o maior projeto de armazenamento do país. - Os mercados visados incluem minas, centros de dados e parques eólicos da Patagônia. - A CATL apresentou seus sistemas a 35 empresas interessadas em uma licitação governamental. - A fabricante conversou com geradoras de energia e bancos em Buenos Aires. Por que isso importa para empresários e investidores A presença comercial da CATL pode ampliar o acesso de empresas argentinas a sistemas de armazenamento para redes elétricas, mineração, centros de dados e geração eólica. Fornecedores, financiadores e operadores de infraestrutura podem encontrar oportunidades em instalação, integração, manutenção e crédito para novos projetos. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão dependerá do resultado da licitação governamental e da conversão das conversas comerciais em contratos. Como a fonte não informa valores, cronogramas, capacidade dos sistemas ou compromissos firmes, ainda não é possível dimensionar o investimento nem seu efeito efetivo sobre o mercado argentino.

artigo.texto: LOWELL, Mich. — The debate over a potential data center in Lowell Charter Township is continuing, with township leaders now considering new rules for future developments. WATCH: Lowell Township leaders review proposed ordinance for potential data center developments During Monday night's township board meeting, an advisory committee presented a nearly 30-page proposed ordinance outlining requirements developers would have to meet before a data center project could move forward. The proposal received mixed reactions from neighbors. “I think this ordinance has some work to do still,” one neighbor said during public comment. Another neighbor described the proposal as “a great first start.” Tristam Harrington, who has been following the townships data center discussions, said he came into Monday night's meeting skeptical of the proposed ordinance. “We have one chance to get this right because once it goes in, it's over,” Harrington said to the Township Board Monday night. “If we don't put all of the proper and detailed and effective safeguards in place, we have run the real risk of ruining this community forever.” The proposed ordinance would establish requirements for where data centers could be built, how they operate, and what developers must do to protect surrounding communities. That includes addressing concerns such as noise, water consumption, environmental impacts, and emergency response- issues neighbors have raised throughout more than 20 meetings since the project was first announced last November. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: No decision reached after lengthy Lowell Township meeting on Microsoft data center proposal The advisory ordinance committee recommended bringing in third-party consultants to help further develop the proposal and address any remaining gaps. Township Supervisor Jerry Hale agreed with that recommendation. “I think that we do need to hire all the experts to fill in the gaps,” Hale said. After hearing the committee's presentation, Harrington said he came away with a better understanding of the work being done to address neighbors' concerns. “I feel really encouraged by the process and everything that they've done,” Harrington said. “I think we're going to be in a much better position moving forward.” What's next? The proposed ordinance will now go to the Lowell Charter Township Planning Commission for review and recommendations. Township leaders are encouraging members of the advisory committee to participate in that review. “There's still a lot of steps in the process to get to a final ordinance legally,” Township Attorney Bradley Fowler said. After the Planning Commission reviews the proposal, a public hearing will need to be scheduled and held before the ordinance returns to the township board for further consideration. FOX 17 will continue following the township's discussions and provide updates as the process moves forward.

artigo.texto: QUINCY TOWNSHIP, MI (WTVB) – Developers of a proposed battery storage facility in Quincy Township will hold an open house Tuesday to answer community questions, ahead of their application for approval of the project. EDF proposed the Santina Energy facility earlier this year on a 45-acre site in Quincy Township, with about 20 to 25 acres designated for battery equipment. The company says the site on Boone Road was selected partly because it is near ITC transmission lines along the Indiana Northeast Railroad right-of-way. The Bloomington, Minnesota-based company will hold the open house Tuesday from 5:00-7:00 p.m. at Quincy Middle School, with project information and a site plan available for the public to view and comment on. Quincy Township recently adopted new zoning rules and a compatible renewable energy ordinance to maintain local control over projects of this type, limiting battery systems to industrial zones, while EDF proposed an agricultural site. Under state law, EDF could ask the State Public Service Commission to provide approval, regardless of local zoning.

artigo.texto: Floating data centers could help build resilient digital infrastructure in new environments and beyond traditional locations. ABB and Hanwha Ocean have signed an MOU to advance power and control technologies for floating data centers, combining Hanwha Ocean’s offshore design and construction expertise with ABB’s electrification, automation and data center power capabilities. Through May 2027, the companies will explore power system design and operational control technologies suited to the marine environment. This includes assessing power system reliability and quality, and developing control logic to support efficient operations as computing demand changes. The collaboration will also explore how LNG engines and electrical systems can respond to changing data center power demands, helping advance reliable and resilient power solutions for floating data centers.Together, ABB and Hanwha Ocean are combining engineering expertise and power systems know-how to help build the foundations for future marine digital infrastructure. Floating data centers are data centers built on offshore floating platforms, equipped with servers, power systems, and cooling facilities. As the demand for data processing surges, land-based data centers face numerous constraints regarding site selection and power supply; consequently, floating data centers are gaining increasing attention as an alternative solution.

artigo.texto: Locally produced LFP prismatic SBB 2.0 to spearhead North American push World's first LSFT-certified UPS battery solution makes its debut Samsung SDI is set to accelerate its push into the North American market by unveiling a broad lineup of next-generation battery solutions in the United States. The company announced Sunday that it will participate in RE+ (Renewable Energy Plus) 2026 — North America's largest energy industry exhibition — which opens Tuesday (local time) in Las Vegas for a three-day run. Under the slogan "AI imagines it, batteries make it real," Samsung SDI will showcase a battery total solution lineup aimed at leading the North American market, including its ESS solution Samsung Battery Box (SBB), a high-output prismatic battery solution for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, and a high-output cylindrical battery for battery backup units (BBU). The SBB 2.0 — which drew recognition for its technological innovation when it debuted last year — serves as the flagship model for Samsung SDI's North American ESS push. The company said it has recently completed the buildout of a local production system and will begin full-scale supply. The SBB is a power-grid ESS battery solution that installs battery cells and safety devices inside a 20-foot container, optimizing customer convenience and performance. It is equipped with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Samsung SDI applied differentiated materials and electrode technology to its proprietary prismatic form factor, significantly improving safety and longevity. Also making its North American debut is the U8A3, a prismatic battery solution for UPS systems that recently became the world's first to satisfy all criteria of the Indoor Large-Scale Fire Test (LSFT) administered by global safety certification body UL Solutions. The U8A3 uses lithium manganese oxide (LMO) prismatic battery cells and achieves industry-leading safety through multi-layered safety design across every stage — cell, module and rack. It can also respond effectively to sudden fluctuations in power load, such as the sharp spikes and drops in electricity consumption seen in AI data centers. In addition, a cylindrical battery lineup for BBU applications — combining high output and high capacity — will be on display. Visitors will be able to review Samsung SDI's product portfolio, which spans high-nickel NCA to LFP chemistries, backed by technology and reliability built up since the company began supplying battery solutions for data centers in 2017. "We will present locally tailored products and technology targeting the rapidly growing US market," a Samsung SDI official said. "Our strategy is to lead the North American market with technology purpose-built for the AI era." Meanwhile, Samsung SDI is also expanding its footprint in the electric vehicle battery market, having recently been selected as a new cell supplier for BMW's sixth-generation battery while strengthening partnerships with global EV manufacturers. likehyo85@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: MOUs signed with GGGI, ICVCM; ministry says GVCM issuance body to be established next year Eight countries, including Singapore, have expressed their intent to join the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM), a high-integrity carbon market initiative led by South Korea. With the latest additions, the total number of signatories to the GVCM cooperation letter of intent stands at nine: South Korea, the Dominican Republic, Morocco, Burkina Faso, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Uganda, Côte d'Ivoire and Paraguay. According to the Ministry of Economy and Finance on Sunday, the nine countries signed the joint cooperation letter of intent on Saturday (local time) at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, held in Antalya, Turkey. The GVCM is a multilateral carbon market framework the government is developing to provide common carbon credit issuance standards and infrastructure that multiple countries can use jointly to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Companies will be able to use the framework to pursue greenhouse gas reduction projects in developing countries, generate carbon credits and trade them on international carbon markets. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il said in a video opening address that the GVCM is "a platform built together by reflecting the diverse experiences and development needs of participating countries," adding that it "carries great significance as a new multilateral model in which three or more countries participate simultaneously — not a bilateral arrangement." The ministry also signed a trilateral memorandum of understanding with the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) and the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) to enhance the credibility and quality of the GVCM. The three organizations will pursue knowledge sharing on Core Carbon Principles (CCPs) and provide education and training for GVCM participating countries to improve the market's quality. Moon Ji-seong, director general for international economic affairs at the ministry, said the MOU signing was an opportunity to raise the quality of the GVCM by sharing ICVCM's expertise and experience. The ministry said it plans to complete the establishment of the GVCM issuance body next year and will work to bring in more countries, international organizations and private institutions going forward. oskymoon@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: SK Telecom said Monday it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Hyosung Heavy Industries to cooperate on developing gigawatt-scale AI data centers. The two companies will work on securing key equipment for 345-kilovolt substations, testing 800-volt direct-current power distribution technology and identifying new data center projects. Under the agreement, SK Telecom will contribute its AI data center development and operational expertise, while Hyosung Heavy Industries will provide its power infrastructure manufacturing and engineering capabilities. The companies will coordinate supply plans for major equipment, including transformers, to prevent procurement delays from affecting construction schedules. They will also jointly review and test 800V DC distribution, which can reduce power conversion stages and improve data center energy efficiency. They also plan to share expertise in operating and maintaining ultra-high-voltage substations to improve power supply stability and reliability once data centers are operational. The partnership will eventually extend to AI data center development and construction, with both companies seeking new business opportunities and joint business models. "This partnership will help secure the core power infrastructure needed for AI data centers and expand into cooperation on developing and building large-scale facilities," SK Telecom CEO Jung Jai-hun said. "We will strengthen our capabilities in gigawatt-scale AI data center development and take a leading role in the global AI infrastructure market." Hyosung Heavy Industries CEO Woo Tae-hee said the agreement would combine the company's power technology with SK Telecom's data center expertise to establish a stable foundation for electricity supply. jyoungseon8@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: LS Electric, a South Korean electrical equipment manufacturer, said Monday it secured a $93.83 million contract to supply power distribution systems for a hyper-scale artificial intelligence data center in the US. Under the agreement, the company will deliver 38-kilovolt high-voltage switchgear and low-voltage switchgear in phases to an unnamed global technology company. Switchgear controls and protects electrical circuits, helping distribute electricity safely throughout large facilities. The latest order extends LS Electric’s involvement in the client's data center project from the initial construction phase to a subsequent expansion. As AI adoption accelerates, demand for computing capacity has grown, placing greater emphasis on “time to power,” the period required for a data center to secure an operational electricity supply. To meet delivery schedules, LS Electric operates manufacturing facilities in Cheongju, South Korea, and the US states of Utah and Texas. The company said its production network enables it to meet the tight delivery timelines of data center projects. Beyond conventional alternating current (AC) distribution, the manufacturer is expanding into direct current (DC) systems, which can reduce energy losses by limiting the power conversions required to operate servers. At its Cheonan plant, LS Electric operates a DC-powered factory equipped with solid-state transformers for voltage conversion, solid-state circuit breakers for electrical protection and energy storage systems. The facility serves as a testing ground for next-generation power grids and data center applications. “The latest contract reflects the quality of our power equipment and our ability to execute projects in North America,” an LS Electric official said. “We will continue expanding our business by providing solutions tailored to the needs of major technology customers.” yejinlim@heraldcorp.com

Breaks Into the Solid-State Battery Mass-Production Market With an Order in the ₩20 Billion Range From a Global Company - Input - 2026-11-16 08:46:51 - Updated - 2026-11-16 08:49:41 [Financial News] mPlus Corp., a company specializing in rechargeable-battery assembly equipment, is stepping up its push into the next-generation battery market after securing an order worth around ₩20 billion for solid-state battery equipment from a global company. The deal is drawing attention because it marks an expansion of the company’s equipment business, previously centered on electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESS), into solid-state battery mass-production processes. According to industry sources on the 16th, mPlus Corp. recently secured an order worth around ₩20 billion from a global company for solid-state battery assembly and electrode-line equipment. The equipment is expected to be used to build the global company’s solid-state battery production line. The equipment to be supplied incorporates technologies developed in-house by mPlus Corp., including notching, stacking and precision dispensing. The company is also developing Roll Press technology needed for solid-state battery manufacturing. It plans to use these technologies to expand the range of equipment it can supply for solid-state battery production. Solid-state batteries are next-generation batteries that replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density. However, their complex manufacturing processes make securing reliable mass-production technology a key challenge for commercialization. As a result, technological competition is intensifying not only among battery manufacturers but also among makers of equipment for key manufacturing processes. With this order as a springboard, mPlus Corp. plans to focus on securing global customers and diversifying its business. It has also recently been pursuing entry into the market for defense and special-purpose battery equipment, targeting European battery companies. The strategy is to broaden its order base to include solid-state and special-purpose batteries, in addition to equipment for EVs and ESS. Industry observers expect order opportunities for related equipment makers to grow as the solid-state battery market moves beyond research and development and begins preparing for commercialization. In particular, they say that a track record of supplying initial production lines could be a factor in gauging competitiveness in future orders for mass-production facilities. A company representative said, "This order is significant because it gives us a track record of supplying a global customer in the solid-state battery assembly-equipment sector," and added, "We also expect opportunities for additional orders as our customers expand mass production." Meanwhile, mPlus Corp. is expanding its business portfolio to include pouch-type, prismatic and solid-state battery assembly equipment, as well as autonomous mobile robots (AIMR) and control systems. artigo.texto: The Turkish business sector is embracing global carbon markets by leveraging the UN climate change summit, the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31), being held in Antalya. The summit serves as a platform for firms and stakeholders to discuss emerging financial regulations and sustainability standards. Alongside the summit, a carbon market conference was hosted by SEKA Investment and financial services firm StoneX. The conference highlighted that mandatory global carbon trading volumes topped $100 billion per year. Serhat Kisakurek, managing partner at SEKA Investment, said the strong attendance by Turkish firms at COP31 showed the sector’s commitment to the new economic ecosystem, despite some uncertainties over initial carbon pricing. Kisakurek noted that carbon compliance has become a key factor in securing long-term deals and accessing affordable financing for corporations. While industrial giants have adapted to green frameworks, small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are lagging behind, he said, urging these firms to follow suit to maintain their global competitive edge. He added that Türkiye has a significant regional advantage in the green transition due to its established climate laws and regulatory infrastructure supporting compliance. Alfredo Nicastro, global director of carbon markets at StoneX, said the summit is connecting private sector innovators with policymakers, while the global turnout at the event continues to demonstrate growing momentum in Türkiye’s green financial sector. He added that COP31 represents a turning point for Türkiye in becoming a central carbon trading hub for the EU and the wider region.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI to supply LFP batteries to Jupiter Power SEOUL, Nov. 16 (Yonhap) -- Samsung SDI Co., South Korea's second-largest battery maker, said Monday its U.S. subsidiary has secured a deal estimated to be worth trillions of won to supply lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to a U.S. energy storage company. Samsung SDI America signed a three-year, 16-gigawatt-hour (GWh) battery supply agreement with Jupiter Power, a U.S. energy storage system (ESS) developer owned by BlackRock, the South Korean company said in a press release. Under the agreement, Samsung SDI will supply LFP batteries for Jupiter Power's ESS, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2029. Combined with an earlier agreement, the latest deal brings Samsung SDI's cumulative orders from Jupiter Power to about 27 GWh. The batteries will be manufactured at StarPlus Energy, a U.S. joint venture between Samsung SDI and Stellantis NV, in the U.S. state of Indiana. Jupiter Power, owned by U.S. asset management giant BlackRock, is one of the largest developers and operators of energy storage projects in the United States. The contract comes shortly after Samsung SDI began mass production of LFP batteries at the Indiana facility. Industry observers said the deal could help Samsung SDI gain a foothold in the ESS battery market, which has long been dominated by Chinese manufacturers, by leveraging its U.S. production capabilities and non-Chinese supply chain. (END)

artigo.texto: Data centers tiveram ampla derrota nas eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA. Foto: Dado Galdieri/Bloomberg Indústrias e ativistas imaginam que parte da capacidade planejada para estados americanos possa vir parar em território brasileiro Bruno Romani Repórter de tecnologia O “tsunami azul” que varreu Donald Trump nas eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA foi também um grande plebiscito sobre inteligência artificial (IA), com candidatos favoráveis à regulação — e opositores dos grandes bilionários do setor — conseguindo ampla votação. Mais especificamente, as urnas deram um grande recado sobre o que a população de lá pensa da presença de data centers em suas comunidades. Agora, indústria e ativistas imaginam que parte dessa demanda possa vir parar no Brasil — para o bem e para o mal. Vale lembrar que o processo eleitoral americano não escolheu apenas novos membros do Legislativo federal e dos Executivos estaduais. Houve também referendos sobre diversos temas, entre eles a paralisação ou a restrição de data centers em vários condados do país. A rejeição foi ampla: segundo a consultoria Redbud, dos 47 referendos, 44 tiveram resultado negativo para o setor e apenas um foi favorável (outros dois ainda não têm resultado). O Goldman Sachs alertou os investidores de que o resultado poderia afetar 45% da expansão de capacidade planejada para o território americano — se isso acontecer, a própria expansão da indústria da IA fica em xeque e começa a se formar um clima terrível de bolha. Na semana passada, essa simples perspectiva fez as empresas de tecnologia perderem US$ 2,5 trilhões em valor de mercado. Elon Musk correu para o X: “Os data centers no espaço parecem bastante atraentes no momento”. Ele, claro, já está fazendo propaganda de um potencial serviço que a SpaceX pode oferecer. Mas nem é preciso ir tão longe: o Brasil já aparece como opção. Sérgio Sgobbi, diretor de relações institucionais e governamentais da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom), me explicou o que coloca o país em jogo: O cenário nos EUA cria uma oportunidade para o Brasil. Lá, criou-se uma resistência muito forte a data centers, mais por questões econômicas do que ambientais, reflexo da demanda por energia. A gente tem uma matriz diversa. A outra característica é a interligação. A gente tem problemas de distribuição, mas tem uma capacidade interligada que outros países não têm. A Brasscom previa que o Brasil receberia US$ 92 bilhões em investimentos acumulados em equipamentos de TI até 2031 — e o tamanho do bolo é maior, porque a conta não considera custos de construção e de infraestrutura física de suporte, como geradores, sistemas de ar-condicionado/refrigeração, sistemas de combate a incêndio, baterias e no-breaks. Sgobbi admite que a entidade pode voltar à prancheta para refazer as contas após as eleições americanas. Ainda não é possível saber qual será o novo número. Na semana passada, Marcos Peigo, CEO da Scala, disse ao jornal Valor Econômico que o Brasil está diante de uma oportunidade de US$ 500 bilhões. Já o representante da Brasscom tenta dar uma ideia de outra forma. Ele afirma que os aportes em hardware, redes e data centers para IA equivaleram a 1,5% do PIB dos EUA no 1º trimestre de 2026 (contra uma média histórica de 0,7% entre 2015 e 2022). É claro que não haverá transferência automática de toda essa capacidade para o Brasil, mas uma fração disso já significaria valores históricos para o país. Victor Arnaud, presidente da Equinix no Brasil, lembra que o país não é o destino natural da demanda expulsa dos EUA. O norte da Europa, por exemplo, tem mais capacidade instalada do que toda a América Latina — o Google decidiu investir € 13 bilhões na Finlândia. A gigante também anunciou outros US$ 15 bilhões para a Malásia em 2027 e 2028, uma clara indicação de que o Sudeste Asiático também está na fila do pão. E há ainda os rivais locais na América do Sul, cada um com seus atrativos e problemas. A Argentina tem a amizade entre Milei e Trump e o frio da Patagônia (vale lembrar, porém, que um suposto projeto da OpenAI por lá está parado); o Paraguai tem Itaipu e um regramento mais relaxado (mas também uma crise política profunda); e o Chile tem o seu histórico no setor (e um movimento de rejeição que o acompanha). Arnaud reforça que a regulamentação do Redata, a harmonização do ICMS entre os estados e a futura aprovação do Marco da IA são reformas que viabilizam o Brasil, independentemente de onde venha a demanda por data centers. Na sexta (6), a ministra-chefe da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, afirmou que a regulamentação do Redata deverá ser debatida com o presidente Lula após a viagem dele à Ásia. Ainda que toda essa tramitação demore a ocorrer, o executivo da Equinix lembrou que um dos principais atrativos do Brasil permanece: O Brasil continua sendo o maior mercado da América Latina e vai continuar crescendo. O usuário daqui não vai falar que não usa mais o celular ou que gosta quando o vídeo demora para carregar. O Pix, o streaming e a vida digital já garantem o crescimento. A Equinix vinha investindo numa média de R$ 1 bilhão por ano e, nos últimos 12 meses, aumentou isso em 50%. Até aqui, com o Redata, a ideia do Brasil era trazer para o território nacional infraestrutura para reduzir o nosso déficit computacional — segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, 60% da nossa demanda roda no exterior. Então, como o país poderia surgir como opção para fornecer capacidade a outros mercados? Sgobbi diz que um data center de grande porte é construído para 100 megawatts (MW), mas costuma iniciar a operação com “apenas 5 MW e expandir conforme a venda de capacidade”. Uma eventual absorção da carga americana poderia fazer os novos data centers no país iniciarem com capacidade maior. Segundo a Bloomberg, o resultado das eleições nos EUA está fazendo a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, estudar a ampliação da capacidade de seus novos data centers no Nordeste. artigo.texto: Hithium has signed a memorandum of understanding with the University of Cambridge to collaborate on long-duration energy storage research, battery technology and the commercialisation of academic work. The agreement was signed during the Global Energy Storage Colloquium in Xiamen, China, on 12 November. Hithium said the partnership will combine Cambridge’s work in materials science, engineering and fundamental research with its own experience in battery development, long-duration energy storage and large-scale deployment. The two organisations plan to establish joint management and research mechanisms, develop research projects, facilitate scientific exchanges and support the translation of research into industrial applications. Hithium said Cambridge researchers will contribute to work on fundamental scientific questions and emerging energy storage technologies, while the manufacturer will provide engineering validation and industrial application scenarios. No individual research programmes, funding commitments or development timescales were disclosed. The partnership comes as Hithium expands its focus on lithium iron phosphate batteries designed for longer-duration stationary storage. BESTmag reported in August that Hithium began production at its $1.8 billion LFP long-duration energy storage manufacturing park in Shandong. The 80-hectare development includes battery cells, modules and complete storage systems alongside materials and upstream processing. The company’s current LDES strategy includes large-format LFP cells intended for discharge durations of four to eight hours. Hithium was also ranked as the world’s second-largest supplier of BESS cells in the first half of 2026, behind CATL. Hithium and Cambridge strengthening bridge from research to deployment Hithium and Cambridge said the collaboration is intended to strengthen links between fundamental battery research, product development and industrial deployment. The agreement also forms part of Hithium’s plans to expand its international research network through partnerships with universities and research institutions. The Xiamen colloquium at which the agreement was signed brought together researchers and industry representatives to discuss battery materials, degradation and lifetime prediction, grid integration, power electronics, thermal-runaway detection and virtual power plants. Hithium said it intends to use the collaboration to bring technical challenges encountered in commercial energy storage projects into academic research, while accelerating the engineering validation of research findings. artigo.texto: Data Centers DID YOU KNOW? the Potomac River basin has the largest concentration of data centers in the world. Most of which are nestled in Northern Virginia, now known as “Data Center Alley” – a mega hub of data center infrastructure estimated to handle 70% of all global internet traffic. Northern Virginia is home to one of the world’s largest clusters of data centers. And as more facilities are proposed across the Potomac watershed, there’s a question worth asking: What does all this growth mean for the rivers, streams, and drinking water we depend on? Every time we stream a show, store a photo, or use an AI tool, data centers help make it possible. These large facilities house the computers that keep our digital lives running. But they also need electricity, cooling, and land. Their effects on water vary widely depending on how and where they are built—and with so many projects on the horizon, we need to look at the bigger picture. A data center is an industrial facility that houses expansive, high-powered computing equipment to continuously store and process data for users globally. An average AI data center contains 200,000 computer servers, miles of wiring, batteries, water systems, hundreds of air conditioning units, and is supported by dozens of high-powered, industrial backup diesel generators. Data centers operate constantly, using massive amounts of water in order to cool and power their systems. In our region, they draw this water from Potomac-fed water supplies. This is especially important during the hottest days of the year, when data center water demand spikes at the most water-stressed time of year. Why This Matters for the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers Data center proposals are multiplying across our region. AI is helping drive that growth, though not every proposed project will necessarily be built. What happens next matters: choices about water use, wastewater, construction, and power infrastructure can shape the health of the Potomac and Shenandoah for years to come. The Potomac River watershed remains a legacy hub and now has more than 350 operating data centers and is projected to surpass 1,000 – placing 200 million square feet of buildings on roughly 20,000 acres of land. Because of the unprecedented construction of these facilities in our watershed, the exact impacts on the environment and water quality remain unclear. However, the primary concerns associated with data centers include: - Water drawdowns - Periodic cooling system discharge - Increased polluted runoff - Construction site pollution - Threats from fuel spills - Threats to drinking water intakes - Risk of substation fires - Toxic e-waste in landfills - Developments on toxic sites - Impacts from power line construction - Power plant operation threats Rapid data center expansion helped the Potomac River earn the title of America’s Most Endangered River in 2026. How PRKN is taking action The extent of data center impacts on river systems and waterways is still not fully understood, and comprehensive analyses and assessments are needed to begin to grasp their effects on our rivers. What we do know is that when unchecked, these installations can pose serious risks to the watershed and the primary clean drinking water source for six million people in the Potomac River basin. PRKN is keeping a watchful eye on the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers for data center impacts and fighting for adequacy of state permitting, such as for cooling system releases, and will call for more public stream monitoring on tributaries where high concentrations of these facilities are upstream from drinking water intakes. Importantly, PRKN will be a voice to ensure that clean water protections are seriously managed in data center development.

artigo.texto: An aerial view of the world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage power station, Yuanchu No 1, in Northwest China's Gansu Province. Photo: CCTV News The world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage (CAES) power station has been connected to the grid in Northwest China's Gansu Province, marking a major step in bringing the technology from experimental testing to large-scale engineering applications, CCTV News reported on Monday, citing China Energy Engineering Corporation (China Energy). The project, known as Yuanchu No 1, provides a new engineering example for diversifying China's compressed air energy storage technologies. The station has four air-storage caverns excavated in rock formations about 110 meters underground. It is equipped with a 300-MW generating unit and has an energy storage capacity of 1,800 megawatt-hours. With a round-trip efficiency of 72 percent, the facility can generate electricity continuously for six hours on a single discharge and has a projected annual power output of 600 million kilowatt-hours. Compressed air energy storage works by converting electricity into energy stored in compressed air, which can later be converted back into electricity when needed. Artificially excavated hard-rock caverns offer an alternative to natural underground storage spaces such as salt caverns. Suitable rock formations are more widely distributed, allowing greater flexibility in site selection, although construction costs are relatively high, according to a report by China Electric Power News published on the website of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Engineering Thermophysics. The report noted that suitable salt formations are concentrated in parts of central, eastern and southern China, while the country's northern regions, which have extensive wind and solar power installations and strong demand for large-scale energy storage, lack suitable geological conditions for salt cavern storage. The Gansu project reached a key testing milestone in September, when an initial air-injection test at its No. 4 underground storage cavern succeeded, with pressure reaching 12.63 mega-pascals, setting a record for compressed air storage in large artificial caverns, according to China Energy. The grid connection comes amid rapid growth in China's new energy storage sector. The country's installed new energy storage capacity reached 136 million kilowatts by the end of 2025, up 84 percent from a year earlier, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Lithium-ion batteries accounted for 96.1 percent of the total, while compressed air storage, flow batteries, flywheels and other technologies made up the remaining 3.9 percent. Energy storage projects with a duration of four hours or longer accounted for 27.6 percent of total installed capacity, up about 12 percentage points from the end of 2024, the NEA said. China is also seeking to diversify its energy storage technologies under its development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan, jointly issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA, sets a target of 300 million kilowatts of installed new energy storage capacity by 2030, with an average storage duration of about three hours. artigo.texto: Israel risks becoming a pollution haven in the global race to build AI data centers As the Electricity Authority opens the door to another 1,000MW of data center capacity, the Environmental Protection Ministry warns of rising emissions, health costs and pressure on the country's natural gas reserves. The Electricity Authority has announced plans to position Israel as a global leader in connecting data centers to the power grid. But a senior official at the Ministry of Environmental Protection is warning of significant consequences. "Air pollutant emissions will rise by more than 10% once data centers with a capacity of 3,000 megawatts are established, causing economic damage through increased morbidity and mortality, lost workdays and other costs," she said. The ministry estimates that Israel’s rapid push to establish data centers will cause approximately NIS 2 billion in annual economic damage from the additional electricity generation they require, plus more than NIS 1 billion from the operation of backup generators. The anticipated costs also include higher greenhouse gas emissions and faster depletion of Israel’s natural gas reserves. Beyond the financial damage, the ministry warns of an increase in annual deaths caused by air pollution, which is already responsible for an estimated 5,500 premature deaths in Israel each year. AI is reshaping the global energy landscape, as major technology companies race to build massive data centers around the world. According to the latest forecast from the International Energy Agency (IEA), electricity consumption by data centers is expected to nearly double, from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, accounting for approximately 3% of global electricity consumption. Over the same period, electricity consumption by data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence is expected to triple. For comparison, 950 TWh is slightly more than Japan’s current annual electricity consumption. In the United States, data centers are expected to account for nearly half of the projected growth in electricity demand through 2030. Local communities are increasingly bearing the costs of this technological expansion, including higher air pollution from facilities that operate polluting backup generators, consume vast amounts of electricity and require large quantities of water for cooling. Data centers are also affecting electricity prices. According to the Federal Reserve, wholesale electricity prices rose by 6.9% last year, driven in part by demand from these facilities. Opposition to data center developments is growing in communities around the world, where residents are also concerned about the large tracts of land these facilities occupy. In the United States, the issue even influenced this month's midterm elections. A September poll by Quinnipiac found that nearly three out of four Americans opposed having a data center in their community. During the elections, 41 ballot measures concerning data centers were put to a vote, with voters rejecting the proposed developments in all but one case. In an NBC exit poll, 23% of voters said data centers were a "decisive" factor in their congressional vote, while another 33% described them as a "significant" factor. The day after the election, Nvidia lost $450 billion in market value. OpenAI has since pledged to use closed-loop cooling systems and to pay for the electricity consumed by its data centers. It has also moved to rebrand its facilities as "computing campuses." In July, the Electricity Authority froze the processing of grid connection requests for data centers with electricity demands exceeding eight megawatts, after approving 2,000MW of capacity. Developers had submitted requests totaling 27,000MW, roughly three times Israel's current electricity consumption and well above the country's record peak demand. The authority recently announced plans to release an additional 1,000MW of capacity, potentially enabling the construction of facilities as large as 200MW, a scale not yet seen elsewhere in the world. "Realizing this allocation is expected to result in data centers accounting for approximately 20% of national electricity consumption, positioning Israel among the world's leaders in the integration of data centers relative to total consumption," the Electricity Authority said. Opening the door to these large facilities is expected to require the construction of at least three new polluting power plants in Israel to meet their electricity needs. But alongside the potential economic benefits, the expansion carries significant environmental and public-health costs that will ultimately be borne by Israeli residents. The concern is that, at a time when communities in other countries are increasingly resisting data center developments, Israel could become a "backyard" for the sector's pollution. In a sharply worded letter, Shuli Nazar, Deputy Director General for Environmental Regulation and Risk Prevention at the Ministry of Environmental Protection, warned of a broad range of risks. In addition to increased air pollution and the resulting rise in morbidity and mortality, she said, higher greenhouse gas emissions would make it harder for Israel to meet its climate targets. According to Nazar, offsetting the additional emissions from data centers would require Israel to set a target of approximately 45% renewable energy by 2035, about 10 percentage points higher than the target recommended by the Electricity Authority. There is considerable skepticism within the energy sector about whether Israel can meet even its existing renewable energy targets. Nazar also warned that implementing the Electricity Authority's plan would accelerate the depletion of Israel's domestic natural gas reserves and shorten their expected lifespan. artigo.texto: Enlight and Shemen join race for Israeli data centers with 150MW Haifa project The companies plan to invest in a facility at Hof Shemen, with a NIS 334 million electricity guarantee and a 25-year land lease. The project enters a crowded market as developers compete for the remaining 1,000MW of capacity earmarked for data centers. New names are joining the growing list of entrepreneurs seeking to establish data centers in Israel. Enlight and Shemen Real Estate announced this morning that they have signed an agreement to develop a 150-megawatt data center at Hof Shemen in Haifa. The two companies will jointly establish a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) for the project and have already submitted an application to connect the facility to the electricity grid. Under the Electricity Authority’s regulatory framework, applicants must provide financial guarantees to secure grid connections. The guarantee required for the project is estimated at NIS 334 million, which the two companies will fund in equal shares. The data center is planned to cover between 41 and 82 dunams. The project’s SPV will lease the land from Shemen for 25 years. Annual lease payments will start at NIS 27,000 per dunam during the development phase, gradually rising to NIS 433,000 per dunam once the data center becomes operational. Enlight has also secured an option to purchase 50% of the land designated for the data center at a minimum price of NIS 6.32 million per dunam. The price may increase under a pre-agreed mechanism, and the option can be exercised 30 months after the agreement was signed. Enlight and Shemen are joining a growing field of developers competing for approximately 1,000 megawatts of additional electricity capacity earmarked for data centers. Under the regulatory framework published by the Electricity Authority, up to 20% of Israel’s national electricity supply, equivalent to approximately 3,000 MW, is expected to be allocated to data centers by 2030. Of that amount, approximately 2,000 MW is accounted for by connection requests that have already been approved. The remaining 1,000 MW has become the focus of intense competition among developers seeking to build data centers. For Enlight, a renewable energy company, this is not its first investment in an Israeli data center. In March 2025, it won a tender issued by the Israel Land Authority to build a data center alongside a solar energy facility in Ashalim, in the Negev. Shemen Yielding Real Estate is the successor to Shemen Industries, a company previously engaged in oil production. It is held by Memorandum, a company owned by Haim Fink (44.2%); Zvika Ben-Zvi (22.1%), who also owns logistics company Orsher; and real estate investment fund JTLV3 (22.1%).

artigo.texto: South Korea Joins 'Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets' as New Member International carbon market partnership South Korea to take part in talks on setting rules Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Seonghwan is being interviewed by The Asia Business Daily at the Han River Flood Control Office in Dongjak-gu, Seoul. 2026.9.21 Photo by Kim Hyunmin View original image South Korea has officially joined the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets (OCCCM), an international partnership on carbon markets involving the European Union (EU), China and other participants. As a new member, South Korea has secured voting rights at the coalition's high-level meetings and will take part in discussions on international carbon market rules, including Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes and offset credits. Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Seonghwan officially announced South Korea's membership at a high-level meeting of the coalition held on the sidelines of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on the 16th. The coalition is an international partnership that shares experience with compliance carbon markets, such as greenhouse gas emissions trading systems and carbon taxes, and promotes mutual understanding and cooperation among its members on topics including measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), carbon accounting and high-quality offset systems. Brazil proposed the coalition at COP30 last year, and it was launched in May this year with major carbon market operators, including the EU and China, as its core participants. Thirteen countries are currently members. South Korea joined after receiving an invitation from the EU in June, as a follow-up to Korea-EU summit diplomacy. To become a member, a country or regional economic integration organization must have or be developing a domestic compliance carbon market or carbon pricing system. Members can exercise voting rights at high-level meetings. With its membership, South Korea will be able to participate in future discussions on international carbon market rules, including the generation of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and the establishment of common principles for high-integrity offset credits. artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] Ecuador Applies Zero VAT and Currency Outflow Tax to Solar and Storage Equipment Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa signed Executive Decree 530, published on November 11 in the Fifth Supplement to Official Gazette No. 407, setting a 0% rate for value-added tax and the tax on foreign currency outflows (ISD) on electricity-sector equipment including solar PV and energy storage systems. A subsequent ministerial agreement, MAE-MAE-2026-0118-AM, lists 55 categories of goods eligible for the 0% VAT rate in the domestic market — solar cells, modules, inverters, power optimisers, controllers, mounting structures, trackers and DC cables — and 104 tariff subheadings eligible for the 0% ISD rate on imports, with storage goods covering stationary cells and modules, battery banks, integrated systems, bidirectional converters and battery management equipment. The new rates took effect on November 12, and the decree lets taxpayers deduct VAT paid on qualifying purchases and imports made between January 1, 2026 and entry into force as an expense for the 2026 income tax year. The measure removes import and transaction taxes on solar and storage equipment, part of Ecuador's push to accelerate private renewable investment after the 2024 supply shortfalls and blackouts.

artigo.texto: A new legislative review estimates that Virginia’s data center tax break generated 22 cents in state tax revenue for every dollar companies saved. Staff for the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission presented the findings Monday. The report estimates that data centers saved an average of $811.5 million a year from fiscal 2021 through 2025. Researchers estimated that the business activity the tax break attracted generated $179.4 million a year in state taxes, leaving a difference of $632.1 million a year. The revenue estimate excludes local taxes, including property taxes that cities and counties collect from data centers. The exemption lets qualifying data center operators and tenants buy computer equipment and software without paying sales and use tax. Five years of savings from that one tax break accounted for 60% of the $6.8 billion in tax breaks, grants and other business incentives the commission counted over a decade. To figure out what Virginia got back, researchers had to estimate how much data center business would have come to the state anyway. Earlier reviews assumed the tax break drove at least 90% of data center location and expansion activity in Virginia. The new review puts that share at about half. It draws on research into how sales and use tax exemptions affected the number, square footage and energy use of data centers across states. The Virginia Economic Development Partnership said in an Oct. 28 letter that the change had a substantial effect on the estimates. The partnership urged the commission to explain how much its findings depend on that assumption and to keep evaluating its method as more Virginia-specific evidence becomes available. The commission estimated that the exemption supported about 18,100 private-sector jobs a year, including jobs at businesses that supply data centers. It also estimated that the exemption added about $3.9 billion a year to Virginia’s gross domestic product over those five years. A Senate proposal to end the sales tax exemption early helped stall state budget talks this spring. Lawmakers kept the exemption in place in June and added a separate tax on electricity used by data center operators. The electricity tax took effect July 1 and runs through June 30, 2028. The state budget caps deposits from the tax into Virginia’s general fund at $600 million per fiscal year. Lawmakers are still split over the exemption. At an Oct. 26 meeting, Senate Finance Chairwoman Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, backed repealing it. House Appropriations Chairman Luke Torian, D-Prince William, urged the state to honor its commitments to the industry while addressing the effects of data center growth on communities. artigo.texto: By Alex Adi At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, global leaders and climate negotiators are focusing on one of the mechanisms for financing climate action: carbon credits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries can trade emission reductions and removals through international carbon markets. But what exactly is a carbon credit, and how can Ghana position itself to turn its environmental initiatives into revenue, create jobs and build cleaner cities? A carbon credit represents one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) reduced, avoided or removed from the atmosphere. For instance, when Ghana protects its forests, converts organic waste into compost instead of allowing it to decompose in landfills, or replaces diesel generators with solar power, it can reduce greenhouse gas emissions. When these reductions or removals are properly measured, independently verified and certified under an approved standard, they can generate carbon credits that are traded in the market. Companies and countries can purchase these credits to meet certain climate commitments or offset emissions, depending on the rules governing the market. In simple terms, Ghana can earn revenue by undertaking activities that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions and selling the resulting verified credits. Ghana’s growing carbon market Ghana has established a Carbon Market Office and a framework to regulate carbon market activities and international transactions. One example of the country’s involvement in the market is the Jospong Group’s Integrated Recycling and Compost Plants. The company secured a bilateral agreement with the Swiss Government at COP28, with carbon credit transactions estimated to be worth US$20 million by 2030. Beyond waste management, Ghana is also generating carbon credits through forest conservation initiatives, including the Ghana Cocoa Forest REDD+ Programme. For a developing economy such as Ghana, the carbon market presents several potential opportunities. Revenue without additional borrowing Carbon credit transactions could provide Ghana with a source of foreign revenue and attract investment without increasing the country’s public debt. Employment opportunities Investment in reforestation, waste sorting, recycling and renewable energy could create jobs for young people, particularly in communities involved in environmental protection and sustainable resource management. Cleaner cities Carbon finance could provide additional incentives for improved municipal waste management, including recycling and composting. These activities could help reduce the volume of waste sent to landfills and ease sanitation challenges in urban communities. Supporting the energy transition Revenue from carbon credits could also support solar energy and clean cooking initiatives, helping households and businesses adopt cleaner energy sources. The need for transparency and accountability Despite the opportunities, carbon market experts have cautioned that Ghana must establish strong safeguards to ensure that the benefits are properly managed and shared. Transparency, independent verification and clear benefit-sharing arrangements are essential to preventing greenwashing and ensuring that carbon credits represent genuine emission reductions or removals. There are also concerns that communities, farmers and other groups directly involved in protecting forests and natural resources could be excluded from the financial benefits if appropriate arrangements are not put in place. For Ghana, therefore, participation in the carbon market must go beyond generating and selling credits. It must also ensure that the people and communities contributing to environmental protection receive a fair share of the proceeds. Carbon trading is not simply a form of aid or charity. It is a market that depends on credible data, proper measurement, independent verification and compliance with established standards. If Ghana strengthens its regulatory framework and ensures that the benefits are fairly distributed, its forests, waste management systems and clean energy initiatives could become valuable sources of climate finance and international investment.

artigo.texto: Today, a team led by Harvard researchers published a highly anticipated study in Nature Sustainability. For the first time since generative AI took off, we have a peer-reviewed estimate of how much climate pollution comes from keeping America’s biggest data centers running. Headlines about it are already popping up all over. The study estimates that hyperscale data centers across America are emitting up to 31 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, roughly as much CO₂ as Denmark emitted in 2024. It also estimates the facilities are taking up roughly 2 percent of U.S. electricity consumption. These are big, important numbers! And yet, they’re also massive underestimations. There are a few reasons why today’s study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution coming from these ever-buzzing internet slop factories. One is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power. But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants. For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied. For the facilities they did study, the researchers couldn’t tell how much power came from the grid and how much was generated on-site. So they applied the regional grid mix to all estimated electricity use, which can undercount emissions at facilities that burn their own gas. Another reason the climate impact of hyperscale data centers is likely understated is that electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do—methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant. In addition, there are potentially hundreds of hyperscale data centers that were left out of today’s study on the climate impacts of these facilities. Yes—hundreds. That’s because we don’t actually know how many hyperscale data centers are currently up and running in the United States. (Hyperscale means “the largest and most powerful class of data centers,” according to the study. These are the kinds of facilities that can train and run large language models. See footnote to see how the study defines them).1 The researchers only landed on their number—403—after painstakingly going through a list of 675 possible hyperscale data center locations given to them by a company called Baxtel, which tracks data centers. And by that I mean they had to pull up satellite images for every single facility to answer questions like Is this the data center, or just another building on the same campus? Has it even been built yet, or is this satellite photo just old? And even after they found the right building, they still had to figure out whether it was running before they could figure out how much electricity it might be using. All told, the researchers had to leave 272 possible hyperscale data centers out of the study because they couldn’t find out enough about them. Finally, the study period ends in April 2025—meaning the climate impact of data centers has likely grown substantially. Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author, acknowledged this in Monday’s release. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025,” he said. “New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” And yet, even with all of these limitations (most acknowledged by the study itself, which is how I know about them), the researchers were able to pull out some important findings. They include: - The generative AI boom is mostly powered by fossil fuels. 53.9 percent of the electricity consumption of hyperscale data centers is fossil-fuel generated, with 38.2 percent coming from methane gas and 15.2 percent coming from coal. - Hyperscale data centers use as much electricity as some U.S. states. They used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year (68–99 terawatt-hours of electricity across scenarios). That’s as much electricity as some individual U.S. states over the course of a year, with the upper estimate approaching the annual electricity consumption of Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee. It represents about 1.8% of all U.S. electricity consumption. - Hyperscale data centers are consuming more than 3 times as much electricity as they were in 2018. An earlier study done before the generative AI boom put U.S. data centers’ electricity use at about 23 terawatt-hours in 2018. The new study’s central estimate is about 3.6 times as high. - Virginia alone accounted for about a quarter of the electricity use. The researchers counted 142 facilities in Virginia, more than twice as many as in any other state. Powering those facilities was associated with about 7 million metric tons of CO₂. Together, Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half the electricity used by the data centers in the study. Now, to be totally clear, I’m not saying any of this to bash the study! Quite the contrary: I think it represents an important, Herculean effort, especially given how little information Congress and state governments require tech companies to give u

artigo.texto: The Minneapolis City Council passed an ordinance Thursday in a 7-6 vote to strengthen regulations on data centers ahead of the expiration of a six-month suspension on new development passed in June. If approved by Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, the law will institute overlay zoning, which gives the City Council and City Planning Commission the ability to evaluate new data center proposals on a case-by-case basis. The ordinance also limits the size and geographic location of data centers, which provide storage and transmission of data for internet services. The development of new data centers is limited to two downtown districts that primarily consist of office buildings in an effort to avoid densely populated residential areas. Under the ordinance, data centers using only nonrenewable energy are capped at 50,000 square feet, while those that purchase local green energy can use up to 150,000 square feet. There are eight existing data centers in Minneapolis, with Cologix Data Center being the largest at 45,000 square feet. In an effort to limit noise pollution, servers must be located 20 feet inside a building and at least 100 feet from residential properties. The ordinance also requires potential developers to share expected water and energy use, and how they plan to manage noise. Supporters say case-by-case evaluations by elected officials will strengthen the democratic process. “This amendment is fundamentally about whether we believe residents deserve a meaningful voice in decisions that will shape the future of their neighborhoods,” Ward 2 Council Member Robin Wonsley, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis and the University of Minnesota area, said. The ordinance follows a failed attempt Monday by progressive council members to pass a full ban, intended to reflect the wishes of the majority of the 1,600 Minneapolis residents who submitted comments to the City Council, Wonsley said. “It doesn’t bring a people-centered downtown, it’s not gonna be our ticket out of our financial woes, and our neighbors don’t want it,” Council Member Soren Stevenson, who represents parts of south central Minneapolis, said. “We should ban it.” The ban did not receive enough support from council members or Mayor Frey to pass. Data centers have been at the center of political deliberations in communities across the country, as the quickly developing Artificial Intelligence industry has increased demand for computational power. Residents in communities with large-scale data centers have faced air, noise and water pollution, as well as lower property values and strain on local energy resources, resulting in frequent power outages and higher utility costs. Council members who oppose stricter regulations say Minneapolis should prioritize the economic investment brought by data center developers. “We need a plan for economic growth, for a thriving downtown core. Being anti-jobs, anti-labor, anti-investment is not a strategy,” Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer, who represents parts of downtown and southwest Minneapolis, said. Council members supporting overlay zoning hope that evaluating individual applications could effectively respond to the rapidly changing conditions of the AI and data center industries. “The industry is rapidly evolving. It changes week by week, both in its financial conditions, in the way that the tech is evolving and also the way that the industry is finding gaps in local policies,” Council Member Aurin Chowdhury, who represents parts of southeast Minneapolis, said. Other council members preferred the existing primary zoning laws, which would establish standardized rules for all data center applications, in order to avoid tedious deliberation. “It’s better for us to have rules, apply them evenly, and not make every data center application a political fight,” Shaffer said. At a rally outside Minneapolis City Hall on Tuesday evening, residents protested in favor of a total ban and, in its absence, the adoption of overlay zoning over primary zoning. Many expressed worry about the pollution and quality-of-life risks from living near large data centers. Kalani Matus of the Climate Justice Committee spoke at the rally opposing any data center development, citing inflated demand driven by intense industry competition and speculation. City Council President Elliott Payne echoed these sentiments in support of overlay zoning at Thursday’s meeting. “The large frontier models are taking on significant debt to build these out under the speculation of future demand that might not actually ever show up,” Payne said. “It’s all speculation. It is a gold rush right now.” J.P. Morgan estimated that the industry’s five largest development companies will spend $697 billion on data center investments by the end of 2026, while major AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are not expected to make a profit for several years. The City Council’s ordinance will now go to the desk of Frey, who will either approve or veto it. Frey has spoken in support of overlay zoning before, though he has also supported allowing data center development in a larger range of Minneapolis neighborhoods than the ordinance proposes.

artigo.texto: Md. Shahidul Haque Anralya, Turkuye. Bangladesh and Singapore have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen cooperation in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, create new opportunities for climate finance, and promote joint initiatives to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The MoU was signed on Saturday morning (14 November) at the Singapore Pavilion during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye. Sheikh Faridul Islam, State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, signed the MoU on behalf of Bangladesh, while Melvin Ong, Secretary of Singapore's Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, signed on behalf of Singapore. The MoU marks a significant milestone in facilitating Bangladesh's effective participation in international carbon markets, expanding opportunities for carbon financing and environmentally sustainable investments, and supporting the implementation of the country's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0). Speaking at the signing ceremony, State Minister Sheikh Faridul Islam said, Bangladesh warmly welcomes this important partnership with Singapore under the Paris Agreement. This cooperation will play a significant role in unlocking new opportunities for carbon finance, developing high-quality and transparent carbon markets, and supporting the implementation of Bangladesh's NDC 3.0. Bangladesh is committed to working closely with Singapore to advance sustainable development, achieve ambitious climate goals, and strengthen effective global climate action. Under the MoU, the two countries have agreed to exchange information, knowledge, and experience related to carbon credits and strengthen future cooperation on carbon emission reduction projects based on mutual interests and benefits. This collaboration will help accelerate climate change mitigation efforts by leveraging opportunities for international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The initiative is expected to support the development of internationally recognized carbon markets in Bangladesh, facilitate the transfer of climate-friendly technologies, attract greater private sector investment, and create new opportunities for international climate finance. It will also contribute to advancing the country's sustainable and low-carbon development initiatives and achieving its national climate targets. As a follow-up to the MoU, Bangladesh and Singapore are expected to sign an Implementation Agreement at COP32, scheduled to be held in Ethiopia next year. The agreement is expected to further strengthen the effectiveness, institutional framework, and practical implementation of bilateral cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
