artigo.texto: Data center moratorium extension recommended for Bloomington BLOOMINGTON (25News Now) -Bloomington’s planning commission recommends pushing the data center moratorium out for another 12 months. Since the first public event, staff made several changes to their proposed rules, based on public feedback. The commission voted to recommend extending the current moratorium for a year, instead of another six months, to come up with data center regulations. Some of the proposed changes include banning non-disclosure agreements about data centers, no matter what size the center would be, and higher fines for developers who violate city regulations. Some stakeholders, like the Citizens’ Utility Board, sent a representative who said he was pleased with proposed regulations on energy. “Relating to the energy use provisions of the ordinance, I’ve read through the draft, and I find them to be more than reasonable, really, they look a lot better than other ordinances I’ve seen around the state,” said Scott Allen of CUB. The planning commission recommended the moratorium that expires on Nov. 27 should be extended for a year, but the city council will take final action on that. artigo.texto: German energy giant RWE has just broken ground on a colossal 262.5-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery that is capable of supplying roughly 21,000 households with electricity during peak evening hours. The 62.5-megawatt (MW) battery is reportedly RWE’s first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. Located in the city of Ragusa in Sicily, it will be fitted with 42 containers housing lithium-ion batteries. RWE representatives revealed that the system will have a total storage capacity of 262.5 megawatt-hours (MWh). It will be capable of delivering its maximum output for four hours. This will be enough to cover the evening peak electricity demand of around 21,000 Italian households. The company expects to commission the project by the end of 2027. “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone,” Sopna Sury, CEO of RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said. “We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun.” Power for peak demand Sury explained that the battery will support the balance between electricity supply and demand. “In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilizing the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most,” Sury continued. More from Energy See All Unlike conventional power plants, renewable energy sources depend on weather conditions. Battery storage systems can store excess electricity when production is high and release it when the demand increases. RWE said its new battery will provide balancing energy to stabilize the electricity grid. It will also feature technology capable of delivering grid-forming services such as instantaneous reserve, also known as inertia. Apart from installing the batteries, RWE will build the necessary grid infrastructure, including a high-voltage transformer that will link the system to the 150-kilovolt (kV) electricity grid. “[The] Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for four hours,” Sury added. More battery capacity With the project, RWE aims to expand its battery storage business across Europe and other parts of the world. The company currently operates approximately 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage capacity worldwide. At the same time, another three GW are under construction. Additionally, RWE has established a strong presence in Italy’s renewable energy market. It currently operates 18 onshore wind farms, one solar power plant, and three agrivoltaic facilities. Together, these projects have an installed capacity of approximately 670 MW. This is enough to supply renewable electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households. The company is also constructing 200 MW of additional wind and solar capacity across the country. The Ragusa project will complement these renewable energy operations. Meanwhile, RWE plans to develop further battery storage capacity in Italy alongside its existing wind and solar projects. “We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system,” Sury said in a press release. He explained that the expansion will make Italy’s electricity grid more reliable.

artigo.texto: Korea has joined the Carbon Market Club of Clubs (OCCCM), an international coalition on carbon markets that includes the European Union (EU) and China. With this, Korea will take part in talks that set rules for the international carbon market, including internationally transferred mitigation outcomes and offset credits. Kim Sunghwan, Minister of the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, announced Korea's entry at a high-level meeting of the Carbon Market Club of Clubs held on the sidelines of the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on the 16th local time. The Carbon Market Club of Clubs is an international cooperation body that shares experience operating compliance carbon markets such as emissions trading systems and carbon taxes, and discusses measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), carbon accounting, and high-quality offset systems. Brazil proposed creating the group at COP30 last year, and it launched in May this year with the EU, China, and other major operators of carbon markets at its core. Korea joined after receiving an invitation from the EU as a follow-up to Korea-EU summit diplomacy in June. Membership is open to countries or regional economic integration organizations that operate or are developing a domestic compliance carbon market or carbon pricing system. Members have voting rights at high-level meetings. Announcing the accession, Minister Kim said, "Korea was the first in East Asia to introduce and operate a nationwide emissions trading system in 2015," adding, "We now manage more than 70% of the country's greenhouse gas emissions." He added, "We will share with member states our MRV system built for a manufacturing-centered industrial structure, our market design and operation, and our experience running an offset program within the ETS." Kim also said Korea is working to shift from a fossil fuel–based economy to an 'electric nation' centered on zero-carbon power, and introduced the government's Korea Green Transformation (K-GX) strategy released last month. By joining, Korea can now take part in setting international carbon market rules, including creating internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and establishing common principles for high-integrity offset credits. Meanwhile, the high-level meeting adopted the 'COP31 Carbon Market Club of Clubs Declaration,' which welcomes new members and commits to developing the coalition into a core consultative body for international cooperation on compliance carbon markets.

artigo.texto: Data centers: acordo entre Amazon e Blackstone abrange 13 prédios em Indiana e no Mississippi (Adobe Stock/Divulgação) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h10. Última atualização em 16 de novembro de 2026 às 10h11. A Amazon anunciou em 16 de novembro de 2026 a venda do controle de 13 prédios de data centers nos Estados Unidos, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões, para a Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone. A Amazon Web Services (AWS) continuará ocupando todos os imóveis como inquilina, com contratos de prazo médio inicial de 12 anos, que podem chegar a 32 anos com as renovações, e reajuste de 2,75% ao ano. A Amazon receberá dinheiro e ficará com 24,9% das duas sociedades conjuntas que serão donas dos complexos, localizados em Indiana e no Mississippi, que somam 647 megawatts de capacidade. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde o IPO, em maio, e a conclusão está prevista para até o fim de 2026. O modelo lembra a sociedade fechada pela Meta com fundos da Blue Owl, em 2025, para o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. A Amazon vai passar de proprietária a sócia minoritária e inquilina de 13 prédios de data centers recém-construídos nos Estados Unidos. Em acordo anunciado nesta segunda-feira, 16, um veículo imobiliário administrado por uma afiliada da Blackstone comprará o controle das sociedades que ficarão com os imóveis, avaliados em US$ 5 bilhões. A Amazon Web Services (AWS), braço de computação em nuvem do grupo, vai alugar todos os prédios e continuar usando a infraestrutura. A operação dá à Amazon uma forma de levantar dinheiro com instalações que já construiu e manter a capacidade disponível para seus clientes. Em troca, a companhia assume aluguéis com prazo inicial médio de 12 anos. Se todas as opções de renovação forem exercidas, a média sobe para 32 anos. O reajuste previsto é de 2,75% ao ano, e a própria Amazon garante os pagamentos da subsidiária. Os US$ 5 bilhões correspondem à avaliação bruta dos dois complexos. Na conclusão da operação, a Amazon vai transferir os imóveis para duas sociedades conjuntas, uma para cada complexo, e receber dinheiro e uma fatia de 24,9% em cada uma. A Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, negociada na Bolsa de Nova York sob o código BXDC, ficará com os outros 75,1%. O pagamento em dinheiro será financiado por duas fontes. A BXDC espera aportar US$ 1,9 bilhão em recursos levantados no IPO. Subsidiárias das sociedades conjuntas devem contratar cerca de US$ 2,5 bilhões em empréstimos hipotecários, garantidos pelos próprios imóveis. Como parte do financiamento também cobrirá custos da transação, a soma dessas duas fontes indica o volume de recursos mobilizados, e o valor líquido a ser recebido pela Amazon ainda depende dos termos do fechamento. É o primeiro investimento da BXDC desde a abertura de capital, em maio. A oferta inicial foi de US$ 1,75 bilhão e, depois que os bancos exerceram integralmente a opção de vender ações adicionais, a captação líquida chegou a cerca de US$ 1,9 bilhão. A conclusão da compra está prevista para até o fim de 2026, sujeita às condições do acordo. O acordo reúne nove prédios no norte de Indiana, no mercado de data centers da região de Chicago, e quatro no Mississippi. Juntos, eles somam 647 megawatts de capacidade elétrica para equipamentos de TI. O número indica a potência que a infraestrutura pode disponibilizar a equipamentos como servidores e sistemas de rede. Para a BXDC, a compra dá acesso a prédios novos com um contrato para ocupar 100% do portfólio. Para a AWS, a locação mantém disponíveis os imóveis de que a operação depende. O contrato segue o modelo conhecido como triple net, em que o inquilino arca, além do aluguel, com despesas como impostos imobiliários, seguro e manutenção. A aquisição foi precificada a uma taxa inicial de capitalização de 7%. O indicador relaciona a renda operacional anual dos imóveis ao valor atribuído a eles. Ele serve para avaliar o preço pago pelo portfólio. O retorno para o acionista da BXDC também depende do custo da dívida e das demais despesas da operação. A parceria permite à Amazon recuperar parte do capital investido nas instalações e continuar usando os prédios. O dinheiro entra no fechamento. Os aluguéis serão pagos ao longo dos anos, com reajuste anual. Para o investidor imobiliário, o atrativo é justamente o fluxo de pagamentos de uma única locatária, respaldado pela garantia da Amazon. Prasad Kalyanaraman, vice-presidente de infraestrutura da AWS, afirmou no comunicado que a parceria permite à empresa continuar ampliando sua operação à medida que cresce a demanda dos clientes. No terceiro trimestre, a receita da AWS cresceu 39%, para US$ 46 bilhões. A expansão exige investimentos em terrenos, energia e prédios, além dos chips e servidores instalados neles. O acordo com a Blackstone traz um investidor para a parte imobiliária dessa conta. A Meta recorreu a uma sociedade com fundos da Blue Owl em outubro de 2025 para desenvolver o complexo Hyperion, na Louisiana. Os fundos ficaram com 80%, e a Meta, com 20%. Os US$ 27 bilhões divulgados naquele acordo correspondem ao custo estimado de desenvolvimento, incluindo construção e infraestrutura de energia, refrigeração e conectividade. No caso da Amazon, os US$ 5 bilhões são a avaliação de imóveis já construídos, que a AWS continuará usando como inquilina. A AWS vai alugar todos os 13 prédios. A Amazon também manterá 24,9% das sociedades que serão donas dos imóveis. Os US$ 5 bilhões são o valor bruto atribuído aos dois complexos. Na conclusão do negócio, a Amazon receberá uma parcela em dinheiro e manterá uma participação minoritária nas sociedades. A BXDC espera concluir a transação até o fim de 2026. O fechamento depende das condições do acordo e do financiamento previsto. artigo.texto: Ascenty constrói data center de IA em Sumaré Projeto tem cliente âncora contratado; companhia mantém três unidades em construção e quatro em expansão no Brasil. A Ascenty está construindo em Sumaré, no interior de São Paulo, um data center dedicado à inteligência artificial, com capacidade inicial de 60 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de TI e 90 MW de potência total. O empreendimento, chamado Sumaré 3, já tem um cliente âncora contratado, segundo Rodrigo Radaieski, CTO da companhia, em entrevista ao TV.Síntese. O vídeo vai ao ar hoje, às 19h. “É um hyperscale”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, as bases e os pilares da construção já foram executados. A previsão é disponibilizar a primeira fase em setembro de 2027. O projeto faz parte da expansão da empresa no Brasil, dona de 21 data centers em operação, três em construção e quatro em expansão. Na América Latina, a companhia contabiliza 26 unidades operacionais e um total de 40 ao incluir os empreendimentos em construção e desenvolvimento. Expansão concentrada em São Paulo As obras de expansão no Brasil estão concentradas em São Paulo. Segundo o CTO, a localização atende à demanda dos clientes e à necessidade de reduzir a latência, ou seja, o tempo de comunicação entre os dispositivos dos usuários e os data centers. O executivo afirma que essa proximidade também importa para aplicações de inteligência artificial. A empresa mantém unidades no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. Radaieski também conta das negociações para novos projetos, que atribuiu ao avanço do Redata, regime de incentivos ao setor. “O Redata acelerou bastante o mercado, então tem muitas discussões, a gente deve fazer anúncios em breve”, disse. No caso de Sumaré 3, a intenção é solicitar o enquadramento no regime após a regulamentação. Além daquela projeto, a Ascenty está adaptando instalações existentes para receber cargas de maior densidade. “Só no ano de 2025 nós fizemos 400 ações dentro dos data centers para buscar essa eficiência energética”, afirmou. Entre os exemplos citados estão ajustes de temperatura, posicionamento de grelhas e circulação do ar. Rede de fibra integra a estratégia A expansão dos data centers é acompanhada pela infraestrutura própria de conectividade. Segundo o CTO, a Ascenty possui 4 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica, somando as redes no Brasil e no México. Essa infraestrutura conecta unidades da empresa, data centers de outros operadores e estações de chegada de cabos submarinos. No Brasil, a rede própria tem conexões em São Paulo, incluindo Praia Grande, no Rio de Janeiro e em Fortaleza. A rede atende tanto clientes corporativos que contratam links quanto empresas que demandam fibras apagadas, dedicadas à conexão entre instalações. Segundo o executivo, os hyperscalers contratam grandes quantidades dessas fibras para interligar data centers, replicar dados e manter redundância. Ele diz que o ativo é estratégico e não há nenhum plano de spin off dele.

artigo.texto: HADLEY — Lightning Hill is the name generations of Hadley residents have given to the peak of Breckenridge Road, where a gravel pit could soon become the location of a stand-alone battery energy storage system. “It is incredibly prone to lightning strikes,” said Linda Hannum, of Sylvia Heights. For residents who have organized to halt the placement of a 5-megawatt facility in the 5-acre site above Zatyrka Park, where there is a playground, gazebo and walking trails, the fact that lightning regularly splits trees and tears off bark makes the location above the town’s aquifer unsuitable for this project. On Thursday, nearly 30 people went to the Hadley Senior Center dining room, joined by another dozen or more attending virtually, to appeal to the Board of Health to take a stand against the development. They contend that the Board of Health could intervene after the Planning Board last month approved site plans, a solar project special permit and a business use in aquifer special permit for ZP Battery Devco’s 5-megawatt system. The meeting came two nights after the Conservation Commission voted 3-0 against the project. Commission members cautioned that they typically only weigh in on matters when wetlands are involved but still determined the project likely wasn’t appropriate for the neighborhood. “We are asking for you to join the Conservation Commission in opposing this project outright,” Hannum said. Planners had initially rejected the development in January 2025, concerned with potential impacts on the aquifer and public safety should there be a fire or leaks, before facing a lawsuit in Hampshire Superior Court in which the company argued the board’s decision was legally untenable and “unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious.” The Lightning Hill nickname for the top of Breckenridge Road, along with the gravel pit remaining an active site with unstable material at its base, are among neighbors’ many objections to the development. Since the agenda only called for public comment on the project, the Board of Health made no decision and took no action on the request. Neither the developer nor the landowner, Karl’s Excavating, was present to rebut any of the information presented. Hannum said she understands that the health board will likely have to prove there is a risk to the aquifer. Her hope is that the information residents provided, supplemented with photographic evidence from the site and pictures of a similar development that caught on fire and burned in Warwick, New York, will be sufficient. Members of the group organizing opposition, though, said they understand this is only a starting point. The aquifer is the big concern for Carol Soules of Sylvia Heights. Soules said the porous soil and fragile and unstable embankments should have necessitated a hydrogeologic study, which was not required for the proposal to proceed. “I feel like there are risks to [the] health and safety of residents,” Soules said. “The developer should find a safer place.” There are potential noise concerns, too. Donna Kurkul of Frallo Drive said residents below the gravel pit can already hear everything that happens there, and the battery noise will be excessive. Gail Mengel of Sylvia Heights said that a catastrophe could happen, and it’s unclear if the town has the resources to handle an emergency, whether a fire or a leak. Greg Owen of Breckenridge Road said the town should mitigate the threat and plan for the worst-case scenarios, adding that the best hazard prevention would be to prohibit such a development altogether. Others suggested that the project would be more appropriate along Route 9, where there are already areas paved over and fewer residential homes. Kristi Nelson of Sylvia Heights said that those concerned with the development are green energy advocates who understand the need to support solar and battery energy storage, but harming drinking water is not a good trade-off. “We feel very strongly it should not be in this location,” Nelson said.

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution is set to launch an offensive in the North American AI power infrastructure market by unveiling an integrated energy solution that covers everything from power storage to supply and management for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. On Nov. 15, LG Energy Solution announced its participation in ‘RE+ 2026,’ North America’s largest renewable energy exhibition, which will be held in Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, from the 17th to the 19th (local time). This year’s exhibition theme is “Energy for the Future of AI – Reliability, Resilience, and Intelligence.” LG Energy Solution has prepared an exhibition space of 279 square meters, approximately 20% larger than last year, where it will showcase integrated power infrastructure for AI data centers and next-generation battery technology. The core of the exhibition is “AI Data Center Integrated Power Infrastructure,” which combines Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS), Battery Backup Units (BBU), and Energy Management Systems (EMS). A key feature is that it provides power storage and supply, as well as functions to respond to emergencies such as power outages, all within a single system. The company will also introduce its recent achievement of being selected as a partner in NVIDIA’s “DSX Ready BESS” program. In the field of grid-scale Energy Storage Systems (ESS), LG Energy Solution will unveil the “JF3 AC LINK,” based on Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries. This product utilizes LFP batteries produced locally in the United States and increases energy density per site by approximately 26% compared to existing products. It is designed to supply power stably to data centers and large-scale power grids by applying digital twin technology (a technique that replicates real-world facilities or systems in a virtual computer space to analyze and predict operating conditions) and AI-based power stabilization technology. As for next-generation battery technology, the company will showcase a system combining sodium-ion batteries with Solid-State Transformers (SST). This technology combines the thermal stability of sodium-ion batteries with the power conversion function of SSTs to respond to frequent charging and discharging cycles as well as sudden changes in power demand. In addition, LG Energy Solution will exhibit next-generation “JP6 UPS Rack” systems and BBU products utilizing cylindrical 2170 batteries. These products supply power immediately to servers during a power outage while enhancing data center space utilization through high-density battery design. LG Energy Solution also plans to emphasize its production capacity of over 50 GWh secured in North America. The company is expanding its business scope from system design and construction to operation, optimization, and asset management by leveraging Vertech, a specialized legal entity for the ESS business, and the integrated software platform “AEROS Suite.” Kang Chang-beom, vice president of LG Energy Solution’s ESS Battery Business Division, said, “The growth of the AI industry demands new energy solutions that encompass stable power storage and supply, as well as efficient operation.” He added, “By combining local production competitiveness in North America with differentiated technological capabilities, system construction expertise, and intelligent operational capabilities, we will accelerate our growth into an energy platform company.”

artigo.texto: EcoPro is stepping up efforts to strengthen its global competitiveness by showcasing its secondary battery materials ecosystem in Pohang, North Gyeongsang Province, and its next-generation battery materials technologies. EcoPro said Sunday that it participated in the International Battery Expo 2026 Pohang, held for three days from Nov. 13 at Manindang Gymnasium in Pohang. Now in its second year, the expo is a specialized exhibition showcasing technologies and future visions across the entire battery industry, from materials and components to recycling used batteries. EcoPro organized its exhibition booth around seven themes, including cooperation with the Pohang community, global supply chains, high-nickel cathode materials and next-generation battery materials. Since 2017, EcoPro has invested approximately 3.3 trillion won in Pohang to build a secondary battery materials ecosystem linking precursor and cathode material production with used battery recycling. The company is strengthening its supply chain competitiveness through a closed-loop system that connects raw material procurement, production and recycling. The company also introduced its global production network. It is building an integrated supply chain linking its BNSI nickel smelter in Indonesia, its cathode materials plant in Debrecen, Hungary, and its domestic production facilities, connecting raw material sourcing with finished product manufacturing. EcoPro also showcased its next-generation battery materials technologies. Its lineup included high-nickel ternary cathode materials, known for their high energy density, as well as mid-nickel cathode materials, materials for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. The company also presented its solid electrolyte technology, a key material for all-solid-state batteries, outlining its strategy to expand its product portfolio. High-nickel cathode materials, in particular, are expected to find wider applications beyond electric vehicles in emerging industries requiring high energy density, including humanoid robots, urban air mobility (UAM) and aerospace. EcoPro also highlighted its contributions to the local community. Through social initiatives such as supporting childbirth in vulnerable households, providing safety umbrellas for children and developing community welfare villages, the company has been recognized as a community-contributing company for seven consecutive years. "Having grown in Pohang, EcoPro feels a strong responsibility to contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of Korea's battery industry alongside the local community," EcoPro CEO Choi Sang-woon said. "We will do our utmost to boost our global competitiveness through continued investment and technological innovation while helping revitalize the local economy and create quality jobs."

artigo.texto: Pela regra, os operadores de data centers nos cinco países vão precisar de autorização do governo americano para comprar chips de IA avançados da Nvidia e de outros fabricantes americanos. O objetivo é impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA usem capacidade computacional instalada fora do país e baseada em processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. “A regra foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso à tecnologia americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota que envolvam data centers em terceiros países”, afirmou o departamento em comunicado. Segundo o órgão, os avanços na computação em nuvem tornaram cada vez mais viável acessar remotamente os sistemas americanos de IA. A nova regra busca alinhar esse tipo de acesso às normas que já valem para o acesso físico à tecnologia. As ações da Nvidia chegaram a cair 2,9% nesta segunda-feira, e o índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia recuou até 5,5% Como a regra afeta o Brasil e os outros países da lista Os pedidos de licença serão analisados caso a caso. Empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos cinco países ficam de fora da exigência e podem continuar enviando chips de IA para lá sem licença. A isenção também vale para data centers usados em sistemas de recomendação de varejistas online e redes sociais. O texto divulgado na segunda-feira prevê que as novas exigências entram em vigor quando a regra for publicada no Federal Register, o diário oficial do governo americano. Escândalo na Nvidia pressiona o Departamento de Comércio A regra saiu dias depois de Jensen Huang deixar o cargo de CEO da Nvidia. Ele admitiu ter tido um caso com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa com sede em Singapura. Os EUA suspeitam que Alice seja espiã chinesa, e hoje ela está na China. A Megaspeed é investigada nos EUA por possíveis violações dos controles de exportação e nega irregularidades. Depois da saída repentina de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades como o secretário Howard Lutnick passaram a ser mais cobrados pela forma como conduzem os programas de controle de exportação. Nos últimos dias, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, culpou Lutnick por não fazer o suficiente para aplicar as restrições que já existem. “Como eu disse, muitos outros departamentos estavam pressionando por isso, e quem redigia era o Comércio”, afirmou Bessent no programa Sunday Morning Futures, da Fox News. O comunicado do Departamento de Comércio diz que a regra foi escrita pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, e por orientação deles. Isso sugere que a pressão de autoridades de fora do Comércio pesou na publicação. Na semana passada, o site Axios informou que Trump havia autorizado uma nova ofensiva contra empresas suspeitas de desviar chips avançados de IA para a China, mas que Lutnick atrasou a execução da ordem. Nesta segunda-feira, Trump disse que Jensen Huang não colocou a segurança nacional em risco.

artigo.texto: Chris Meiter & Ed Evans from AMAG Technology and Eric Zei from Salient Systems examine why data center security gaps often stem from unfinished integration and unclear ownership, rather than outdated technology. Article Chapters Toggle Data centers are going up faster than almost any other facility type, and the security problem inside them resembles nothing else. A large colocation site moves tens of thousands of people through its doors in a year, working for hundreds of separate tenant companies, most of whom the operator does not employ. Community opposition and organized protests are trying to reshape where these buildings go and how their perimeters get designed. Drones are a concern, though not for what they can see: everything in a data center comes back to cooling, and material dropped into an intake causes an operational event without anyone crossing the fence. Even video retention, a policy question in most buildings, is a contractual obligation with real money attached. Salient Systems and AMAG Technology have worked on these buildings together since 2012. AMAG is among Salient’s closest technology partners, and the work we do together concentrates in exactly this segment: the large operators running multi-tenant sites at scale. So, when an operator tells one of us that the security system isn’t doing what they expected, we compare notes. Comparing notes works because the two halves are not as separate as they look. Access control is often treated as finished technology: badge, reader, door. Visibility is treated as something happening on the video and analytics side. But that mistakes maturity for being solved. A protocol can be decades old and entirely stable, yet still be poorly managed. It is also backwards. Analytics are only ever as good as the access data they compare themselves against. Access events arrive in the video system with the cardholder attached to the alarm, which is what allows an operator to see who badged and to pull the recorded video by clicking the event rather than hunting for a camera and a time. The traffic runs both ways: video can trigger a lockdown, and a credential flagged as stolen can raise an alert with the right camera already attached to it. Video used to be evidence you went back for after somebody reported an incident. Now it is meant to raise the alarm while the incident is still underway. That only works if the access side is alerting personnel to something worth raising. Tailgating is the clearest case. Access control records one valid swipe. Video, counting people, sees two bodies come through. Neither system flags anything alone, because the log says a valid credential was granted and video has no view on how many people should have passed. The alert exists only in the comparison. And in a data center, the second person is rarely an intruder. It is a colleague who did not badge, or a contractor’s second technician on one credential, walking past cages that belong to somebody else. That is what the two systems do when they work. Far more often, what we hear is that they don’t. The complaint is always the same sentence. What is causing it almost never is. In one building the recording servers are eleven years old and the software is four versions behind. That is a budget conversation, and there is no clever way around it. In the other, everything is current and everything works. Nothing was ever finished: the detection zones are drawn so wide that somebody switched the alarms off, the cameras and the doors carry different names in each system, and the clocks drifted apart two years ago without anyone noticing. That one is an afternoon of work. From the operator’s chair the two are indistinguishable. Ed Evans of AMAG Technology puts it at four out of five being the second kind, and suspects that estimate is generous. Neither got that way by accident, and the routes are different. The first route is money. Hardware debt accumulates because security sits behind other IT in the funding order, and a department whose failures stay invisible is easy to defer. Nobody runs a laptop for eleven years. A recording server that has been writing continuously for eleven years draws no comment at all. Version drift is quieter still. One operator can run a dozen sites on the same platform with eight different builds among them and never log it as a fault. That is why someone will watch a capability demonstrated at a trade show and insist their own system cannot do it. It can. Theirs is four versions back. The second route is easier to travel because nothing along it announces itself. A detection zone, a door name, a drifted clock: none of it registers as an incident on its own. Collectively they are the distance between the system as designed and the system as installed, and almost nobody measures that distance. “The system does what it’s told,” Ed says. “It’s just being told the wrong thing.” Colocation multiplies everything that has to be told correctly. “The big thing colocation has to deal with that single-tenant and hyperscale rarely do, is keeping tenants separated from each other, not just keeping outsiders out,” Ed adds. That one difference reaches into every part of the design. Segmentation has to go down to the cage and sometimes the cabinet. Every tenant runs its own authorized-personnel list, with its own churn. Audit evidence has to come out per tenant, PCI for one and HIPAA for the next. And a tailgate into the wrong cage is not an internal write-up. It is a contract problem with a paying customer. An unfinished system is not a technology failure. It is a failure of ownership, and a data center project is structured in a way that almost produces it. On paper, commissioning splits three ways: “Nobody is structurally incentivized to find the gaps,” Ed says. Verification falls to whoever volunteers, and frequently nobody does. artigo.texto: COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkiye, have exposed a major imbalance in international carbon markets: governments and project developers are preparing billions of tonnes of carbon credits for sale, but actual transactions, verified emission reductions and financing reaching climate projects remain far smaller. A new COP31 report identifies $70.9 billion in potential Article 6 carbon-credit supply through 2030, compared with only $1.6 billion in contracted government demand. The State of the Article 6 Carbon Market 2026 report, released on November 13, estimates that 2.36 billion tonnes of carbon credits could become available by 2030. However, sovereign buyers have contracted approximately 53 million tonnes, representing just 2.2 percent of identified potential supply. Only 151,566 tonnes of internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) have actually moved between countries. These figures highlight the difference between potential carbon-credit supply, signed purchasing agreements, completed transfers and measurable climate investment. The report estimates demand associated with national climate commitments at approximately 200 million tonnes by 2030, worth $6 billion at the same assumed price. Since October 2025, governments have announced new tenders and agreements covering 27.3 million tonnes, valued at approximately $819 million. The volume includes Singapore’s procurement programme and Norway’s agreement to purchase up to 12 million tonnes from Indonesia, announced during COP31. These transactions could generate financing for emissions-reduction projects, but contract announcements alone do not establish that developers have received payment or delivered verified credits. Carbon Credit Prices: From $9 Forest Credits to $36 Government Purchases Carbon-credit prices vary significantly according to project type, verification, buyer requirements and eligibility under international climate agreements. According to OPIS’s November 9 COP31 carbon market assessment, Switzerland paid an average of approximately $36.58 per tonne for internationally transferred credits in 2025. Singapore’s initial procurement averaged approximately $27.30 per tonne, while Japanese Joint Crediting Mechanism credits were offered by a trader at $18–22 per tonne during 2026. Some forest-related credits were assessed at substantially lower prices, with OPIS reporting a broad REDD+ price assessment range extending from $0.15 to $9.20 per tonne. OPIS, A Dow Jones Company Sources: OPIS and Fastmarkets. Prices reflect different credit types, contract structures and dates; they are not directly interchangeable. Lower prices are not automatic evidence of fraudulent credits, just as higher prices do not guarantee genuine emissions reductions. The decisive factors are additionality, conservative emissions accounting, permanence, independent verification and safeguards against double counting. Voluntary Carbon Market: 169 Million Credits Retired in 2025 The Fastmarkets 2026 carbon-credit assessment shows that retirements across seven major registries reached approximately 169 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in 2025, compared with 174.5 million tonnes in 2024. This represents a decline of approximately 3.2 percent, indicating that demand for voluntary credits remained relatively weak despite growing corporate climate commitments. Shell was the largest identified corporate user, retiring 9.75 million credits in 2025, down from more than 14 million in 2024. Eni retired 6.44 million credits, an increase exceeding 80 percent. Gold Standard’s 2025 annual report provides another important comparison. Gold Standard’s 37 million retirements represented approximately 46 percent of its 81 million issuances during 2025. However, credits retired in a particular year may have been issued in earlier years, so this ratio is not a project-level retirement rate. Its $12.4 billion shared-value estimate includes environmental and socioeconomic benefits. It is not carbon-credit sales revenue or verified cash investment. India Leads Historical Voluntary Credit Issuance With 405 Million Tonnes The Berkeley Carbon Trading Project’s voluntary offset database tracks carbon-credit issuance and retirement across major international registries. An analysis published by the US Congressional Research Service found that Indian projects accounted for approximately 405 million tonnes of cumulative voluntary carbon-credit issuance from 2004 through 2025, across 1,855 projects. India ranked first in the dataset for both issued credits and project count. Worldwide voluntary credit issuance reached approximately 253 million tonnes during 2025. India’s domestic carbon market is also developing. According to the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s November 2026 analysis, approximately 490 industrial facilities across seven sectors completed their first compliance reporting cycle under India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme in July 2026. For Indian developers, Article 6 creates potential export opportunities for verified reductions from eligible projects, including methane abatement and qualifying clean-energy activities. However, international transfers require appropriate authorization and accounting adjustments, while domestic compliance credits follow a separate regulatory framework. Can Renewable Energy and Methane Projects Generate Credible Carbon Revenue? Renewable-energy carbon credits face increasing scrutiny because solar and wind projects are commercially competitive in many markets. A developer must demonstrate that carbon-credit revenue supports emissions reductions that would not otherwise occur. Methane-abatement projects can offer more directly measurable benefits when emissions are monitored through reliable equipment and independently verified against credible baselines. The Verra Verified Carbon Standard requires projects to undergo validation, monitoring and third-party verification before credits are issued

artigo.texto: Data center estaria em trâmite na ONS Mapa traz data center anunciado há quase 2 anos para Maringá, mas ministério não registra criação de ZPE Embora não seja apareça publicamente com o pedido de criação de uma Zona de Processamento de Exportação, no Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Maringá consta do Mapa da ONS – Mapa de Datacenters do Brasil do Maravalley, comunidade que mostra a distribuição dos datacenters em operação, construção e planejamento no país. Para se implantar um datacenter é necessário ter uma ZPE, criada mediante edição de decreto presidencial após terem tido seus projetos aprovados pelo Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE). Até julho não havia nenhum pedido protocolizado no MDIC. A informação no mapa é que, ao lado de outros 17 projetos, foi encaminhado ao Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) e está sob análise do ONS – Operacionador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico. No site não possível constatar a existência do protocolo. Hoje no país são quatro ZPEs ativas: Pecém (PE), Paranaíba (PI), Cáceres (MT) e Uberaba (MG), e outras em instalação: Açu (RJ), Aracruz (ES), Araguaína (TO), Bacabeira (MA), Barcarena (PA), Bataguassu (MS), Imbituba (SC), Senador Guiomard (AC) e Suape (PE). Em 23 de janeiro do ano passado o prefeito Silvio Barros (PP) anunciou que Maringá tinha iniciado à tramitação junto ao governo federal para a criação de uma ZPE, que abrigaria o maior data center de inteligência artificial da América Latina, em parceria com a RT-One, que anunciou recentemente a implantação modular e poderá alcançar capacidade de até 400 megawatts (MW) para equipamentos de tecnologia. A empresa informou que o investimento será de R$ 6 bilhões e que adotará sistema direct-to-chip em circuito fechado (resfriamento líquido). A expansão acelerada dos grandes data centers (especialmente voltados para IA) gerou uma forte polêmica em torno do consumo de energia e recursos naturais. Os servidores funcionam 24 horas por dia e exigem uma quantidade colossal de eletricidade, comparável ao consumo de grandes cidades ou a centenas de milhares de residências por unidade. Além disso, pode impactar na conta de luz, dada a expectativa de que o consumo gere escassez. Além da eletricidade, os sistemas de resfriamento consomem grandes volumes de água e geram ilhas de calor e poluição sonora nas comunidades vizinhas. Oficiamente, o governo federal presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu que a energia “do povo” não deve subsidiar ou ser consumida por essas grandes infraestruturas estrangeiras, sugerindo condicionar a instalação de data centers à autoprodução de energia (como geração própria ou contratos específicos). A recente vitória dos democratas nos Esta Unidos fez investidores das bolsas da Europa ponderarem sobre as incertezas relacionadas ao futuro da inteligência artificial e dos data centers. artigo.texto: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. “Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” says Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study. To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study. “Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.” While based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the new study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers. “Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study. The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent. While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

artigo.texto: On November 12, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published a comprehensive Finance and Economics Discussion Series working paper documenting that while U.S. capital commitments for artificial intelligence data centers have surged past $1 trillion, aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted. For university research leaders, economics scholars, and facility directors, the empirical findings highlight severe upstream hardware inflation, substantial import leakage, and mounting compute procurement pressures across higher education. FEDS 2026-074: Quantifying the Capital Boom in Artificial Intelligence Authored by Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina, and Joseph Nichols, working paper FEDS 2026-074—titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence (DOI: 10.17016/FEDS.2026.074)—evaluates how generative AI infrastructure is rippling through national accounts. Crucially, this working paper investigates real macroeconomic variables, capital accumulation, and industry output, keeping its analysis distinct from the central bank’s semi-annual Federal Reserve Financial Stability Report, which focused on debt liquidity and bank credit exposures. The paper documents a massive escalation in planned domestic data-center construction, which climbed from roughly $300 billion in 2024 to more than $1 trillion in announced pipelines by 2025. Applying the project forecasting methodology from Brandsaas et al. (2025), the authors estimate that baseline annual data-center investment will step up from $100 billion in 2024 to over $880 billion by the end of 2027, exceeding 2.0% of U.S. GDP. Approximately one-third of this outlay funds physical structures, while two-thirds is absorbed by high-tech equipment including GPUs, TPUs, high-density memory, and server cooling systems. Data-Center Capex Projections, Import Leakage, and Component Inflation The pace of data-center capital deployment has generated distinct supply-chain pressures and macroeconomic offsets. Key benchmarks established in FEDS 2026-074 include: Crucially, Carollo and colleagues calculate an import share of roughly 50% for high-tech compute hardware, with components primarily sourced from East Asian fabrication and packaging corridors. Because imported equipment enters national accounts as a deduction, this substantial leakage moderates the direct domestic output multiplier. Concurrently, direct inputs like high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and specialized printed circuit boards experienced annualized price increases of nearly 8% through early 2026, reversing a multi-decade trend of technological price deflation. Surging electricity requirements also prompted a sharp rise in power-generation interconnection requests in late 2025. These local infrastructure dynamics align with NBER research by Alvarez et al. (2026), which shows that data centers generate brief construction bursts but minimal long-term local employment. The Solow Productivity Paradox in the Generative Era Despite heavy capital commitments, FEDS 2026-074 finds that generative AI has yielded negligible measurable impact on aggregate U.S. labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity (TFP). Addressing this gap on November 13, 2026, at the UC San Diego Economics Roundtable, Federal Reserve Board Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a keynote address titled New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy. Jefferson invoked Robert Solow’s famous 1987 paradox that ‘you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.’ Jefferson noted that early personal computer investment in the late 1980s required more than a decade of organizational adaptation before aggregate productivity accelerated. Econometric decomposition in FEDS 2026-074 indicates that recent post-2023 productivity pickups primarily reflect cyclical supply-chain normalization rather than AI diffusion. Furthermore, the authors review growth literature: Daron Acemoglu (2025) estimates cumulative TFP gains of only 0.7% over the next decade, while optimistic projections by Filippucci et al. (2025) reach 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points annually. Task-level studies by Jones and Tonetti (2026) and Demirer, Musolff, and Yang (2026) confirm that coding agents accelerate syntax generation, but software deployment remains tightly bounded by human review and integration testing. Federal Reserve Leadership Perspectives: Barr and Waller on Labor and Inequality Central bank governors expanded on these macroeconomic themes during November 2026 addresses. On November 12 at Yale University, Governor Michael S. Barr presented remarks on American Inequality and the Future of AI, analyzing findings from the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Barr warned that because AI infrastructure requires massive capital reserves, financial gains are heavily concentrated among top software firms and high-wealth equity holders, raising distributional risks if routine entry-level cognitive tasks face wage erosion. Conversely, Governor Christopher J. Waller emphasized labor resilience in his November 10 speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference on The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism. Waller noted that aggregate claims, vacancies, and payrolls show no sign of widespread displacement. This stability is corroborated by New York Fed research (Abel et al., 2025) and independent market analysis from TradingView, which report that only ~10% of workers use AI daily, with firms primarily augmenting existing roles rather than reducing headcounts. artigo.texto: Data centers precisam se conectar às comunidades Sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios, avalia Ana Cunha, da Deerns Por Ana Cunha* – A expansão da IA mudou a forma como projetamos e operamos data centers. Com o aumento da densidade e potência dos racks e da demanda por capacidade computacional, questões como energia, água, resfriamento, disponibilidade de rede, emissões e adaptação tecnológica deixam de ser questões isoladas e passam a fazer parte de uma mesma equação que define estrategicamente o valor do ativo “data center” e até a viabilidade do seu licenciamento (permiting) técnico e social. Nesse cenário, falar em sustentabilidade significa ir além da eficiência energética, passando pela otimização de múltiplos recursos e pela criação de impacto positivo, especialmente para as comunidades que abrigam esses edifícios. Torna-se prioritário compreender como diferentes dimensões ambientais, técnicas, regulatórias e sociais se relacionam e como afetam a resiliência e o valor do ativo no longo prazo. Uma mudança que já é perceptível na Europa. Obrigações de reporte e instrumentos como a Taxonomia Europeia, a EED (Diretiva da Eficiência Energética) e a CSRD (Diretiva europeia sobre Relatórios de Sustentabilidade Corporativa) aproximam cada vez mais o desempenho de sustentabilidade das decisões de financiamento, investimento e de relacionamento ou captação de clientes. Sustentabilidade deixa, assim, de ser apenas uma agenda de conformidade e passa a integrar a equação econômica do empreendimento e de aceitação social na fase de licenciamento. Indicadores de desempenho sustentável e operacional também podem influenciar a avaliação de risco econômico e reputacional, a atratividade do ativo e o acesso a instrumentos de financiamento, tão importantes na fase atual de capital “caro”. Isso não significa que o Brasil deva reproduzir o modelo europeu. Os mercados partem de condições diferentes, mas os clientes de data centers de grande escala são cada vez mais internacionais e buscam otimizar práticas, indicadores e valor. A Europa possui um ambiente regulatório mais maduro e enfrenta restrições importantes relacionadas à água, à energia renovável e à capacidade (ou saturação) da rede. O Brasil, por sua vez, conta com uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e vive uma fase de expansão da infraestrutura digital. O ponto de convergência entre eles está na relação entre sustentabilidade e capital. Enquanto o mercado europeu utiliza critérios de desempenho e mecanismos financeiros cada vez mais associados à sustentabilidade, o Brasil pode combinar suas características energéticas com mecanismos fiscais para estimular novos investimentos. O Redata se insere nesse contexto como parte de uma nova equação para a expansão da infraestrutura digital brasileira, embora seus efeitos concretos devam ser avaliados à medida que o mecanismo avance. Mas existe um risco em transformar essa discussão em uma competição por indicadores. O PUE (Eficácia no Uso de Energia) continua sendo uma métrica fundamental para avaliar a eficiência energética de um data center, mas nenhum indicador isolado conta toda a história. Muitas vezes uma solução pode melhorar o PUE e piorar o WUE (Eficácia no Uso de Água); outra pode otimizar o consumo energético e, ao mesmo tempo, dificultar o reaproveitamento do calor residual. Além de que um local energeticamente eficiente ainda pode operar com energia não renovável tendo assim um fraco REF (Fator de Energia Renovável). É por isso que precisamos de uma abordagem sistêmica e multicritérios refletida desde as fases preliminares. Uma decisão de engenharia e de consultoria estratégica de sustentabilidade produz efeitos em diferentes dimensões do projeto, que precisam ser consideradas não só desde a concepção do ativo, mas até mesmo desde a seleção do terreno. Essa visão ganha ainda mais importância diante da inteligência artificial. Um data center preparado para cargas convencionais de cloud não necessariamente terá as mesmas características de uma instalação voltada para cargas de IA. A maior densidade de potência exige novas estratégias e tecnologias de resfriamento e modifica requisitos de infraestrutura. Por isso, a sustentabilidade começa antes do primeiro megawatt. A escolha do terreno, a disponibilidade de energia e água, os riscos climáticos, a arquitetura, o sistema de resfriamento, a possibilidade de reutilização de calor e a capacidade de adaptação futura precisam fazer parte das primeiras decisões. Inovação, porém, não significa simplesmente adotar a tecnologia mais nova. Em infraestrutura crítica, novas soluções precisam ser acompanhadas de segurança operacional e gestão de riscos. A experiência técnica é fundamental para avaliar sua aplicabilidade e integrá-las ao projeto sem dissociar sustentabilidade de funcionalidade, resiliência e custo total de propriedade (“Total Cost of Ownership”). Há ainda uma dimensão que muitas vezes fica fora das discussões predominantemente técnicas que é o território. Um data center não existe isoladamente, pois depende de energia, conectividade, fornecedores, trabalhadores e serviços. Sua implantação também pode gerar impactos sobre a região, e questões como ruído, impacto visual, demanda por água e energia ou ausência de benefícios locais podem comprometer a aceitação do projeto. Por outro lado, a infraestrutura digital também pode contribuir para o desenvolvimento desse local. Reaproveitamento de calor, capacitação profissional, contratação local, conectividade e integração com outros edifícios e sistemas urbanos podem criar benefícios que ultrapassam os limites físicos do data center. É na fase inicial, desde a seleção do terreno, que podem ser identificar as oportunidades de sinergias entre o data center e o território onde será instalado. artigo.texto: How data centers lost in the midterm elections COLUMBUS, Ohio - Beyond political parties and individual candidates, there was a clear loser in the 2026 midterms: data centers. As these essential pieces of AI infrastructure have dropped in popularity, they’ve been met with staunch resistance at the ballot box. Data centers lost on the ballot in the midterms By the numbers: According to research by Rosebud Consulting, voters in cities across the nation approved 44 ballot measures restricting data centers this November. Nearly half of those ballot measures came out of cities in Ohio, one of the nation’s largest data center markets. Ohio has more than 250 data centers. That’s the fifth most in the nation. Voters in Kansas, Illinois, Wisconsin, Maine, New Jersey, Florida, California and Nevada also approved restrictive ballot measures. By contrast, a single community voted in favor of data centers on a ballot measure. That was in Harwood, North Dakota — a town of less than a thousand residents. Data centers proved unpopular Dig deeper: AI proponents took a shellacking in Ohio, where midterm voters approved 21 restrictions for data centers in cities across the state. And that’s no surprise for researchers at Ohio Northern University. "These election results reflect a well-established majority consensus across Ohio communities demanding greater local control and strict oversight." said Keith Durkin, a professor at Ohio Northern University. He’s also director of the university’s Institute for Civics and Public Policy. The college released a study in October that found widespread opposition to data centers. "Our statewide Northern Poll found that 55% of Ohio adults oppose data center construction in their communities, and 57% support legal restrictions and megawatt caps on hyperscale development." Durkin said. Big Tech growing pains appear to go beyond a rural and urban or political divide. "The underlying voter sentiment shows minimal geographical differences in the state of Ohio," Durkin said. "Concerns over escalating home electric bills and grid vulnerability resonate equally across urban centers, suburban developments, and rural farming communities. The demand for ratepayer protection and community zoning authority spans all geographic demographics." Ohio's Senate race: Data centers may have been a factor in Ohio’s Senate race. While Ohio has typically been a stronghold for Donald Trump — he carried the state in the last three presidential elections — this year, Ohio voters rejected his endorsed Senate candidate and instead sent Democrat Sherrod Brown to Washington D.C. Brown, who previously served in the Senate, labeled his competitor Republican Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers" in a campaign ad. In another, Brown’s campaign called Husted, who was the incumbent in the race, the "chief reason Ohio has so many data centers." Meanwhile, President Trump, who endorsed Husted, has vocally supported AI and data centers, saying communities that reject them are destined to become "backwards and poor." Brown ultimately won his seat with 50% of the vote. Husted trailed with 45.1%, according to the Associated Press. Anti-data center sucesses: Beyond Ohio, candidates looking to battle Big Tech performed well on election night. Gina Hinojsa, the Democrat and Texas Governor-elect who unseated Republican Greg Abbott, has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers. Likewise, in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who won a bitter Senate race, was also outspoken on data centers. Their wins help to validate survey results from Pew Research Center, which found that a large portion of Americans are feeling pessimistic about data centers. Six in 10 adults surveyed said they would not be comfortable with a new data center in their area. Another 58% said they disliked politicians who supported building data centers near their homes or communities. However, Dirkin, the professor from Ohio Northern University, cautioned against drawing a straight line between candidate success or failure and anti-AI sentiment. "While data center expansion and tax subsidies carry clear public unpopularity, it is difficult to draw a direct causal line to candidate losses," Dirkin said. "Multi-issue elections are complex, and our findings indicate that data center concerns do not operate in a vacuum—they are tied to a larger, overarching voter focus on overall economic affordability, household utility costs, and community tax policy." Are data center laws going to change? Big picture view: It’s unclear if the anti-data center sentiment that came through in the midterms will result in new laws governing AI’s continued buildout. Wall Street appeared fearful of a data center slowdown, leaning into a multi trillion-dollar post-election sell-off of AI stocks. At the same time, some in the Big Tech world are asking for clarity in future laws. "New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies," wrote OpenAI, the owner of ChatGPT, in a Nov. 5 statement. "Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared." The company also offered a new set of data center commitments, saying it will pay the full costs of electricity and infrastructure and introduce new environmental protection plans. The Source: This story was written using interviews with a Northern Ohio professor, Pew Research Center and Rosebud Consulting data, election night results and public statements made by candidates and OpenAI. It was reported from Eden Prairie, Minnesota.

artigo.texto: India's renewable energy ambitions have reached a stage where generating clean electricity is no longer the only challenge. The more difficult task is ensuring that electricity generated during sunny and windy hours remains available when households, industries and businesses need it. With solar and wind capacity expanding rapidly, India faces a fundamental question: how can intermittent renewable energy become a dependable source of round-the-clock electricity?The Union Cabinet's approval of a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme on November 4, 2026, represents a major intervention in addressing this challenge. The programme envisages developing 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between 2026–27 and 2030–31, involving an estimated investment of ₹97,600 crore.Of the proposed capacity, 60 GWh will come from pumped hydro storage projects, 30 GWh from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and 2 GWh from emerging storage technologies. The programme also introduces a minimum domestic content requirement of 40% for battery storage projects, reflecting the government's intention to strengthen indigenous manufacturing.The significance of this initiative extends beyond the installation of batteries and storage infrastructure. It represents an attempt to transform the operating architecture of India's electricity system, which has traditionally depended on coal-fired generation to provide reliable power when renewable energy production fluctuates.Solar power generation peaks during daylight hours, while electricity consumption frequently rises in the evening. Wind generation also varies according to weather conditions. Without sufficient storage, renewable electricity may be curtailed during periods of surplus generation, while conventional power plants must compensate when output declines.Battery storage can absorb surplus electricity and release it during peak demand. Pumped hydro storage performs a similar function by using electricity to move water to an elevated reservoir and subsequently releasing it through turbines.Together, these technologies can reduce renewable energy curtailment, improve grid flexibility and limit the need for additional coal-based balancing capacity. However, storage cannot eliminate coal dependence immediately, particularly during prolonged periods of low renewable generation.According to the Ministry of Power, India's grid-scale energy storage requirement is projected to reach 411 GWh by 2031–32. The newly approved programme is therefore an important addition, but it will meet only part of the country's anticipated requirement.A more complex challenge lies in India's dependence on China for battery cells, components and processing technologies. China dominates several critical stages of the global lithium-ion battery supply chain, particularly lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which are widely used for stationary energy storage because of their cost advantages and durability.According to a May 2026 analysis by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), China accounts for approximately 74% of global lithium refining, 80% of cobalt refining and 98% of LFP cathode active material production. India's domestic lithium refining capacity remains negligible, while its battery cell manufacturing industry is still developing.The same analysis estimated that India's advanced chemistry cell battery demand could increase from 28 GWh in 2025 to approximately 272 GWh by FY2030. Despite the government's ₹18,100 crore production-linked incentive programme, only 1.4 GWh of cell manufacturing capacity had been commissioned under the scheme by early 2026.This creates a strategic contradiction. India is investing heavily in renewable energy to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, but its transition could create another form of external dependence through imported batteries and processed minerals.Assembling battery packs domestically does not necessarily constitute technological self-reliance if the cells, cathodes, anodes, electrolytes and manufacturing equipment continue to come from China. Changing this situation requires coordinated intervention across the entire battery value chain.India must accelerate domestic cell manufacturing while developing facilities for processing lithium, nickel and other critical minerals. The Cabinet's simultaneous approval of a ₹2,814 crore capital-support scheme for critical mineral processing provides an opportunity to connect mineral refining with battery manufacturing.India should also expand long-term mineral supply partnerships with countries such as Australia, Argentina and Chile, encourage Indian companies to acquire overseas mineral assets, and develop recycling facilities capable of recovering valuable materials from used batteries.Equally important is investment in alternative battery technologies, including sodium-ion systems, which could reduce dependence on lithium for some stationary storage applications. Domestic research institutions and manufacturers need sustained support to commercialise these technologies at competitive costs.The Ministry of Heavy Industries has acknowledged that Chinese dominance in technology and mineral processing creates difficulties for Indian manufacturers, including restricted access to some refining technologies. Addressing these constraints will require technology development, international partnerships and a predictable domestic market.Financing presents another major challenge. Battery storage projects require substantial upfront investment, while revenues depend on electricity price differences, storage utilisation, contractual arrangements and the financial health of electricity distribution companies.The VGF scheme can improve project viability by reducing initial capital costs. artigo.texto: Saída de Jensen Huang da Nvidia e o risco oculto dos data centers no Brasil A troca de comando na Nvidia não é só questão de liderança. Para o Brasil, que atrai bilhões em data centers, o risco real é a dependência de um único fornecedor de chips. Jensen Huang deixou a presidência da Nvidia em 12 de novembro sem um sucessor definitivo. O mercado reagiu ao fato como uma questão de liderança corporativa. Mas o problema mais relevante está a milhares de quilômetros de Santa Clara: no Brasil, que começa a receber investimentos bilionários em infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, a troca de comando expõe uma fragilidade estrutural que pouca gente está discutindo. A dependência quase total de um único fornecedor de tecnologia transforma qualquer instabilidade na Nvidia em risco financeiro direto para projetos brasileiros. Por que a Nvidia domina os data centers e o que isso significa A Nvidia não vende apenas chips. Ela entrega o pacote completo: processadores de aceleração, servidores, redes de interconexão e o ecossistema de software CUDA, usado por milhões de desenvolvedores no mundo. É como comprar um carro inteiro de um único fabricante, do motor ao sistema de navegação. Para o cliente, isso reduz a complexidade da instalação. Para a Nvidia, cria uma relação de dependência difícil de romper. Essa estratégia deu à empresa uma participação estimada acima de 80% no mercado de chips para treinamento de IA. Os concorrentes existem, como mostram os resultados recentes da AMD no segmento de data centers, mas nenhum se aproxima da escala e da integração que a Nvidia oferece. O lançamento sequencial de gerações como Blackwell e Rubin reforça a vantagem competitiva, e a reserva antecipada de capacidade fabril nas fundições especializadas torna quase impossível para rivais escalarem na mesma velocidade. O custo invisível da dependência tecnológica Para entender o risco brasileiro, é preciso pensar em termos concretos. Um data center de grande porte no Brasil exige centenas de milhões de reais em investimento inicial. Parte desse capital vai para equipamentos Nvidia: servidores com GPUs de última geração, sistemas de rede proprietários e licenças de software. Depois da instalação, trocar de fornecedor significa retreinar equipes, substituir hardware e reescrever código otimizado para CUDA. Economistas chamam isso de custo de mudança de fornecedor, um problema clássico de investimentos em ativos específicos. Projetos como o supercomputador planejado para o Nordeste do Brasil já ilustram essa dinâmica. O investimento é feito em função de uma tecnologia específica, com cronogramas de entrega amarrados ao roadmap de produto da Nvidia. Se a troca de comando alterar prioridades comerciais, atrasar lançamentos ou redirecionar produção para mercados mais lucrativos, o impacto no Brasil é imediato: equipamentos atrasados, custos financeiros correndo sem geração de receita e financiadores exigindo juros mais altos. Essa situação não é hipotética. A tensão geopolítica envolvendo a Nvidia e a China já demonstrou que decisões estratégicas da empresa afetam cadeias de fornecimento globais. Uma mudança de liderança adiciona incerteza a um cenário que já era complexo. O que a manchete não conta: risco financeiro de segunda ordem O problema não se limita ao dono do data center. Ele atinge toda a cadeia de financiamento. Quando um banco ou fundo de investimento financia um projeto de infraestrutura de IA, ele projeta fluxos de caixa para os próximos anos com base em premissas de entrega de equipamentos, vida útil da tecnologia e continuidade do suporte. Qualquer dúvida sobre esses fatores altera o perfil de risco do projeto. Na prática, isso significa que uma transição de liderança na Nvidia pode encarecer o custo de capital de um data center brasileiro mesmo sem nenhuma mudança na economia local. É um canal de transmissão de risco que foge do radar da maioria dos analistas, porque não aparece em indicadores macroeconômicos tradicionais. A Malásia entendeu essa dinâmica ao diversificar suas fontes de investimento em infraestrutura de IA, atraindo tanto empresas americanas quanto chinesas. O Brasil, até aqui, não demonstrou a mesma sofisticação na negociação desses contratos. O melhor argumento contra essa preocupação É justo reconhecer que a Nvidia é maior do que uma pessoa. A empresa tem 30 mil funcionários, uma estrutura de engenharia consolidada e contratos de longo prazo com as maiores empresas do mundo. A saída de um CEO, mesmo um tão identificado com a marca, não significa colapso operacional. A Apple sobreviveu a Steve Jobs. A Microsoft floresceu depois de Bill Gates. Empresas maduras costumam ter resiliência institucional. Além disso, o mercado de chips para IA é tão aquecido que a demanda por GPUs Nvidia continuará superando a oferta independente de quem estiver no comando. Os investimentos globais em data centers já ultrapassaram centenas de bilhões de dólares anuais e seguem acelerando. Esses argumentos são válidos, mas não eliminam o risco de curto e médio prazo. A Nvidia sob Huang tinha uma visão de produto e uma capacidade de execução que eram indissociáveis da figura do fundador. Uma transição mal conduzida pode não destruir a empresa, mas pode criar exatamente o tipo de incerteza que encarece projetos em mercados emergentes como o Brasil. O que o Brasil precisa fazer diferente Atrair investimentos em data centers é necessário, mas não suficiente. O desafio brasileiro é transformar compra de tecnologia em capacidade produtiva autônoma. Isso exige pelo menos três frentes simultâneas. Primeira: negociar contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo com cláusulas de proteção contra atrasos e mudanças estratégicas do fornecedor. Segunda: investir na formação de profissionais brasileiros capazes de operar e adaptar essas tecnologias, reduzindo a dependência do ecossistema proprietário. Terceira: evitar concentração excessiva em um único fornecedor, abrindo espaço para alternativas como AMD, Intel e até chips
