artigo.texto: RWE starts construction of its first battery in Italy Essen/Rome, 10 November 2026 RWE has started construction of its first Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Italy. The 62,5-megawatts (MW) Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for 4 hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262,5 megawatt hours (MWh). Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. ”We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for 4 hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. Battery storage at RWE As a driver of the energy transition, RWE develops, builds and operates battery storage systems in the US, Europe and Australia. Globally, RWE currently operates battery storage systems with a total capacity of around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) and 3 GW are under construction. As an integral part of its growth strategy, RWE plans to significantly expand its battery storage capacities worldwide. RWE Renewables Italia – strong presence in Italy’s renewables market RWE is a key player in the Italian renewables market. The company takes an integrated project approach that incorporates the development, construction and operation as well as the marketing of wind farms and solar plants. With 18 onshore wind farms, one photovoltaic plant and three agrivoltaic plants in operation, RWE currently manages a total installed capacity of approximately 670 MW in Italy, enough to supply green electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households. In addition, RWE currently has around 200 MW of further wind and solar capacity under construction in Italy. artigo.texto: A recent report compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project found, to quote from coverage of the report in The Guardian by Tom Perkins, “Data centers are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines.” A federal records review completed as part of the report identified 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, which would collectively span some 17,000 miles. The pipelines would help serve at least 98 gas-fired power plants meant to serve data centers. If all lines are completed, they would carry about 40% more natural gas daily than what the existing system carries. The U.S. already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, according to data from the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, which is housed within the U.S. Department of Transportation. “The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands,” Perkins continues. “At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres of federal protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.” Gov. Patrick Morrisey has just announced that Appalachian Power will commit $17 billion to building three new natural gas-fired plants in the state, expected to be operational by 2031, and $7.5 billion to upgrade its coal-fired plants in the state through 2050. Meanwhile, according to a piece in The Guardian by Oliver Millman, the nonprofit institute Climate Action Tracker has found that “The world is heading for an ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions.” An analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund recently found that the Trump administration handed out $950 million in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants. So, when do utility ratepayers get some relief? Because this buildout of data centers and the fossil fuels infrastructure that will power the vast majority of them is driving up our costs, as fossil fuels use always does, even as they contaminate our lives and destabilize our only home in the cosmos. The 2026 election results nationwide made one thing abundantly clear: Americans are tired. We’re tired of skyrocketing costs, endless corruption and criminality from the executive branch, corporate handouts at our expense and total disregard for our concerns regarding things AI, datacenters, surveillance systems like Flock cameras and a lot more. Even in West Virginia, though turnout was an abysmal 38% of registered voters statewide, every county moved double-digits toward the Democratic Party from previous elections. We’re more than coal, oil, gas and plastics and petrochemicals. We’ve been an extraction colony and sacrifice zone since June 20, 1863, and we just can’t take it anymore. All the economic development zones and fast-tracking of permits and approvals in the world do not lead to thriving communities where people want to come or return and build lives. Our public schools are shuttering as we hemorrhage population. We have growing food deserts and huge swaths of the state where communities lack potable water and safe sewage disposal systems. Despite all the pledges and dollars allocated, we still lack sufficient rural broadband. West Virginia should be one of the wealthiest and most prosperous places on the planet with all the resource wealth we’ve shipped out of here, but it’s only been a resource curse to us. Change starts with public policy that enables it. The Morrisey administration and Republican supermajority in the Legislature are telling us to swallow more of the same and like it. Let’s hope that, by 2028, more people realize the importance of getting to the polls in this state and demanding better, as people in so many states across the country just did on Election Day.

artigo.texto: A Turquia, país que sedia a COP31, em Antália, recebeu do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB) a aprovação de US$ 1,6 bilhão para acelerar sua política climática. O financiamento foi aprovado em 22 de outubro de 2026, semanas antes da conferência, segundo a página oficial do projeto no banco. O AIIB é um banco multilateral criado por iniciativa da China, com sede em Pequim, que financia infraestrutura na Ásia e em outras regiões. Como funciona o dinheiro O pacote tem duas partes de US$ 800 milhões cada. A primeira é um financiamento atrelado a políticas climáticas, e a segunda vem de um fundo do banco para energia, segurança alimentar e resiliência econômica. Nos dois casos, o dinheiro só sai se a Turquia cumprir 12 medidas acertadas antes, com metas acompanhadas por indicadores. O prazo previsto para o fim do empréstimo é dezembro de 2028. Os três eixos - Mercado de carbono e finanças verdes: pôr em funcionamento o sistema turco de comércio de emissões e criar regras para as finanças verdes; - Descarbonização: reduzir emissões em energia, indústria e transporte, com melhor monitoramento; - Adaptação: governança climática local, segurança hídrica, sumidouros de carbono e riscos do clima para a saúde nas 81 províncias do país. Por que a Turquia precisa Segundo o AIIB, a Turquia é o 17º maior emissor de gases de efeito estufa do mundo. O banco cita duas pressões sobre o país: o imposto de carbono na fronteira da União Europeia, que vai encarecer exportações de produtos com muitas emissões, e o custo maior da energia importada com a situação no Oriente Médio. O programa apoia a nova meta climática turca e a Lei do Clima do país, que o banco descreve como o marco legal climático mais substancial da Turquia até hoje. A anfitriã sob os holofotes Sediar uma COP coloca o país anfitrião sob escrutínio. A Turquia levou à conferência prioridades como eletrificação e redução de resíduos, mas ainda depende bastante de carvão e gás. O financiamento do AIIB é um dos instrumentos com que o país tenta mostrar avanço na própria casa. O paralelo com o Brasil O Brasil também tem um sistema de comércio de emissões aprovado por lei e em fase de regulamentação. Na COP31, o BNDES anunciou fundos que podem mobilizar R$ 39 bilhões para transição energética, com apoio do Fundo Verde para o Clima da ONU. Acompanhe a cobertura diária na página especial da COP 31. Perguntas frequentes Quanto a Turquia recebeu do AIIB? US$ 1,6 bilhão, em duas parcelas de US$ 800 milhões, segundo o banco. O que é o AIIB? O Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura, banco multilateral com sede em Pequim. Com informações do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Gostou desta reportagem? artigo.texto: SubTel Forum Issue 151 – Data Centers & New Technology OUT NOW! SubTel Forum Press Release November 16, 2026 Sterling, Virginia – Submarine Telecoms Forum, Inc. announces Issue 151 of Submarine Telecoms Forum Magazine, a special 25th anniversary edition exploring Data Centers & New Technology. AI and cloud services depend on physical networks. This edition examines the cables, landing stations, data centers and interconnected infrastructure that support those services, along with the security, planning and operational challenges facing the people who build and maintain them. What’s Inside Issue 151 The November edition explores how data center growth is changing the requirements for subsea connectivity. Contributors examine Loudoun’s next chapter, the role of shorter unrepeatered systems and the influence of cable route diversity on where cloud and AI infrastructure is built. Security and resilience run throughout the issue, from submarine cable protection to the connection between a landing station and a data center. Other features consider repair readiness, future Atlantic routing constraints, integration across network domains and the work still needed to connect African schools. Feature Articles - The Next Chapter of Loudoun’s Data Center Alley: Applying the Lessons of Scale and Experience by Buddy Rizer - Understanding the Security Layers in Submarine Cables by Sharat Sinha - Short Spans, Big Shifts: Unrepeatered Cable, Data Centers and the New Map of Subsea Projects by Christian T. Priess - The Internet Runs Through Cables We Rarely Think About by Kiran S. Pillai - No Cable, No Cloud, No AI: Why Subsea Networks Decide Where Data Centers Are Built by Natalia López Céspedes - The Shore End Is the Weak End: Securing the Cable-to-Data-Center Seam in the AI Era by José Silva Amaro - Painful Connectivity Cuts: Why Readiness Must Begin Before the Race to Repair by Olivier Côté and Gwenn Amice - The Coming Challenge of Deep-Water Cable Congestion: Using Automated Route Engineering to Forecast Future Routing Constraints in the Atlantic by Adrian Jelffs and Nick Harrington - The End of the Single-Domain Network by Bob Brumley and Alex Vaxmonsky - We Invested Billions in Subsea Cables, Yet Children Are Still Waiting: What Will It Take to Connect Africa’s Future Generation? by Aleksandra Chmielewska, Ben Roberts and Naroa Zurutuza Looking Ahead to PTC’27 A conversation with PTC CEO Brian Moon explores the conference’s relevance to the subsea community. The edition also includes an agenda preview and a guide to attending PTC’27, connecting the issue’s technology theme with the discussions shaping digital infrastructure. Celebrating 25 Years SubTel Forum looks back at the publication’s beginnings in November 2001 and the community that has grown around it. Anniversary features recognize the authors and company sponsors whose contributions have supported its work over a quarter-century. Regular Departments Cable map updates, analytics, Sustainable Subsea and cableship coverage sit alongside Permitting Pathways, Fault Lines, Legal & Regulatory Matters, Back Reflection and Advertiser’s Corner. Redesigned News Now and On the Move pages bring a refreshed presentation to industry developments and personnel news. Special Thanks to Our Issue 151 Advertisers We thank the advertisers and partners supporting this edition: Their support helps keep the magazine freely available to readers across the submarine telecommunications community. About Submarine Telecoms Forum, Inc. Submarine Telecoms Forum publishes news, analysis and reference resources for the submarine telecommunications industry. Its magazine, Almanac, Industry Report, maps and online tools help readers follow projects, explore industry developments and connect technical, commercial and policy perspectives. Read Issue 151 online. The next magazine, Issue 152, is planned for January 2027 with a Global Outlook theme. news via inbox Sign up to get the latest updates straight to your inbox!

artigo.texto: Could a data center’s waste heat warm a North Carolina town? In the Carolinas, Ohio, Texas, and many other states, Democrats routed incumbent Republicans in this month’s elections at least in part because voters fear an onslaught of AI data centers — the massive computer warehouses that threaten to suck up water supplies, increase climate and air pollution, and drive up energy costs. Voters didn’t just take their anger out on politicians. In red and blue areas alike, they also approved dozens of ballot measures pausing or restricting data centers, adding to the over 450 moratoriums already in place across the country. The backlash has left state and local leaders grappling with how to put guardrails on the facilities and ensure they benefit nearby communities. A forthcoming deal between a data center and Enfield, North Carolina — an overwhelmingly poor, majority Black town of 2,000 — could offer a groundbreaking example of what such development might look like. For years, Enfield leaders and their allies have been working toward a clean energy vision that includes a solar farm to supply residents with power, a new substation to help distribute those renewable electrons, and a thermal energy network — a shallow form of geothermal that could replace inefficient water heating, space heating, and cooling. But they’ve faced a dearth of funding and fierce policy headwinds under President Donald Trump. Then, this summer, Halifax County, where Enfield sits, announced it was selling property to Wyoming-based Quiet Data Centers, a land development firm, for a 100,000 square-foot facility. The industrial site is 2 miles outside the town but needs to tap into its wastewater systems. For Enfield Mayor Mondale Robinson, that presented a bargaining opportunity. Now, he and top officials from Quiet are negotiating a community benefits agreement, a legally binding document that ties developers to certain benchmarks. Among other commitments, Robinson wants the company to fund the entire $16.2 million clean energy plan. What’s more, he wants the data center to join the thermal energy network, which could provide a surge of excess heat to meet the whole town’s needs. If the plans come to fruition, it would be the first time in the U.S. that a data center has connected to such a system. Brendan Morris, Quiet’s chief development officer, confirmed to Canary Media that the discussions were ongoing and that all of Enfield’s aims were on the table. “I think things are possible,” he said. “We’re new to this community and new to the county. We look around and see how a new business and a new data center coming into the area can make a positive impact.” Robinson, a self-proclaimed progressive, acknowledges that the midterms were a rebuke of the tech sector’s buildout. “Everybody should be against dirty data centers,” he said. But he believes the not-in-my-backyard approach has too often stuck communities like Enfield with polluting projects rejected by wealthier areas. That’s why he wants a data center that’s built sustainably and with community input. “There’s nothing progressive about saying we are against something, without saying what we are for,” he added. A cheap, quiet option for cooling data centers A year ago, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, became the first local government in the country to sign a community benefits agreement with a data center project, according to researchers at the World Resources Institute. The agreements have long been used for other types of developments, from manufacturing plants to solar farms, said Danielle Riedl, research associate at the nonprofit. “But now, of course, the conversation — seemingly everywhere — is focused on data center development,” she said. Still, the agreements are no silver bullets. “You really want to see CBAs as one tool, together with zoning policies, development agreements, and other accountability mechanisms.” In Halifax County, Quiet has pledged to mitigate some common data center complaints. At a public meeting this summer, the company said the 88-megawatt facility will plug into the Dominion Energy grid on its own dime and pay for all the electricity it needs, according to the local news outlet RRSpin. It will run backup generators for no more than 30 minutes a month, on average, unless there is an outage. But the company also has to alleviate the immense heat generated by racks of computers inside the facility. And while Quiet has pledged to use closed-loop cooling — a less-water-intensive process than sending waste heat to cooling towers, where water then evaporates — the technology is expensive and noisy. That’s where the thermal energy network comes in. The system is essentially a network of ground-source heat pumps. They’re analogous to air-source heat pumps, but move heat between the buildings and the earth rather than the outside air, thanks to a water-based solution that flows through a system of buried pipes. Some data centers in Europe are already plugged into such systems as a way to release excess heat. The same technology could be used in Enfield, providing cooling without the noise and at less cost, said Eric Bosworth, a pioneer on utility-run thermal energy networks who runs his own consultancy called Thermal Energy Insights. “It gives a layer of resiliency, and it’s going to save them money on cooling, too,” Bosworth said, referring to Quiet. “Every [unit] of heat that they send to the network is going to be cheaper than putting it up through their chillers.” The nonprofit Enfield Energy Futures won a seed grant earlier this year to design the thermal energy network. But receiving funding from Quiet for the geothermal project — and the entire clean energy plan — would be game-changing. artigo.texto: Singapore is expanding its international carbon market network after authorizing its first carbon credit project in Rwanda and signing a new carbon trading agreement with Bangladesh. Both developments, announced at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, show how Singapore is turning its Article 6 partnerships into practical projects and new sources of climate finance. The Rwanda project is expected to reduce about 780,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) between 2026 and 2030. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters to households and early childhood centres, giving more people access to safe drinking water. Singapore also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Bangladesh to explore future carbon trading. The two countries will work toward a formal agreement that could allow Bangladesh to transfer eligible carbon credits to Singapore. These steps form part of a wider plan to build a regional carbon market hub. Singapore is also working with the World Bank and private groups to improve project funding, carbon registries, and access to buyers. Singapore Approves First Rwanda Carbon Project Under Article 6 On November 14, Singapore’s National Environment Agency (NEA) announced its first project authorization under its carbon market agreement with Rwanda. Singapore-based Climate Bridge International developed the Safe Water Supply Project. It will distribute 300,000 ceramic water filters across Rwanda, focusing on the Western Province. The filters will provide clean drinking water without the need to boil it using firewood or charcoal. This can lower fuel use, reduce emissions, and improve indoor air quality. - The project is expected to benefit around 1.8 million people and reduce about 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e from 2026 to 2030. The first 10,000 filters began distribution in June 2026, with the rest planned for 2027. This is the first project authorized under Singapore’s six operationalised Article 6 agreements. More than 20 other projects are also being assessed under its agreement with Rwanda. However, authorization does not mean that all 780,000 credits have already been issued or transferred. The project must still undergo independent checks and credit issuance. The two countries must also approve the transfer of eligible credits. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries must make a corresponding adjustment when they transfer credits internationally. This prevents both countries from counting the same emissions reduction toward their climate targets. The Singaporean official document reads: “The Singapore-Rwanda IA comprises three stages, corresponding to different stages of a carbon credit project’s development and implementation. At each stage, Singapore and Rwanda assess applications against their respective requirements. For Singapore, projects must meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria for International Carbon Credits (ICCs).” Singapore and Bangladesh Explore Carbon Trading Singapore and Bangladesh also signed an MoU on November 14 to develop carbon market cooperation under Article 6. The agreement sets the stage for talks on a legally binding implementation agreement. This would establish how both countries approve projects and transfer eligible carbon credits from Bangladesh to Singapore. The two governments also plan to share knowledge and support the growth of high-quality carbon markets. Bangladesh could gain new funding for projects that cut emissions and support sustainable development. Singapore could gain another source of international credits for companies covered by its carbon tax. Permanent Secretary Melvyn Ong remarked: “Carbon markets are a new area of partnership for Singapore and Bangladesh, and this MOU is an exciting next step in our relationship. Together, we will work towards an Implementation Agreement and enable the development of high-integrity carbon credit projects that support both countries’ climate goals.” The MoU is an early step, however. It does not yet allow Bangladesh to transfer credits for use under Singapore’s carbon tax system. That will require a formal agreement and approved projects. The deal adds to Singapore’s growing network of carbon market partners across Asia, Africa, and South America. Singapore Expands Its Article 6 Network Singapore has signed carbon market agreements with 12 countries: Papua New Guinea, Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Chile, Rwanda, Paraguay, Thailand, Mongolia, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Laos. Six agreements have been operationalized, with project application processes open for Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda, Thailand, and Mongolia. These partnerships follow Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to trade emissions reductions toward their climate goals. Singapore’s rules also include safeguards. Five percent of proceeds from authorised credits must support climate adaptation in host countries or the UN Adaptation Fund. In addition, 2% of authorised credits must be cancelled at issuance to help reduce global emissions. These rules aim to ensure that carbon trading supports wider climate action, rather than simply moving credits between countries. The two partners signed a 2027–2029 activity plan under the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme at COP31. - The plan will focus on three areas: carbon market systems, project funding, and technical support. It will help countries develop carbon registries and digital systems to track and verify emissions reductions. artigo.texto: The Anutin government last Thursday discussed with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to expand its data centers in Thailand, according to local publication Banmuang. The Thai government also outlined plans for a data center one-stop service, faster investment approvals, clean energy procurement and workforce development. This came following Thailand’s tightening of data center rules to chart a sustainable growth path for its booming data center industry. To support the growth of data centers, AWS affirmed its commitment to clean energy, including direct PPA and air cooling technology. The tech giant has previously pledged to invest more than US$ 5 billion over 15 years in Thailand. The first phase of the data center project worth more than 24,800 million baht and the AWS Asia Pacific (Thailand) Region have been previously launched. At the same time, AWS continues to develop the skills of the Thai digital workforce through partnerships with universities and educational institutions. The proposed Data Center One Stop Service seeks to promote the Board of Investment’s Thailand Fast Pass Service measures while at the same time reducing the approval and permitting processes in order to create a conducive environment for investment. Besides Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnwirakul, executives of the Board of Investment (BOI) and the Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC) were also present at the discussion.

artigo.texto: St. Cloud moves closer to data center moratorium Following a lengthy and, at times, heated debate, city leaders in St. Cloud failed to pass the data center policy and ordinance changes they had in front of them. It did approve moving forward more discussion, including setting a public hearing for Dec 21, surrounding placing a one-year moratorium on data centers. Still, some council members expressed concerns with the negative impact a moratorium would have on the city’s economic growth. The changes would have created a policy statement about data centers — which would have included how data centers would benefit the city and the importance of carefully considering projects to address community concerns — and ordinances to address several factors of any future projects. City staff said there are no proposed data centers in the city; this was just an effort to be prepared for future proposals, pointing to the city’s infrastructure, resources and desire to grow the city’s tax base as reasons data centers could be an important aspect of the city’s future. The policy statement would have also stressed the need to carefully consider all projects to “avoid projects with an unreasonable detrimental effect on surrounding properties and the environment.” The ordinance changes would have required developers to share how much energy and water they expect to use, where data centers can operate — including larger hyper-scale data centers being at least a quarter mile from homes — and the need for projects to have council support. In what was at times a convoluted meeting with council members trying to navigate proposed amendments and changes to the items in front of them, the council did not move forward with both the policy statement and ordinance changes. Many community members pushed back during the public hearing — most stressing the potential harmful impacts to the environment. Ahead of the meeting, some protested with signs outside city hall, including Sue Hanley, who’s called St. Cloud home for a year and a half with no plans to move. “What do they bring to the table? We know the resources they need, absolutely: energy, water, all kinds of things that are going to be taken from our community. What do we get in return for that sacrifice?” Hanley told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS. Another big issue people have is with the tax breaks and subsidies that have been offered to data center projects across the state. We pressed the city, mayor and all city council members on whether the city has offered tax breaks and subsidies to data center developers or if it plans to do so in the future. Only the city administrator wrote back to us, sharing, “No, the City has not given any tax breaks or subsidies to any data centers.”

artigo.texto: 16 November 2026 Thailand Carbon Markets Club Joins Carbon Market Partners in ASEAN to Renew Memorandum of Collaboration at COP31 in Turkey On November 12, 2026, the signatories to the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), comprising Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), the Malaysia Carbon Market Association (MCMA), the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), the Indonesia Carbon Trade Association (IDCTA), and the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets (AACM), signed a renewal of their Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) for a further two years at COP31 in Türkiye. The renewal reaffirmed their shared commitment to regional cooperation and to developing high-integrity, interoperable carbon markets across ASEAN. As part of the renewal, Aboitiz Foundation, Inc. from the Philippines formally joined the ACCF and signed the MoC as an observer. Its participation broadens regional representation in the ACCF and reflects growing interest among ASEAN member states in linking national carbon market development with regional coordination. The renewal also marks progress in aligning approaches on the demand side. AACM and CMC joined IDCTA, SSFA, and MCMA in supporting the Shared Principles under the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a government-led initiative co-chaired by Kenya, Singapore, and the United Kingdom. Launched in November 2025 at the COP30 Business and Finance Forum, the Shared Principles set out six pillars for the credible corporate use of carbon credits alongside deep decarbonization. With all five signatories now supporting the Shared Principles, the ACCF will explore ways to contribute to and advise global initiatives, including those led by the Coalition, so that carbon market development reflects ASEAN’s circumstances. Under SSFA’s chairmanship, which began in the second half of 2026, the ACCF established five priorities for its 2026–2028 strategy. - Bring the ACCF’s work into formal ASEAN processes. - Broaden the signatory base to ensure wider and more balanced regional representation. - Bring ASEAN carbon markets into closer alignment with global standards. - Coordinate with the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and contribute ASEAN perspectives to its work. - Establish an ASEAN Community of Practice (CoP) as a structured platform for sharing knowledge and consulting on longer-term ACCF projects. The ACCF’s work covers three main areas. - Supply and demand - Develop interim guidance for companies on using high-integrity carbon credits to support demand. Build capacity among financiers through a preliminary due diligence framework for assessing key criteria for carbon project financing. - Market infrastructure - Examine the legal nature and status of verified carbon credits and explore ways to reduce cross-border barriers, better align market rules, and enable the use of credits interchangeably across ASEAN carbon markets. - Capacity building - Work with international partners to provide technical and advisory support for carbon project financing and bring the ACCF’s work to ASEAN forums. Since its establishment at COP29 in November 2024, with MCMA serving as chair for the first 18 months, the ACCF has gained wider regional recognition. It was acknowledged in the Joint Media Statement of the 57th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and the ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP30. It was also cited in the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum’s Guidance for an ASEAN Voluntary Carbon Market. Over the past year, the ACCF has supported national and independent carbon standards aligned with benchmarks set by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), helping strengthen the integrity and market acceptance of ASEAN carbon credits. Under its renewed strategy, the ACCF will prioritize putting its work plans into practice alongside policy alignment and capacity building. These efforts aim to strengthen confidence in ASEAN-origin carbon credits, facilitate cross-border cooperation, and support the region’s climate objectives. Mrs. Gloyta Nathalang, Senior Executive Vice President, Sustainability Management and Corporate Communications, Bangchak Corporation Public Company Limited, and Chair of Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC), said, “ASEAN’s strength lies in its diversity. Through these efforts, we hope to help channel financing toward high-quality projects that deliver measurable emissions reductions and benefits for local communities.” Ms. Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF Co-Chair, Co-Lead of SSFA’s Carbon Markets Workstream, and CEO of Climate Impact X, said, “This renewal marks the next phase for the ACCF. artigo.texto: Arrests and scuffles with police. Shouts of “shame.” Litigation, petitions and public comment sessions stretching past midnight. This is how Coloradans are reacting to the arrival of large-scale data centers in the Centennial State. Smaller data centers have operated in Colorado for years, tucked into unassuming office parks and downtown skyscrapers. But a new era of hyperscale data centers made for the age of artificial intelligence has begun in Colorado and — despite near-universal pushback in the communities where they are planned — more developments are underway as governments and regulators struggle to keep up. “This has moved so fast, the data center demand is so incredibly strong and powerful that it’s really caught local governments like us off-guard,” Aurora mayor Mike Coffman said. “There’s a feeling of vulnerability right now. It came so fast, so hard, it’s forced me to push back – and I’m pretty pro-business.” Four large data centers are in the planning phases or under construction in Colorado, several of which are competing to become the state’s largest. Combined, their max power needs could equal those of more than 819,000 homes — or 16 times the amount of power used by Denver International Airport. The development comes despite a patchwork of regulations, moratoriums and local opposition that has slowed — though not stopped — industry growth. In Aurora, plans for a 500-megawatt facility next to a neighborhood are moving forward, despite the mayor’s pledge to stop it at all costs. If built, the facility’s power needs could outstrip the city’s entire residential use. In Weld County, a successful petition drive sought to stop an artificial intelligence data center planned there, but it’s unclear whether a ballot measure could halt the project. In Colorado Springs, the City Council voted to put off a vote on a data center until the spring, but the developer said he plans to continue working on the project in the interim. If built, the data center would be the largest power user in the city, by far. There is no standard definition of “hyperscale” data centers, but the term is generally used to describe large facilities that use lots of power and often the computing power needed for artificial intelligence. The Colorado utility regulators writing new rules for large electrical loads (like data centers) are looking at facilities that draw at least 50 megawatts, though they are considering lowering that threshold to 20 megawatts for new customers. A megawatt of power can power approximately 1,100 homes, according to Xcel Energy. Local governments remain the primary regulators of data centers big and small in Colorado. The state lacks broad regulation of the industry, prompting city councils and county commissions of a variety of political persuasions to pass their own rules or enact moratoriums. Larimer County is seeking public comment on a proposed ban on hyperscale data centers, defined as any facility that would draw more than 30 megawatts of power. Brighton in late October enacted a moratorium weeks after residents learned of a 2.5 million-square-foot data center proposed for the Adams County town. The company later withdrew its application. Denver, Arvada, Commerce City, Pagosa Springs, Boulder County and Jefferson County are some of the more than one dozen local governments that enacted a temporary moratorium on data center development. The topic has drawn the attention of governor-elect Phil Weiser, who said at an event in October that his first legislative priority would be a bill to “put guardrails on data centers,” though he did not support an all-out ban. “Communities need to be listened to,” he said. “These data centers shouldn’t be shoved down the throat of communities.” Opposition to data centers is not always about the specifics of a project, said Jason Green, whose company Raeden is building a 50-megawatt facility in Colorado Springs. Instead, developers feel like they are defending against the broad swell of growing hostility against the industry — and the artificial intelligence technology it fuels — as a whole. “There isn’t a data center project in the U.S. that in some form isn’t caught up in the referendum of data centers,” said Green, who has worked in the data center industry for more than 25 years. That broader conversation is also playing out in discussions about potential statewide legislation regulating the industry, said state Sen. Cathy Kipp, who sponsored a failed bill in the last legislative session to regulate data centers. The issue is not about left or right politics, she said, but about regular people bearing the costs to their quality of life from projects that make huge amounts of profit for wealthy companies. “People see these very wealthy companies coming in, building whatever they want, taking our precious resources and people are saying, ‘Why should we support this?'” she said. “It’s no longer left or right, it’s up and down.” Data center capital of the state? When Amy Wiles bought her home in Aurora in 2020, the realtor told her that the open fields abutting her neighborhood would eventually become a small, walkable cluster of shops and restaurants on the eastern edge of Colorado’s third-largest city. Wiles never got her neighborhood coffee shop. Instead, the land became home to the state’s largest data center. And Wiles, now a city councilmember, has found herself deeply embroiled in the debate about how local communities should regulate the booming, unpopular industry. The ward she represents sprawls across the city’s northeast corner and has a lot of attributes data center developers value: large parcels of undeveloped land, relatively easy access to power and water resources, proximity to an urban core and — an increasing rarity on the Front Range — a lack of a moratorium against data center development. artigo.texto: Battery storage: avoid auto sector mistakes The Express Tribune • • 1 min read The Express Tribune published an argument on November 15 that Pakistan should approach battery-storage investment cautiously, rather than repeat the protected assembly model seen in automobiles and mobile phones. The article says producing battery cells requires significant capital, specialised skills and technology, and notes that China held more than 80% of global manufacturing capacity and cell production in 2025. It proposes starting with assembly using imported cells while building local capabilities, but cautions that falling prices, changing technology and the National Tariff Policy 2025-30 could undermine reliance on tariff protection. It argues that investment should be judged by domestic value addition, technology transfer, productivity and eventual exports. At a glance - Pakistan imported 4.57 GWh of lithium battery capacity worth $274 million in early 2026. - The article favours assembly with imported cells alongside gradual development of local capabilities. - It warns that tariff changes and falling battery prices could challenge protected assembly. artigo.texto: 13/11/2026 A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. Fonte: Agência Infra

artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms LS ELECTRIC to Supply Switchgear for US AI Data Center Expansion Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Key PointsLS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data… View more - LS ELECTRIC's new $93.83 million contract is a follow-on order from an existing data center customer. - Repeat awards hinge on meeting hyperscale delivery schedules across its Korea and US production sites. - LS ELECTRIC is also developing DC distribution systems at its Cheonan facility for future AI data centers. LS ELECTRIC announced on November 16, 2026, that it had signed a power-system supply contract worth approximately $93.83 million (KRW 130 billion) for a global big-tech company’s U.S. hyperscale AI data center project. The contract covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear and low-voltage switchgear, which will be supplied sequentially for the data center’s power network. The high-voltage equipment distributes incoming electricity to individual facilities and protects equipment when power abnormalities occur. LS ELECTRIC participated in the customer’s large local data-center project from its initial construction phase. The new contract continues its high-voltage switchgear awards into the expansion phase, making it a follow-on order from an existing customer and directly connecting the supplier’s role to the project’s continued buildout. Delivery Capacity Underpins the Expansion Order LS ELECTRIC identifies time to power—the interval before a data center receives electricity and can begin operating—as a central competitive concern in AI infrastructure. It attributes its repeat awards to meeting the customer’s quality requirements and hyperscale delivery schedules from the project’s early stages. Its named production bases are the Cheongju smart factory in South Korea, LS ELECTRIC Utah and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. The company presents that footprint as the foundation of its delivery competitiveness. For this expansion order, the delivery requirement has a concrete operational dimension: the equipment contract depends on industrial capacity and scheduling as well as product specifications. Recent Contracts Span the Power System A separate October 2026 announcement disclosed a KRW 168.9 billion ($125.23 million) long-term agreement with another U.S. big-tech company covering 2027–2028. The announced amount represents products scheduled for delivery in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business remains subject to further discussions. That agreement covers 38 kV high-voltage switchgear. Possible additional supplies of low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers and ring main units remain under discussion, creating a potential broader equipment package around the committed deliveries. LS ELECTRIC announced on October 1, 2026 a KRW 181.2 billion ($133.41 million) contract for 345 kV extra-high-voltage transformers. Deliveries are scheduled in phases to nine substations through 2030 for a North American hyperscale AI data center project. Read together, the company’s records describe work across both data-center distribution equipment and the higher-voltage infrastructure required to power large AI projects. AC Business and DC Development Beyond conventional alternating-current (AC) distribution, LS ELECTRIC is pursuing next-generation direct-current (DC) systems for AI data centers. It describes its Cheonan DC Factory as the first manufacturing site to commercialize DC distribution. Solid-state transformers, solid-state circuit breakers and energy-storage systems are used there to test next-generation grids and data-center environments. The contract highlights the commercial connection between power delivery and AI compute: new capacity cannot be energized until electrical equipment is in place. LS ELECTRIC’s repeat role ties its switchgear business to that schedule, while the Cheonan test site provides a route into future DC designs as hyperscale projects expand and their power architecture evolves.

artigo.texto: Ormat Technologies, Inc. (NYSE:ORA) ranked seventh in our recently published list of the 10 Best Renewable & Clean Energy Stocks To Buy According to Analysts. Clean energy has returned to investors' attention as a Democratic Congress raises expectations that federal green subsidies and tax credits will receive stronger protection and that project approvals could move faster. Reuters reported renewed interest in solar manufacturers, residential installers, and equipment suppliers following the election. The policy outlook matters because developers commit capital well before a power plant starts generating revenue. Greater confidence in the incentives available when a project is completed can make it easier to finance construction, place equipment orders, and secure customers for its electricity. New Storage Projects Lift Revenue Ormat combines geothermal power generation with an expanding battery-storage business. Geothermal plants can supply electricity around the clock, making them useful to customers seeking dependable renewable power. Batteries add a different source of revenue by shifting electricity between periods of low and high demand. Our discussion of Ormat's stable cash flows and growing storage business examines how that combination supports its development plans. Storage drove much of the improvement in the third quarter of 2026. Segment revenue increased 145% year over year to $49.9 million as new facilities entered service and market conditions supported existing assets. Net income attributable to shareholders rose 32% to $31.9 million. The results demonstrate how incremental storage capacity can contribute to earnings, although favorable wholesale electricity prices also helped the comparison. Contracts Add Revenue Visibility Contract structure matters when judging how much of that growth can recur. Ormat's planned 100-megawatt Denali battery has a 20-year tolling agreement that gives the customer access to capacity and provides greater revenue visibility for Ormat. Projects earning more of their income from wholesale markets face a different risk profile because charging and discharging margins fluctuate. The balance between contracted payments and market revenue will influence how predictable the storage business becomes as it grows. Geothermal Expansion and Analyst Sentiment Geothermal development provides another opportunity. Ormat identified potential for 5 to 6 gigawatts of enhanced geothermal capacity on its land, while commercial terms and drilling at Dixie Valley remained to be established. That resource potential requires successful development before it contributes to cash flow. Morgan Stanley initiated coverage at Overweight with a $123 target, highlighting cash generation from the existing fleet. The same median target implies 32.29% upside in our screen. With 32 Q2 hedge fund holders, investors have an established operating business from which to assess the expansion. artigo.texto: Superando desafios e abraçando o superciclo de investimentos em data centers. Segundo Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, os data centers em todo o mundo estão apresentando um forte crescimento. Este também é o momento em que o mercado está entrando em um super ciclo de investimentos. O rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial ( IA ), da computação em nuvem e da economia digital está transformando os centros de dados, de meras infraestruturas de armazenamento em plataformas essenciais para a economia digital. À medida que a IA se desenvolve, a demanda por poder computacional, armazenamento, conectividade e processamento de dados aumenta, exigindo que a infraestrutura dos centros de dados seja moderna, flexível e escalável. Em seu discurso no recente seminário "Data Centers no Vietnã: Infraestrutura Estratégica para a Era da IA", organizado pelo jornal Industry and Trade Newspaper, o Sr. Ha Dang Son, Presidente do Centro de Pesquisa em Energia e Crescimento Verde, afirmou que a tendência de transformação digital e a revolução digital são necessidades urgentes para o Vietnã e a região no período vindouro. Segundo pesquisadores do mundo todo, o mercado de data centers e serviços relacionados à digitalização e inteligência artificial na região Ásia-Pacífico representa atualmente cerca de 34% da demanda global, sendo que a ASEAN sozinha responde por aproximadamente metade desse valor. A tendência de digitalização e desenvolvimento de data centers já está presente em países vizinhos como Singapura , Tailândia e Malásia. No entanto, o Vietnã é considerado um dos países de crescimento mais rápido da região. “Isso também representa um desafio significativo para o investimento em infraestrutura e a preparação de serviços relacionados para garantir o desenvolvimento. Os investimentos em data centers devem assegurar sustentabilidade e competitividade com outros países da região”, afirmou Ha Dang Son. O Sr. Ha Dang Son analisou que, com o aumento da densidade e da eficiência dos centros de dados, a densidade energética por rack disparou em comparação com o passado, chegando a ser de 3 a 4 vezes maior. Para modelos específicos, o nível é ainda mais alto (podendo atingir 1 MW para uma única unidade de gerenciamento de dados). "Isso levanta a questão de como ainda podemos criar centros de dados altamente eficientes, garantindo simultaneamente um fornecimento de energia sustentável que esteja alinhado com a tendência verde emergente", afirmou o Sr. Son. Além disso, o sistema de refrigeração (que representa aproximadamente 20-30% do consumo de energia) também precisa ser otimizado. Este é um problema relacionado ao planejamento e à seleção dos padrões mais adequados às características específicas do Vietnã, visto que cada país terá características diferentes dependendo da localização do data center. Do ponto de vista de uma unidade de investimento e operação de data centers, o Sr. Nguyen Tien Long, Diretor Adjunto de Negócios da FPT International Telecommunications Co., Ltd. (FTI), uma subsidiária da FPT Telecom, identificou três tendências em mudança nos sistemas de data center que atendem à IA. Você também pode gostar Em primeiro lugar, a eficiência energética por unidade de área, bem como por utilização de racks, aumentou significativamente nos últimos tempos. Em segundo lugar, o investimento em sistemas de refrigeração é necessário para atender às demandas de sistemas de computação de alto desempenho. O Sr. Long explicou que estávamos acostumados com data centers tradicionais que utilizavam sistemas de refrigeração a ar. No entanto, para data centers de alta densidade, precisamos migrar para um novo sistema chamado Refrigeração Líquida. Em terceiro lugar, esses sistemas exigem velocidades de conexão muito altas. Antes, nos conectávamos a 1G, 10G ou até mesmo 100G, mas agora precisamos de conexões de 800G ou 1 Terabit. Segundo o Sr. Long, os atuais centros de dados do Vietnã utilizam principalmente refrigeração a ar. Portanto, o desafio é a modernização para um novo sistema de refrigeração líquida, bem como a atualização de outros componentes dentro do centro de dados. Isso apresenta desafios técnicos significativos e exige um cronograma de implementação rigoroso para atender às demandas dos clientes e do mercado. 60% dos novos centros de dados serão destinados a aplicações de IA. A respeito desse assunto, o Sr. Do Thanh Thang, Diretor de Otimização de Operações para o Leste Asiático da Schneider Electric, afirmou o forte desenvolvimento de data centers em todo o mundo. Segundo o Sr. Thang, estamos em um superciclo de investimentos em data centers. O relatório mais recente da JLL, do início de 2026, indica que o mundo deverá adicionar aproximadamente 100 GW de data centers globalmente entre agora e 2030, o que representa uma duplicação da capacidade. Desse total, 60% dos novos data centers atenderão aplicações de IA. “Em países vizinhos, já surgiram grandes data centers (também conhecidos como fábricas de IA). Essas fábricas de IA são projetadas especificamente para atender a todas as necessidades ao longo do ciclo de vida da aplicação de IA, desde o treinamento e o refinamento até a consulta e a inferência”, explicou o Sr. Thang. Como parceira global em tecnologia de energia, a Schneider Electric observa um forte impacto dessa onda de investimentos nas necessidades de fornecimento de energia, sistemas de refrigeração e gerenciamento de energia para data centers. Você também pode gostar O Sr. Do Thanh Thang salientou que a densidade de potência normal atual ronda os 5 a 10 kW por rack, mas que será muito superior no futuro. Os fabricantes já estão mesmo a considerar um cenário de 1 MW por rack. Além disso, os centros de dados de IA operam de maneira muito diferente dos centros de dados convencionais. Por exemplo, o treinamento de IA exige a mobilização de um número muito grande de chips de GPU, às vezes milhares funcionando simultanea

artigo.texto: St. Cloud is latest Minnesota city to consider new rules for data centers Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read St. Cloud officials will hear from residents Monday night about possible new restrictions for data centers. St. Cloud hasn't yet received any proposals from developers who want to build a large data center, as other Minnesota communities have, but the City Council is considering adopting an ordinance so it's prepared for any future requests. The proposed rules would separate smaller data centers from hyperscale facilities — those with at least 2,000 computer servers housed in buildings larger than 10,000 square feet, or that use at least 50 megawatts of electricity. Under the ordinance, hyperscale data centers could only be located in the city's industrial district, at least a quarter mile from residential areas, and would require a conditional use permit. They must be connected to the city’s water system. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Data center developers also would have to study noise, vibration, environmental and community impacts. They would also be required to incorporate sustainability measures, including water conservation and renewable energy. After Monday’s public hearing, the council could vote on the ordinance or postpone action. Why Minnesota is attracting data centers Tech companies are eyeing Minnesota for data centers because of its relatively cool climate and available land, water and electricity. More than a dozen large projects have been proposed around the state. Meta is already building a hyperscale data center in Rosemount. Google plans to build massive data center campuses in Hermantown and Pine Island, although environmental groups are fighting those projects in court. Many Minnesotans have raised concerns about the impacts of a mega-sized facilities, including noise and light pollution, water and energy use. Proponents say they will bring construction jobs, property tax revenue and other economic benefits. Some of St. Cloud’s neighboring cities, including Waite Park and St. Joseph, have passed one-year moratoriums on new data centers. Others, including Sartell, have adopted similar regulations. Monticello, a city about 25 miles southeast of St. Cloud, adopted a data center ordinance in April. Its City Council will consider at a Nov. 30 meeting whether to allow a hyperscale project to move forward. In Minneapolis, a temporary moratorium that blocks most new data centers, with some exceptions downtown, expires Nov. 21. On Thursday, the Minneapolis City Council narrowly approved new data center regulations on a 7-6 vote, including a controversial proposal to require council approval of any new data center. The Minneapolis City Council plans to reconvene Nov. 20 to address a possible veto — one day before the moratorium ends.

artigo.texto: Maharashtra’s emissions trading scheme is being presented as a way to make industrial pollution control financially meaningful rather than relying only on penalties and restrictions. Announced at an Impact Assembly in Mumbai organised by The Earthshot Prize, the proposed expansion will initially cover Maharashtra before being extended to Rajasthan, according to a report by Loksatta – Mumbai. The initiative is expected by its proponents to help improve air quality for about 21 crore people across the two states. The central idea is to place an overall limit on the pollution that participating factories can emit and allow permits linked to unused pollution capacity to be traded. A factory that emits less than its permitted level could sell its surplus allowance to another industrial unit. In theory, this creates two simultaneous pressures: cleaner factories can gain financially, while factories that continue to emit more face a higher economic cost. That design changes the logic of industrial regulation. Conventional enforcement generally focuses on setting standards, inspecting facilities and penalising violations. An emissions market adds a price signal to those requirements. The purpose is not to make pollution acceptable, but to make pollution reduction financially valuable and continued high emissions financially burdensome. Whether that shift produces cleaner air will depend on how the cap is set, how emissions are measured and how consistently the system is enforced. The supplied announcement does not provide those operational details. The model is based on Gujarat’s experience, which the report describes as a successful experiment and as the world’s first system to establish an economic trading mechanism around industrial pollution. Under the model, factories receive an overall pollution limit. Units that remain below their limits can trade their unused permissions, while units that exceed their own reduction capacity can bear the cost of acquiring additional permissions. The arrangement is intended to reward investment in pollution-control equipment and production systems. A factory that reduces particulate emissions could potentially create a tradable surplus, giving it a financial return in addition to the environmental benefit. The incentive is therefore different from a rule that simply requires every unit to install the same equipment or meet the same reduction pathway. It attempts to direct reductions towards facilities that can achieve them more efficiently, although the source material does not specify how the Maharashtra programme will identify those facilities. Particulate matter is the immediate pollution concern identified in the announcement. Fine particles released by industrial activity contribute to deteriorating air quality, and industrial development can intensify that problem when emissions controls do not keep pace with production. The Maharashtra proposal thus links industrial policy with urban and regional public health. The impact will not be confined to factory premises: emissions move through the air sheds in which workers, nearby communities and urban residents live. This is particularly important for a state with large industrial and urban regions, but the announcement does not identify the districts, industrial clusters or categories of factories that will enter the first phase. It also does not state the number of facilities to be covered, the initial emissions cap, the particulate pollutants to be traded or the date on which trading will begin. Those details are not peripheral. They will determine whether the scheme operates as a meaningful reduction programme or merely as a compliance mechanism with limited effect on actual air quality. The institutional arrangement announced so far places the Emissions Market Accelerator in a supporting role. The organisation will assist with expanding the Gujarat model to Maharashtra and later Rajasthan. The report does not identify the precise responsibilities of the Maharashtra government, the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board or other regulatory bodies in administering the market. It also does not specify who will issue allowances, verify factory emissions, maintain the trading platform or impose consequences for inaccurate reporting. Those administrative functions are central to the credibility of any pollution market. A tradable allowance has value only when the underlying emissions data are reliable and when the total quantity of allowances is controlled. If a factory’s emissions are under-measured, its apparent compliance may not reflect its actual pollution. If the overall cap is too generous, trading can continue without delivering a significant reduction. If enforcement is inconsistent, firms that invest in cleaner technology may not receive the expected economic advantage. The announcement’s reference to approximately 21 crore people is a measure of the proposed geographic reach rather than evidence of an achieved health outcome. That figure combines the populations of Maharashtra and Rajasthan as the scheme is expanded. The supplied material does not include baseline air-quality data, projected particulate reductions, health indicators or an implementation timetable. It therefore establishes the scale of the policy ambition, but not yet its measurable environmental performance. The sequencing is also significant. Maharashtra is to receive the first phase of the expansion, followed by Rajasthan. This suggests that the programme will be adapted across states rather than introduced simultaneously. However, the report does not explain whether both states will use the same emissions limits, monitoring standards or trading rules. Differences in industrial composition, regulatory capacity and pollution sources could affect how the model works in each jurisdiction. artigo.texto: ANOTHER TOWN may be taking the first steps toward its own comprehensive data center bylaw amid a wider trend of towns adopting effective prohibitions on large-scale data center facilities. The Tewksbury Select Board has an item on its agenda Tuesday for a discussion on a data center bylaw with little information beyond that. The agenda item comes after residents spoke during recent Select Board meetings about the desire to implement Tewksbury’s own moratorium on data centers. When resident Sandra Poole spoke during the Nov. 4 Select Board meeting, she noted that she had drafted a data center moratorium policy herself. She expressed concern that the town could find itself in a similar situation to the Hillman Street battery storage site proposal, which drew backlash from surrounding residents and ultimately fell through earlier this year after the company withdrew its application. Board members Eric Ryder and Mark Kratman both noted that they had wanted to make it through the special Town Meeting last month before taking this issue up, and suggested that the conversation starting now would allow a bylaw proposal to make it to the annual Town Meeting next spring. “I have looked at what some of our surrounding communities have done, and it is something I intend on discussing with the town manager and other board members as well to get their inputs,” Ryder said during the Nov. 4 meeting. It will take some time before we can say what form a data center ban or moratorium would take in Tewksbury, if there is a big enough desire for such a thing at all, but if the town follows the same route as other nearby communities it could be one less option for a location for large scale data centers. In its fall Town Meeting last month, Chelmsford Town Meeting representatives voted to impose a total ban on medium- and large-scale data centers, leaving room for smaller data centers already commonly in use. This Saturday, Wilmington’s special Town Meeting will consider a similar prohibition. Data centers have been around in some form since the widespread adoption of the internet, but as the demand increases for larger facilities increases in our still young artificial intelligence era, so too do the concerns about the resource draw required by these facilities, and the effects they may have on the surrounding area via pollution or persistent noise. Notably, Tewksbury already has a definition for data center in its bylaws, but it is very much behind on the times. In Tewksbury’s zoning bylaws, a data center is defined as “A physical location that stores computing machines and their related hardware equipment. It contains the computing infrastructure that IT systems require, such as servers, data storage drives, and network equipment. It is the physical facility that stores a company’s digital data.” There is no mention there of the physical footprint of the facility, its water use, energy requirements, or any of the things people have been expressing concern over when it comes to data centers in the age of AI. If there is a desire to prohibit large data centers in Tewksbury, or any community without explicit policies toward them in 2026, those factors will be the likely place to start. — Peter Currier Will another one bite the dust? AFTER DRACUT finally caved and approved MBTA Communities zoning, Wilmington remains the last community in Greater Lowell to still be out of compliance with the state law. Dracut’s decision last week followed a similar change of heart from Tewksbury last month as the number of noncompliant towns ticks down. On Saturday Wilmington will consider effectively the same zoning overlay Town Meeting has considered twice before, the only difference being that the town has had the opportunity to be hit with the consequences of noncompliance, namely through lost grant funding and the potential for the state to come in and set its own zoning. Instead of losing any say in the matter, Wilmington is going through the “paper compliance” strategy, where a zoning overlay is created in areas where there is not likely to be any new multifamily housing built in the near future. The slow capitulation of the noncompliant communities also comes after voters in Massachusetts very narrowly rejected a ballot measure to allow single-family homes to be built on lots as small as 5,000 square feet. That kind of measure wouldn’t have solved the housing crisis on its own by any means, but paired with other solutions, and cities and towns not pretending like the housing crisis is every other community’s problem but their own, it could have helped. Instead we get state mandates that anger large parts of the population and don’t actually accomplish what they set out to do because they made too big of a loophole. — Peter Currier It is TIF season in Lowell A WEEK after the Lowell City Council approved a tax increment financing agreement with Draper, TIFs are on the agenda again on Tuesday in the form of a motion by Councilor Corey Robinson and Mayor Erik Gitschier. The motion in question is a request for the City Council to freeze all decisions on TIFs and tax increment exemptions pending the creation of a sliding scale tax incentive package that incorporates community- and council-led initiatives. The reasons for this motion will certainly be made clear Tuesday night, but it comes after the Draper TIF vote had been delayed by a week due to it first appearing on the agenda on election night earlier this month, and amid complaints from local trade unions about a lack of commitment to local construction hires in the agreement. That commitment came in a separate agreement the unions of the Merrimack Valley Building and Construction Trades Council made with Wexford Science & Technology, the project developer, and construction management firm Shawmut. artigo.texto: Malásia vai monitorar conta de luz de data centers para caçar contrabando de chips de IA da Nvidia Nova legislação quer usar picos anômalos de consumo elétrico e inventário obrigatório para flagrar servidores clandestinos com GPUs sob embargo. O governo da Malásia está preparando uma ofensiva regulatória sem precedentes para frear esquemas internacionais de contrabando de semicondutores. O país asiático planeja aprovar uma nova legislação que utilizará o monitoramento detalhado do consumo de energia elétrica em data centers para identificar e rastrear aceleradores gráficos de inteligência artificial da Nvidia que entram ilegalmente ou são desviados para mercados sancionados pelos Estados Unidos, como a China. Nos últimos dois anos, a Malásia tornou-se o principal polo de expansão de infraestrutura em nuvem do Sudeste Asiático, atraindo investimentos bilionários em polos tecnológicos como o estado de Johor. Contudo, esse crescimento meteórico também abriu brechas para operações de fachada, onde empresas fantasmas importavam hardware avançado sob o pretexto de hospedar servidores locais, apenas para posteriormente reexportar os chips de forma clandestina. Declaração obrigatória de chips e telemetria elétrica Pela nova proposta legislativa articulada pelo Ministério Digital e pelas autoridades de comércio exterior malaias, todos os proprietários e operadores de data centers sediados no país serão obrigados por lei a: - Inventário rigoroso de hardware: Declarar a contagem exata, número de série e modelo específico de cada chip acelerador (GPU) importado e instalado em suas instalações. - Transparência de clientes e hyperscalers: Fornecer a identidade dos verdadeiros beneficiários e empresas proprietárias das cargas de trabalho alocadas nos racks. - Relatórios contínuos de consumo de energia: Compartilhar dados detalhados de demanda elétrica em tempo real com a concessionária nacional de energia, a Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB). O princípio básico das autoridades é cruzar o perfil de consumo elétrico registrado nas subestações com a potência térmica declarada (TDP – Thermal Design Power) dos chips instalados. Se um galpão alegar operar apenas placas de servidores modestas, mas exibir picos contínuos de centenas de quilowatts compatíveis com fazendas de superchips Nvidia Blackwell ou Hopper, fiscais poderão deflagrar operações de busca e apreensão no local. Fim da “demanda fantasma” e multas dez vezes maiores A regulamentação também ataca outro problema crítico que ameaçava desestabilizar a rede elétrica do país: a especulação energética por parte de fundos de investimento em tecnologia. Muitos desenvolvedores de data centers vinham reservando gigantescos blocos de megawatts com anos de antecedência, criando uma “demanda fantasma” que travava a expansão de indústrias locais e residências. Para acabar com essa reserva especulativa, a nova regra forçará os operadores a pagarem pela capacidade reservada na rede independentemente de ela estar sendo utilizada ou não. Além disso, a taxa de penalidade para empreendimentos cujo pico real de consumo fique muito abaixo do volume contratado (Connected Load Charge – CLC) foi multiplicada por mais de dez vezes, saltando de RM 8,50 para RM 89,64 por quilowatt. Limitações técnicas: a variação de TDP na prática Apesar da ambição do projeto, especialistas em engenharia de computação alertam para gargalos técnicos relevantes. Na prática, o consumo elétrico de um servidor de IA não é uma linha reta constante: “O cálculo de potência térmica projetada (TDP) em folhas de especificações raramente reflete a realidade operacional. Dependendo da densidade dos modelos, se o sistema está executando inferência leve ou treinamento distribuído com FP8 ou FP16, a demanda energética de uma GPU pode flutuar de 30% a 100% de sua capacidade máxima em questão de segundos”, apontam analistas do setor de infraestrutura. Sem vistorias físicas periódicas e auditorias diretas nos racks para inspecionar os números de série soldados nos silícios, estimativas puramente baseadas na conta de luz podem gerar falsos positivos ou permitir que contrabandistas refinem suas técnicas de dispersão de carga para driblar os limites de monitoramento. Ainda assim, a movimentação da Malásia envia um recado explícito a Washington e ao mercado global de tecnologia: o país não aceitará se transformar em um entreposto clandestino para desvios de tecnologia militar e comercial em meio à guerra fria dos semicondutores.
