artigo.texto: San Francisco lawmakers will have a busy, varied agenda this week as they consider legislation on issues ranging from hotel workers’ ability to sue their employers over health issues to restrictions on data centers, along with hearings on traffic safety and revitalizing Market Street. Meanwhile, commissions review surveillance policy and the state of cleanup at the former Hunters Point shipyard. El Niño, data centers, and traffic safety One of the first events on this week’s calendar is a Monday meeting of the city’s Disaster Council, chaired by Mayor Daniel Lurie and Department of Emergency Management Executive Director Mary Ellen Carroll, to review preparations for anticipated extreme weather events associated with El Niño. The meeting comes as officials consider the potential for heavier rainfall, flooding, and other weather-related disruptions from the climate pattern, and Lurie’s declaration of a city emergency last month, to expedite department response. The council includes the heads of the Police and Fire departments, Public Health, Public Works, the Port, the Municipal Transportation Agency and other city departments. A presentation for the meeting obtained by The Voice outlines the roles of different departments to coordinate preparedness, protect the city’s waterfront, drainage systems, transport, and public spaces from flooding, and generally “mitigate what we can and prepare to respond to impacts we cannot prevent.” Later that day, the Supervisors’ Land Use Committee considers items related to the interim moratorium on data centers, including a move to extend the freeze for another 10 months. The debate comes amid growing scrutiny of the potential environmental and land-use consequences of data centers, including their substantial electricity and water requirements. The committee will likely refer the extension and other items to the full board for approval on Tuesday; as an extension of emergency legislation, it will require nine votes for passage. The committee will also reopen a hearing convened by Board President Rafael Mandelman, along with colleagues Stephen Sherrill and Danny Sauter, on traffic enforcement and street safety. The hearing was originally convened in 2022, when it revealed significant deficits in enforcement, including a 97 percent decline in citations between 2014 and 2022, with less than half issued for the five violations most commonly associated with serious collisions. Subsequent meetings have found little improvement, and a 2025 Civil Grand Jury report found that police failed to prioritize traffic safety and had inadequate staffing. Health Commission reviews Hunters Point cleanup Also on Monday, the Health Commission will hear a presentation from the Department of Public Health on the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. The presentation, by Health Officer Susan Philip and other department officials, will cover remediation and restoration updates, health promotion in Bayview-Hunters Point, community outreach and regulatory oversight. The presentation includes updates on the July 2026 vegetation fire at the shipyard’s Parcel E-2 landfill, which burned an estimated two to three acres and damaged monitoring equipment and stormwater controls. The Navy subsequently repaired the damaged systems, while state regulators and the Health Department monitored the response. Full board: Strengthening the Healthy Buildings Ordinance Set for approval on first reading at Tuesday’s Board of Supervisors meeting is a Covid-era ordinance requiring hotels to follow specified cleaning and disease-prevention practices, including frequent cleaning of high-contact common areas. A proposed amendment would allow hotel employees and their unions to sue hotels for civil penalties and other remedies. The bill is sponsored by District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen, with Mandelman and colleagues Connie Chan, Shamann Walton and Jackie Fielder as cosponsors. After being held on ice at the Rules Committee since April, it was revived with amendments earlier this month. In a Nov. 14 oped in the Chronicle, Lynn S. Mohrfeld, president and CEO of the California Hotel and Lodging Association, criticized the proposal as expanding outdated pandemic-era requirements. The group has also placed ads on social media to coincide with the vote. Budget Committee: Can relocating courts jumpstart Mid-Market? On Wednesday, the supervisors’ Budget and Finance Committee will consider a bill sponsored by District 6 member Matt Dorsey and almost all his colleagues to enable “Sober Spaces” by increasing availability of public facilities such as community rooms to recovery groups at no cost, along with a fund to support such meetings when hosted by private nonprofit-owned facilities. Dorsey will also preside over a hearing on how to use city-owned assets to help revitalize Market Street. One presentation associated with the hearing explores the leveraging of courthouses for economic impact, and Dorsey has floated the idea of moving the Hall of Justice and related offices to the struggling Mid- Market area. Police Commission: Surveillance cameras Meanwhile the Police Commission will hear a briefing on on its live monitoring of surveillance cameras owned by private entities and other non-city organizations. Current city laws allow officers to access private camera feeds in emergencies involving imminent danger, certain significant public-safety events and active criminal investigations, with restrictions. They were enacted after a controversy in 2020 over the practice during the George Floyd protests. The department’s presentation reports that all requests for live monitoring from the third quarter of 2023 through the first half of 2026 were approved. During the first six months of this year, SFPD made 11 requests, involving 40 hours and 58 minutes of monitoring, and reported 10 arrests. artigo.texto: O que são mega data centers, onde estão os projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para proteger o povo e a natureza das Big Techs. A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida tecnológica que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers? São centros de dados de hiperescala que concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros, sobrecarregando as redes elétricas locais e milhões de litros de água potável. A principal diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: os data centers operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já os mega data centers são instalações computacionais de escala industrial e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs para desenvolvimento de IA. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers? Diferente de estruturas menores, os mega data centers causam danos de proporção industrial e prejudicam principalmente a população local: - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas projetos de hiperescala estão chegando em todo país: instalações maiores e com muito mais impactos. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam violações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com i

artigo.texto: SpaceX plans $50B data center campus in Cochise County COCHISE COUNTY, AZ (AZFamily) — SpaceX has announced plans to build a $50 billion data center campus in Cochise County, and several community groups are organizing to stop it. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, has created an online link for the facility that includes a rendering of the proposed campus. The data center would sit on nearly 750 acres near Willcox Playa and would be the largest in the state. Developers have changed their tactics amid opposition to data center facilities. Many now are trying to work with communities to get projects approved. SpaceX is highlighting the economic impact of the project. Residents raise concerns Tara Clayton lives in Cochise County and is the organizing director for Rural Arizona Engagement. The group fought and killed a large data center project in Pinal County over the summer. “I’ve been hearing from the community that they’re extremely concerned about the integrity of this SpaceX data center,” Clayton said. “Whether they’re telling us the absolute truth about some of these benefits that we might be receiving or the chemicals that might be involved in this facility, how it could potentially impact our water supply here locally or local wildlife, quality of life,” Clayton said. Clayton said it’s important that the county leaders listen to the community and take their opinions into account. Environmental questions Ken Gillingham, a professor of environmental and energy economics at Yale University, has been researching data centers. He said SpaceX has used diesel generators to power some of its facilities. “SpaceX has acquired a reputation for not being the most environmentally oriented of the large hyperscalers,” Gillingham said. “There are other claims that they have not been following environmental protections in a very, very serious way.” Jobs, grid upgrades and state review SpaceX said the project would create more than 5,000 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs. According to the company’s application, SpaceX would invest more than $3 billion in power grid upgrades. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said in an interview with On Your Side’s Christine Stanwood that she has concerns and that her office is taking a closer look. Mayes raised the question of “whether that would destabilize our grid in the southwest and maybe even potentially in the West.” SpaceX claims the project would reduce neighbors’ electricity bills and lower property taxes. What’s next The project still must go before the county’s Planning and Zoning Board, which will hold a hearing Dec. 9. Arizona’s Family Investigates called and emailed the Planning and Zoning department and all three members of the Board of Supervisors but has not heard back. artigo.texto: America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability. The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers. American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say. “Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions. They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh. More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark. Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption. However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid. “For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.” Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF. The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025. The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably. “We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

artigo.texto: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category. That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent. Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

artigo.texto: Proposta já está pronta no Ministério da Fazenda e, se aprovada pelo presidente, deve virar medida provisória no início de 2027. Um órgão com cerca de 150 funcionários e um colegiado de cinco diretores, com mandatos, pode passar a comandar o mercado regulado de carbono do Brasil. A proposta de criação de uma autarquia especial está pronta no governo federal e aguarda a decisão do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, segundo a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Cristina Reis, em entrevista ao UOL publicada em 10 de novembro de 2026. A expectativa é que o tema seja levado ao presidente ainda neste ano. Havendo aval, será editada uma medida provisória para criar a estrutura. Uma solução “engatilhada” para depois da COP31 Cristina Reis afirmou que o desenho do novo órgão já está concluído e que o debate deve ganhar força após a conferência do clima. A proposta está pronta. A gente está com uma solução engatilhada. Nessa volta da COP31, essa discussão vai ser mais aprofundada. Apesar disso, a secretária admite que o calendário é incerto. A proposta ainda depende de discussões dentro do governo e da palavra final da Presidência. “Tem muitas discussões a serem feitas, então é mais provável que fique para o começo do ano que vem”, disse. Como seria o novo órgão A autarquia teria um colegiado de cinco diretores, incluindo um diretor-presidente, todos com mandatos definidos. O quadro de pessoal seria de aproximadamente 150 funcionários. O órgão ficaria vinculado ao Ministério da Fazenda e teria estrutura própria para conduzir a regulamentação e a operação do mercado. Ele substituiria a Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, criada para conduzir a primeira fase de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), nome formal do mercado regulado de carbono no país. Até que a autarquia esteja efetivamente constituída, com pessoal contratado e estrutura montada, a Secretaria Extraordinária continuaria em funcionamento. A transição, portanto, evita um vazio de gestão. Quem vai pagar a conta O financiamento é o ponto ainda pendente. Inicialmente, a autarquia dependerá de recursos do Orçamento da União, o que exige definição antes da criação formal da estrutura. No futuro, o próprio mercado deve ajudar a custear a governança do sistema. Pela legislação, 15% das receitas arrecadadas por meio de leilões e outros mecanismos de cobrança poderão ser destinados à governança, o que inclui a manutenção da autarquia. Para onde vai o restante do dinheiro A mesma regra define o destino das demais receitas. Outros 75% serão direcionados ao Fundo Clima, e 10% poderão financiar projetos de interesse público, especialmente iniciativas sociais envolvendo comunidades tradicionais e povos indígenas. Para a Amazônia, esse último ponto é o que mais tende a ter efeito direto. A região concentra grande parte dos territórios indígenas e das comunidades tradicionais do país, potenciais beneficiárias dessa fatia, embora os critérios de acesso dependam da regulamentação que o novo órgão terá de conduzir. Os próximos passos O primeiro passo é a discussão da proposta com o presidente Lula, prevista para este ano. Se houver aprovação, a medida provisória que criaria a autarquia deve ser editada, na estimativa da secretária, no começo de 2027, enquanto a definição do financiamento segue em aberto. artigo.texto: CARMEL – Soon-to-be-retiring Putnam Legislator William Gouldman is concerned about energy storage systems that he said could create risk to drinking water, streams, and wetlands in the Hudson River watershed. The Putnam Valley lawmaker introduced a resolution opposing such systems. The county legislature’s Rules Committee approved it and forwarded the data to the full legislature for ratification next month. Battery energy storage systems support New York’s transition to renewable energy by storing surplus electricity for use when solar and wind power generation falls short. Several neighboring communities have already addressed the situation. Yorktown approved a townwide ban that the state is challenging. Two years ago, the Town of Carmel adopted a six-month moratorium and temporarily halted proposals for commercial solar installations. Putnam Valley has also enacted a moratorium of up to one year on such systems and wind-power projects so that its Building and Zoning Department could work with its Planning Board on regulations.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA A LS ELECTRIC fornecerá equipamentos de manobra para a expansão de um data center de IA nos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um… Ver mais - O novo contrato de US$ 93,83 milhões da LS ELECTRIC é um pedido de acompanhamento de um cliente existente de data center. - As premiações repetidas dependem do cumprimento dos cronogramas de entrega de hyperscale em suas unidades de produção na Coreia e nos EUA. - A LS ELECTRIC também está desenvolvendo sistemas de distribuição DC em sua instalação de Cheonan para futuros data centers de IA. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 16 de novembro de 2026, que havia assinado um contrato de fornecimento de sistemas de energia no valor de aproximadamente US$ 93,83 milhões (130 bilhões de KRW) para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável nos EUA de uma empresa global de tecnologia de grande porte. O contrato abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV e painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, que serão fornecidos em etapas para a rede elétrica do data center. Os equipamentos de alta tensão distribuem a eletricidade recebida às instalações individuais e protegem os equipamentos quando ocorrem anomalias no fornecimento de energia. A LS ELECTRIC participou do grande projeto de data center local do cliente desde a fase inicial de construção. O novo contrato dá continuidade às encomendas de painéis de manobra de alta tensão na fase de expansão, tornando-se um pedido subsequente de um cliente existente e vinculando diretamente a atuação da fornecedora à continuidade da construção do projeto. Capacidade de entrega sustenta o pedido de expansão A LS ELECTRIC identifica o prazo até a energização — o intervalo antes que um data center receba eletricidade e possa começar a operar — como uma preocupação competitiva central na infraestrutura de IA. A empresa atribui os pedidos recorrentes ao atendimento dos requisitos de qualidade do cliente e dos cronogramas de entrega para instalações hiperescaláveis desde as etapas iniciais do projeto. Suas bases de produção nomeadas são a fábrica inteligente de Cheongju, na Coreia do Sul, a LS ELECTRIC Utah e o Bastrop Campus, no Texas. A empresa apresenta essa presença como o alicerce de sua competitividade em entregas. Neste pedido de expansão, o requisito de entrega tem uma dimensão operacional concreta: o contrato de equipamentos depende tanto da capacidade industrial e do cronograma quanto das especificações dos produtos. Contratos recentes abrangem todo o sistema elétrico Um comunicado separado de outubro de 2026 divulgou um acordo de longo prazo no valor de 168,9 bilhões de KRW (US$ 125,23 milhões) com outra empresa de tecnologia de grande porte dos EUA, abrangendo 2027–2028. O valor anunciado corresponde aos produtos programados para entrega em 2027, enquanto a dimensão dos negócios de 2028 continua sujeita a novas discussões. Esse acordo abrange painéis de manobra de alta tensão de 38 kV. O possível fornecimento adicional de painéis de manobra de baixa tensão, transformadores de distribuição e unidades de manobra em anel continua em discussão, criando a possibilidade de um pacote de equipamentos mais amplo em torno das entregas já comprometidas. A LS ELECTRIC anunciou, em 1º de outubro de 2026, um contrato de 181,2 bilhões de KRW (US$ 133,41 milhões) para transformadores de tensão extra-alta de 345 kV. As entregas estão programadas em etapas para nove subestações até 2030, para um projeto de data center de IA hiperescalável na América do Norte. Em conjunto, os registros da empresa descrevem atividades tanto em equipamentos de distribuição para data centers quanto na infraestrutura de tensão mais alta necessária para fornecer energia a grandes projetos de IA. Negócios em corrente alternada e desenvolvimento em corrente contínua Além da distribuição convencional em corrente alternada (CA), a LS ELECTRIC está desenvolvendo sistemas de próxima geração em corrente contínua (CC) para data centers de IA. A empresa descreve sua Cheonan DC Factory como a primeira unidade fabril a comercializar a distribuição em corrente contínua. Transformadores de estado sólido, disjuntores de estado sólido e sistemas de armazenamento de energia são usados ali para testar redes elétricas de próxima geração e ambientes de data center. O contrato destaca a relação comercial entre o fornecimento de energia e a capacidade computacional de IA: não é possível energizar uma nova capacidade até que os equipamentos elétricos estejam instalados. A atuação recorrente da LS ELECTRIC vincula seu negócio de equipamentos de manobra a esse cronograma, enquanto a unidade de testes de Cheonan oferece um caminho para projetos futuros em corrente contínua, à medida que os projetos hiperescaláveis se expandem e sua arquitetura de energia evolui.

artigo.texto: SALEM — The massive, whitewashed buildings of Shetland Park loom over Salem Harbor, looking much like the cotton mills they used to be. Decades ago, with its mechanical looms and thousands of low-paid textile workers, this was probably the noisiest spot in town. Today, it’s remarkably quiet. The modern tenants — law offices, a food pantry, a medical clinic, a charter school — make good neighbors for the apartment dwellers just across Congress Street, in the low-income neighborhood known as The Point. But now Shetland Park’s owner has designs on bringing back the thrum of industry. It has proposed a small-scale data center for the complex, one that would bring the constant hum of cooling fans and the occasional roar of three big diesel generators. Many in Salem want no part of it. “There’s probably a place for data centers,” City Councilor Ty Hapworth said. “It’s probably not in a dense city like Salem.” The outcry against the Salem proposal echoes the surging nationwide resistance to giant “hyperscale” data centers. In October, public opposition halted a $4 billion project in Westfield. And in a town near Worcester, Sutton residents turned out in force last week to oppose a plan by the Kraft Group to build one of the nation’s biggest hyperscale facilities. Such massive data centers are essential for training powerful artificial intelligence systems from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Their developers are up against ferocious opposition from citizens in Massachusetts and across the country, who fear the data centers will drain local water supplies, jack up electricity rates, and generate intense noise and air pollution. The Pew Research Center estimates there are about 3,000 data centers in the United States. Most of them are relatively small — like the one that’s been sitting atop the Macy’s department store in Boston’s Downtown Crossing for nearly 30 years — and use little cooling water or electricity. We rely on them for nearly every part of our digital lives, from shopping and banking to streaming video, yet until recently, few people noticed they existed. Lately, though, anything called a “data center” draws fire, however small. In Salem, upstate New York-based Prime Group Holding, which owns the 30-acre Shetland Park, had no trouble getting a building permit in May. But in September, amid intense backlash from city residents, Salem’s zoning board of appeals canceled the permit. The about-face was driven in part by concerns that Prime Group hadn’t been entirely honest about its intentions. The company had originally proposed a much smaller facility, claiming it would be used by an unnamed “IT services company.” Only after getting the permit was the project scaled up to drugstore size, requiring three diesel generators to provide backup power instead of the single generator in the original plan. Prime Group has a less-than-transparent name for the new version, calling it a “low-latency inference point,” and insists it’s not a data center, even though it would be a roomful of computers providing artificial intelligence services to local businesses. “It did feel a bit disconcerting that they would change plans midstream and try to characterize their project as something that it clearly was not,” Salem Mayor Dominick Pangallo said. Now, the city has banned the construction of data centers, except by organizations that need them for their own use, such as hospitals or government agencies. Prime Group did not respond to requests for comment. The company has until late November to challenge the zoning board’s decision in court. Across the state line, in Concord, N.H., a similar battle is playing out. City planners are having second thoughts about an already approved plan for a small data center on vacant commercial land near Interstate 93 in East Concord. The planning board may vote later this month to halt the development. Kelly Morgan, an S&P Global analyst who tracks the data center industry, said 110 US data center projects had been canceled or delayed this year through October, with the overwhelming majority scrubbed because of citizen opposition. Most were to be large data centers, using at least 50 megawatts of electric power from the local grid. But Morgan listed the cancellation or delay of eight projects requiring 36 megawatts or less. And her list did not include the Salem and Concord data centers. “I suspect it is people hearing the word ‘data center’ and not distinguishing by size or impact, just reflexively saying, ‘No thanks,’” Morgan said. Levitate, a Bothell, Wash.-based AI infrastructure and data center company, obtained a building permit in East Concord to erect a 15-megawatt, 7,500-square-foot data facility on a parcel of undeveloped land about a quarter mile from Interstate 93. The area couldn’t be more different from Salem. There’s little nearby except trees and a few businesses, including a shipping company, a data networking contractor, and a company that repairs roads and bridges. No homes, no apartment buildings. Just trees and traffic whirring past on the interstate. During a recent visit, managers of local businesses declined to speak on the record, but expressed no concern about a possible data center in the neighborhood. One seemed mystified that anybody would object. But object they did, after Concord’s city planner ruled in June that the Levitate project was a permissible use of land zoned for industrial use. Faced with broad opposition, the board deferred final action until Nov. 18. Speaking at the hearing, Levitate chief executive Ryan Howard described the data center as “a small compact design with an intentionally low impact on public resources.” He said that local power company Unitil could deliver the needed electricity without driving up electric rates. artigo.texto: The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) has launched its second Bulk Energy Storage solicitation to procure approximately 1 GW of energy storage capacity. The solicitation is open to various eligible energy storage technologies and is part of a plan to procure 3 GW of bulk energy storage through at least three annual solicitations. The initiative is part of the state’s 2022 Energy Storage Roadmap, which aims to deploy 6 GW of energy storage by 2030. Projects supported under the programme will be required to comply with updated energy storage safety codes, including requirements for safe site selection, first responder training, and emergency response plans. NYSERDA will provide incentives through its Index Storage Credit mechanism, but payments will only begin after projects have received the necessary permits, been installed and become operational, and passed peer reviews and quality assurance inspections. NY Green Bank will also offer financing options to developers and investors to support project development. In September 2026, NYSERDA awarded contracts to eight battery storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects. Together, these projects represent 1.7 GW of new capacity and over $3.7 billion in private investment. BESS projects will add 950 MW of capacity, with durations ranging from four to eight hours while the 13 renewable energy projects will add over 719 MW of capacity and comprise solar, onshore wind, and hydropower. The projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2030.

artigo.texto: This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford SPOTSYLVANIA, Va. (7News) — Two important hearings will take place this week in Spotsylvania and Stafford counties on proposed massive data center projects. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, the Stafford County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the massive Kings Corridor data center complex on and near the Rappahannock River. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors will hold a public hearing on the Crossroad Technology Campus in the Lee Hill area. The data center applicant is requesting a special use permit in Spotsylvania County to develop a 555-acre data center campus. One property is at 3215 Eagle Drive. The other two properties have not been assigned addresses. According to the county, the properties are located on the north side of Eagle Drive (Route 736), Lee Hill School Drive (Route 635), and Mills Drive (Route 17) and lie adjacent to the CSX Railroad corridor on the west side. RELATED | Spotsylvania Planners recommend approval for 555-acre Amazon data center In September, 7News reported that the Spotsylvania County Planning Commission recommended approving a new data center campus in the Lee Hill area. The planning commission voted 4-2 to approve the Crossroads Technology Campus. The data center mega-site would sit across the street from a park, and homeowners have told 7News they’re concerned about how close it will be to their homes. Right now, the 550-acre site is filled with trees and wildlife. Much of it would be leveled for a data center campus with multiple buildings, including three substations to power the data center complex. RELATED | Spotsylvania residents push back on data centers and the county’s low data center tax Over the summer, 7News reporter Nick Minock spoke with homeowners living next to the proposed data center development. “We are worried about all sorts of things. Will it affect our home prices?” asked Trillane Burlar. “Will we be able to sleep at night with the noise? Will our children get asthma from the additional particulates in the air from the generators?” “I would really like to see a limit on how many data centers we bring here,” said Cynthia Staats. “At the bare minimum, we need to slow it down. We need to understand what the long-term impacts are to our neighborhoods, communities, water, [and] utilities.” “Not only do we love our home because it's our sanctuary and it's our place where we come to restore and revive, but we also have invested a lot of money in our home, and we would like to know that it continues to appraise,” said Sarah Burlar. “I've been looking much more into the environmental impacts, the noise problem that's going to be affecting everyone, because constant hum and noise is actually bad for our health,” said Kevin Johnson. “We wouldn't be able to sit on our decks and enjoy the peacefulness of our neighborhood with having the 24/7 light and noise pollution; that is a big, big concern of ours,” said Catherine Williams. “3,100 feet is too close.” RELATED | Stafford residents oppose massive data centers proposed near Rappahannock River Meanwhile, several Stafford County residents who live in a neighborhood on the Rappahannock River are concerned about a proposal that would place data centers and a substation near – and in some cases right next to – their homes. “I hate it,” said Arlene, who would live directly next to the data centers. “It makes me want to cry.” The data center complex, known as Kings Corridor, would cast a shadow over Arlene’s house during the day, and bright lights from the data centers would shine through her windows at night. “It makes me very sad, and I'm praying that it doesn't come about,” said Arlene. “And we should keep it farm.” The location the data center developer is eyeing is currently farmland and an agricultural area with homes and subdivisions next door. The developer is proposing four sites along Route 3, also known as Kings Highway, for massive data center complexes. Homes are right next to all four locations. The newly proposed data center alley is a short drive from Fredericksburg, King George County, and George Washington’s boyhood home in Stafford County. One of the data center locations is right across the river in Spotsylvania County. The homeowners there would have a view of an industrial site instead of a serene river with trees at Bald Eagle's nest. David lives in the house right next to Arlene’s home, and he’s concerned about data center noise. “I've had a choice [to live anywhere in] the entire country,” said David, who is a veteran and physician. “I chose here, and this is an idyllic area with a lot of nature. We've got a river here. We've got eagles. We've got wildlife. That'll all disappear.” The Parsons are concerned about their property value and the data centers impacting the water next to their homes, which run on well water, but that’s not all. “I'm just worried about the Rappahannock because it is an endangered river,” said Sharon Parsons. artigo.texto: Investing.com -- Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has told customers it will stop selling chips to data-centre operators that rent more than half of their graphics processing units (GPUs) to Chinese companies, CNBC reported on Tuesday, as Washington moves to tighten restrictions on China's access to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The chipmaker has in recent months warned buyers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act (RASA) would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, similar to its powers over physical hardware, CNBC reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia also warned that the legislation could expose both chipmakers and buyers to legal risks, the report said. The Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia had verbally told data-centre clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts. RASA passed the U.S. House of Representatives in January but has yet to clear the Senate, CNBC reported. U.S. export controls restrict Nvidia's advanced chips from being sold to China, but regulators have had limited powers to restrict access through cloud services hosted overseas. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an interim final rule on Monday aimed at preventing Chinese companies from remotely accessing AI chips, CNBC reported. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese artificial intelligence startup Moonshot AI had sought access to Nvidia chips through data centres in Europe. The Trump administration accused Moonshot in July of accessing the chips through data centres in East Asia. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia following the departure of Chief Executive Jensen Huang, amid reports of an alleged extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China, CNBC reported. Bessent suggested that other Nvidia executives should also face scrutiny over compliance with export controls. He told Fox News he wanted to know whether the company had pushed what he described as seemingly illicit sales to boost revenue and earnings.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis Downtown Council CEO calls for veto of data center ordinance MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - A new Minneapolis data center ordinance is setting up a fight between downtown business leaders and the City Council. Downtown business group pushes back Adam Duininck said he has spent the past six months trying to convince council members that some of downtown's 9 million vacant square feet could be used for data centers. He said that could help shift more of the property tax burden away from homeowners and renters. Local perspective: Duininck pointed to the Sleep Number building in downtown Minneapolis as an example he wants to repeat. The building recently sold for $235 million, which was about eight times its previous assessed value of about $30 million, and Duininck credited the AI data center inside for that increase. "We took I think 10 of the council members through the Sleep Number building behind us on a tour," said Duininck. "We want to try to make things easier for people to invest money in the city, it should be a clear process, a clear timeline," said Duininck. The backstory: Duininck said he worked with the council on some regulations, including square footage and location, but said the final approval amendment added at the end could push developers away. "I think it’s just a total non-starter," said Duininck. He said the extra council vote would add more time and risk to projects that already go through the planning commission process. "Every developer would have to plan in time and risk and do a fair amount of community engagement. That sort of thing is going to happen anyways through the planning commission. This is just another step for the city council to insert themselves in the process," said Duininck. What the new ordinance does Late last week, the City Council passed the ordinance after a full ban failed. As part of that compromise, any new data center would need council approval, could go only in existing buildings and could not be the primary use of a building. "We want to make sure that our community is protected from data centers, the impacts that it has on our planet. We want to better understand the impacts that it has on our water, and we want to have a better say on how we shape our city," said Councilmember Aurin Chowdhury, who authored the ordinance. By the numbers: The city says downtown now has eight data centers serving tech companies. City staff said many more around Minneapolis support the computing needs of existing businesses, and council members said they heard from Xcel Energy that there is interest in up to eight more downtown projects. The ordinance also bars data centers from the first or second floor, requires disclosure of energy, water and generator use, calls for a sound attenuation plan and requires a decommissioning plan if a site stops operating. Data centers larger than 50,000 square feet would also have to enter an Xcel Energy program and pay a premium for renewable energy credits, according to Chowdhury. What we don't know: FOX 9 reached out to ask whether Frey will veto the ordinance, but had not heard back. Frey must decide by Nov. 19, and the city's six-month moratorium on data centers expires Nov. 21. Duininck said there are two to three data center projects in talks downtown right now, but he said those projects could be in jeopardy if the ordinance moves forward. "It’s unfortunate and now we’ll have to figure out a way forward," said Duininck. The Source: A Minneapolis City Council press conference, Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck, property records and past FOX 9 reporting.

artigo.texto: Osaka, Japan-headquartered Kansai Electric Power is acquiring a minority interest in Prospect Power Storage, a 150-MW/600-MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) owned by Elevate Infrastructure and ArcLight Capital Partners. Elevate (a portfolio company of ArcLight) and ArcLight announced the deal on November 16. Prospect Power currently is the largest standalone BESS in commercial operation in the PJM Interconnection, the power grid operator that serves all or part of 13 states across the U.S. Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions. Prospect Power is located in Rockingham County, Virginia. The companies on Monday said the investment by Kansai is part of Elevate’s strategy “to develop and operate critical energy infrastructure at scale while attracting sophisticated long-term strategic capital.” The groups said the BESS is an important installation in an area with growing electricity demand driven by data centers, artificial intelligence, and electrification. Utility-Scale Battery Energy Storage “Prospect Power demonstrates Elevate’s ability to execute utility-scale battery storage projects from acquisition through commercial operation and deliver flexible capacity where the grid needs it most,” said Joshua Rogol, CEO of Elevate. “As electricity demand accelerates, projects like Prospect Power are increasingly important to strengthening grid reliability and supporting economic growth. We look forward to continuing to bring projects of this scale online across our portfolio.” The groups said that Kansai’s investment “further expands the group of global strategic and institutional investors partnering with Elevate and ArcLight and reinforces the ability of the platform to combine deep energy infrastructure expertise, operational execution, and long-term capital.” “Battery storage is becoming increasingly critical as energy demand grows and power markets require greater flexibility and reliability,” said Angelo Acconcia, managing partner of ArcLight. “Prospect Power demonstrates the value of bringing large-scale storage infrastructure into service in high-growth markets, and Kansai’s investment is a strong validation of both the quality of the asset and the growing need for storage as part of the nation’s power infrastructure.” “Prospect Power is a high-quality operating asset in an important U.S. power market, and we are pleased to partner with Elevate and ArcLight through this investment – our first battery storage project outside Japan,” said Takayuki Doi, executive officer of Kansai’s Global Business. “We look forward to leveraging the experience gained through Prospect Power and exploring opportunities for further collaboration in battery storage and other energy infrastructure in the United States.” Elevate brought Prospect Power into commercial operation in May of this year. The project is fully contracted under a 15-year power purchase agreement with Dominion Energy Virginia. —Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

artigo.texto: EUA restringem venda de chips de IA para data centers no Brasil Regra exige licença para exportar semicondutores avançados ao País; medida também restringe oferta de serviços de computação em nuvem. O governo dos Estados Unidos incluiu o Brasil em uma lista de cinco países que passarão a depender de licenciamento específico para adquirir determinados semicondutores avançados utilizados em inteligência artificial. A medida, anunciada hoje (16) pelo Departamento de Comércio norte-americano, também abrange Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia e estabelece tratamento diferenciado para empresas controladas por grupos sediados nos Estados Unidos. A exigência consta da regulamentação provisória Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors, identificada pelo código RIN-0694-AK50 e divulgada pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão responsável pelo controle de exportações norte-americanas. O documento estabelece que a exportação, reexportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados para os cinco países dependerá de autorização do governo dos Estados Unidos, ressalvadas as exceções previstas. Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, esses destinos apresentam risco de desvio de equipamentos superior ao considerado normal pelas autoridades norte-americanas. Trata-se de uma classificação adotada pelo governo dos EUA para justificar os novos controles, sem identificação, no documento, de operações irregulares específicas realizadas no Brasil. A medida não representa uma proibição geral de comercialização desses processadores. Os pedidos de licença serão analisados individualmente, considerando critérios de segurança nacional e política externa dos Estados Unidos. Empresas norte-americanas terão exceção à exigência A regulamentação estabelece que a nova exigência de licença baseada no país de destino não será aplicada a semicondutores destinados a empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos ou cuja controladora final tenha sede naquele país, desde que sejam cumpridas as obrigações de informação previstas pelo BIS. Isso significa que a localização dos equipamentos no Brasil não será o único critério considerado. A estrutura societária da empresa destinatária também determinará a aplicação da exigência específica de licenciamento. A exceção, porém, não representa dispensa de todas as demais regras norte-americanas de controle de exportações. Para os pedidos sujeitos à autorização, o BIS informa que considerará a eficácia dos mecanismos nacionais de controle de exportações e o grau de cooperação das autoridades do país destinatário com o governo dos Estados Unidos. O Departamento de Comércio também poderá adotar medidas adicionais contra países que, segundo sua avaliação, tolerem tentativas de contornar as restrições. Entre as possibilidades estão novas exigências de licenciamento, restrições comerciais e inclusão de empresas em listas de controle. Regra também alcança acesso remoto a data centers Além das restrições de exportação para o Brasil e os outros quatro países, a norma cria um mecanismo separado de controle sobre a utilização remota de capacidade computacional instalada em data centers. Nesse caso, o objetivo declarado pelo governo norte-americano é impedir que empresas sujeitas a restrições tenham acesso indireto a processadores avançados por meio de serviços de computação em nuvem oferecidos em outros países. O mecanismo estabelece a necessidade de licença para determinadas operações com semicondutores destinados a data centers que forneçam, direta ou indiretamente, capacidade computacional superior a 12 milhões de unidades agregadas de Total Processing Performance (TPP) a empresas sediadas, ou controladas por companhias sediadas, em Macau ou em países classificados no grupo D:5. O limite considera a capacidade disponibilizada por uma instalação individual ou por diferentes data centers conectados digitalmente. Essa exigência é distinta da nova regra de licenciamento baseada no destino dos semicondutores. Portanto, o limite de 12 milhões de TPP não constitui um teto geral de processamento para data centers brasileiros. A regulamentação também prevê obrigações de identificação dos clientes e verificação de suas estruturas de controle societário. Há uma exceção específica para sistemas comerciais de recomendação, como os empregados por plataformas de comércio eletrônico e redes sociais, vinculada ao controle de acesso remoto, e não à exigência geral de licenciamento aplicável aos cinco países. Restrição surge após sanção do ReData no Brasil A mudança na política norte-americana ocorre dois meses depois da sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (ReData), instituído pela Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026. O programa brasileiro estabelece incentivos tributários para investimentos na instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers, incluindo infraestruturas destinadas à computação em nuvem, ao processamento de alto desempenho e ao treinamento e à inferência de modelos de IA. O regime prevê benefícios para a aquisição de equipamentos destinados ao ativo imobilizado de empresas habilitadas, condicionados ao atendimento de contrapartidas estabelecidas na legislação. Entre as obrigações está a disponibilização de pelo menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados beneficiada pelo regime para o mercado interno, além do cumprimento de requisitos de sustentabilidade e investimentos em pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. A nova exigência norte-americana acrescenta uma condição de licenciamento às operações de aquisição de determinados semicondutores avançados destinados ao Brasil, independentemente dos incentivos tributários previstos na legislação brasileira. Vigência depende de publicação oficial A regulamentação também formaliza a revogação dos dispositivos da chamada AI Diffusion Rule, anunciada em janeiro de 2025, durante o governo Joe Biden. artigo.texto: Rochester City Council approves one-year pause on data centers Interim ordinance passes 5-1 after public hearing ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – The Rochester City Council approved a one-year moratorium on data centers within city limits through passage of an interim ordinance. The Monday evening vote followed a public hearing on the topic. The majority of those who spoke were in support of the measure. The council heard from 10 people. Eight supported the interim ordinance, which was prepared by Rochester’s Community Development Department. Several social and environmental issues were raised. Those opposing the move said a one-year moratorium isn’t necessary for the council to responsibly address potential data center projects. According to city leaders, there are no pending applications. “There’s a lot of questions at this table. There’s a lot of questions in the audience. And we need to know more about how it’s going to impact our community,” said Randy Schubring, Rochester City Council president. The vote was 5-1. Councilmember Shaun Palmer opposed the proposal and raised concerns over the wording of the interim ordinance. In addition to the one-year moratorium, the action authorizes a comprehensive study on best practices related to data center developments. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA* A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) pretende apresentar uma ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) para questionar o custeio do leilão de baterias, disseram fontes à Agência iNFRA. Pelas regras atuais, os encargos da contratação dos sistemas de armazenamento serão pagos apenas pelos geradores. Mesmo com o risco de um “desgaste político”, os agentes temem que o leilão marcado para dezembro ocorra com “fragilidades regulatórias”, de acordo com interlocutores. Também está previsto que empresas associadas entrem com uma ACP (Ação Civil Pública) na Justiça pedindo a suspensão do certame até a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716/2026, que compartilha os encargos com os consumidores. O objetivo, de acordo com fontes, é pressionar pela rápida tramitação do projeto no Congresso. A estratégia foi aprovada no conselho da Abeeólica há cerca de três semanas, mas foi decidido que só dariam andamento a ela após se certificarem de que o PL não seria aprovado a tempo do certame. Segundo fontes, a expectativa era que o projeto fosse debatido na reunião de líderes partidários da Câmara dos Deputados na última terça-feira (10) e votado no plenário nesta quinta-feira (12). Isso viabilizaria a apreciação no Senado na próxima semana. A matéria, no entanto, não entrou na pauta da Câmara. O leilão está previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Relatório Contribui para a percepção de risco do setor a probabilidade de que outros temas do setor sejam incluídos na matéria. Isso poderia atrasar ainda mais a aprovação do texto. A avaliação de fontes é que há margem para uma tentativa de rever pontos debatidos na MP (Medida Provisória) 1.304, transformada na Lei da Reforma do Setor Elétrico (Lei 15.269/2025). O PL está sob relatoria do deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE), próximo a pautas de agentes renováveis, mas que não são consensuais no setor e entre os parlamentares. Um dos principais temas já defendidos pelo deputado é a ampliação do ressarcimento financeiro aos geradores pelo curtailment (cortes de geração obrigatórios). Ele conseguiu aprovar uma emenda na Câmara durante a tramitação da MP 1.304, mas que foi vetada pelo presidente Lula. Outros temas que podem estar no relatório, como circula nos bastidores, são a obrigatoriedade de que projetos de hidrogênio verde contratem energia de usinas novas ou recém-construídas, além do retorno dos incentivos nos custos dos fios de transmissão para fontes renováveis. Apesar de serem pautas benéficas às eólicas, segundo fontes, a Abeeólica defende que o relatório do PL 3.716 fique livre de temas polêmicos. Isso facilitaria a aprovação de forma célere, sem colocar em risco a realização do certame na data prevista. Mudanças no edital O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, disse à imprensa que qualquer modificação legal sobre o leilão iria requerer o adiamento do certame. Segundo ele, a reguladora precisaria de prazo para ajustes no edital. No MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), no entanto, a percepção é que o edital aprovado não exige alterações caso o custeio seja estendido aos consumidores, disseram fontes. Existe ainda a possibilidade de incluir no projeto que tramita no Congresso emenda para dispensar a ANEEL do prazo necessário para modificações no edital. Contudo, há relatos de resistências a isso. Posição do governo O governo federal evitou apoio ao PL antes das eleições, pelo risco de ter atrelado a si o discurso de aumento de custos aos consumidores de energia elétrica. No entanto, técnicos do MME estariam alinhados à proposta, de acordo com fontes. O tema também foi levado à Casa Civil, que teria solicitado aos geradores um estudo comprovando que a medida não seria prejudicial aos consumidores e de que forma contribuiria para o sistema elétrico. Segundo relatos, a avaliação é que o órgão da Presidência da República estaria mais sensibilizado à pauta. *Colaboraram: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr.

artigo.texto: Samsung’s Solid-State Battery and the Shaky 64% Silver Demand Claim Key Takeaways - The 64% silver claim traces to one X post from August 2024, and its author later described the figure as "completely unverified" after Kitco, MarketWatch and Morningstar carried it. - Samsung SDI has not disclosed silver loading per cell or pack; the Ag-C layer is a five-micrometre-class coating, so a plausible range is a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack. - The claim needs 16 million vehicles, equal to four of every five EVs sold in 2025, yet Samsung targets mass production only in the second half of 2027, starting with luxury vehicles and robots. - Against the Silver Institute's 2025 data, the 16,000-tonne figure falls to about 61% of mine production and about 46% of total demand. - Silver's demand case stands without Samsung; the signals to watch are a Samsung loading disclosure, real 2027 production volumes and the pace of Toyota's 2027-2028 rollout. The most quoted number in the silver bull case right now is not a Samsung number. The claim that Samsung‘s solid-state battery could consume 64% of the world’s annual silver mine supply traces back to a single post on X in August 2024. Its author later called his own figure “completely unverified”. That admission has not slowed the figure down. Kitco, MarketWatch, Morningstar and a long tail of silver-investment sites have carried it, and each retelling made it sound more solid than the last. If you hold silver or are thinking about it, you may be pricing in a story rather than a specification. This piece separates what Samsung has disclosed from what was guessed, and gives you a method for testing the next commodity demand claim that lands in your feed. Where did the 64% silver claim come from? In August 2024, Kevin Bambrough, a retired investment professional, posted an estimate of how much silver Samsung’s planned battery might need. About ten days later, Kitco published it on 19 August 2024, and the figure began its run through financial media. His arithmetic took four steps: - Each cell might use as much as 5 g of silver. - A typical 100 kWh EV pack might hold about 200 cells, giving roughly 1 kg of silver per vehicle. - Roughly 20% of about 80 million vehicles built each year (about 16 million) might adopt the battery. - That adds up to 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. Set against a rough 25,000-tonne annual mine output, you get 64%. Use the Silver Institute’s 2025 mine production of 846.6 Moz (about 26,300 tonnes) and the figure drops to about 61%. Against total 2025 demand of 1,130.6 Moz (about 35,166 tonnes), it falls to about 46%. The viral 64% figure relies on cascading estimates, concluding that 16 million vehicles would require 16,000 tonnes of silver a year. How the caveats disappeared The original post was hedged. Bambrough said official figures were unavailable, that 5 g might be high and that the true number could be as low as 0.5 g per cell. In replies, he said he had used AI to estimate grams per cell and cells per pack, and he cited a 3-10 g range without naming its source. None of that survived the trip into headlines. By late 2025, he was pushing back on people treating it as fact: His later verdict on his own estimate: “completely unverified.” Then, in 2026, a widely circulated analysis attributed the figure to technical disclosures from Samsung SDI. No such documents have been published. The same retellings blended a 600-mile range, a 20-year life and a 9-minute charge into one battery, even though those benchmarks came from separate Samsung announcements. A headline figure that cannot be traced to a primary source is a hypothesis. You should treat it as one before it shapes any allocation decision. Readers who want the bullish framing in full can read it in our deep-dive into the solid-state battery silver thesis, which sets out the mispricing pattern commodity investors repeat. When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first What has Samsung actually disclosed about silver in its battery? Strip out the guesswork and a real technology remains. Samsung SDI describes its all-solid-state battery as anode-free, meaning the cell is built without a conventional graphite or lithium-metal anode. Instead, lithium plates onto the current collector during charging and forms the anode in place. That is where silver comes in. A thin silver-carbon (Ag-C) layer helps lithium spread evenly rather than clumping, according to Korea JoongAng Daily (1 July 2026). Reports describe it as thinner than a hair, a five-micrometre-class coating. The pouch cell matters because robot packs hold a couple of kWh, against roughly 70-75 kWh in an average EV. Silver scales with stored energy, so early robot cells would use little of it. The production timing is a company target, not a guarantee. The gaps are wider than the facts: - The silver-to-carbon ratio in the layer - Silver per cell, per kWh and per pack - Final cell size for the prismatic EV product - Whether recipes differ between pouch and prismatic formats A plausible range runs from a few hundred grams to about 1 kg per EV pack; even Bambrough’s low-end 3 g per cell gives 600 g. Because the silver sits in an interfacial layer rather than a bulk electrode, you should read 1 kg as the ceiling of that range, not the baseline. How does silver demand work, and why do adoption assumptions matter? A new use for silver only matters relative to the size of the market it enters. Mine supply is the metal dug out each year. Total demand adds industrial use, jewellery, silverware and investment buying, and the gap is filled by recycling and existing stocks. Now test the adoption assumption against those totals. The International Energy Agency (IEA) counted just over 20 million electric cars sold in 2025 (about 21 million in its Global Energy Review), roughly a quarter of new-car sales. The speculative claim of 16,000 tonnes of battery demand represents a massive share of the 846.6 Moz (~26,300 tonnes)

artigo.texto: Eight area emergency departments extinguished a Poynette garage fire just after noon on Sunday, Nov. 15. No one was injured by the blaze. According to an update from Carie Myers, public information officer for the Poynette-Dekora Fire Department, a call at 12:19 p.m. reported flames coming from a garage near Seward Street in the Village of Poynette. Fire units were enroute by 12:26 p.m. Both Poynette-Dekora EMS units were on calls at the time, so medical support was requested from Arlington EMS. “Our partners with the Poynette Police Department were first to arrive on the scene, locating the garage fire in the alley behind the residence,” wrote Myers on Facebook. “Our PPD officer immediately took action, initiating an aggressive attack on the fire with a fire extinguisher until fire resources arrived.” Crews kept the fire contained to the garage and the fire was reported under control by 12:53 p.m. Battery safety An official cause has not been determined, Myers wrote, but “preliminary information indicates the fire may have originated from an e-bike battery that was charging inside the garage.” She noted that the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has highlighted lithium-ion battery safety as part of its fire prevention education efforts, “Incidents like this serve as an important reminder of the potential dangers associated with these batteries when they are not property stored, charged or maintained,” she wrote. The NFPA advises consumers to stop using these batteries if they observe odor, a change in color, too much heat, a change in shape, leaking or odd noises. Lithium-ion batteries should not be disposed of in traditional recycling bins or they could ignite, the NFPA states. Instead, they should be taken to a safe battery recycling location, such as those listed at call2recycle.org.

artigo.texto: Residents urged to speak up as Salix weighs data center ordinances SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Community members gathered in Salix Monday evening for an informational meeting to discuss how local ordinances could shape the future of their community. This comes amid debate over a proposed Google data center. Attendees learned about data centers and asked questions about their potential local impact. Salix City Council members Gene Monk and Tim Skidmore attended the meeting. Organizers encouraged residents who want to see changes to continue speaking at City Council meetings and contacting elected leaders. “I think people need to show up. If there’s no one at the city council meeting, no one calling their numbers, they’re not going to change their minds,” said Jessica Mazour, conservation program coordinator for the Iowa Sierra Club. Woodbury County homeowner Janet Yanak said one of her biggest takeaways was the importance of getting local ordinances right. She also expressed concern about a data center’s potential impact on water and air quality. “The one thing that really did stick with me is how important it is to get these ordinances in and get them right,” Yanak said. “We really need some strict, some protective ordinances to protect not only the cities, but the citizens.” Residents were also encouraged to talk with their neighbors, write letters to the editor and contact state lawmakers about data center legislation. artigo.texto: No cumprimento de seus compromissos para enfrentar as mudanças climáticas, o Vietnã identificou o estabelecimento de um mercado de carbono como uma das principais soluções para criar incentivos à redução de emissões, promover a transição verde e atrair investimentos. No entanto, para que o mercado opere de forma eficaz, é necessário aprimorar ainda mais o arcabouço institucional, garantir a transparência dos dados de emissão e aumentar a participação das empresas. Esses temas foram debatidos por especialistas nacionais e internacionais no evento paralelo "Promovendo o Mercado de Carbono do Vietnã: Transparência, Eficiência e Cooperação Internacional", realizado no Pavilhão do Vietnã no âmbito da 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP31). Transformar a redução de emissões em um fator de incentivo ao investimento. O Sr. Bui Duc Hieu, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas ( Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente ), afirmou que o desenvolvimento de um mercado de carbono é uma das soluções importantes para o Vietnã cumprir seus compromissos nacionais de resposta às mudanças climáticas, visando emissões líquidas zero até 2050. Um mercado de carbono fornece uma ferramenta para gerenciar as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, ao mesmo tempo que incentiva as empresas a inovar em tecnologia, melhorar a eficiência energética e investir proativamente em soluções de produção de baixa emissão. Para concretizar essa direção, o Vietnã está acelerando a conclusão dos marcos institucionais e a construção da infraestrutura necessária para apoiar a operação do mercado. No período de 2025-2026, o Governo aprovou uma cota piloto total de emissões de aproximadamente 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente, alocada a 110 instalações em três setores: energia térmica, produção de ferro e aço e cimento. Todas essas indústrias apresentam altos níveis de emissão e desempenham um papel crucial na produção industrial e no desenvolvimento econômico . A fase piloto do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) deverá durar até o final de 2028, preparando o terreno para que o mercado de carbono entre em sua fase operacional oficial a partir de 2029. Essa implementação gradual visa ajudar as agências reguladoras a aprimorarem progressivamente os mecanismos de monitoramento, permitindo também que as empresas se adaptem às novas exigências de inventário, gestão e redução de emissões. Ao avaliar o progresso do desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no Vietnã, John Robert Cotton, Diretor da Parceria para a Transição Energética do Sudeste Asiático (ETP) do Escritório das Nações Unidas de Serviços para Projetos (UNOPS), observou que o Vietnã está avançando rapidamente no estabelecimento de um arcabouço legal e na implementação de um mecanismo de mercado obrigatório. Comparado a muitos países, o Vietnã está acelerando a transição da formulação de políticas para a implementação de um sistema de comércio de emissões em um ritmo notável. No entanto, um grande desafio para o Vietnã é o enorme capital de investimento necessário para a transição verde e para atingir as metas de emissões líquidas zero, que excede a capacidade do orçamento estatal. Nesse contexto, a precificação do carbono é vista como uma ferramenta econômica capaz de promover investimentos em atividades produtivas e comerciais ambientalmente sustentáveis. John Robert Cotton analisou que, em primeiro lugar, a precificação do carbono ajuda a incorporar os custos de emissão na contabilidade financeira e no balanço patrimonial de uma empresa. Em vez de simplesmente implementar medidas de redução de emissões para atender aos requisitos regulatórios, as empresas terão que calcular a eficiência econômica de cada opção de investimento, na qual a inovação tecnológica, a economia de energia e a redução de emissões se tornam fatores que impactam diretamente os custos de produção e a competitividade. Além disso, espera-se que a implementação de um mecanismo de leilão de cotas de emissão a partir de 2029 gere receitas adicionais para o orçamento do Estado. Esses recursos podem ser reinvestidos em programas de redução de emissões no setor industrial, apoiando a transformação tecnológica e aprimorando a eficiência energética. Em particular, através dos mecanismos de cooperação internacional estipulados no Artigo 6.º do Acordo de Paris, o mercado de carbono pode abrir oportunidades de acesso a financiamento internacional para projetos de redução de emissões que têm dificuldade em angariar capital através de métodos tradicionais. A capacidade de atrair esses recursos é crucial para economias em desenvolvimento como a do Vietnã, pois a transição verde exige capital a longo prazo, enquanto muitos projetos de tecnologia limpa têm altos custos iniciais de investimento e longos períodos de retorno. O estabelecimento de um mecanismo transparente de precificação de carbono pode contribuir para melhorar a eficiência financeira dos projetos e criar mais incentivos para que o setor privado participe de investimentos na redução de emissões. No entanto, para que essas oportunidades financeiras se traduzam em fluxos de capital reais, o mercado precisa de mecanismos operacionais claros, um sistema de dados confiável e uma conectividade eficaz entre empresas nacionais e investidores e parceiros internacionais. Transparência de dados para desbloquear recursos internacionais. Apesar dos avanços na criação de um arcabouço legal, especialistas acreditam que a formação de um mercado de carbono é apenas o começo. Os maiores desafios residem na capacidade de organizá-lo e operá-lo, garantir a transparência das transações, a qualidade dos créditos de carbono e a efetiva redução das emissões.
