artigo.texto: The last several days have not been good for big tech. On Thursday, Microsoft Outlook, which handles most of the business email in America, suddenly shut down. Then, on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country, apparently because of technical upgrades that went wrong. These fiber-optic faceplants happen to come at a moment when much of the country, mostly at the local level, is seeing fierce opposition to data centers, not only because of environmental concerns and energy prices but also because of real concerns that tech is becoming too big a part of our lives. In Maryland, the story of Taylor Frazier-McCollum, a community activist who helped block a $5 billion data center project planned for the site of an abandoned mall, went viral, with the left praising the power and bravery of the individual and the right mocking her alternative idea for the site: a trampoline park. In fairness, this Maryland activist does not come across as particularly adroit or searing in her insights. On the other hand, like many Americans, she understands implicitly the advantages a trampoline park or a Topgolf location can bring to her community. The benefits of a data center seem murky by comparison. This kind of attitude toward data centers has many very smart people pulling their hair out in frustration. For them, the economic and technological benefits, including beating China in the AI race, obviously far outweigh the concerns of nonexperts like Frazier-McCollum. In fact, many proponents of data centers argue that China is funding propaganda to slow our growth in the sector, even as data centers start popping up all over China like umbrella salesmen in a Manhattan rainstorm. This is true. China, the Eddie Haskell of the planet, is absolutely "giving us the business" by stoking anti-data center fervor. But it is important to remember that data centers aren’t controversial because of Chinese information operations; rather, Chinese information operations exist because data centers are controversial. FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS Up until about six months ago, data centers were not a major national news story. In fact, the place one was most likely to hear about them was local talk radio in small towns across rural America, where many people care more about who the county commissioner is than who lives at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. The concerns you hear from callers on these shows sound downright mundane compared to the fervent calls from experts to win the new space race against China and unleash the power of AI. But for many who live there, water rights and easements mean more than geopolitical fisticuffs. This is why, in a strange way, this week’s tech mishaps, which inconvenienced millions of Americans at work and at airports, present an opportunity for the tech industry to explain in more practical terms why we need so many data centers. Implicit in the pro-data center argument has been the idea, often offered with a bit of disdain, that it is absurd to oppose data centers by posting about them on devices that cannot operate without data centers. And OK, point taken, but the snark doesn’t help. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS In fact, Democrats, one could say cynically, capitalized on the anger many Americans felt at being talked down to by the big tech set, using it to great electoral advantage, especially in traditionally right-leaning rural areas. But Democrats, no matter who leads them, cannot maintain their blanket disapproval of data centers for long, as this weekend showed. It was safe enough to call for data center moratoriums in the races of 2026, but as they seek to govern, Democrats will need data centers. Let’s face it, nobody is going back to typewriters and fax machines, and nobody wants to sit in seat 24B for five hours on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS At the local level, much of the data center fuss is already working itself out through the sausage-making of politics and the courts. Some communities, like the Amish, will eschew the infrastructure projects completely and lose out on the pot of gold. But most will find a happy compromise once enough concessions are pried from developers. For now, proponents of data centers would be wise to point to events like the Outlook outage and the flight groundings, without sneering, as the very reason we need so many data centers to power the conveniences we have all grown accustomed to. artigo.texto: GCC and EXIST Sign Carbon Market Cooperation Agreement at COP31 The Global Carbon Council and Turkiye's Energy Exchange, Enerji Piyasalari Isletme A.S., known internationally as Energy Exchange Istanbul (EXIST), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to deepen cooperation on carbon market development and to examine trading of GCC-issued carbon credits in Turkiye, according to QNA. The agreement was signed at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by the GCC and the League of Arab States, during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkiye. The memorandum was signed by Dr. Yousef Alhorr, Founding Chairman of the GCC, and Taha Meli Arvas, CEO and Vice Chairman of the Board of EPIAS. The cooperation is intended to facilitate use of the GCC's internationally recognized carbon crediting program in Turkiye, open new paths for market participants to access high-integrity carbon credits, and reinforce technical capacity as the country builds its carbon market framework. Combining Standards Expertise with Market Operations The arrangement pairs the GCC's experience in carbon crediting standards, project registration and credit issuance with EPIAS's expertise in running organized energy and environmental markets. It aims to support transparent market mechanisms that connect credible emissions reduction projects with buyers and investors, while contributing to corporate climate strategies and national climate objectives. Under the memorandum, the two organizations will explore listing and trading of the GCC's Approved Carbon Credits on EPIAS trading platforms, subject to applicable regulations and market requirements. They will also examine whether the credits could be recognized under Turkiye's future compliance carbon market framework. The proposed cooperation could widen market access for project developers and buyers and encourage the registration, issuance and use of high-quality carbon credits through transparent trading processes. Capacity Building and Technical Support Beyond trading, the agreement emphasizes capacity building and knowledge exchange. The GCC and EPIAS intend to hold workshops, webinars, seminars and other activities to improve understanding of carbon market requirements among potential participants and local stakeholders. The GCC will also support access to publicly available information on its crediting program, registry and methodologies. The cooperation may draw on the expertise of the Gulf Organisation for Research and Development, the GCC's parent organization, to support market readiness and technical capacity development in Turkiye. Possible areas of support include training on greenhouse gas accounting, monitoring, reporting and verification, carbon border adjustment requirements, and sustainability disclosure under the Turkish Sustainability Reporting Standards, which are aligned with IFRS S1 and S2. The parties may also explore applying GORD digital solutions, including SustainoAI, for greenhouse gas accounting, ESG reporting and financed-emissions calculations, along with broader technical assistance on decarbonization and energy efficiency. Positions of the Signatories Dr. Alhorr commented that credible carbon markets depend on connecting high-integrity credits with transparent, well-functioning market infrastructure, and that the cooperation with EPIAS creates an opportunity to strengthen those connections in Turkiye while supporting the knowledge and institutional capacity markets need to grow responsibly. He indicated that a broader objective is to help climate projects attract investment, deliver measurable emissions reductions and contribute to sustainable economic development. Taha Meli Arvas commented that effective carbon markets require more than trading platforms, depending instead on reliable standards, transparent processes and participants with the knowledge and capacity to engage confidently. He said the cooperation with the GCC aims to explore new opportunities for carbon credit trading, strengthen technical expertise and support market development in line with Turkiye's regulatory priorities and evolving market needs. The agreement reflects a shared interest in strengthening Turkiye's carbon market ecosystem through internationally recognized standards, technical cooperation and the exchange of expertise. artigo.texto: Rwanda carbon market goes to Antalya with 29 projects on its register Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects and opened its Article 6 agreement with Singapore to renewable energy and clean cooking proposals, and at COP31 in Antalya, where Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva leads the delegation, its pavilion programme includes the launch of a carbon registry and a distributed renewable energy fund. Credits from Rwandan carbon projects have sold at between $14 and $45 a tonne and brought in about $1.5 million, the Rwanda Environment Management Authority (REMA) said in September, from a register of 29 projects running across renewable energy, electric mobility, forestry, waste management, agriculture and land conservation. Some of those projects are already selling credits and others are with external auditors for verification, according to REMA, whose Deputy Director General, Faustin Munyazikwiye, said the projects “are at different stages of development”. Rwanda became Singapore’s first East African partner under Article 6 when the two governments signed an implementation agreement on 6 May 2025, Singapore’s sixth such agreement overall, under which Singapore-based companies can use eligible Rwandan credits to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions. Singapore will put the value of 5% of the authorised credits towards adaptation in Rwanda and cancel 2% at first issuance, and the call for proposals that opened on 30 January covers renewable energy and efficiency alongside clean cooking, electric mobility, waste management and improved forest management. The joint committee overseeing the agreement, which Munyazikwiye co-chairs, met in Kigali on 16 October to speed up approvals, and the lessons from it are the subject of a session at Rwanda’s COP31 pavilion that will also launch the country’s carbon registry. At the same pavilion the Rwanda Green Fund is launching its Distributed Renewable Energy Fund, the first fund of its investment arm, the Ministry of Environment said on 10 November, alongside a biodiversity window and the Cabinet-endorsed Country Platform for Climate and Development, which coordinates national climate priorities with the investment raised for them. Household electricity access reached 85.4% by the end of 2025, with 60.1% of households on the national grid and 25.3% relying on solar, according to Rwanda Energy Group, and the government’s target is universal access by 2029. The World Bank’s Renewable Energy Fund project, which runs subsidies and loans for solar home systems through local savings and credit cooperatives, aims to connect at least 445,000 households from a $15 million subsidy window, and Franz Drees-Gross, the World Bank Group’s Regional Director for Infrastructure in Western and Central Africa, called Rwanda “a shining example for Africa of what it takes to electrify a country”, The New Times reported in October. Under its third nationally determined contribution, submitted last year, Rwanda commits to a 53% cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035, about 14.86 million tonnes, with 7% of the reduction to come from its own resources and 46% depending on external finance or technical support, against a total finance need of $12 billion to 2035. Its delegation is asking COP31 for a clear roadmap to the $300 billion a year climate finance goal agreed at COP29, and for high-integrity carbon markets under Article 6. Rwanda will also use COP31 to call for universal ratification of the Kigali Amendment, which commits countries to cut their use of climate-warming hydrofluorocarbons by 80% by 2047, after Kigali hosted the 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol from 2 November on the amendment’s tenth anniversary. Full implementation could avoid up to 0.5°C of warming by 2100, and close to 1°C with more efficient cooling, and the Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, told the Kigali meeting that “signals only matter when they are backed by clear rules”. Speaking in Kigali in October, Arakwiye said the government is studying whether “a share of the proceeds from carbon transactions can be recycled through the Rwanda Green Fund”, so that the credits Rwanda sells now pay for the feasibility studies and baseline data its next projects need before investors will look at them. artigo.texto: St Bess collects $413m in property taxes up to October Loading article... WESTERN BUREAU: Despite the widespread devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa, St Elizabeth is reporting a steady collection in property tax payments, netting $413.6 million in the first seven months of the 2026-2027 financial year. The improved revenue performance has triggered calls from councillors for a greater portion of the revenue to be channelled into community development projects, particularly in areas still recovering from the hurricane. Black River Mayor Richard Solomon, who is also the chairman of the St Elizabeth Municipal Corporation, said the $413,626,794 collected up to October 31 represents 64.2 per cent of its $644.26-million annual target. The sum collected is approximately $144.14 million short of matching the $557.76 million collected for the entire 2025-2026 financial year, with five months remaining. Deputy Mayor Donald Simpson, councillor for the Malvern Division, commended the residents for honouring their tax obligations despite the financial challenges. “I think it’s a great achievement. We really have to congratulate the citizens of the parish because, you know, people in general don’t like to be taxed,” he said. “But when you go through these sorts of circumstances and you still remember that you have to pay your property tax and you make it your duty to pay property tax, I think we really have to congratulate the citizens of St Elizabeth.” Solomon endorsed the sentiments, noting that property tax revenue is important for the efficient operation of municipal corporations and funding for local government services. He hailed the collection team for its outreach efforts, particularly the mobile collection unit, which has been visiting communities to facilitate payments. According to the corporation’s report, property tax collections for October 2026 exceeded those collected in the corresponding month last year by approximately $10.27 million. The parish’s annual property tax target was reduced by approximately $11.85 million, from $656.12 million in 2025-2026 to $644.26 million for the current financial year. Audie Myers, councillor for the Siloah Division, stressed that residents should reap tangible benefits from the funds collected. “We want to see it reflected now in the parish. It’s time for us to get something now within the parish to do something on the roads,” said Myers, declaring that residents were making sacrifices to meet their tax obligations. Everton Fisher, councillor for the Balaclava Division, suggested that the funds could be used to assist communities still struggling with the hurricane’s impact. Solomon also acknowledged the need for taxpayers to see direct benefits from improved collections. “We have to revisit the timetable and see how best we can connect this programme, so that people can realise the benefits that can be derived from the improved collection,” he said. albert.ferguson@gleanerjm.com

artigo.texto: Why Immersion Cooling Still Hasn't Gone Mainstream Immersion cooling offers clear efficiency benefits, but high upfront costs and the need to rethink data center design and operations still limit adoption. There is a great deal for data center operators to love about immersion cooling, a technique that keeps IT equipment cool by immersing it in liquid. It is highly efficient from an energy perspective. It requires no water. And because it eliminates many of the moving parts and airflow dependencies associated with traditional cooling, it can reduce certain operational risks. And yet, very few data centers are actually using immersion cooling or appear to be planning a large-scale shift to it. Other liquid cooling methods – such as direct-to-chip cooling, which circulates coolant through pipes placed adjacent to processors rather than immersing entire servers – are projected to grow rapidly. Immersion cooling, by contrast, remains a niche. That raises an obvious question: If immersion cooling is so effective and sustainable, why aren’t more data centers using it? And what technical, financial, or operational changes would the industry need to make for immersion cooling to take off? To answer that, it is worth taking a closer look at the current state of immersion cooling, the barriers holding it back, and the odds that it becomes more mainstream in the years ahead. Why Immersion Is Still a Niche Immersion cooling technology has been around for decades. As of 2026, however, it still has not become a mainstream production cooling strategy among major data center operators. Most of the headlines on immersion cooling in recent years have focused on pilots, demonstrations, and proofs of concept, such as Microsoft’s well-known experiment earlier this decade. Some of the large AI data centers under construction may be planning to deploy immersion cooling. In some respects, the technology is a natural fit for facilities designed for extremely high power densities and significant heat loads. But if large operators were preparing to embrace immersion cooling at scale, you might expect them to say so loudly. So far, few have. What’s Holding Immersion Back Why aren’t more data centers taking advantage of immersion cooling, given that it is a proven and reliable way to dissipate heat? Two factors likely explain much of the hesitation. 1. The Economics Are Hard to Ignore First, immersion cooling systems are significantly more expensive to install than most alternatives. Estimates vary, but immersion generally carries materially higher upfront costs than direct-to-chip cooling and vastly higher capital costs than conventional evaporative or air-based approaches. According to one study, it costs about $1 million per MW of IT load to implement an immersion cooling system, compared to $650,000 using direct-to-chip. From a CapEx standpoint, it is hard to make immersion look attractive, especially for operators under pressure to bring new capacity online quickly and cost-effectively. To be sure, immersion cooling can deliver savings over time through lower operating costs. It can reduce energy required for cooling, improve thermal efficiency, and shrink the physical footprint needed to support a given amount of compute. Adam Silva Consulting estimates that “cooling a 64-rack AI cluster over 10 years costs $42M with advanced air, $31M with direct-to-chip liquid, and $28M with single-phase immersion.” But those long-term benefits do not automatically outweigh the short-term economics. Data center operators may still be too focused on near-term financial targets to invest in systems whose payoff could take years to materialize. It may also be that, when compared to direct-to-chip cooling in particular, immersion’s operational savings are not compelling enough to justify the extra upfront expense. 2. The Industry Doesn’t Change Easily Cost, however, is probably not the only factor. Part of the issue may also be cultural. The data center industry is accustomed to designing and operating facilities in ways that have remained fundamentally consistent for decades. Those norms include placing servers in conventional racks, arranging hardware in familiar floor layouts, and relying on established approaches to maintenance, monitoring, and serviceability. Immersion cooling upends much of that model. With immersion systems, airflow is no longer a primary design constraint, which means data center architecture and white-space layouts can and arguably should change in more fundamental ways. Maintenance procedures change, too, because servers are no longer housed in traditional cabinets and are not accessed in the same way. Monitoring practices, service workflows, and technician training all have to evolve. Direct-to-chip cooling also requires changes to data center design and operations, but overall, those changes are less disruptive than those immersion cooling demands. Direct-to-chip allows operators to preserve more of the conventional server-and-rack paradigm, making incremental adoption easier. The cultural barriers to immersion cooling can be overcome. But doing so would require architects, operators, and technicians to rethink not just how they cool IT equipment, but what a data center should look like and how it should function. Adoption Will Depend on Future Pressures Whether that rethinking happens, and whether operators decide to make the financial commitments that immersion cooling requires, will largely depend on how data center cooling demands evolve in the coming years. If power-hungry, heat-intensive workloads such as AI training and inference continue to expand, immersion cooling could become increasingly attractive. The denser and hotter the compute environment becomes, the stronger the case for cooling technologies that can efficiently handle extreme thermal loads. But if the AI boom plateaus before immersion gains real momentum, the technology may remain largely experimental in the data center market. A

artigo.texto: A SOLV Energy (NASDAQ:MWH) anunciou uma carteira de projetos de US$ 9,2 bilhões em 30 de setembro de 2026, ao apresentar suas atividades comerciais e planos de desenvolvimento de infraestrutura durante a conferência de energia limpa RE+ 2026 em Las Vegas. A empresa afirmou que o tamanho médio de seus projetos agora ultrapassa 400 megawatts de capacidade de corrente contínua (MWdc), com o crescimento dos negócios concentrado nas regiões Sudoeste, Centro-Sul e Centro-Oeste dos Estados Unidos. A conferência marca a primeira participação da SOLV Energy na RE+ desde que se tornou uma empresa de capital aberto no início de 2026. A empresa fornece serviços de engenharia, aquisição e construção, além de operações e manutenção, suporte técnico e soluções de infraestrutura de alta tensão para projetos de energia. A aquisição amplia os serviços de transmissão e alta tensão A SOLV Energy destacou sua recente aquisição da ASB Energy Services, que amplia suas capacidades em transmissão, distribuição, infraestrutura de alta tensão e serviços de campo. A aquisição amplia a gama de serviços que a empresa pode fornecer nas fases de desenvolvimento, construção e operação de projetos de infraestrutura energética. A SOLV Energy afirmou que a maioria de seus clientes atualmente utiliza mais de um de seus serviços, incluindo engenharia, aquisição e construção, operação e manutenção, serviços técnicos e soluções de alta tensão. A empresa indicou que esse modelo de serviço permite dar suporte aos clientes em diferentes estágios da vida útil de um ativo energético. George Hershman, CEO da SOLV Energy, comentou sobre a demanda por infraestrutura energética. “A necessidade de energia confiável e escalável continua a crescer, criando oportunidades em todas as etapas do ciclo de vida dos ativos de energia”, disse Hershman. “Os clientes procuram parceiros que possam entregar projetos com sucesso e dar suporte ao desempenho dos ativos a longo prazo.” Os clientes estão cada vez mais focados em requisitos de infraestrutura de longo prazo A SOLV Energy afirmou que seus clientes estão cada vez mais considerando suas necessidades de infraestrutura em períodos mais longos, em vez de abordar projetos individuais de forma independente. A empresa atribuiu essa tendência à mudança na demanda por eletricidade e à necessidade de desenvolvimento e gestão coordenados dos ativos energéticos. Helena Kimball, Diretora de Receitas da SOLV Energy, afirmou que os clientes estão buscando parcerias com fornecedores de serviços capazes de dar suporte a múltiplos projetos à medida que suas necessidades aumentam. “Em vez de avaliar projetos individualmente, muitos estão buscando estabelecer relacionamentos com parceiros em quem confiam e com quem podem crescer ao longo do tempo”, disse Kimball. A empresa afirmou que sua combinação de serviços de construção, manutenção, técnicos e de alta tensão visa atender a essas necessidades de longo prazo. O crescimento do armazenamento de energia e dos centros de dados está entre as prioridades do setor A SOLV Energy também confirmou que Hershman tem participação agendada em um debate informal organizado pela Associação das Indústrias de Energia Solar (SEIA) no dia 17 de novembro. A discussão abordará os desenvolvimentos na infraestrutura de energia, incluindo o papel do armazenamento de energia e a expansão dos centros de dados. Essas áreas estão se tornando parte de discussões mais amplas do setor sobre demanda de eletricidade, capacidade de infraestrutura e integração de recursos adicionais de geração de energia. A participação da SOLV Energy no evento ocorre após a divulgação de sua carteira de pedidos de US$ 9,2 bilhões e do aumento no tamanho médio dos projetos para mais de 400 MWdc. A empresa não forneceu projeções financeiras adicionais nem um cronograma revisado para converter sua carteira de pedidos em receita nas informações apresentadas. artigo.texto: Supported by Congress Looks to Charge Data Centers Billions in Sweeping Energy Plan The permitting bill could make it easier to build data centers for A.I. but a novel provision would also force data centers to pay much more for power. Weeks after voters lashed out at data centers in the midterms, Congress is debating a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting rules that could help tech companies more quickly build the facilities. The bill would speed up federal environmental reviews of a variety of energy projects, including transmission lines and gas pipelines, making it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers. But that help comes with a huge catch: Data centers would also have to pay much more for their electricity under a provision in the bill that would charge the facilities extra for access to the electric grid. That measure would upend decades of federal power rules and potentially save billions of dollars over the next decade for households and other ratepayers. The push to impose higher costs on data centers underscores how thorny the politics around A.I. have become in Washington. Massive, energy-hungry data centers are spreading rapidly across the country, straining electrical networks and triggering anger in many communities. Voters this month approved at least 40 local ballot initiatives to restrict the facilities. Some environmentalists who oppose the permitting bill have cast it as a boon to tech companies, arguing that the legislation could accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas. The bill would pare back federal environmental laws to speed construction of a many types of projects, including gas pipelines, wind and solar projects, high-voltage transmission lines, roads, public transit and housing. By contrast, supporters have framed the bill as an opportunity to get tough on A.I. firms. “The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes,” said Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island and a co-author of the bill. “Data centers now have to pay for the extra costs that they bring to the grid when they come online. They do not get to have all that extra cost dumped out onto the utility’s rate base and picked up by all of the other ratepayers.” Related Content Advertisement

artigo.texto: The U.S. Commerce Department on November 16 issued an interim rule that restricts indirect access to advanced American AI chips through overseas data centers, Bloomberg reported, as President Donald Trump prepared to travel to the Philippines and China. The rule adds export-license requirements for covered chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. It also gives overseas data centers that serve certain foreign customers 90 days to obtain licenses. We already walked through the mechanics in our earlier report on the five-country license requirement and 90-day deadline. This piece takes a different angle. It asks what these AI chip curbs mean for the people who rent GPU time, train models and serve inference from Southeast Asia and Brazil, and for the AI model market that leans on that compute. Trump was scheduled to meet Xi Jinping in China, and the timing colors how Washington, Beijing and regional capitals read the move. Reporting so far leaves several details open, including chip model numbers, performance thresholds and the names of affected data centers. We mark those gaps as we go, and we keep every figure tied to what outlets have actually confirmed. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The AI Chip Curbs at a Glance Start with what is on the record. The measure is an interim rule from the Commerce Department, and it works through export licensing rather than a ban on any single product. It covers advanced chips from NVIDIA Corporation and other U.S. manufacturers. It also reaches the data centers that sell access to that hardware, which is the part that makes it different from a classic shipment rule. One caution on framing. Some headlines say the curbs hit Asian data centers. That wording summarizes the story, but the confirmed measure is a licensing and remote-compute restriction that applies to specified countries and uses. Brazil sits on the list too, so the geography is wider than Asia alone. Why Remote Access to AI Chips Became the Target Traditional export controls govern boxes crossing borders. A buyer who cannot import accelerators directly can still rent time on servers somewhere else, send training jobs over the internet and collect the results. That path never touches a customs desk. The new rule goes after it by putting obligations on the data centers that provide the computing power, not only on the sellers of the silicon. The Associated Press framed the action as an effort to restrict China from indirect access to AI technology. That matches the language in the rule as reported, which targets overseas data centers providing “significant volumes of computing power” to companies headquartered in countries including China, Russia and Iran. Those data centers must obtain U.S. licenses and conduct end-user checks. This shift matters because earlier limits focused almost entirely on hardware. Our analysis of why US chip export controls fell short showed how much room remained once a buyer found a third-country intermediary. Washington now treats rented compute as the same kind of exposure as purchased compute. Whether that works in practice depends on enforcement, and the reporting does not describe any company-specific enforcement action yet. The Five Countries and the Higher-Than-Normal Risk Label Reuters reported that the rule names Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as places where advanced chips face a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion or rerouting to unauthorized buyers. Shipments of covered chips to those countries now need a U.S. export license. The label describes risk, not a finding of wrongdoing, and the reporting we reviewed does not accuse any of the five governments of facilitating diversion. The list reads like a map of where data center capital has been landing. Singapore and Malaysia have drawn heavy investment in server capacity, and Bloomberg’s headline called the region an Asian data center hotbed. Indonesia and Thailand are building out as well. Brazil is the odd one out geographically, which tells you the logic here is about transshipment risk and compute hosting, not a regional campaign against Asia. For operators in those countries, a license requirement changes timelines more than it changes demand. A shipment that used to clear in routine fashion now waits on a federal decision. Procurement teams will need to model that delay into capacity plans. How long licenses take is not stated in the reporting, so any estimate today is a guess. The 90-Day Clock for Overseas Data Centers Covered overseas data centers have 90 days to obtain licenses if they want to keep providing the specified services. If the clock runs from the November 16 announcement, that window closes around mid-February 2027. Reports do not say when the 90 days formally begin, so treat that date as arithmetic and not as a published deadline. What happens at the end of the window is also unclear. The practical reading is that a site without a license must stop providing the covered service to the restricted customers, or lose access to further covered chips. The reporting available does not spell out penalties, and we will not guess at them here. Compare that with the usual rhythm of export policy. Rules often land with immediate effect and leave industry scrambling. A 90-day runway gives operators time to audit customer lists, find out who sits behind each account and file paperwork. It also gives Washington leverage, because a data center that wants a license has a reason to cooperate on end-user checks. Who Is Exempt: U.S.-Headquartered Operators The new country-specific licensing requirements do not apply to U.S.-headquartered companies operating data centers in the five countries. artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign Thursday and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. artigo.texto: Relatórios Estudo de Harvard conclui que os combustíveis fósseis fornecem energia à maioria dos data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveOs combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos… Ver mais - Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída aos data centers de hiperescala dos EUA. - As emissões atribuídas a um data center dependem da matriz de geração da sua rede regional. - O estudo não conseguiu separar o uso de eletricidade específico da IA da computação de uso geral em instalações individuais. Um estudo liderado por Harvard, publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 na Nature Sustainability, estima que 403 data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA consumiram aproximadamente 82 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade no cenário central, o equivalente a cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA. Os combustíveis fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da geração atribuída, principalmente gás natural, com 38%, e carvão, com 15%. A estimativa central das emissões atribuíveis de dióxido de carbono (CO2) foi de aproximadamente 25,7 milhões de toneladas métricas, dentro de uma faixa de 21 a 31 milhões de toneladas métricas entre os cenários. Nos diferentes cenários de carga das instalações, o consumo estimado de eletricidade variou de aproximadamente 68 a 99 TWh. Harvard afirmou que a estimativa mais alta se aproxima do consumo anual de eletricidade de estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee. Como foram elaboradas as estimativas das instalações As estimativas abrangem o período de maio de 2024 a abril de 2025. Os pesquisadores usaram imagens de satélite para compilar a lista de instalações e modelaram o consumo anual de eletricidade de cada local em diferentes cenários operacionais. Em seguida, usaram dados da Agência de Proteção Ambiental para atribuir as emissões de acordo com a combinação de usinas de energia na rede regional de cada instalação. O artigo descreve seu método central de contabilização como um método de atribuição baseado na localização e na produção total da autoridade de balanceamento. Na prática, a abordagem distribui entre as instalações a geração e as emissões das usinas da rede regional pertinente. O resultado é uma estimativa das fontes de eletricidade e das emissões discriminada por instalação, em vez de leituras diretas dos medidores de cada local. As redes regionais moldam a pegada Segundo a medida de produção total ponderada pelo consumo de eletricidade usada no artigo, a intensidade de carbono foi de aproximadamente 314 gramas de CO2 por quilowatt-hora, em comparação com a média de produção total dos EUA, de aproximadamente 348 gramas. Essa média agregada mais baixa coexiste com grandes variações regionais: cerca de um quarto da eletricidade foi consumida em regiões da rede com intensidade de carbono acima da média nacional, e muitas instalações estavam concentradas em áreas onde a geração a carvão contribui significativamente para o abastecimento. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, em conjunto, por mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Portanto, uma média nacional não representa todos os complexos de data centers; as emissões atribuídas a uma instalação dependem da combinação de fontes de geração de sua rede regional. O que as estimativas não esclarecem Os dados disponíveis não abrangiam todos os data centers hiperescaláveis dos EUA, e os pesquisadores não conseguiram separar, em cada instalação, a eletricidade usada em operações especializadas em IA daquela destinada à computação de uso geral. As instalações dão suporte a serviços como computação em nuvem, treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem e implantação global de ferramentas de IA; por isso, os totais não podem ser interpretados como consumo exclusivo de IA. O autor principal, Gianluca Guidi, afirmou no anúncio de Harvard que o consumo de eletricidade e a pegada de carbono relatados “já podem ser substancialmente maiores agora, em 2026”. Trata-se de uma projeção baseada nas instalações construídas e nos complexos ampliados após o período do estudo, além do crescimento contínuo da demanda por computação de IA, e não de uma nova medição. O estudo não mediu diretamente os efeitos sobre a saúde, que os pesquisadores planejam investigar em trabalhos futuros. A autora correspondente, Francesca Dominici, descreveu duas vias: o dióxido de carbono impulsiona as mudanças climáticas, que afetam a saúde por meio de ondas de calor, fumaça de incêndios florestais, inundações e outras vias; além disso, as usinas de combustíveis fósseis liberam material particulado fino, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, associados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura. As pessoas que vivem perto dessas usinas e a favor do vento em relação a elas podem arcar com custos para a saúde mesmo estando longe do próprio data center. Dominici afirmou que o objetivo é oferecer ao público, aos formuladores de políticas, aos investidores e aos incorporadores uma base mais concreta para decidir onde instalar data centers e como abastecê-los de energia. Essa estrutura amplia a contabilização, que deixa de se limitar a um único total nacional e passa a abranger as redes regionais e suas usinas — o nível em que se encontram a escolha de locais para data centers hiperescaláveis, o fornecimento de eletricidade e as emissões atribuíveis.

artigo.texto: SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future. ‘Meteoric growth’ Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. “The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.” Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. “As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. “It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.” Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. “They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.” The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. artigo.texto: Oklahoma currently has 64 data centers operating or in progress. Editor’s note: This story was updated on 11/16/2026 with new information from the U.S. Data Center map, and updates to local project. Our Data Center Info Hub features an interactive map, data center profiles, frequently asked questions, and a form to ask us your questions about data centers in your area. Driven by affordable land, access to power, and growing demand for cloud and AI services, companies ranging from global tech giants to regional providers are expanding their presence in Oklahoma. According to the US Data Center Map, data as of Oct 2026. https://dcmap.us, Oklahoma has: - 64 data center projects overall - 34 operational data centers - 6 data centers under construction - 20 data centers planned - 2 paused data center projects - 2 inactive data centers Below is a running list of data center projects across the state. This article will be updated as new facilities are announced, approved, or completed. Claremore Project Mustang (Approved) Project Mustang is an approved data center development at the Claremore Industrial Park by Beale Infrastructure. Plans call for multiple data center buildings and office space, with power supplied by Grand River Dam Authority and water and wastewater services provided by the City of Claremore. City leaders say the property is already zoned for industrial use and that the developer would pay for required infrastructure upgrades. The Claremore City Council approved plans Monday, May 18, for “Project Mustang.” Claremore City Hall reached standing-room capacity during the meeting, with dozens of people waiting outside and rotating in to comply with fire code limits. Public comment lasted nearly two hours before the council voted on the proposal. Related Story: Claremore approves Project Mustang data center plan The agreement allows Beale Infrastructure to seek a 25-year ad valorem tax exemption for each phase of the project. Company representatives said the development would still contribute more than $250 million toward Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. Some residents have raised concerns about water usage, environmental impacts and transparency. City officials and the developer say the project would not raise taxes or utility rates and could bring long-term investment and jobs. Muskogee County Google Data Centers (Summit and Council Hill) (Early Development) Google plans to build two new data center campuses near Summit and Council Hill as part of a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma. The facilities are expected to support Google’s cloud and AI services, including Search, Maps and Google Cloud. The company says the projects will be paired with clean energy agreements expected to add hundreds of megawatts of renewable power to Oklahoma’s grid. Construction timelines have not been released. Related Story: Google to build two data centers in Muskogee County as part of $9B Oklahoma investment In April, OG&E announced that it will power the Muskogee data centers as well as a data center coming to Stillwater (see below) “OG&E is pleased to support Google and together advance growth in our home state, ensuring our current customers benefit from data center expansion that meets the technology needs of the 21st century economy at some of the lowest rates in the country,” said Sean Trauschke, Chairman, President and CEO of OGE Energy Corp. “This unique agreement is a model for future data center partnerships and forms the basis for a new large-load tariff that OG&E will submit in the coming weeks that protects our current customers from bearing the costs of this growing demand and Oklahoma’s goals for economic growth.” Core Scientific (Under Construction) A Core Scientific data center in Muskogee at 4800 S 24th St W. is operational, as of Aug. 14, 2026, according to the U.S. Data Center map. Two more Core Scientific high-performance computing (HPC) data centers in Muskogee are under construction. Oklahoma City American Tower EDC Oklahoma (Planned) American Tower EDC Oklahoma is a construction-ready edge data center* development located at 1309 Northeast 122nd Street in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. According to American Tower, the facility would be on 83.5 acres and provide 4MW of capacity. The American Tower EDC Oklahoma company says that zoning has been approved and that the facility can be ready in 18 months once a customer signs an anchor lease. *An edge data center is a smaller, decentralized facility positioned near the source of data generation. Cerebras Systems operates a 10-megawatt data center in Oklahoma City in partnership with Scale Datacenters. The facility supports large-scale AI computing and uses a closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus - 3 Data Centers (Under Construction) The CloudBurst Oklahoma City Campus is planned to be an expansive location with a total capacity of 200MW covering at least three data centers. It is planned for the area near 2000 S Council Rd. Cogent Data Center (Operational) The Cogent Data Center in Oklahoma City is 5,294 square feet of colocation space designed for 42U cabinets. The Cogent data center is what’s known as a “carrier hotel,” meaning that it has equipment, space, and/or bandwidth available for rental to retail customers. Lumen Technologies operates the Oklahoma City 1 data center, supporting enterprise, government and network infrastructure. MIDCON Recovery Solutions operates a 60,000-square-foot data center in northwest Oklahoma City’s Quail Springs Business Park, designed to meet Tier IV standards. RACK59 operates a 30,000-square-foot colocation data center at 7725 West Reno Avenue, offering redundant power and on-site substation access. TierPoint operates multiple Oklahoma City facilities providing colocation and enterprise services ValorC3 operates a 65,000-square-foot Tier III+ data center designed to withstand severe weather, including EF5 tornadoes.

artigo.texto: Pakistan’s next opportunity in battery technology may lie in a mineral we have known for centuries. At Khewra, visitors marvel at the pink salt that has become one of the country’s most recognisable natural products. Less celebrated is the fact that the same town has been home to an industrial soda ash plant since 1944. As Pakistan prepares to welcome investors to the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026, this combination of mineral wealth and chemical manufacturing raises an intriguing question: could our abundant salt help Pakistan enter the emerging sodium-ion battery industry? The idea is more credible than it might initially sound. Sodium-ion batteries are attracting increasing international attention as an alternative to conventional lithium-ion technologies. Sodium is widely available, and its use could help diversify battery supply chains that remain heavily dependent on a relatively small number of countries. Pakistan certainly has the raw material. According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, the country extracted approximately 2.9 million tonnes of rock salt during FY2024-25. Lucky Core Industries, meanwhile, reports an installed soda ash manufacturing capacity of 560,000 tonnes annually at Khewra. These are not insignificant foundations for a country hoping to develop new industries around its mineral resources. Rather than rushing towards large-scale manufacturing, Pakistan should begin with a focused programme linking chemical manufacturers, universities, battery researchers and energy companies. Yet there is a fundamental distinction that must not be overlooked. Having sodium is not the same as knowing how to manufacture a sodium-ion battery. Ordinary salt is sodium chloride. A rechargeable battery, however, requires carefully engineered electrode materials, specialised electrolytes and sophisticated manufacturing processes. Its performance depends not merely on the presence of sodium but on how effectively sodium ions move between the electrodes during thousands of charging and discharging cycles. The difference is considerable. A battery’s capacity, lifespan, charging performance and safety are influenced by the chemical composition and microscopic structure of its materials. Even small impurities can affect performance. The transformation from inexpensive industrial chemicals to reliable battery components therefore demands scientific expertise, precision manufacturing and rigorous quality control. This is where Pakistan must be careful not to mistake geological abundance for industrial competitiveness. China offers an instructive example. Companies such as CATL and BYD are investing heavily in sodium-ion technology, but their progress rests on decades of experience in battery research, materials processing, manufacturing equipment and supply-chain development. Their advantage is not simply access to raw materials; it is the ability to convert scientific advances into reliable products at competitive prices. The International Energy Agency’s February 2026 assessment puts the industry’s progress into perspective. Advanced sodium-ion cells can achieve energy densities of around 175 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with up to 205 Wh/kg for lithium iron phosphate batteries. Global sodium-ion production in 2025 was still less than one per cent of lithium-ion production. The technology is advancing, but established lithium iron phosphate batteries remain difficult to beat on cost, performance and manufacturing maturity. Moreover, China already dominates sodium-ion battery production and the supply of critical components. For Pakistan, this presents both a warning and an opportunity. Entering an emerging industry is attractive, but competing directly with established manufacturers without first developing the necessary expertise would be an expensive gamble. A more promising starting point may be the materials that go into these batteries. Pakistan’s existing chemical industry could investigate producing high-purity sodium compounds and cathode precursors. Khewra’s soda ash manufacturing experience is particularly relevant, although substantial additional processing and qualification would be necessary before any product could meet battery-grade specifications. There is another possibility that deserves attention: agricultural waste. Many sodium-ion batteries use a specialised anode material known as hard carbon. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries that commonly rely on graphite, sodium-ion technology can utilise carbon materials produced from various organic feedstocks. Pakistan generates substantial agricultural residues, including rice husks and sugarcane bagasse. With appropriate research and processing, some of these materials could potentially serve as feedstocks for hard-carbon anodes. This is an area where our universities and chemical-processing industries could make a meaningful contribution. The challenge would be to develop production methods that deliver the required electrochemical performance without making the final material prohibitively expensive. High energy consumption, inconsistent feedstock quality and impurities could otherwise undermine the economics. Such research is not merely theoretical. The United States Department of Energy has supported projects investigating alternative hard-carbon production processes and advanced sodium-based cathode manufacturing. This illustrates how countries seeking a place in emerging battery supply chains are investing in specific technological capabilities. Pakistan could adopt a similarly selective approach, concentrating on the parts of the industry where its existing resources and expertise offer a realistic advantage. The domestic energy market also merits consideration. artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – A Botetourt County judge is taking more time to decide whether construction on a controversial 300-acre Google data center campus should be halted. Following a hearing Monday, the judge gave attorneys for the three parties involved, Botetourt County, Google shell company Helio, and Botetourt County resident Robert Dallas, until Friday to submit additional briefs explaining their arguments. The judge said he wants more time to review the evidence and relevant case law before deciding whether the county violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act. John Fishwick, who represents Dallas, argued the county failed to adequately disclose that supervisors would be voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Fishwick said the county did not provide the public with enough information about the agreement before the vote, arguing that the lack of disclosure violated state law. “We think we have a strong case. We think we’ve made it,” Fishwick said. “We’re pleased with how the evidence came in today. We put a lot of evidence in front of the judge. Ultimately, that’ll be his call.” The county maintains it made information about the project available to the public, including posting the performance agreement online after the deal was finalized. “Once the deal was consummated, it was all out in the open. Anyone could issue a FOIA request for the deal. The deal was placed on the website,” said Julian Harf, an attorney representing Botetourt County. However, the judge questioned the timing of that disclosure, pointing out that the details of the agreement were not made public until several hours after supervisors voted on it. “I have a fundamental disagreement as far as the temporal issue and whether you can disclose three and a half hours after the vote, and that somehow satisfies the statutes,” the judge said. The judge also acknowledged a fundamental disagreement between the parties over what qualifies as disclosure under the state’s open meeting requirements. A ruling could come as early as Monday, after the judge has had additional time to review the arguments and determine whether the remedies Dallas is seeking are permitted under the Freedom of Information Act.

artigo.texto: (3 Minutes Read) Electricity access has risen to 85.5%, with Tanzania targeting universal coverage by 2030, expanding clean cooking and seeking international investment in carbon projects. Tanzania is stepping up efforts to transform its energy sector, combining expanded electricity access, renewable energy development and clean cooking initiatives with plans to attract international investment in carbon markets.Electricity access has increased from 78.4% in 2020 to 85.5% in 2026, according to the country’s energy sector commitments. Under its Mission 300 National Energy Compact, Tanzania aims to achieve universal electricity access by 2030 while targeting a 75% renewable energy share. The government is also focusing on ensuring that improved electricity access translates into productive economic activity, particularly in agricultural processing, manufacturing, small businesses and emerging green industries. President Samia Suluhu Hassan has stressed that reliable energy infrastructure will be critical to achieving Tanzania’s ambition of becoming a USD 1 trillion economy by 2050. The forthcoming Energy Transition and Investment Plan (ETIP) is expected to provide a framework for aligning infrastructure development with long-term economic transformation and identifying investment opportunities. Tanzania is also positioning itself as a regional advocate for clean cooking. Its National Clean Cooking Strategy targets 80% adoption by 2034, with particular attention to schools and healthcare facilities. Replacing traditional fuels with cleaner alternatives is expected to improve public health, reduce operating costs and limit pressure on forests. At the COP31 discussions in Antalya, participants also examined how carbon markets, including cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, could mobilise results-based financing for institutional clean cooking programmes. Meanwhile, UK-based Carbon Bridge has expressed interest in investing in Tanzania’s carbon market, identifying opportunities in forestry, agriculture, energy, water and waste management. During discussions with the National Carbon Monitoring Centre (NCMC) on the sidelines of COP31, the company cited the country’s investment environment, project potential and government-backed regulatory framework as key attractions. artigo.texto: Chinese automaker BAIC’s electric vehicle brand Arcfox has launched two new battery-swappable models in China, expanding the technology into a more affordable segment of the market. The Beta S3 535 Ultra+ LiDAR Swappable Edition and Beta T1 Swappable Edition both use CATL’s Chocolate battery-swapping network, with prices starting at 52,000 yuan ($7,800) under a battery-leasing arrangement. The launch builds on a partnership between BAIC and CATL to develop a shared battery-swapping ecosystem. Both cars can swap depleted battery packs in about 99 seconds, allowing drivers to resume their journeys without waiting for conventional charging. Beta S3 gets LiDAR and 535-km range According to Car News China, the Beta S3 535 Ultra+ is a front-wheel-drive electric sedan powered by a permanent-magnet synchronous motor producing 159 kW (213 hp) and 250 Nm of torque. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (62 mph) in 7.1 seconds and has a top speed of 165 km/h (103 mph). Its battery delivers a claimed range of 535 km (332 miles) under China’s CLTC testing cycle. The vehicle also supports conventional fast charging. The new edition’s main technology highlight is its driver-assistance system. It combines a 192-line LiDAR sensor with Horizon Robotics’ Journey J6M computing chip to support highway and urban navigation assistance, as well as automated parking. More from Transportation See All Inside, the sedan features a 15.6-inch central touchscreen, an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8155 cockpit processor. Its starting price is 78,800 yuan ($11,800) with battery leasing. Beta T1 brings swapping to a lower price The smaller Beta T1 targets buyers looking for a more affordable electric car. It measures 4,337 mm (170.7 in) long, 1,860 mm (73.2 in) wide, and 1,572 mm (61.9 in) tall, with a 2,770-mm (109.1 in) wheelbase. Its electric motor produces 95 kW (127 hp), while its CATL-manufactured lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supports the swapping system. The car has a top speed of 150 km/h (93 mph), although Arcfox has not disclosed the range of this new edition. The T1 starts at 52,000 yuan ($7,800), with a higher trim priced at 60,000 yuan ($9,000), both under battery-leasing plans. CATL expands its battery-swapping network The two launches are part of CATL’s wider effort to make battery swapping available across multiple vehicle brands. BAIC, CATL, and service partner CAES signed a cooperation agreement in April 2026 covering compatible vehicle development and battery-swapping infrastructure. CATL reported that its Chocolate network had more than 1,470 stations across 99 Chinese cities at the time, with a target of exceeding 3,000 stations by the end of 2026. In October, BAIC and CATL also announced a broader partnership targeting one million battery-swapping vehicles. Under battery leasing, customers purchase the car without owning its battery outright, paying a recurring fee to use a pack maintained within the swapping network. For the new Arcfox models, monthly plans start at 399 yuan ($60) for a 5,000-km (about 6,200 miles) allowance, while unlimited monthly mileage costs 599 yuan ($90). Arcfox is also offering buyers 10,000 km (about 3,100 miles) of free battery-swapping mileage through 20 vouchers. The promotion applies to Beta S3 swapping-edition purchases made by January 31, 2027, and to Beta T1 customers. The challenge for the technology will be expanding station availability. A battery exchange that takes just 99 seconds is useful only when compatible infrastructure is accessible. By bringing more affordable vehicles into the same network, BAIC and CATL are betting that shared infrastructure can make battery swapping a more practical alternative to conventional EV charging.

artigo.texto: In March, Super Micro faced a crisis. Two employees at the U.S. server giant, including one of its co-founders, had just been charged in federal court with attempting to transfer Nvidia AI chips to China, in violation of U.S. export laws. Weeks later, Super Micro retained the services of Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm known for its close ties to the Trump administration. Ballard would help the company with “advocacy regarding AI data center infrastructure policy” and “export control regulations affecting advanced computing hardware,” according to records maintained under the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Super Micro is one of three firms involved in Southeast Asia’s data center boom that have called on Ballard since the beginning of Trump’s second term. The region has emerged as a hotbed for server companies providing remote access to Nvidia chips for Chinese AI companies. Ballard’s other clients include EdgeConneX, a U.S. firm that operates data centers in Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta, with three more under construction elsewhere in Malaysia and the Philippines, and Equinix, another data center operator for which Ballard has been “tracking executive orders and action regarding power, energy, and data center development.” Equinix, too, has expanded operations in Southeast Asia since Trump retook office. Ballard’s work on behalf of data center operators raises questions about vectors of influence in the Trump administration, whose approach to chip export policy has come under fresh scrutiny following revelations about Jensen Huang’s affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (黃樂). Super Micro has also returned to the spotlight this week, following a statement from Singapore’s government saying that the company had provided “limited cooperation” with its investigation into Alice Huang last year. Since the second quarter of this year, Super Micro has paid Ballard $100,000 each month as the company has come under increasing scrutiny for its role in a network of AI infrastructure providers that Nvidia assembled in East Asia to get around U.S. export controls. The lobbyists on the Super Micro account include two former high-level officials with recent experience in the Trump White House. Thomas Boodry, a former aide to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, served as special assistant to President Trump and senior director for legislative affairs at the National Security Council. Micah Ketchel served as a Trump special assistant, too, and a senior advisor to the former national security advisor, Michael Waltz. Domino Theory has reached out to Boodry for comment. Ketchel could not immediately be contacted. Both men left the administration around the time that Waltz — who accidentally added a journalist to a group chat containing classified battle plans for Yemen — transitioned out of his role as national security advisor. Founded in Tallahassee, Florida, in 1998, Ballard Partners did not expand outside of Florida until 2017, establishing an office in Washington when Trump became president. Brian Ballard, the firm’s founder, has had close ties to the president for more than a decade. When Trump first ran for president in 2016, Ballard chaired the campaign’s finance committee in Florida. Ballard Partners has also acted as a talent pipeline for Trump. The firm’s alumni include his former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. In a recent interview, Calley Means, a former top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told CBS News that Ballard “controlled” White House policy. Ballard’s more than $88 million in lobbying revenue in 2025 was the highest of any firm since the Lobbying Disclosure Act went into effect in 1996, even after adjusting for inflation, according to CBS News. In the first three quarters of this year, it has already earned $98 million. The firm’s clients have included Lenovo, a Chinese computer maker that a House committee accused of building a back door for the Chinese government to spy on users in late 2023. Lenovo denied these allegations. Ballard has also worked for ByteDance, the Chinese tech giant that struck a joint venture deal to keep operating its social media platform TikTok in the U.S. earlier this year. More than $1 million of Ballard’s recent revenue has come from EdgeConneX, which first hired them in late 2024 for lobbying related to “International Data Center development opportunities,” according to disclosure records. Ballard’s most recent lobbying disclosure on behalf of EdgeConneX came in the third quarter of 2025, when it contacted an office at the White House. Since then, it has continued to receive $50,000 each month for its services, despite reporting no further lobbying activity. EdgeConneX has been rapidly expanding its AI data center capacity in Malaysia, where Chinese AI firms have increasingly turned for remote access to Nvidia-powered servers. It is currently building two data center campuses, in Cyberjaya and Johor, designed specifically to handle AI workloads. “These facilities also serve as gateways for global cloud and cloud-based services expanding throughout Southeast Asia and beyond,” reads a description of the project on the company’s website. There is no evidence that EdgeConneX has been involved in any illicit chip diversion to China. The company does, however, maintain a substantial presence in the Chinese market.
