artigo.texto: A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) entrou com uma ação civil pública nesta segunda-feira, 16 de novembro, para suspender os leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A entidade questiona a constitucionalidade da regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio da contratação e aponta insegurança jurídica pela ausência de regulamentação definitiva sobre o rateio do encargo. A ação, apresentada contra a União e a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), tramita na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, e inclui pedido de tutela de urgência para impedir a realização dos certames nas condições atuais. O principal questionamento recai sobre o parágrafo 6º do artigo 3º-A da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determinou que os custos da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia, conforme regulamentação da Aneel. Segundo a associação, a regra contraria o modelo geral de contratação de reserva de capacidade, no qual os custos são distribuídos entre os usuários finais do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A entidade ressalta que a potência contratada beneficia os consumidores, ao garantir segurança e confiabilidade ao fornecimento, e não exclusivamente os agentes de geração. A Abeeólica ainda aponta que a diferenciação do custeio conforme a tecnologia contratada viola princípios constitucionais, como isonomia, livre concorrência, legalidade e segurança jurídica. Além disso, destaca que a mudança pode comprometer investimentos realizados sob regras anteriores, especialmente em projetos eólicos e solares. Abeeólica: rateio ainda não foi regulamentado Na ação, a Abeeólica aponta que ausência de uma metodologia definitiva para distribuir os custos entre os geradores. A Aneel submeteu o tema à consulta pública 37/2026, encerrada em 6 de novembro, mas a regulamentação ainda não foi concluída A proposta discutida pela agência considera diferentes níveis de flexibilidade das fontes de geração, com fatores de participação no encargo que variam de 25% a 100%. Na avaliação da Abeeólica, o modelo pode fazer com que determinados geradores paguem até quatro vezes mais que outros, sem que a legislação tenha estabelecido critérios para essa diferenciação. A associação ressalta que a indefinição impede os agentes de estimar adequadamente os impactos econômicos da contratação, cujos contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Além disso, a entidade contesta a possibilidade de repasse integral dos custos aos consumidores. Segundo a petição, contratos do mercado regulado podem prever mecanismos de recomposição de encargos, mas essa possibilidade não está necessariamente assegurada nos contratos do mercado livre, o que poderia transferir parte do ônus diretamente aos geradores. Na ação, impetrada pelo escritório Justen, Pereira, Oliveira & Talamini, a entidade declara que não pretende impedir a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento, mas evitar que os leilões sejam realizados antes da resolução das controvérsias jurídicas e regulatórias. A Abeeólica pede que a Justiça impeça a realização dos certames nas condições atuais, preservando a possibilidade de sua realização após a correção dos vícios apontados. Mudança legal Em 27 de outubro, a Aneel entendeu que uma eventual mudança na lei que atribui aos geradores o custeio da contratação exigirá nova avaliação da agência sobre os efeitos nos contratos. A MegaWhat conversou com o deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania – SP), que entende que a aprovação do projeto de lei (PL) nº 3.716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos de contratação de baterias como reserva de capacidade, pode ser viabilizada com a manutenção do foco na proposta original, sem a inclusão de outros temas do setor elétrico. Se o projeto de lei original for aprovado, as baterias passarão a seguir a regra geral de rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade, com cobrança dos consumidores de energia elétrica. Associações ligadas à geração hídrica, eólica e solar, junto a entidades que representam o setor de baterias e hidrogênio verde, manifestaram apoio ao PL. As associações afirmam que os custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias serão repassados aos consumidores de qualquer forma, mesmo que a cobrança seja concentrada nos agentes de geração.

artigo.texto: Economia Brasil pode contestar restrições dos EUA à venda de chips para data centers O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva está considerando a possibilidade de questionar as novas limitações impostas pelos Estados Unidos sobre a comercialização de chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a data centers no Brasil. Essa medida, anunciada nesta segunda-feira, colocou o Brasil entre cinco países que precisarão de autorização do governo americano para importar esses componentes, utilizados em grandes centros de processamento de dados. Fontes próximas ao governo dizem que uma possível negociação com os EUA ou contestação das regras ainda está em aberto. Por enquanto, o tema não gerou grande preocupação dentro do Executivo, e não há uma decisão tomada sobre eventuais respostas à decisão dos americanos. Os Estados Unidos detêm um controle significativo sobre a fabricação e distribuição desses chips, que são essenciais para o funcionamento de sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial, o que lhes confere forte influência sobre o comércio internacional desse mercado. Os data centers são locais que reúnem servidores e equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar grandes quantidades de informações. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, esses centros passaram a exigir chips mais potentes, capazes de realizar os cálculos necessários para desenvolver e operar essas tecnologias. A nova regulamentação foi divulgada pelo Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos e também inclui Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. O objetivo é evitar que empresas chinesas acessem tecnologia americana por meio de centros de dados instalados em outros países, burlando as restrições já impostas por Washington. Desde 2022, os EUA limitam a venda de chips avançados para a China, exigindo autorização para a exportação de certos componentes e equipamentos usados na fabricação desses chips. Em 2023, as regras foram reforçadas e agora abrangem novas exigências para países que o governo americano considera mais vulneráveis ao uso indevido dessas tecnologias. Membros do governo brasileiro apontam que anteriormente houve preocupação com a possível escassez de chips no mercado global, devido ao aumento da demanda por equipamentos para inteligência artificial, mas essa preocupação foi superada. Segundo as novas regras, as empresas afetadas terão que obter licenças do governo dos EUA para importar determinados chips avançados. A regulamentação prevê exceções para empresas baseadas nos Estados Unidos, desde que cumpram os requisitos de fornecimento de informações, e determina que os pedidos de autorização serão analisados caso a caso pelas autoridades americanas.

artigo.texto: Hitachi Energy fecha primeiro contrato de IA para energia de data center no Brasil Acordo com a BCR-i prevê manutenção preditiva em subestação de 560 MVA que atende data center no estado de São Paulo. A Hitachi Energy assinou seu primeiro contrato HMAX Energy no Brasil com a BCR-i Brasil para implementar um sistema de monitoramento e manutenção preditiva em uma subestação de 560 MVA que atende um data center no estado de São Paulo. O acordo prevê o uso de IA para analisar as condições dos equipamentos elétricos e identificar riscos de falhas operacionais. A solução combina informações coletadas dos ativos elétricos, monitoramento em tempo quase real e modelos analíticos para orientar intervenções técnicas. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o serviço busca substituir parte das rotinas de manutenção baseadas em intervalos predeterminados por procedimentos orientados pelas condições dos equipamentos. Subestação atende infraestrutura digital A instalação é operada pela BCR-i Brasil, grupo especializado em gestão de infraestrutura e serviços técnicos, e a capacidade de 560 MVA corresponde à potência aparente da subestação. Raphael Campos, Head de Operação e Manutenção da BCR-i Brasil, afirma que o contrato permitirá integrar os serviços de operação elétrica da companhia às ferramentas de análise de dados fornecidas pela Hitachi Energy. “Garantir a máxima confiabilidade no fornecimento de energia é fundamental para atender a setores que exigem alta disponibilidade, como os data centers”, afirma o executivo. A Hitachi Energy ficará responsável pelo fornecimento do HMAX Energy, que reúne serviços de acompanhamento técnico e ferramentas de IA aplicadas à gestão dos ativos durante seu ciclo de vida. “Os data centers estão no centro da era da IA e operam com a expectativa de 100% de disponibilidade. Isso exige uma transformação na forma como a infraestrutura energética é gerenciada, incorporando mais inteligência, capacidade de antecipação e integração”, diz Fernanda Alves, gerente do Service Hub para a América Latina na Hitachi Energy. Expansão pressiona demanda por energia O acordo ocorre em meio ao crescimento da infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados no Brasil, associado à expansão da computação em nuvem e das aplicações de IA. Segundo projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) citadas pelas empresas, o consumo de eletricidade no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) deverá crescer 4% ao ano até 2030, quando a carga elétrica total poderá atingir 98,8 GW. A expansão dos data centers é apontada como um dos fatores de aumento da demanda. A continuidade do fornecimento elétrico é um requisito operacional dessas instalações, que dependem de energia para servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, equipamentos de rede e refrigeração. Nesse contexto, o modelo contratado pela BCR-i busca identificar alterações no desempenho dos componentes elétricos antes que provoquem interrupções nos serviços. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Criticism of data centers is less about the physical building infrastructure and more about the public’s broad concerns about artificial intelligence and tech companies, according to several University of Virginia studies. Maura Austin, a research scientist at the University of Virginia’s National Security Institute, said that as data center pushback has intensified over the last few months, it’s largely been bipartisan. But, Austin said, people are thinking about data centers “as combined with their thoughts on AI, and they are harboring a strong distrust for the federal government and for Big Tech as well. And those feelings of distrust translate into an uneasiness about the future and about the economic instability that they believe is being wrought by AI and the developments there, and they’re taking out that unease in their resistance to data centers.” Broadly, Austin said, many people have a negative feeling about data centers but can’t explain why. As a result, they point to the physical buildings. There are hundreds of data centers across Northern Virginia, and many are in Loudoun County. In some cases, local governments are working to change the way data center projects are approved, in an effort to slow their growth. Generally, Austin said, residents who live close to new data center projects don’t envision benefits locally. “They don’t expect data centers to bring jobs,” Austin said. “They don’t expect to experience any more benefits from AI by having a data center close by, which makes sense. I don’t think that you get faster access to AI models just because you have a data center down the street.” There are concerns about noise, water usage and data centers driving up energy bills, Austin said, which means data centers are “occupying this particularly tricky space, where they are not bringing any known benefits to the local community, and they are bringing a lot of expectations for costs and burdens.” Some tech companies, Austin said, are working to make water use more transparent or taking responsibility for energy infrastructure and announcing they’ll absorb the costs. But, based on the studies’ findings, “What people are looking for is to feel more secure in their economic futures,” she said. Spending on proenvironmental efforts, local libraries or schools, or direct payments to households would all increase support for data center projects, Austin said the research found. Direct payments to households were the best-performing initiative to increase the public’s support for data centers. “We’re relying on the acceptance of the people in these communities in order to continue this critical infrastructure build-out, and the way forward is to meet the people at the negotiations table, and that means listening to their concerns and listening to their needs,” Austin said. artigo.texto: Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state’s plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change. Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers are requiring so much electricity that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released Monday found. The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with the new demands from the data centers being used to power artificial intelligence. That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats. “Fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals,” said Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at Respiratory Health Association in Chicago. “These are chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people.” In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed. Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. Those peaker plants are limited-use, oil-fueled or gas-power sources shut down for most days in any given year, but are designed to guard against blackouts and can be fired up when energy use is peaking, like on the hottest day of the year, when many air conditioners are running. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation. “That’s disappointing,” said Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County. She said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. “Our community is tired of dirty energy.” Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants but that is not being advised, state officials said. The state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants in hopes of producing more energy which is free of carbon dioxide, according to the reports. Enough power for now Illinois is not running out of power yet but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity. Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city. State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month. Hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and the Integrated Resource Plan, released by the Illinois Commerce Commission. artigo.texto: Expansão de data centers nos EUA pode desacelerar após eleições legislativas | Vero NotíciasExpansão de data centers nos EUA pode desacelerar após eleições legislativas A expansão dos data centers de inteligência artificialnos Estados Unidos pode perder força após as eleições de meio de mandato, diante da pressão de democratas por restrições à construção de novas instalações. Entre as preocupações estão o elevado consumo de energia, o aumento das tarifas de eletricidade e os impactos ambientais. A senadora Elizabeth Warren defende uma moratória para novos empreendimentos. Analistas avaliam que possíveis restrições podem reduzir investimentos em inteligência artificial e pressionar ações de tecnologia na Nasdaq, enquanto os títulos públicos americanos ganham atratividade. Dados da CNN. O secretário de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, Howard Lutnick, enfrenta críticas de integrantes do governo Trump por sua relação com Jensen Huang, ex-CEO da Nvidia, e pela demora em restringir exportações de chips avançados à China. Autoridades questionam a decisão de não incluir a empresa Megaspeed, suspeita de repassar tecnologia americana ao mercado chinês, em uma lista de restrições comerciais. Os Correios registraram prejuízo de R$ 1,9 bilhão no terceiro trimestre de 2026, alta de 19% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. Entre janeiro e setembro, as perdas acumuladas chegaram a R$ 7,48 bilhões, crescimento de 27%. A estatal atribui parte das dificuldades à queda nas receitas com encomendas e entregas internacionais, além do aumento de despesas judiciais e financeiras. O Brasil poderá receber até R$ 1 trilhão em investimentos em data centers até 2036, segundo estimativa da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC). O crescimento é impulsionado pela inteligência artificial, por incentivos fiscais e pela oferta de energia renovável. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) projeta que o setor responderá por cerca de 3% do consumo nacional de eletricidade em 2036, aumentando a necessidade de fontes capazes de garantir fornecimento contínuo. Cinco economistas avaliam que o ajuste fiscal do governo Lula, voltado a alcançar superávit de 0,5% do PIB em 2027, é insuficiente para conter o crescimento da dívida pública, próxima de 83% do PIB. Entre as propostas estão mudanças na correção do salário mínimo, revisão dos pisos de gastos com saúde e educação e maior controle das despesas obrigatórias. As medidas buscam estabilizar a dívida e abrir espaço para a redução dos juros. O presidente do Federal Reserve de Kansas City, Jeff Schmid, afirmou neste domingo (15) que a inflação nos Estados Unidos permanece acima da meta de 2% e apresenta uma trajetória preocupante. Durante uma conferência no Havaí, Schmid destacou que o banco central possui instrumentos para controlar a alta dos preços, mas não defendeu explicitamente novos aumentos dos juros.

artigo.texto: A demora na regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) e a possibilidade de exigências ambientais excessivamente restritivas para o uso de gás natural podem comprometer a atração de investimentos para o Brasil. O alerta foi feito por Pietro Mendes, diretor da Agência Natural do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP), durante a Conferência Ibero-Brasileira de Energia (Coniben) 2026, realizada em Lisboa, em Portugal. Pietro também cobrou maior agilidade do governo na definição das regras do Redata, diante da competição internacional por investimentos em infraestrutura digital. “A gente vai perdendo oportunidade, vai perdendo investimento, aí sim o capital vai para outro lugar”, afirmou. Embora o gás natural já esteja contemplado na legislação do programa, Pietro Mendes criticou discussões sobre a adoção de critérios que condicionariam a participação das termelétricas a gás ao uso de tecnologias de captura e armazenamento de carbono (CCS) ou priorizariam o suprimento com biometano. Segundo ele, o biometano tem papel importante na transição energética, mas ainda não dispõe de escala de produção suficiente para atender à demanda de grandes termelétricas. Mendes ainda ressaltou que a definição de critérios muito restritivos pode penalizar o gás natural em um país cuja matriz elétrica já apresenta elevada participação de fontes renováveis. Segurança do suprimento No mesmo painel, Christiano Vieira, diretor de Regulação da Eneva, defendeu que a regulamentação do Redata considere não apenas a origem renovável da energia contratada pelos data centers, mas também os custos associados à segurança do suprimento. Segundo o executivo, os empreendimentos possuem demanda contínua de eletricidade, enquanto fontes como solar e eólica apresentam variações de produção ao longo do dia. Nesse cenário, mesmo que um data center contrate energia exclusivamente renovável, o sistema elétrico continuará precisando de recursos capazes de garantir o atendimento nos períodos de menor geração. “Não tem sentido você fazer um modelo energético só com renováveis […] e deixar a conta da segurança ser arcada por todos os usuários do sistema”, disse o diretor da Eneva. Para Christiano Vieira, a regulamentação deve preservar os objetivos de descarbonização do programa, mas também permitir que os empreendedores apresentem soluções competitivas de potência e confiabilidade, incluindo térmicas a gás natural e sistemas de armazenamento. O executivo citou como exemplo a instalação de data centers com demandas de 300 MW a 500 MW, que podem exigir recursos adicionais para assegurar o fornecimento de energia. As baterias também devem desempenhar um papel importante, especialmente na qualidade do suprimento para aplicações de inteligência artificial. No entanto, segundo ele, o armazenamento não elimina a necessidade de soluções capazes de sustentar o atendimento contínuo. Segundo Christiano, na integração entre gás e eletricidade, a Eneva consegue oferecer flexibilidade de atendimento por contar com produção própria de gás e infraestrutura de regaseificação, mas mecanismos semelhantes precisam ser viabilizados para outras usinas conectadas à malha de transporte. O executivo também defendeu tarifas de transporte competitivas e criticou tratamentos regulatórios diferenciados que favoreçam determinadas fontes sem necessariamente produzir ganhos de eficiência.

artigo.texto: A busca por maior autonomia e controle sobre informações corporativas sensíveis levou organizações brasileiras a intensificarem a alocação de cargas críticas em infraestruturas locais de computação em novembro de 2026, conforme avaliação divulgada pela fornecedora de data center e serviços gerenciados Global Gate. O movimento, sustentado por exigências crescentes de conformidade regulatória e mitigação de vulnerabilidades transfronteiriças, estabelece a soberania de dados como parâmetro central na tomada de decisões tecnológicas de alta gestão, superando o modelo de contratação pautado exclusivamente em custos nominais de armazenamento e disponibilidade. A discussão institucionalizada no ecossistema corporativo transcende o conceito básico de residência física de hardware. A soberania de dados compreende a capacidade irrestrita de uma organização estabelecer protocolos proprietários de acesso, determinar a governança do tratamento de ativos intangíveis e blindar operações contra legislações externas. Segundo a análise da empresa, oscilações nas relações diplomáticas, alterações em tratados de comércio internacional e revisões regulatórias em potências estrangeiras passaram a figurar na matriz de risco corporativo de companhias que mantêm sistemas dependentes de jurisdições externas. Geopolítica digital e riscos de extraterritorialidade O panorama macroeconômico global impõe desafios complexos aos departamentos de tecnologia da informação. Mecanismos normativos internacionais, a exemplo de legislações extraterritoriais que autorizam requisições governamentais de registros digitais independentemente da localização física de servidores multinacionais, aumentaram a insegurança jurídica entre corporações brasileiras. A interdependência de ecossistemas em nuvem pública operados fora do território nacional expõe operações estratégicas a sanções unilaterais, embargos tecnológicos ou alterações súbitas de termos de uso impostas por cortes estrangeiras. Para as companhias com atuação no mercado nacional, a adequação integral à Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD) e às exigências de órgãos fiscalizadores setoriais demanda previsibilidade na custódia de arquivos. A manutenção de ambientes digitais sob a autoridade jurídica exclusiva dos tribunais brasileiros simplifica auditorias e resguarda segredos industriais. Jean Jader Martins, diretor da Global Gate — divisão do Grupo Bludata, conglomerado com mais de quatro décadas de experiência tecnológica —, avalia que a evolução das prioridades corporativas decorre de uma readequação estrutural de portfólio. Conforme sustenta Martins, o processo decisório tradicional concentrava-se em métricas operacionais diretas de escala volumétrica e valor por gigabyte. Atualmente, os comitês de governança priorizam o conhecimento da cadeia de custódia, as credenciais de manipulação de dados e as garantias institucionais de conformidade. A proximidade física com o provedor e a transparência em relação aos protocolos de defesa cibernética constituem salvaguardas essenciais para a sustentabilidade e a continuidade operacional dos negócios. Pesquisa global reflete apreensão da liderança executiva A percepção de vulnerabilidade no ambiente digital não está restrita aos quadros técnicos de segurança da informação e engenharia de sistemas. Levantamento conduzido internacionalmente pela consultoria Everpure indicou que falhas ligadas à soberania de dados atingiram patamar crítico de responsabilização funcional. De acordo com o relatório, 88% dos executivos de nível C-level consideram que incidentes de inconformidade jurisdicional ou perda de controle regulatório sobre dados podem culminar na rescisão de seus próprios contratos de trabalho. A mesma sondagem apontou que 91% dos líderes entrevistados temem repercussões financeiras severas e prejuízos duradouros à reputação corporativa em decorrência de eventos associados à custódia irregular de informações. O receio de desvalorização de marca e imposição de multas regulatórias catalisa a revisão de arquiteturas corporativas de nuvem, impulsionando a busca por parceiros locais capazes de assegurar atendimento a marcos legais locais. Parâmetros técnicos de infraestrutura e padrões Tier III A migração para centros de processamento nacionais requer garantias técnicas de tolerância a falhas e contingência operacional contínua. Para viabilizar a hospedagem de cargas críticas sem interrupções operacionais, o mercado B2B direciona investimentos para instalações certificadas pelo padrão Tier III do Uptime Institute. Esta classificação atesta a existência de manutenção concorrente, assegurando que qualquer componente de distribuição de energia ou climatização possa ser reparado ou substituído sem a paralisação dos sistemas de processamento. Dentro desse arranjo estrutural, a fornecedora reporta a operação de dois centros de dados desenhados para atender sistemas de alta sensibilidade. O primeiro complexo está localizado em Blumenau (SC), constituindo o primeiro data center do estado catarinense a receber a certificação Tier III. O segundo ponto de presença atua na região metropolitana de Vinhedo (SP), oferecendo redundância geográfica e capacidade de balanceamento de carga para clientes corporativos de diversas regiões industriais do país. - Residência jurídica estrita: Salvaguarda contratual e técnica de que os volumes armazenados respondem exclusivamente ao ordenamento processual e civil brasileiro. - Arquiteturas de Disaster Recovery: Rotinas de contingência automatizadas entre sítios remotos com baixa latência, reduzindo o tempo de recuperação (RTO) e o ponto de recuperação (RPO). - Isolamento de nuvem privada: Estruturas dedicadas que mitigam os riscos de ataques laterais comuns a ambientes compartilhados hiperconvergentes. - SLA de sustentação assistida: Suporte técnico local com responsabilidade única sobre hardware, conectividade e segurança de borda. artigo.texto: Pulaski County Judge-elect Wendell Griffen has asked to intervene in a federal lawsuit brought by a company working to build a $6 billion data center near Wrightsville. AVAIO Digital, the company behind the data center, sued Pulaski County in federal court over an ordinance the Quorum Court passed recently, saying they would be harmed if the measure, which puts limits on the construction and operation of huge industrial sites, goes into effect. On top of the lawsuit, AVAIO filed a request for a temporary injunction in an attempt to stop the ordinance from being implemented while the case is under consideration. Griffen said he should be allowed to intervene because AVAIO’s lawsuit will be his responsibility in just a few weeks. “I am the county judge-elect and on Jan. 1, I will be legally obligated to defend the implementation of that ordinance,” he said in an interview on Monday. “Between now and Jan. 1, I need to be able to see how the county is defending against the lawsuit, which I believe is baseless and without merit.” The case is before U.S. District Court Judge Lee Rudofsky, who is scheduled to hear the arguments relating to the temporary injunction order on Friday. The ordinance was passed in September and then vetoed by County Judge Barry Hyde, who gave a number of reasons for his action, including that he thought the ordinance opened the county to legal action. The Quorum Court, however, was able to override Hyde’s veto. Griffen used Hyde’s stance as another reason to be allowed to intervene. “The incumbent County Judge’s opposition to the Ordinance creates a potential divergence between the current administration’s litigation position and the interests of the incoming administration,” Griffen wrote in his request to the court. In hopes of being allowed to intervene, Griffen also readied his legal position further, filing another two motions, one addressing a rebuttal to AVAIO’s argument for a temporary injunction and the other a paragraph-by-paragraph response to AVAIO’s lawsuit. At this point, Griffen said in his response to the temporary injunction request, there is no reason to seek injunctive relief. “The county has not implemented the ordinance, meaning there has not been a stop-work order so their construction is continuing as we speak,” Griffen said.

artigo.texto: Last December, a Wythe County Board of Supervisors meeting was standing room only. Residents at the time said they were blindsided by the announcement of the first data center in the county, to be built on public land in an industrial park. The following year involved the announcement of a second, bigger data center on private land, sparking fears from local opponents that more were on the way. After an open house with one of the data center developers in October, many said they were still searching for answers. “Our ecosystems in Southwest Virginia are what make us so special,” said Maranda Edwards, a Wytheville resident, while at the open house. “We need to preserve that. People like looking out their windows and seeing the deer. With data centers, that’s going to go away, and that’s frustrating to know.” For Edwards and her family members, who live out in the county, zoning regulations could have shone light on plans for the data centers before they were a done deal, she said. Wythe County is one of a handful of localities in Virginia that has no zoning codes. Data centers — or any other development — can be built on private land without public notice or government intervention aside from state permitting in limited circumstances. As of early November, the process to put codes in place has been progressing at the urging of dozens of county residents who say they want the regulations to act as a deterrent for data center developers. Several said that as conservatives who otherwise wouldn’t want zoning implemented, they see a need for it in their community because of data centers. Across several counties in Southwest Virginia, a similar movement has taken root in meeting halls where officials have stressed the importance of getting specific data center zoning ordinances on the books. Most residents who speak at their public meetings have said they agree their localities need rules for data centers, though some are skeptical of their efficacy and have asked for multi-year moratoriums. No locality in Southwest Virginia has enacted a moratorium so far. For local governments, data centers can be a source of millions of dollars in property tax revenue, and some local officials have said they don’t want to write them off entirely. Wythe County zoning In early November, the Wythe County Planning Commission voted 5-2 to send its drafted ordinance and map for a board of supervisors public hearing, the next step in a process to get zoning codes on record. The commission recommended a July 1 implementation date. A vote on the ordinance and the map would occur after the public hearing, which hasn’t been scheduled yet. The process started several years ago before data centers became a major concern for people in Wythe County, according to Matt Hankins, deputy county administrator. At the time, it was another major type of development rankling residents: solar farms. In 2023, solar farm companies began building on hundreds of acres in the county, to the chagrin of residents around them, Hankins said in an interview. After looking at the options, he found the only way the county could make it possible to regulate solar farms on a local level was by enacting zoning codes. “We’ve had that conversation,” he said. “As part of it, residents said, ‘We’ve looked at zoning before. Come back to us with a light-touch ordinance that respects personal property rights and gives us some level of input and management over these projects as they come in.’” The data center issue is similar in nature to solar farms, he said, and has motivated groups of residents to advocate for zoning. The ordinance he and his team have worked on isn’t perfect, Hankins said, but it reflects the character of the county and the end goal of putting it in place, which is to ensure public input for major changes to the county’s landscape. The new codes would require a special exceptions permit for data centers, according to the draft document, which involves a public hearing and a vote from the board of supervisors. They would be allowed in commercial and industrial zones. Though some have called for a complete ban, Hankins said that it’s not legal to strike a particular use of private property from all areas of the county. The two data centers already in the works will also have to be grandfathered into the new codes, Hankins said. Wythe County residents have organized protests and spoken in droves at public meetings over the past year, asking for a way to halt the development of the data centers that have already been announced. They’ve voiced concerns over potential environmental impacts to the air and water, and the damage to their rural quality of life, if large-scale processing centers are built near their homes. At a public hearing hosted by the planning commission in late October, the majority of 17 people who spoke said they were in favor of zoning, specifically to protect the county from data centers. Those who were against zoning said they did not believe the codes would be protective enough against data centers to warrant restrictions on what they could do with their property. “Maybe we do need zoning to keep them out,” said Virginia Riggins, a county resident, during the October hearing. “But if they’re already here, it’s too late. Too little too late.” But for others, the possibility of Wythe County becoming a hotspot for dozens of data centers is the primary fear. Andrew Kegley has lived in the county for 46 years, he said in an interview. Like some, he believes the zoning has come too late, he said, but he is relieved it’s close to the finish line. He thinks it’s a dire need before other data center developers begin to see the county as a place to build without friction from the local government. artigo.texto: Soneil Spark revela Sistema Móvel de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias rebocável na RE+ 2026 A Soneil Spark apresentou esta semana seu Sistema Móvel de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias, uma unidade de bateria modular portátil instalada em um reboque rebocável, segundo a Solar Power World. A empresa, que oferece soluções modulares de energia sob medida, exibe o produto na RE+ 2026. O Mobile BESS foi projetado para fornecer energia de reserva temporária e energia fora da rede, captando eletricidade da rede elétrica, de um gerador ou de fontes solares. Sonya Jain, diretora-executiva da empresa, afirmou em comunicado que a energia acompanha o negócio aonde ele for e que a unidade pode ser rebocada até locais onde a demanda por energia cresce; os clientes podem começar com uma única unidade e acrescentar outras conforme as necessidades mudarem, acrescentou ela. A Soneil Spark descreveu a instalação como simples, sem necessidade de guindaste, valas ou espera por interligação à rede elétrica. A empresa posiciona o sistema para canteiros de obras que podem estar a meses de receber o serviço permanente, sets de filmagem e eventos em que o ruído e a fumaça dos geradores são problemáticos, equipes de concessionárias que restabelecem a energia após tempestades e minas ou fazendas remotas além do alcance da rede. Em locais que já usam geradores, o Mobile BESS se sincroniza com eles para cobrir picos e lacunas de partida, permitindo que os geradores operem por menos horas. Em locais onde o uso de diesel é restrito, a empresa afirmou que a unidade oferece uma alternativa silenciosa. Diferentemente do armazenamento em contêineres, destinado a ser instalado uma única vez, o Mobile BESS foi construído para ser rebocado e operar em qualquer clima, segundo a empresa. Entre as aplicações-alvo estão locação de geradores e equipamentos, construção civil, energia de emergência e de reserva, concessionárias, empreiteiras elétricas, eventos, cinema e entretenimento, além de locais fora da rede, como mineração e agricultura. Uma opção híbrida acrescenta a recarga de veículos elétricos. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado global de acumuladores elétricos, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. artigo.texto: AI companies are missing a key reason people hate data centers: They’re ugly Of all of the millions of dollars being spent on these sites, barely anything is allocated to visual design. The U.S. is experiencing a huge boom in AI investment, and data centers are at the epicenter. But amid power outages, criticisms around water usage, and moral quandaries, the infrastructure is facing intense backlash from communities earmarked for site development. The new AI Infrastructure Coalition (AIIC)—a trade organization whose members include Google, Meta, Microsoft, and other tech giants—hopes that pledges to limit resource use, prioritize local hiring, and invest in community projects will ease the mounting friction. But all this forgets one crucial thing: People don’t want to live next to eyesores. Of all of the millions of dollars that data center developers are spending on these structures, barely anything is allocated to their visual design. And while I would expect the largest expenses to be what they are—AI servers, electrical and power infrastructure, cooling systems, and labor—the buildings’ aesthetics mustn’t be sidelined. Far more time and money must be spent on this part of the equation. Otherwise, AI companies risk simply adding to the growing list of reasons to resist construction. Neighborhoods are already resisting development and the backlash is reaching the leading data center locations. In Texas, for example, Governor Greg Abbott has gone so far as to implement a statewide moratorium requiring an energy audit for AI companies, halting grid approvals in the meantime. And the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has said she’ll go farther, with a moratorium until the legislature passes new data center laws “to protect Texans.” AI companies and developers will need to get creative to deal with the scale of the challenge, and while I accept that improving how centers look may not solve everything, investing more in their visual appeal would certainly help. Because, fundamentally, people tend to view nicer-looking things more favorably. We are superficial creatures, and psychological researchers have even found that people attribute greater moral standing to animals, objects, and buildings that they perceive as more beautiful. Data centers could certainly do with that boost. Current designs tend to have the opposite effect. Huge gray commercial units are simply not nice to look at, and economically speaking, can spark homeowner concerns about whether they’ll be able to sell their property if they choose to. Owners are already on edge, given that home sales are down, and property delistings—sellers pulling homes off the market—are hitting near-record rates. At a time when the residential market is volatile, the arrival of a massive gray industrial unit is even more unlikely to be welcomed. It matters to everyone in the local area because Americans have a deep-rooted sense of pride in their communities, especially the way they look. The look and feel of a town really makes a difference to the people who live there, and I regularly see just how much pride a homeowner takes in having a pristine, clean-cut lawn or an aesthetically pleasing home exterior. It is why Homeowners Associations (HOAs) keep popping up. Nationwide there are more than 370,000 communities managed by HOAs, encompassing more than 77 million residents. These HOAs set guidelines for home appearance and waste management, among other matters. The associations take maintaining standards very seriously. Nearly half of all HOA violations are based on landscaping or architectural concerns, and they are met with penalties and fines. It could not be clearer to me that residents care deeply about these kinds of design elements—and that data center developers are missing an easy win with local communities by overlooking sites’ aesthetics. Putting more thought into the building’s shape, ensuring the entrance has a well-maintained lawn and foliage, or making architectural modifications that match other local buildings can make a meaningful difference in how a site looks. And it could go a long way toward making residents more amenable to them. Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying that enhancing visual design will lead to a U-turn in public opinion. There are still plenty of resource-driven concerns that I know will worry communities far more than the building’s exterior. But, by and large, the AIIC is trying to addressing these concerns in its recent pledges. What developers, and the AIIC for that matter, are missing is the aesthetic consideration. It carries a surprising amount of weight, and given that the leading states for data center development—Virginia and Texas—are also home to some of the largest numbers of HOA communities, it cannot be left to fly under the radar any longer. Beautifying data centers is the low-hanging fruit that could help shift the dial back in developers’ favor. Without it, the appearance of these ugly buildings will steadily add more fuel to the flames, with communities continuing to resist construction in their backyards.

artigo.texto: ROCHESTER — A timeline for a temporary moratorium on data center development in Rochester remains uncertain. “I don’t expect it to take longer than a year, and our hope is to get there sooner,” Community Development Director Irene Woodward told the Rochester City Council during a roughly 90-minute review of the proposal Monday. ADVERTISEMENT The council voted 5-1 to approve the moratorium, making way for staff study of potential data center impacts, along with developing definitions and guidelines for future development. The development pause begins with official notice of approval. “It gives us the opportunity to define the application process,” Woodward said, noting the goal is to ensure the community and developers know what is possible and what the development process entails. Council member Shaun Palmer, who cast the sole vote against the moratorium, questioned whether existing model ordinances could be adopted in an effort to reduce the potential timeline to three months. Woodward said model ordinances will be reviewed, but it will take time to tweak one, if used, since staff must ensure it meets community expectations and fits within the city’s unified development code without causing new conflicts. Council member Dan Doering said time is needed, but the move doesn’t mean data centers won’t be allowed under revised ordinances. “It’s not about automatically saying no to them,” he said. “It’s about fully knowing the pros and cons before making a long-term decision that could have a profound impact on our community.” ADVERTISEMENT Woodward said the city cannot outright ban data centers, but regulations can ensure development fits community expectations. While the process for developing future regulations is expected to involve public engagement efforts, the City Council heard concerns from both sides of the issue Monday. With 11 people speaking during a public hearing, the majority encouraged the council to support the moratorium as presented by staff, voicing concerns about environmental impacts and development issues seen in other communities, including Pine Island. “I am pleased that you are looking at this proactively and not just waiting until a center is on our doorstep and a deal is already made and proposed,” Rochester resident Mary Vlazny told the council. Evan Vlaeminck, an asset manager for the Rochester Technology Campus, which sits on the former IBM campus, said he’s concerned the moratorium could harm existing businesses needing to expand their data centers during the moratorium period. “A year is a very long time, certainly with respect to business,” he said. “Many deals can come and go in that time.” Council member Andy Friederichs suggested limiting the moratorium to new development, making way for expansion, but the proposal failed to get the needed support. ADVERTISEMENT The moratorium allows existing operations to operate and adapt to changing needs, but it’s also intended to be broad enough to rule out expansions that could transform existing facilities into something beyond their existing scope. Woodward said existing Rochester data centers were developed before the city implemented its new development code in 2023, and no applications for development or expansions are under city review. Whether an expansion would be restricted by the moratorium would depend on several factors, she said, noting a building permit application would spur a review to determine if the proposed work is allowed. She said the uncertainty related to requirements in existing code is what prompted the moratorium and planned study of data center impacts. “There are different ways to define a data center, and that is what we don’t have clearly defined,” she said. The temporary pause on potential development is the latest effort throughout the state. Egan lays claim to being the first Minnesota city to enact a temporary moratorium on development of new data centers. The Feb. 17 Eagan City Council decision came as four data centers were under construction in the Twin Cities suburb with a population of nearly 69,000. ADVERTISEMENT Meanwhile, a split Minneapolis City Council took action on Nov. 12 to approve new development rules, which will require council approval for individual data centers after proposals are made. The decision follows a review that included a five-month moratorium, which was implemented in June. Woodward said Rochester’s moratorium is designed to end earlier, if the council approves updates to the city’s development code. “We are planning to keep this moving,” she said of the timeline and state statute that allows a one-year moratorium with the possibility of requesting an 18-month extension. “If we bring back an ordinance before that time, the moratorium would expire.”

artigo.texto: By Lucia Yu, Senior Manager of Development, Key Capture Energy MANORVILLE – Long Islanders opened their electric bills this year to increases of up to 20%. The state’s grid operator forecasts that Long Island’s power grid will be operating with very slim margins starting in 2027. Battery energy storage is one of the fastest ways to help address both rising costs and the risk of blackouts. Key Capture Energy is developing battery energy storage projects across Long Island, including KCE NY 37 in Manorville. The two questions our team hears the most are “why here?” and “is battery energy storage safe?” Why Long Island? Long Island’s grid connections to the rest of the state are stretched thin, and getting energy here can be a challenge, especially on summer afternoons and evenings when air conditioners and appliances are all running at once. That raises the risk of blackouts on an island that has already seen its share of outages. In February, a winter storm knocked out power for nearly 50,000 Long Island residents and just a few months later, heavy wind and rain resulted in blackouts and brownouts that impacted more than 10,000 customers. Without continued investment in the grid, even standard weather events could become increasingly difficult for Long Island’s electric grid to manage. Storage is uniquely able to address both costs and the potential of electrical shortfalls. Batteries charge when power is cheap and plentiful and store it for when it’s needed, like on hot summer afternoons that are the hours that strain the grid and drive up prices. That’s why New York set a goal of 6 gigawatts of storage by 2030, a buildout that State regulators have said could save nearly $2 billion in system costs. KCE NY 37 is a part of that buildout. In September, NYSERDA selected it as one of eight projects in the state’s first bulk energy storage solicitation. It will provide millions of dollars in local taxes, union construction wages and other community benefits. Is battery energy storage safe? Simply put, yes. There are roughly 1,000 large scale projects like KCE NY 37 operating across the country and since today’s modern safety testing codes have been in place, the occurrence of fires at BESS facilities has plummeted. Here in New York, the state updated its fire code to be one of the strictest in the country. Today, every project must undergo an independent third-party safety review during the local permitting process to ensure these updated codes are met and develop an Emergency Response Plan in coordination with the local fire department. Developers are also required to offer training for local first responders prior to a facility starting operations and annually afterwards. KCE has met with the Manorville Fire Department and Brookhaven fire officials to discuss the project. We look forward to ongoing dialogue with local emergency personnel to finalize a comprehensive emergency response plan and address any outstanding questions. These steps and the pre-operational fire department training will ensure that first responders are equipped and ready in the very unlikely event of a safety incident at the facility. New York’s fire leaders have said again and again that battery storage is safe when it is built to New York’s updated code. Residents are also right to ask what the 2023 East Hampton battery storage fire means for their community, particularly after PFAS contamination was found in nearby groundwater. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) is continuing to investigate that contamination, but its preliminary findings identify the facility’s fire suppression system, rather than its batteries, as the likely source of any contamination. That system used Novec 1230, a chemical fire-extinguishing agent that can break down into a PFAS compound if combined with water. KCE NY 37 and our projects across Long Island will not use Novec 1230 or a similar suppression agent. Unlike East Hampton’s indoor facility, which also utilized an older battery chemistry called nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC), KCE’s projects will use outdoor systems with lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries built to New York’s updated fire safety codes. Everyone should be confident in the safety of today’s modern BESS systems, including KCE NY 37, because they incorporate the lessons learned from incidents like the East Hampton fire and are specifically designed to prevent and mitigate the impacts of a fire, in the rare case one were to happen. Battery energy storage built to New York’s updated safety codes is safe. It can ease Long Island’s energy challenges, help stabilize electric bills, and ensure businesses and households have the reliable grid needed to power Long Island’s economy. Lucia Yu is Senior Manager of Development at Key Capture Energy (KCE). KCE is a battery energy storage developer and operator headquartered in Albany with projects across New York.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery maker CATL opens office in Argentina — South China Morning Post Chinese battery manufacturer Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd (CATL) has opened a commercial office in Argentina, South China Morning Post reports, citing Argentine media. The company plans to use it to expand supplies of energy storage systems. CATL already supplies batteries for the country’s largest electricity storage project and has presented its solutions to 35 companies interested in a government tender. Last week, CATL representatives met in Buenos Aires with generating companies and banks. The company said it intends to become the leading supplier of energy storage systems in Argentina. The office is also expected to become a base for developing storage projects for mining enterprises, data centers and wind power plants in Patagonia. Projects and tenders Argentina’s largest private electricity producer, Central Puerto, uses CATL cells in two projects with a combined capacity of 205 MW. Construction of the larger one, the 150 MW Nuevo Puerto facility, is about 80% complete. Commercial operation is planned to begin in mid-December under a 15-year contract with distribution company Edenor. Last year, Argentine authorities announced the first tender for 500 MW of energy storage systems near Buenos Aires to reduce the number of power supply disruptions. Due to high demand, contracts were concluded for 713 MW: they were signed directly with distributors, while Cammesa, which manages the wholesale electricity market, acted as guarantor. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. In July, Argentina’s Energy Secretariat allocated another 700.5 MW among 20 projects in other regions of the country. The auction received 235 technical applications, and the estimated investment volume amounted to $700 million. Average prices were about a quarter lower than in the first round. Renewable energy developer Genneia received 421 MW, or about 60% of the total volume. Financing in yuan Financing remains one of the main issues for market participants, as battery containers are imported from China. Christian Damonaz of the Argentine unit of Bank of China proposed lending in yuan and said that this currency offers acceptable rates and stability against the US dollar. ICBC’s Argentine unit provided Genneia with 358.8 million yuan, or $50 million, last year for renewable energy projects. CATL also reported that its revenue from energy storage systems rose 87.5% year-on-year in the first half of the year. According to Harry Lau, the company’s representative in Latin America, CATL has contracts in the region for more than 15 GWh of energy storage systems, including for the Oasis de Atacama project in Chile.

artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — A leaked Ohio bill could allow data centers to qualify as "public utilities," giving them the ability to seize private property. Ohioans rejected data centers on every ballot measure this election, but after that massive loss, Republican lawmakers may be moving to allow tech hubs one way or another. For decades, Gretchan Francis has been fighting to keep her multigenerational family farm. "It's not the farm that it once was," Francis said in an interview. "It's only 60 acres; it's not 160 acres." Using eminent domain law, which allows the government to take property for public use, the state has seized her land numerous times for highway development. "I understand that it is necessary, but I think it has to be done in the right way," she said. While ODOT has always been able to do this, farmers like her are fearing that new legislation would take their livelihoods for a controversial cause. A draft bill leaked to us exclusively would expand the list of who qualifies to take land. The draft changes the definition of "public utility," from just an entity being owned or operated by municipal corporations, an electric cooperative and an agency holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The legislation adds "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities." This could mean a transmission developer may be able to seize land to power or place a data center, according to legal experts. "That would be devastating," Francis said. "I think anybody would feel the same way if their personal land was taken for a data center. That sounds like it's a corporate, private, for-profit type of need, not for a public need." In June, we discovered that the Ohio Business Roundtable, a powerful trade group that lobbies at the Statehouse, recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law, and “should extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.” RELATED: Ohio farmers fear new proposal would allow data centers to take property The Ohio Farm Bureau, which is adamantly against changing eminent domain, had been preparing for this fight since. "We are aware of efforts to further erode the limited protections that landowners have, allowing for quick take of property without first paying for the property and determining a landowner’s rights and compensation through a court of law," the Bureau’s Evan Callicoat said. The Farm Bureau isn't opposed to data centers, but they are opposed to a violation of property rights, Callicoat said. He feared that with this proposed idea, it's broad enough that farmers could lose their land to data centers, not getting paid for it for months or years. The Roundtable calls the program "deposit and build," and it's modeled after a system that 45 other states use. "This recommendation is about making sure that Ohio's grid is reliable and affordable for Ohioans and that economic development can continue in the state," the Roundtable's Alexandra Denney said in an interview Monday. The Ohio Power Siting Board controls the installation of utility facilities, including power lines, some gas pipelines, and wind farms. The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio can also help utility companies acquire land. A utility will approach a homeowner for land and must provide them with a "fair" market price. If the owner refuses to sell, the utility company will take them to court and will need to determine "necessity" for the land. If a court sides with the utility company, deeming it necessary to take, the appraised value of the land is given to a court account. However, the owner can appeal this decision to fight for more money. While this court battle is going on, construction is not allowed to begin. The draft bill changes the appraisal process, making it easier to seize land immediately. "Ratepayers and Ohioans are paying the price because it's driving up costs and it's also delaying the critical infrastructure that we need to have a reliable grid," Denney said about construction delays. While Denney was aware of the appraisal portion of the legislation, she categorically denied any changes to eminent domain. After I read the bill out loud, she said she would need to "look at" the changes in the definition of public utilities. She said that Ohioans choosing to restrict or ban data centers in 21 different cities has nothing to do with the timing of this proposal. "That is not the intent of the Ohio Business Roundtable to expand the ability to use eminent domain to anybody that doesn't already have that ability," Denney said. Soon-to-be Senate President Republican Bill Reineke (R-Tiffin), who is working on the bill, echoed her sentiment. “We keep talking about lowering costs, and one way we can do that is expanding infrastructure for public utilities to keep rates down. That’s what this is about," Reineke said in a statement. "It’s important to me that landowners keep their rights, and this would not extend eminent domain to anyone who doesn’t already have that privilege — rather, it is a framework to simplify our existing process that would put us in line with 45 other states." He added that one of his top focuses was to make sure there was enough energy and lower costs. But the legislation does specifically change who is considered a public utility, both for electrical transmission and for gas. Even without being a private electric transmitter who applies for a certificate, Francis believes it is feasible that a utility company can help take land in order to power a data center. artigo.texto: Data centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard | Vero NotíciasData centers dos EUA emitem tanto CO₂ quanto a Dinamarca, aponta Harvard Os 403 maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos emitiram 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, volume equivalente às emissões anuais da Dinamarca, segundo estudo da Universidade de Harvard. Publicado nesta segunda-feira (16) na revista Nature Sustainability, o levantamento aponta que as emissões desses centros de dados triplicaram desde 2018, impulsionando preocupações sobre o impacto ambiental da infraestrutura digital. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa concentraram mais da metade do consumo de eletricidade analisado. Segundo os pesquisadores, a maioria dos centros utilizava energia gerada a gás, e o estudo busca ampliar a transparência sobre os impactos ambientais da inteligência artificial. Um estudo do Ministério da Fazenda estima que a aprovação do projeto de lei que regulamenta economicamente as big techs pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas brasileiras. Os valores representam entre 0,1% e 0,4% do PIB. O levantamento, elaborado pela Secretaria de Reformas Econômicas, analisou 20 segmentos do mercado digital, incluindo comércio eletrônico, publicidade, aplicativos de transporte e inteligência artificial. Os setores movimentaram cerca de R$ 410 bilhões em 2025. O Ministério da Fazenda estima que ampliar a concorrência entre plataformas digitais pode gerar benefícios de R$ 15,3 bilhões a R$ 50,6 bilhões anuais para consumidores e empresas, com menores preços e comissões. O estudo avalia um projeto que amplia os instrumentos do Cade para fiscalizar grandes plataformas e combater barreiras à concorrência. O texto tramita com urgência na Câmara e aguarda votação no plenário. O ajuste fiscal pode reduzir em R$ 280 milhões os recursos destinados a projetos esportivos, estimam as organizações Atletas pelo Brasil e Instituto Esporte e Educação. As entidades divulgaram comunicado contra a medida. O projeto amplia de 10% para 20% o corte linear de benefícios tributários. As organizações pedem que a Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte seja excluída da redução para preservar o financiamento dos projetos. O Ibovespa caiu 1,83% nesta segunda-feira (16), aos 169.295,41 pontos, em meio a preocupações com as contas públicas brasileiras e ao aumento da aversão ao risco nos mercados internacionais. Investidores avaliam se o pacote fiscal será suficiente para estabilizar as contas. O Morgan Stanley reduziu sua recomendação para o Brasil e projetou o Ibovespa em 160 mil pontos no fim de 2027. O secretário especial da Receita Federal, Robinson Barreirinhas, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (16) que o projeto de ajuste fiscal não restringe os créditos tributários da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS). Segundo Barreirinhas, os créditos da CBS continuarão podendo ser compensados. O texto permite restringir outras compensações tributárias caso o governo esteja distante da meta fiscal, incluindo créditos ligados a benefícios fiscais.

artigo.texto: The Hidden Efficiency Gap in Data Center Containment The Gap Nobody Budgeted For Data center operators measure nearly everything to ensure efficiency at the highest level, from inlet temperatures to rack density, airflow per kilowatt to PUE. Yet an unobtrusive gap above the hot contained aisle or missing roof above the cold contained aisle has been leaking conditioned air, forcing the cooling system to work harder than it needs to be, driving up cooling costs since the day the facility was commissioned. And no one has been measuring its detriment to performance. It’s easy to miss. The open seam sits at ceiling height for HAC or above the racks for CAC and is barely perceptible to some. However, the gap rarely appears on an efficiency dashboard, because it’s not an oversight nor a design defect. The gap is a deliberate allowance, that’s been quietly shaping the cooling bill of almost every contained facility that has relied on it. The real story is not that the gap exists. It’s why the industry has treated it as an unavoidable compromise. Why the Gap Exists The open seam above the hot aisle containment or missing roof above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment is a result of fire code, not a construction fault. In the United States, a combination of national model codes, specialized National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) regulations 13 (installation of sprinkler systems) and 75 (protection of IT equipment) standards, along with the International Fire Code plus state or local municipal amendments enforced by local Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJs), regulate data center fire safety. A sprinkler can only protect what its water spray can reach. Fire code mandates require the unobstructed dispersal of sprinkler heads to protect the space, and a he ad that is blocked, shadowed, or poorly positioned may fail to control the fire. The problem is that a fully sealed ceiling impedes sprinkler coverage. It can be done. The sprinkler layout could be designed at the same time as the rack, tray, and containment layout rather than afterward. But this would require renewed verification and approvals after any increase or relocation of racks and cabinets, change of cable trays or busways, additional lighting or cooling lines, or modification of containment and airflow. With the rapid evolution of AI racks, adding higher-density or higher-power equipment (such as liquid cooling or battery systems) also changes the hazard classification and can trigger additional requirements. To adhere to fire code and not impede sprinkler coverage, data center designers made the easier call and left a gap. It is a reasonable, safety-first decision that allows for adaptation and refitting as and when required. It is also one that operators have paid for ever since, in wasted cooling energy. The industry has long treated this as a fixed trade-off between containment and compliance. While that choice has protected facilities, safety and efficiency have been set against each other, and efficiency has lost by default. This trade-off has gone unchallenged for years, because no one could offer containment that fire protection engineers and code officials would accept as fully sealed. What the Gap Costs at Scale Containment has one job: to keep hot exhaust air and cold supply air from mixing. Every pathway that lets them meet forces the cooling plant to compensate. It matters more than its size suggests. The loss is not a one-off event to be fixed after an incident. It is a constant, built into the facility's operating cost from the first day of operation. Sealed When it Should Be The answer is a contained cold or hot aisle that stays fully sealed in normal operation and changes its behavior in an emergency. Two components work together to make that possible: - A melting fuse plug with airflow flaps: A sealed ceiling with airflow flaps that under normal operating conditions stay closed. If aisle temperatures rise, the melting fuse plug is activated, opening the airflow flaps releasing hot air to the sprinkler activation. - Dissolving panels: When the sprinklers activate, the EPA approved non-combustible panels dissolve on contact with water; sprinkler discharge is never blocked and panels never fall, so there is no obstruction to egress. The principle is simple: containment is in full effect when conditions are normal, but when safety requires the space, the flaps and dissolving panels combine, giving operators efficiency when they need it and safety when it counts. Reviewed and Approved Promising efficiency gains in a life-safety context can often lead to mistrust. Efficiency improvements that cannot demonstrate fire code compliance are not improvements at all. They are liabilities waiting to surface during inspection, or worse, during an incident. Most efficiency gains ask a lot: major capital, long downtime or a redesign from the ground up. The distinction here is that this is not a workaround. It is a design that has been reviewed and approved directly by fire protection engineers and AHJs. It also works for both new builds and legacy facilities. - New builds can specify either fully sealed hot or cold aisles with airflow flaps from the outset, so the gap is never created. - Legacy facilities can close a leak or add a roof system over the cold aisle that has existed since commissioning, without rethinking the architecture. In both cases the result is the same: fully sealed hot aisles with airflow flaps that meet fire code without compromising safety. Compliant Containment The hot aisle seam above hot aisle containment and missing roof system above the cold aisle for cold aisle containment has been tolerated for as long as it was thought to be the price of compliance, but that reasoning no longer holds. Each day these openings stay open is another day of avoidable cooling cost. artigo.texto: Publicidade Receba notícias do Congresso em Foco: Relações exteriores Congresso em Foco 16/11/2026 15:52 O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos passou a exigir licença do governo norte-americano para exportação, reexportação ou transferência de semicondutores avançados de inteligência artificial destinados ao Brasil. A nova regra, divulgada nesta segunda-feira (16) pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão responsável pelos controles de exportação, também alcança Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Segundo o governo dos Estados Unidos, os cinco países foram incluídos na nova exigência por apresentarem um risco considerado "acima do normal" de que equipamentos avançados de computação sejam desviados para empresas ou países submetidos a controles norte-americanos. A medida atinge chips de alto desempenho utilizados, entre outras aplicações, na infraestrutura necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas avançados de inteligência artificial. Os pedidos de licença envolvendo os cinco países serão analisados individualmente pelas autoridades norte-americanas, que avaliarão se a operação pode contrariar interesses de segurança nacional ou de política externa dos Estados Unidos. Há ainda uma exceção para determinadas operações cujo usuário final seja uma empresa sediada nos EUA ou controlada por uma companhia norte-americana, desde que sejam cumpridas exigências de informação ao governo. A regra faz parte de uma ofensiva mais ampla do governo dos Estados Unidos para impedir que empresas de países sujeitos a restrições, especialmente aquelas vinculadas a destinos classificados no grupo D:5, tenham acesso indireto à capacidade computacional de chips norte-americanos. O grupo inclui países como China, Rússia, Irã e Coreia do Norte. O governo norte-americano identificou como uma das preocupações o uso de data centers instalados em terceiros países. Nesse modelo, uma empresa impedida de comprar diretamente determinados semicondutores poderia acessar remotamente a capacidade de processamento de equipamentos instalados em outro território. O Departamento de Comércio afirma que a nova norma busca fechar essa possibilidade e aproximar as regras de acesso remoto das restrições já aplicadas ao envio físico da tecnologia. Tags Temas

artigo.texto: A movement opposing data center development in Rapid City appears to be gaining momentum in City Hall. Put simply, residents pressed the City Council with two options: halt data centers in the community or face potential recall petitions. As City Hall packed Monday night, citizens broke decorum standards, applauding, cheering and offering City Council an ultimatum. No one spoke in favor of data center development at the meeting. Several called back to advocate Jeff Shelton’s comments last week, pushing for a year-long moratorium on the matter, some threatening potential recall petitions, and recommending Council put the matter on the agenda at the Monday meeting. This comes as Council was considering but ultimately pushed back ordinances tied to data center development. Justin Huntley is the former flood plan and air quality manager for the city. He said it’s time to act. “Part of the programs I was involved with – we worked on the data center ordinance," Huntley said. "A lot of people put a lot of time into that. By delaying that ordinance, you’re leaving the window open for things to happen that nobody in this city wants. I would just ask that you, immediately, either approve the ordinance as written and amend it as needed, or apply the moratorium as soon as possible.” Resident Gabbi DeMarce said it simply doesn’t have to be this way. “You are looking at only a fraction of residents in Rapid City that do not support decisions made that subsidize, support, or depend on harmful, unnecessary projects like data centers, simply because it has always been that way," DeMarce said. "I urge you all to extend this moratorium. You have nothing to lose from data center companies and everything to lose in public trust and support.” A recent, Council-backed survey of residents found deep seeded opposition to data center development. Resident Taylor Gunhammer’s impassioned plea perhaps best reflects the growing tension in Council chambers. “It’s not Peter Thiel’s community, it’s not Elon Musk’s community, and we won’t stand for you selling it to them – we don’t want it," Gunhammer said. "We, the people, are not the hammer in your hand, you are the hammer in ours. If you serve the people of this community, as you claim to, there is nothing to discuss. We gave our ruling. You don’t have one. You work for us.” Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun has called upon the Council to act quickly. Council ultimately did not motion put the matter on the Monday night agenda.

artigo.texto: Waaree Energy Storage Solutions Private Limited, a subsidiary of Waaree Energies Limited, has successfully commissioned a new battery pack manufacturing line. The newly established facility, boasting an annual installed capacity of 5.15 GWh, is located at the company's factory in Rola, Valsad, Gujarat. The announcement was made on 14 November 2026, as per a regulatory filing with the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE). This move marks a significant milestone for Waaree Energies, positioning the company to enhance its capacity in the rapidly growing energy storage sector. The addition of this facility is expected to bolster the company's production capabilities and meet the rising demand for energy storage solutions. Waaree Energies Limited is known for its strong presence in the renewable energy sector, particularly in solar power. The expansion into battery manufacturing further diversifies its portfolio and aligns with the broader vision to support clean energy initiatives. The establishment of the manufacturing line at the Valsad facility could potentially lead to increased operational efficiency and expand Waaree's market reach. The move underscores Waaree's commitment to innovation and sustainability in energy storage technology, driving forward India's ambitions in renewable energy. Stakeholders and industry experts view this development as a strategic step that could have a positive impact on the company's growth trajectory. By expanding its manufacturing capabilities, Waaree Energies is poised to play a pivotal role in the evolution of energy storage infrastructure in India. More information regarding this development can be found on the company's official website, www.waaree.com.
