artigo.texto: Publicidade Com a vitória dos democratas nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos, o desenvolvimento das estruturas para inteligência artificial, em especial, os data centers, devem sofrer uma pausa nos estados. Estimativas da XP Investimentos calculam que essas pausas estaduais reduzam de 1% a 5% o capex de inteligência artificial das oito empresas que lideram a construção nos EUA. Segundo os analistas, esse efeito seria causado por atrasos e custos e não por algum movimento na demanda. Após as votações, 40 dos 41 plebiscitos locais realizados em dez estados durante as eleições de meio de mandato, terminaram com a rejeição popular aos projetos das big techs. No Texas, a pausa no estado já existe e deve durar cerca de 13 meses, até uma nova lei estadual passar a vigorar, a partir de agosto de 2027. Apesar de outros estados prometerem pausas parecidas, ainda não há decretos em vigor. Até 2027, não há expectativas de mudanças significativas na produção, uma vez que obras e encomendas já estão sendo executadas e parte da capacidade que atrasaria pode voltar em outros estados ou com geração própria nos próprios data centers. Já de e 2028 a 2030, os caminhos estaduais tiram de 1,2% a 4,9% do capex das empresas e de 4 a 15 GW de capacidade ligada em 2030. De acordo com a XP, o investimento soma US$ 5,1 trilhões neste período, com US$ 1,8 trilhão no último ano, no cenário base. Continua depois da publicidade Conforme os analistas, uma moratória federal, abordada pela casa como cenário de estresse/sensibilidade, mudaria drasticamente a escala, com um corte de cerca de 26% sobre o capex projetado. Impacto nas empresas De acordo com a XP, cada empresa deve sentir as mudanças com base no lugar onde constrói e a perda vai depender de quantos projetos elas têm nos estados com pausa. O grande desafio diz respeito à essas grandes estruturas e todo o sistema para colocá-las em operação. Segundo os analistas, gerar energia no próprio terreno seria a saída natural, mas turbinas e motores já estão vendidos por anos e não resolveriam completamente o problema. Continua depois da publicidade Entre as empresas, Alphabet está melhor posicionada, por ter um maior plano de investimento, afirmam os analistas. Atualmente, a companhia tem o maior plano de investimentos entre as principais empresas e é a que mais deixa de colocar capacidade em operação em números absolutos, com cerca de 2,3 GW a menos em 2030 no caso de vários estados. Por outro lado, SpaceX e CoreWeave perdem mais em proporção, por terem uma fatia maior da expansão nos estados com possibilidade de pausas. Pelo ROIC, métrica de retorno sobre o capital investido, os data centers que entram em operação em 2030 rendem 21,3% mesmo com custo alto, acima dos 15% que consideramos como retorno mínimo. Segundo os analistas, independente de moratórias, os retornos seguem acima da régua mínima de 15% porque a escassez ajuda a compensar. Continua depois da publicidade A XP reiterou a nossa preferência em nomes com menor impacto esperado em cenário de estresse de crédito, como Alphabet, Amazon e Microsoft.

artigo.texto: Japan said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) that Southeast Asian nations will be able to access its crude oil storage facilities as part of efforts to prepare the region for a future energy crisis. The announcement came as leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) met in Manila, where energy security has been high on the agenda. Keep track | ASEAN Summit LIVE updates: PM Modi at ASEAN-India Summit; Quad meeting likely after President Trump arrives Addressing regional leaders, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her country's "hydro-tanks" would be available for use under the proposed initiative for cooperation on oil stockpiling. ASEAN members have been grappling with fuel shortages and price hikes after the West Asia conflict squeezed the flow of crude to the region. The regional bloc has previously called for "unimpeded" passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which was closed following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Under the Japanese POWERR Asia initiative, ASEAN nations will be able to use Japan's excess storage capacity for crude oil. "We have suggested to utilise our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilised," Japan's Foreign Ministry press secretary Toshihiro Kitamura told reporters on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit. "By utilising those unused facilities in Japan, we can stockpile the other countries' crude oil and in case of crisis... it's a kind of joint stockpiling system." Japan has 254 days' worth of oil reserves, Mr. Kitamura said, while at the outbreak of the West Asia war in February some ASEAN countries had less than a month's worth. An ASEAN-backed study for joint stockpiling of oil has also recommended using facilities in Thailand and Indonesia, but Kitamura said a final decision had not been made. "It's under specific discussion," Mr. Kitamura said. "But as a government in Japan, we are ready to work with ASEAN countries to utilise our own facilities," he said. Longer term, Tokyo plans to assist ASEAN countries to build their own "stockpiling facilities". "I think this is very important in order to prepare ourselves for future possibilities, crises." Philippine Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said a memorandum of cooperation signed with Japan on Monday (November 16) included assistance to "put up many more facilities to store more oil, whether (that) is diesel, gas or crude oil", in the archipelago nation. "What this means is the Philippines will be more prepared in ensuring there is adequate oil for our homes and businesses, whatever the situation is," Ms. Garin told reporters. "With our reserves in place, we would be better positioned to support our transport, markets, and industries." Published - November 17, 2026 02:50 pm IST

artigo.texto: Empresas, profissionais e instituições ligados ao setor de data centers podem participar da Pesquisa Nacional de Data Centers, que recebe respostas até o dia 30 de novembro. A iniciativa busca reunir informações sobre o mercado brasileiro e identificar desafios e oportunidades para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura digital no país. A pesquisa é conduzida pela Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI), em parceria com o Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD), como parte do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis. O levantamento pretende reunir dados e opiniões de empresas, operadores, fornecedores, instituições públicas, universidades e outras organizações que atuam no segmento. Entre os temas abordados estão investimentos, infraestrutura, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, formação de profissionais, sustentabilidade, regulação e inovação tecnológica. As informações coletadas serão utilizadas na elaboração de um diagnóstico sobre o setor de data centers no Brasil. O estudo deverá servir de base para identificar oportunidades de expansão, fortalecer a cadeia produtiva nacional e orientar possíveis políticas públicas relacionadas à infraestrutura digital e à soberania tecnológica. Além do questionário, o projeto realizou entrevistas técnicas, visitas presenciais e workshops em diferentes regiões do país. Os encontros foram organizados para discutir questões específicas de cada mercado regional. Em Campinas (SP), os debates abordaram infraestrutura energética e digital, inovação tecnológica, ambiente regulatório e oportunidades para ampliar a participação da indústria nacional na cadeia de data centers. Em Fortaleza (CE), o foco esteve na conectividade internacional por cabos submarinos, no potencial de geração de energia renovável, na infraestrutura de transmissão e nas condições para atrair novos investimentos. Já em Porto Alegre (RS), as discussões trataram da resistência da infraestrutura digital a eventos climáticos extremos, da segurança operacional, da conectividade regional e da continuidade de serviços essenciais. A participação na pesquisa permanece aberta até 30 de novembro e pode ser feita por organizações e profissionais ligados ao setor. Como participar: o questionário está disponível no site da ABDI, na página do Projeto ECOS – Data Centers Sustentáveis: https://www.abdi.com.br/projeto-ecos/#participe-da-pesquisa

artigo.texto: Singapore is stepping up carbon market cooperation with several countries at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference, signing an implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation with Kenya and renewing a memorandum of understanding with Colombia on Monday (16 November). The signing ceremony took place at the Singapore Pavilion at the conference venue. Since signing its first memorandum of understanding on carbon credit trading in 2022, Singapore has established cooperation with more than 30 countries. According to a statement from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, the implementation agreement with Kenya establishes a legally binding bilateral mechanism for transferring high-quality carbon credits with corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Businesses are expected to be able to submit carbon credit projects for government authorisation from 2027. “Corresponding adjustments” refer to an accounting mechanism that ensures the same emissions reductions are not counted by both the buyer and the seller. This is Singapore’s 13th implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation, and its third with an African country, after Ghana and Rwanda. In her speech, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said: “We meet amid global headwinds, but Singapore remains steadfast in our commitment to climate action. No country can tackle climate change alone.” She said it was heartening for Singapore to work with like-minded countries, and praised Kenya for demonstrating considerable leadership in the green transition. In 2024, over 90% of Kenya's electricity was generated from renewable sources. In 2024, Kenyan projects accounted for about one fifth of voluntary carbon market revenues across Africa. Singapore and Kenya signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation in 2023. Typically, the two sides first sign a memorandum of understanding to set the direction for cooperation, before entering substantive negotiations and eventually signing a legally binding implementation agreement. Singapore and Kenya, both founding members of the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, have actively advocated the development of high-quality carbon markets. Fu noted that Singapore and Kenya have complementary strengths. Kenya is one of Africa’s most established carbon markets, with a clear legal framework in place, while Singapore is a financial and carbon services hub. Together, this can help credible projects in Kenya attract the investment they need. Expanding cooperation with Colombia This is Singapore’s second memorandum of understanding on carbon credit cooperation with Colombia. The first memorandum, signed with the South American country in 2022, has expired. The new memorandum of understanding not only continues the partnership but also broadens its scope. It establishes a framework for dialogue, technical cooperation, exchanges of experience and the exploration of opportunities for cooperation in carbon markets and areas related to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Fu stressed that the two countries would work towards a legally binding implementation agreement that could take their cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to the next stage. “Colombia has tremendous potential for high-quality climate action – in its forests and natural ecosystems, in energy and industry, and in waste.” Besides its cooperation with Kenya and Colombia, Singapore also approved its first carbon credit project from Rwanda last Saturday (14 November) and signed a memorandum of understanding on carbon market cooperation with Bangladesh.

artigo.texto: BYD supera Toyota na preferência por eletrificados, diz pesquisa Pesquisa da Webmotors mostra que metade dos donos de eletrificados tem modelos chineses; pós-venda ainda é desafio para novas fabricantes As marcas chinesas estão ganhando espaço na preferência dos consumidores brasileiros e já superam montadoras tradicionais em diferentes indicadores do mercado automotivo, segundo pesquisa da Webmotors Autoinsights. A BYD ultrapassou a Toyota na intenção de compra de veículos eletrificados, enquanto fabricantes como Omoda Jaecoo, Geely e GAC também aparecem entre as marcas emergentes mais consideradas pelos motoristas. No levantamento sobre eletrificados, realizado em junho com mais de 1.200 usuários da plataforma, a BYD lidera a intenção de compra, com 24% das menções, ante 17% em 2025. A Toyota, que ocupava a primeira posição no ano passado, caiu de 28% para 19%. A presença chinesa também aparece entre quem já possui um eletrificado. Cerca de metade dos proprietários ouvidos tem um carro de marca chinesa. A BYD concentra 25% das menções, seguida por Toyota (14,2%), GWM (9,4%) e Caoa Chery (4,7%). Omoda Jaecoo, GAC e Geely também aparecem na lista. O avanço também aparece nas buscas da plataforma. Entre junho de 2025 e junho de 2026, os contatos de compradores com vendedores de eletrificados da BYD cresceram e chegaram a 2,9 vezes o volume registrado pela Toyota. A GWM teve alta de 119% no período. Para Eduardo Jurcevic, CEO da Webmotors, a competitividade das fabricantes chinesas está relacionada à escala de produção e à oferta de tecnologia. "As marcas chinesas chegaram a esse mercado com uma vantagem de escala: a eletrificação já representa 52% das vendas de carros de passeio na China, e o país exportou 2,6 milhões de eletrificados em 2025, alta de 104% em um ano. Isso permitiu trazer um portfólio amplo de híbridos e elétricos, com preços e condições muito competitivos", afirma. Apesar do avanço, a confiança nas fabricantes ainda é um obstáculo. Em outra pesquisa da Webmotors, realizada em setembro, apenas 17,6% disseram que comprariam uma marca nova ou pouco conhecida. Outros 44,8% descartam essa possibilidade. Quando as marcas são apresentadas pelo nome, porém, a resistência diminui. Omoda Jaecoo lidera a intenção de compra entre as fabricantes emergentes, com 30,8%, seguida por Geely (27,9%) e GAC (22,5%). A principal preocupação dos consumidores é a disponibilidade de peças e serviços de manutenção, citada por 28,9% dos entrevistados. O custo-benefício aparece em seguida, com 28,2%. "O pós-venda é, sim, a principal barreira, mas não é a única, e não se vence de uma vez só", afirma Jurcevic, acrescentando que a reputação das fabricantes e o valor de revenda também pesam na decisão de compra.

artigo.texto: Springfield City Council to consider defining data centers, extending pauses on applications Three proposals on Monday’s agenda would add a city code definition and extend pauses through Feb. 24 SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - The Springfield City Council on Monday night will take up three proposals. One would define what a data center is under city code. The other two would extend pauses on development and utility applications while the city works on potential regulations. The current pause expires Tuesday. The proposed extensions would run through Feb. 24. What the proposals would do Council Bill 2026-235 would amend the city’s Land Development Code by adding definitions related to data centers. The bill is up for second reading tonight. Council members can amend or adopt it, and a vote is required for it to be adopted. Unless an amendment is offered, the bill would be voted on tonight. The other two proposals would extend existing pauses on development and utility-related applications through Feb. 24. The ordinance says the Land Development Code does not currently define data centers. It says the amendment establishes a common definition of “data center” and related terms only, as a first step before consideration of later text amendments and public hearings. Steve Childers, the city’s director of planning and development, said the city has not yet written a definition for data centers. He said the city needs that definition before it can establish rules for where data centers can go and how they can operate. “We’re just taking the time to get it right, taking the time to do the due diligence we need in order to be able to do the research, pull it all together and present council with a draft ordinance that they could consider,” Childers said. Any future regulations would still have to go through additional review and public hearings. How the ordinance defines data centers Under the proposed definition, a data center is a building, or a room or portion of a building, used to house information technology equipment for the storage, management, processing or transmission of digital data. The definition lists server farms, artificial intelligence training or processing, image processing, cloud computing, email services, and cryptocurrency or other digital-asset mining, among other uses. The definition also includes backup generators, energy storage systems, on-site electric generation, cooling equipment, electrical equipment, and any substations that primarily serve the data center. The ordinance would classify data centers into three types: - Accessory data center: Located within the principal building on the lot, with a data center floor area of no more than 20% of the building’s gross floor area. It serves only the owner or a tenant of the premises, does not sell, lease, or otherwise provide data storage, processing, or computing capacity to others, and has a maximum power demand of less than 1 megawatt. - Micro data center: Not an accessory data center, with a floor area of no more than 10,000 square feet and a maximum power demand of less than 5 megawatts. - Large-load data center: Not an accessory data center, with a maximum power demand of 5 megawatts or more or a floor area of more than 10,000 square feet. The ordinance says data centers other than accessory data centers that are on the same lot or premises, on adjacent lots, or under common ownership or control and share infrastructure or a point of interconnection with the electric utility would be treated as one data center. Their floor area and maximum power demand would be combined. The ordinance would take effect immediately upon passage. The Planning and Zoning Commission held a public hearing on the amendments Oct. 15 and recommended approval, with additional changes, by a vote of 7 to 0. Existing pause and public input City Council enacted Special Ordinance 28306 on June 29 to delay the acceptance and processing of applications relating to the evaluation, establishment, servicing or expansion of a data center facility until Nov. 17. The ordinance says the city held three public engagement sessions on data centers during the delay, and city staff is reviewing the feedback. The current moratorium has put at least one proposed project on hold. Trent Overhue, who was working to develop a data center at 2900 National Ave., asked a judge for permission to keep moving forward despite the moratorium. The Greene County Circuit Court denied the request for a preliminary injunction Nov. 9. When asked about a formal interview with KY3, Overhue declined. How data centers differ Matt Powell, executive director of the Missouri Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, said many people’s digital lives rely on data centers, from online banking to storing photos and shopping online. He said data centers support technology people use in everyday life, including banks giving customers access to their money, photos and family albums on phones, and GPS on phones. “You know that phrase, it’s on someone else’s computer. That’s essentially what it is,” Powell said. Powell said data centers have large amounts of storage capabilities and are used for accessing and storing people’s data. Powell said not all data centers are the same. Some primarily store information, while others use much more electricity to power the computing behind things like artificial intelligence. Powell said data centers are essentially hubs that allow data to flow throughout the world. “At one point it used to be thought of, well, the internet’s a bunch of invisible wires that connect everyone together,” Powell said. “Well, think of data centers as those hubs. You know, that data is going to ... it goes faster, it’s able to travel further and faster when we have hubs that support that data and push it along, kind of like a relay race, right? So it’s relaying information from one point to another.” The council meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. at the Regional Police-Fire Training Center on Bat

artigo.texto: BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya (UM) are taking their second-life EV battery initiative a step further. After rolling out a solar-powered mobile device charging station at UM Sentral in August, the collaboration has now deployed a larger Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) solution to power an Orang Asli village in Pahang. As part of the RE:GENERATE x Universiti Malaya initiative, the latest project uses retired BMW EV batteries and repurposed solar panels to provide 24-hour electricity to 20 households in the Semai Orang Asli community at Kampung Saweh, Pos Sinderut, Kuala Lipis. The new system not only reduces reliance on fuel-powered generators but also provides a practical example of how EV batteries can continue to serve a useful purpose beyond their automotive lifespan. From four hours of electricity to 24-hour power supply Prior to this, residents at Kampung Saweh relied on petrol and diesel generators, which typically operated for about four hours each night. Electricity usage was largely limited to basic needs such as lighting and fans, and each household were spending about RM10 per day on generator fuel. With the new solar-powered battery storage system, all 20 households now have access to electricity throughout the day and night, at a significantly lower operating cost. More importantly, the continuous power supply opens up possibilities for appliances such as refrigerators, which can make a practical difference to the community. According to BMW Group Malaysia, families who hunt or gather food previously had no reliable means of preserving perishable items such as meat. These items had to be consumed or shared with neighbours immediately to prevent spoilage. The system has been designed to support refrigerators as households acquire them. At the moment, televisions represent the highest individual electricity load in most homes. How does the second-life BMW EV battery system work? The energy storage system was developed by Associate Professor Dr. Tan Chia Kwang and his team of researchers and students at Universiti Malaya’s Power Energy Dedicated Advanced Centre (UMPEDAC). It consists of 30 repurposed BMW EV battery modules, supported by a combined 8kW of inverter power. The system supplies electricity to all 20 households from a single centralised point, with each household allocated 3kWh of energy per day. Instead of having separate battery storage systems for individual homes, the centralised setup allows available capacity to be shared between households based on their current demand. Besides reusing old EV batteries, the solution also utilises second-life solar panels that were retired early from commercial solar farms which still has considerable usable life. During the day, the solar panels charge the batteries, which store energy for use after sunset when household electricity demand is highest. The battery modules are housed in a structure built using wood and bamboo sourced from the surrounding environment. According to BMW Group Malaysia, the repurposed batteries are expected to serve the village for at least another five years under the current system design. This is comparable to or longer than the lifespan of new lead-acid batteries commonly used for rural electrification. The installation was carried out over five days from 23 to 27 October 2026, with the system going live during the team’s visit. Not all retired EV batteries are equal One of the challenges of repurposing EV batteries is that not every battery has the same remaining capacity or condition. According to Universiti Malaya, the research team has spent two years developing a methodology to evaluate and reconfigure used batteries for second-life applications. Each battery undergoes State of Health (SoH) testing at the cell level. Cells that have significantly degraded are removed, while those that meet the required performance thresholds are reassembled into new battery packs. The researchers found that newer-generation BMW batteries typically retain more usable energy, averaging 1.6kWh per pack, while older-generation batteries average around 0.5kWh. This allows the team to match battery packs to different applications based on their remaining capacity. Higher-capacity packs are used for more demanding applications such as rural electrification to power home appliances in off-grid villages. Meanwhile, lower-capacity packs can be used for simpler tasks such as charging smartphones. In August 2026, BMW Group Malaysia and Universiti Malaya deployed their first real-world installation under the partnership, a solar-powered smartphone charging station at the UM Sentral bus stop. The station uses three repurposed BMW battery modules with a combined capacity of 1.5kWh. These modules had retained just 30-40% of their original capacity, demonstrating that even heavily degraded EV batteries can still be useful for less demanding applications. BMW previously repurposed EV batteries for mobile EV charging This isn’t BMW Group Malaysia’s first attempt at giving retired EV batteries a second life. Back in May 2023, BMW Group Malaysia worked with EV Connection to introduce what it described as Malaysia’s first Mobile Charging Vehicle powered by repurposed BMW and MINI EV batteries. Unveiled at the Malaysia Autoshow 2023, the mobile charging solution uses 16 repurposed battery modules with approximately 70% State of Health. The latest rural electrification project builds on this concept by using retired EV batteries as a stationary energy storage solution for an off-grid community. According to Universiti Malaya, repurposing used EV batteries requires extensive testing, grading and modification due to differences in battery condition. The university also highlighted that the cost of supporting components remains substantial, despite receiving retired EV batteries from BMW and donated solar panels. artigo.texto: For all the talk of this month’s election being about a referendum on President Donald Trump, voters had other considerations on their mind, too. Data centers and artificial intelligence had a “huge impact, huge impact,” state Rep.-elect Ryan Kominakis, D-Valparaiso, said. More than 500 state legislative seats were flipped nationwide, he said. “I’ve been in this for a while, and I’ve never seen anything like this ever,” state Rep. Chuck Moseley, D-Portage, said. “I find it hard to believe that that many people could be wrong,” his wife told him. Utilities and data centers were the main topic that came up when Kominakis was knocking on doors in his campaign to unseat incumbent Republican Ed Soliday. “A lot of people are frustrated with the data centers,” Kominakis said, with voters citing the one that had been proposed near Wheeler High School in Union Township and another whether Valparaiso had initially proposed a sports complex. “All these horror stories,” he said, and no regulations made voters wary. Adding to that is the $655 million and counting in tax revenue loss from state economic development giveaways to data center developers. “We’ve got to repeal that law or at bare minimum amend it,” Kominakis said. He has a Dec. 11 deadline to give the Legislative Services Agency, which drafts legislation, his proposal to repeal those tax breaks, require project labor agreements for union wages for data centers that receive scaled-back tax breaks, limit their locations so they can’t be near schools or neighborhoods, and require environmental protection. Kominakis, a Democrat, plans to seek his caucus leadership for advice on the direction his legislation takes. “I want to make sure we’re doing the right thing, making the correct strategic moves,” he said. He credits his Nov. 3 victory to Republicans staying home or switching sides as well as Democrats showing up. “Voters talked about it at the door. Not every door I knocked talked about data centers, but some did,” Moseley said. The Democratic incumbent won re-election. Voters’ concerns ranged from extending big money for tax credits and other incentives to questions about the noise data centers generate. “Everything, everything. It’s just a wide swath with people with different concerns about the things,” Moseley said. “As much as 70% of folks in Indiana are opposed to data centers for various reasons,” Moseley said. “There’s more than likely going to be some discussion about that in the next session, and we’re going to have to see where that goes.” People want realistic answers to their concerns, along with what guardrails to put in place, if any, he said. “I think we’re going to have a good, honest conversation and get everybody at the table,” Moseley said. “We need to be fair and honest.” He said the state needs a task force to look at various concerns surrounding data centers. State Sen.-elect Scott Houldieson, D-Highland, he’s still exploring what’s the purpose of data center development and where it’s going. “What’s the endgame here?” Houldieson said. “These developments are supporting an industry that has produced a lot of wealth inequality in our country, and we should not offer any kind of tax incentives to them.” Houldieson said he’s concerned that its effect on utility rates has yet to be seen, and it’ll take a burden on infrastructure. He also said he’s against non-disclosure agreements. Houldieson previously told the Post-Tribune that he wants to focus on utility affordability at the statehouse. He’s unsure what legislation he’ll support or draft yet. “I’m thinking about all of that,” Houldieson said. “I’m still learning the ropes of the legislature, and I probably will be learning a lot for a while, so I can’t say what legislation I’m going to be putting forward.” State Rep.-elect Nick Neal, D-Crown Point, said it’s important to him that residents’ data center concerns are heard and that utility customers are protected as developments come in. Neal wants the state leaders to look at regulating data centers more closely. “It’s hard for me to say what I’m going to support,” Neal said. “I’m supporting things that are fair and reasonable for all parties involved.” With electric affordability, Neal believes the state legislature should revamp the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, believing it should be a bipartisan group. “We’ve got to do a better job of regulating downstate of those folks who are setting those standards,” Neal said. State Sen.-elect Jay Starkey, R-Demotte, did not respond to a request for comment. U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan, D-Highland, said in a statement Friday that the rising cost of energy is because of “irresponsible policies” from state and federal governments that “have prioritized the interests of Big Tech and Big Coal.” “Affordability was clearly an important issue in this election,” said Mrvan, who won re-election against Republican candidate Barb Regnitz. “The rising costs of household energy and fuel are forcing families to make difficult choices between paying their utility bills, purchasing necessary medications, putting food on the table, and visiting loved ones.” Data center development decisions are made at state and local levels, Mrvan said, but he believes each project should be individually evaluated, looking at its energy demands, demand on natural resources, demands on our existing utility infrastructure and quality of life. Mrvan said he’s concerned that the Trump administration has allowed “Big Tech to operate without meaningful accountability.” He plans to ensure corporations are held accountable and that development doesn’t come at the expense of the environment, economy, or safety and well-being of communities. “When it comes to data centers, I support federal legislation requiring these companies to pay the full cost of the energy and infrastructure necessary to support their operations,” Mrvan said in his statement. “Residential ratepayers should never be forced to subsidize the enorm

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil terão que ter licença prévia dos EUA para comprar chips de IA da Nvidia Medida dos EUA também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia para impedir que empresas chinesas usem chips avançados da Nvidia Resumo - Departamento de Comércio passou a exigir licença prévia para a compra de chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. - Objetivo da medida é impedir que empresas chinesas e de Macau acessem tecnologia americana por meio de servidores no exterior. - A restrição atinge data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. - Exigência vale para centros que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de processamento a empresas de Macau ou do Grupo D:5 (como a China). - Norma foi adotada logo após um escândalo de espionagem forçar a renúncia de Jensen Huang do comando da Nvidia. O governo dos Estados Unidos emitiu nesta segunda-feira, dia 16, uma norma para impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) dos EUA em centros de dados de outros países. Dentre os países afetados estão data centers no Brasil, Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Na prática, data centers que fornecem mais de 12 milhões de unidades de desempenho de processamento a empresas de Macau ou dos países do Grupo D:5, que inclui a China, precisam obter licença prévia do governo americano para comprarem chips avançados de IA da Nvidia. Conforme o Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a norma evita que restrições a tecnologias sensíveis dos EUA sejam contornadas por data centers de países terceiros. As empresas norte-americanas que operam nesses países, incluindo o Brasil, mas bloqueiam o acesso a países restritos ficam isentas da exigência da licença. A medida, adotada pelo Departamento de Comércio americano, é tomada logo após um escândalo de espionagem ter forçado a renúncia de Jensen Huang como diretor-executivo da Nvidia, em meio a relatos de que ele ajudou a facilitar o acesso da China à tecnologia de sua empresa, em violação às normas americanas. Proibição à China Em virtude de medidas sucessivas dos governos de Joe Biden (2021-2025) e Donald Trump, está proibida a venda dos processadores de tecnologia americana mais avançados para empresas chinesas. Washington justifica essas restrições pelo receio de que a China desenvolva uma IA de ponta para fins militares e, mais recentemente, também para conter o avanço de Pequim para a superinteligência. A superinteligência marcaria o momento em que a IA superaria as capacidades humanas de raciocínio e compreensão, e muitos consideram que quem alcançar esse estágio primeiro obterá uma vantagem decisiva nos campos tecnológico e estratégico. O secretário de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, Howard Lutnick, foi acusado por vários observadores de ter trabalhado para flexibilizar as regras de exportação de chips americanos para a China. Na sexta-feira, 13, o secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou publicamente seu colega de governo por essa questão. O documento que apresenta as novas regras de exportação foi publicado pelo Departamento de Comércio, mas foi "redigido pelo Departamento do Tesouro e pelo Conselho de Segurança Nacional, a pedido de ambos", segundo um comunicado do governo americano. Impactos para o Brasil De acordo com o especialista em gestão e governança de riscos digitais, cibersegurança e proteção de dados digitais, Paulo Nascimento, na prática, os data centers brasileiros de grande porte precisam adquirir esses processadores de ponta. “Só que a partir de agora eles precisam de uma autorização dos EUA e essa exigência acaba sendo ativada quando esse poder computacional vai ultrapassando determinado limite, que é de 750 chips NVidia H-100”, exemplifica Nascimento. Ele aponta os principais riscos para os data centers instalados ou em processo de instalação no Ceará. “Primeiro é o atraso e o encarecimento dos projetos porque agora vai depender dessa licença americana, que pode ou não ser concedida. Segundo, a incerteza para novos investimentos. Os investidores vão pensar duas ou três vezes antes de colocar alguns bilhões em projetos que dependem de autorização de um outro país. E o terceiro risco, seria uma vantagem competitiva para as operadoras americanas, que estão isentas dessa exigência”, elenca. De acordo com o professor do Departamento de Telemática do Instituto Federal do Ceará (IFCE), campus Fortaleza, Wendell Rodrigues, a decisão pode, sim, afetar o País. “Isso não vai impactar quem já tenha esse acesso a esses chips, mas nas novas aquisições e novos projetos. Aqui mesmo no Instituto Federal a gente deve adquirir nos próximos meses toda uma plataforma baseada em chips avançados de inteligência artificial conhecida como GPUs”, cita. Para o idealizador do projeto Iracema Digital, Mauro Oliveira, “a regra inclui o Brasil por risco presumido de desvio, sem apresentar um caso concreto envolvendo o País. Somos suspeitos do que poderíamos fazer”. Ele lembra, contudo, que empresas sediadas nos EUA, ou controladas por matrizes americanas ficam dispensadas da licença. “A big tech americana instalada em solo brasileiro segue recebendo seus chips. A empresa brasileira entra na fila”, critica. Por sua vez, o diretor do Fórum Brasileiro de Internet das Coisas, Vivaldo José Breternitz, minimiza o impacto da decisão sobre o Brasil. “É mais oba-oba. Eu acho que o Trump tomou esse tipo de medida pensando nas eleições que aconteceram. Algum atraso pode ocorrer, algum aumento de custo pode ocorrer, mas nada que vá mudar radicalmente o cenário de investimentos nos data centers que estão sendo construídos aqui”, pondera. Já a Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil (Brasscom) disse, por meio de sua assessoria, que não comentaria sobre o assunto. O POVO também tentou contato com as principais empresas do setor de armazenamento de dados que atuam no Ceará, a Omnia e a Tecto Data Centers, e aguarda posicionamento para atualização posterior. (C

artigo.texto: Mercado global de bandejas para cabos (leitos para cabos): Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de bandejas para cabos até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda por gestão de cabos em data centers Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de bandejas para cabos, o mercado chega a 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de bandejas para cabos é um segmento fundamental da infraestrutura elétrica e do gerenciamento de cabos, oferecendo suporte estrutural rígido para o encaminhamento e a proteção de cabos de energia e de dados em edifícios, plantas industriais, data centers e sistemas de transporte. Em 2026, o mercado é moldado pela demanda constante de substituição em mercados de construção maduros e pela aceleração das instalações em projetos de infraestrutura digital e energia renovável. As bandejas para cabos — incluindo configurações tipo escada, calha, tela metálica, fundo sólido e ventiladas — são cada vez mais especificadas por sua capacidade de suporte de carga, propriedades de dissipação de calor e compatibilidade com práticas de construção modular. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 aponta para um crescimento moderado, porém resiliente, com os fundamentos da demanda migrando para lançamentos de cabos de maior densidade em data centers, códigos de segurança e combate a incêndio mais rigorosos em edifícios comerciais e a eletrificação de processos industriais. A escolha de materiais também está evoluindo, com as bandejas de alumínio e à base de polymer ganhando participação onde a resistência à corrosão e a redução de peso são relevantes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados do tamanho do mercado, da segmentação, dos fluxos comerciais e da dinâmica competitiva, fornecendo a fabricantes, distribuidores e especificadores um arcabouço analítico transparente para a tomada de decisão até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de bandejas para cabos prevê expansão constante de 2026 a 2035, com a demanda global crescendo a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual de aproximadamente 4,2%. O crescimento não é uniforme entre regiões ou tipos de produto; reflete, antes, uma rotação da construção comercial tradicional para aplicações em data centers, energia renovável e automação industrial. Nas economias avançadas, as atividades de substituição e modernização em edifícios e plantas existentes sustentam o volume de base, enquanto os mercados emergentes contribuem com demanda incremental por meio da construção de nova infraestrutura. A dinâmica do lado da oferta é moldada pela volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, pela utilização da capacidade de fabricação e pela transição contínua para acabamentos pré-galvanizados e com pintura a pó, que reduzem o tempo de instalação. Espera-se que a intensidade competitiva aumente à medida que fabricantes de metais e integradores de sistemas ampliem seus portfólios de gerenciamento de cabos por meio de aquisições e ofertas de serviços integrados. O índice de mercado, fixado em 100 em 2025, deve alcançar 151 até 2035, refletindo o crescimento acumulado de volume, e não a inflação de preços. Os riscos para as perspectivas incluem quedas no ciclo da construção, atrasos nos investimentos de capital em data centers e mudanças na política comercial que afetam os custos dos insumos metálicos. De modo geral, o mercado é mais bem caracterizado como maduro, mas em evolução, com potencial de alta atrelado às tendências de infraestrutura digital e eletrificação. Fatores de demanda e restrições Principais fatores de demanda - Rápida expansão de data centers de hiperescala e de colocation, que exigem gerenciamento de cabos de alta densidade e soluções de bandejas ventiladas para dissipação de calor - Eletrificação de processos industriais e modernização da automação, impulsionando a demanda por bandejas para cabos duráveis de aço e alumínio em ambientes de plantas - Instalações de energia renovável, incluindo parques solares e eólicos, onde os sistemas de suporte de cabos são essenciais para a coleta e a distribuição de energia - Códigos de construção e segurança contra incêndio mais rigorosos, que exigem suporte e separação adequados de cabos em construções comerciais e institucionais - Adensamento das redes de telecomunicações, incluindo small cells de 5G e expansão de fibra, que exige encaminhamento organizado de cabos em ambientes urbanos e suburbanos - Modernização da infraestrutura ferroviária e de transporte, incluindo sistemas de sinalização e energia que dependem de instalações robustas de bandejas para cabos Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços do aço e do alumínio, que comprime as margens dos fabricantes e atrasa as especificações de projetos - Ciclos longos de licenciamento e construção no setor imobiliário comercial, que podem adiar a demanda por instalação de bandejas para cabos - Disponibilidade de métodos substitutos de gerenciamento de cabos, como eletrodutos e canaletas, em certas aplicações de baixa densidade - Escassez de mão de obra qualificada em contratação elétrica, que pode retardar os prazos de instalação e afetar o cronograma dos projetos - Tarifas comerciais e requisitos de conteúdo regional que afetam os fluxos transfronteiriços de bandejas metálicas fabricadas Estrutura da demanda por setor de uso final Infraestrutura de data centers (participação estimada: 28%) Os data centers são o segmento de uso final de crescimento mais rápido para bandejas para cabos, impulsionado pela construção de instalações de hiperescala e de colocation para atender à computação

artigo.texto: Spartanburg County council takes up 6 data center development agreements Monday Residents speak for and against projects as council considers three final votes and three first votes SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County Council on Monday night took up six data center development agreements, with three up for final votes and three up for first votes, as residents spoke for and against the projects in council chambers. The agenda ran more than 700 pages and included 20 public hearings. Before the 5:15 p.m. public meeting, council met in executive session to discuss contractual terms of several development agreements. The three agreements up for final votes were scheduled for public hearings during the regular council meeting. Resident calls for council members to resign Spartanburg County resident Eric Allison, founder of the Facebook group No Data Centers in Spartanburg, has been leading opposition to data centers in the county. Allison called council members “cowards” and said every member should resign. “Our Spartanburg County Council, every member should be totally ashamed. They need to resign today. It’s a mess. In one meeting, 20 public hearings, 22 second and third votes to move projects forward. It’s absolutely insane,” Allison said. Allison said he believes council is sending residents a message: “We don’t listen to you. We don’t do what you want. We do what we want and our controllers want. Our ears are not for the people of Spartanburg County. Our ears are for other people.” Three of the 20 hearings involve data center development agreements. Valara agreement on South Pine Street The Valara data center at 4000 South Pine Street, which the agenda describes as a high-performance computing center, is under construction. Council took a final vote on a development agreement among the county, Numara LLC and Valara Holdings LLC. It was approved. The agreement will provide the company with long-term development certainty and establish limits on certain future county regulatory actions affecting the project. It will: - Lock in Valara’s development rights for 10 years, protecting the 457-megawatt project from certain future county regulations, moratoriums and zoning changes. - Require the county to determine within 10 days whether development applications are complete. Once an application is determined to be complete, the county would have 45 days to take final action. If the county fails to act within that period, the agreement says the application could be considered approved based on the submitted documentation. - Protect Valara’s ability to continue developing the property, including additional data center buildings, generators, substations and battery storage, subject to the agreement’s terms. In exchange, the company commits to noise mitigation, landscaping and at least one community meeting each year. The agreement calls for an investment of about $2.76 billion. The agreement identifies 27 full-time jobs as a target, not a guarantee. It also requires annual reporting to the county on investment, construction, utilities and employment. Fox Carolina contacted Valara by email to request an interview and a tour of the facility. Jones Road agreement A development agreement with 300 Jones Road Associates LLC for approximately 137 acres at or near 430 Jones Road also received final approval after a vote. The proposal calls for a data center with up to 65 megawatts of IT capacity, an anticipated investment of approximately $1.5 billion and 25 full-time jobs. The agreement also includes $9 million in community benefit payments over five years. The proposal has a history of county opposition. In June, Spartanburg County planning staff denied an earlier application for a data center at the Jones Road property, citing violations of the county’s Unified Land Management Ordinance. The county’s Board of Zoning Appeals upheld that denial on August 25. The developer is now pursuing the project under an exception to the county’s data center moratorium, adopted in September. The exception allows qualifying data centers of 65 megawatts or less on designated industrial park sites or former industrial properties to move forward if they meet additional requirements. The original denial was not overturned. Instead, the county subsequently adopted rules creating another path for certain smaller data center projects to seek approval through development agreements. Monday’s vote was the third and final reading. Tyger River Industrial Park proposals Project Spero was a proposed $3 billion data center development for the Tyger River Industrial Park. In February, Spartanburg County leaders announced they would not approve the tax incentives sought for the project, effectively derailing the proposal following significant public opposition. Jerry Tang, the executive associated with Project Spero, is now associated with four data center proposals in the same industrial park. One, AIB CLT1 at 389 Tyger River Industrial Drive, is an existing bitcoin mining operation proposing to convert its facility into a conventional data center. A final vote was held on Monday on a development agreement. It was approved. The proposed facility would have 50 megawatts of capacity and an estimated investment of $1.2 billion. The other three proposals, AIB CLT2, AIB CLT3 and AIB CLT4, were up for first readings. Each item on the agenda included a proposed special source credit agreement and development agreement. The agreements include tax incentives. Draft agreements indicate the incentives could run for 40 years. FOX Carolina contacted Tang by email to request an interview and a tour of the proposed development sites. artigo.texto: A multi-metallic oxide composite synthesized from nickel cobalt bimetallic oxide and magnesium-copper oxide has demonstrated high electrochemical activity for both water oxidation and asymmetric supercapacitor energy storage in alkaline environments. Synthesized as NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO, the material addresses limitations in the chemical fabrication of multi-metallic oxides for water electrolysis while leveraging the versatile redox properties recognized in transition metal oxides containing nickel and cobalt. The research team developed the composite using a chemical synthesis strategy combined with a modified hydrothermal process. This fabrication method utilized phytochemicals derived from lemon peel extract to facilitate the in situ growth of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite directly onto a nickel foam substrate, creating an integrated electrode structure intended for oxygen evolution reaction half-cell water splitting and asymmetric supercapacitor devices. The introduction of multi-metallic ions into the composite architecture induced electronic disorder and surface defects throughout the material. According to the study, the resulting presence of oxygen surface vacancies alongside trivalent cobalt (Co3+) and trivalent nickel (Ni3+) species contributed significantly to the material’s electrochemical performance and reaction kinetics in alkaline media. Structural validation of the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite was carried out using multiple complementary characterization techniques. The researchers employed scanning electron microscopy, powder X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, which together confirmed the multi-metal oxide composition and the tailor-made structural features of the synthesized electrode material. When evaluated for the oxygen evolution reaction in a 1 M potassium hydroxide electrolyte, the composite exhibited a low overpotential of 370 millivolts at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimeter. In addition to its catalytic efficiency during water oxidation testing, the electrode demonstrated operational durability by sustaining the same catalytic function over 40 continuous hours under alkaline conditions. In asymmetric supercapacitor testing conducted in 3 M potassium hydroxide, the NiCo2O4/MgO-CuO composite delivered a specific capacitance of 551.73 farads per gram. The assembled device attained an energy density of 193.97 watt-hours per kilogram at an applied current density of 1 ampere per gram, while exhibiting high cycling stability by retaining 96.9 percent of its original capacitance after 40,000 galvanic charge-discharge cycles. artigo.texto: Countries take up industry push to loosen UN carbon market rules at COP31 Dozens of countries - from big emerging economies to the world's poorest nations - are calling for the UN's new carbon market to reassess climate integrity rules, in a push that campaigners and researchers have blamed on industry lobbying. At COP31 talks on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) this weekend, the Like-Minded Developing Countries – a group that includes Saudi Arabia, India and China – the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries raised concerns about the requirements project developers must meet, according to sources familiar with the closed-door discussions. They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said. Dozens of countries - from big emerging economies to the world's poorest nations - are calling for the UN's new carbon market to reassess climate integrity rules, in a push that campaigners and researchers have blamed on industry lobbying. At COP31 talks on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) this weekend, the Like-Minded Developing Countries – a group that includes Saudi Arabia, India and China – the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and landlocked developing countries raised concerns about the requirements project developers must meet, according to sources familiar with the closed-door discussions. They warned about the cumulative weight of those requirements developed under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as barriers to implementation. Several countries, including Singapore and some Latin American states, said rules must keep projects financially viable, while South Korea asked for proportionate requirements, the sources said. Their demands closely track arguments from carbon market industry groups, which claim PACM's conservative approach to counting emission reductions is so strict that few projects will ever come to fruition. Industry and NGOs lobby to weaken UN carbon credit rules in “coordinated” push In a letter published ahead of COP31, the lobby groups asked governments to "raise implementation concerns" and to request that the Supervisory Body - the UN body that oversees the market - assess the "combined impact" of its rules on the feasibility of projects. The letter was signed by the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), a business group whose members include fossil fuel giants Shell, BP, Saudi Aramco and Chevron, along with the Project Developer Forum and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which develops forest conservation programmes. Draft text reflects industry demands Those demands are reflected in the first draft of the COP31 decision on the mechanism, published late on Saturday. To guard against over-crediting, PACM’s rules deliberately err on the side of issuing fewer credits when emissions cuts from projects are uncertain. The document asks the Supervisory Body to look at how these cautious assumptions add up across its rules and what that means for the number of credits, project costs and prices. The aim, it says, is to avoid "excessive compounding of conservative adjustments". Other parts of the draft tell the body not to make its rules too cautious or too rigid. That includes efforts to guard against the risk that carbon captured by a project is later released. Most of these passages add that environmental integrity must be maintained. Risk of another 'failure' "Weakening the rules is not climate ambition - it is a license to pollute,” said Erika Lennon, a senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). “As we are on the brink of permanently breaching 1.5C, we cannot afford to turn the carbon market into another loophole for polluters,” she added. Axel Michaelowa, research director at Perspectives Climate Research, said that if attempts to weaken the rules succeed, it could lead to another failure of an international carbon market. Demand for credits rests on trust, he said, and the slightest doubt over integrity erodes buyers' willingness to pay. Calls to revise requirements "must be supported by scientific evidence, not unsupported claims of under-crediting - especially when these assumptions come from private actors whose revenues depend on the volume of transacted credits rather than real mitigation outcomes," Michaelowa said. The EU, Switzerland and Senegal are among a handful of countries pushing back against demands to re-assess the market rules, according to the sources, and are opposing requests to weigh up the profitability of projects or to lower standards. Cookstove credits in focus At the centre of the fight are new methodologies for projects that aim to cut emissions by distributing cleaner cookstoves - one of the carbon market’s most popular credit types and also one of its most criticised for overstating climate benefits. A 2024 study in Nature Sustainability found cookstove projects had been over-credited roughly tenfold. Under the rules adopted by the Supervisory Body in October, cookstove project developers are required to set aside part of their credits in a buffer pool, in case the forests they claim to save later burn or are cleared. artigo.texto: The International Business Aviation Council (IBAC) is urging its affiliated national associations to lobby their governments to demand political pressure to block changes to the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU-ETS). The group, which represents business aviation at ICAO, has backed the EBAA’s opposition to proposals made by the European Commission’s Climate Action directorate-general on the grounds that changes would disproportionately affect the industry to the extent that some operators could find it impossible to comply with requirements. Under proposals issued in July, the introduction of a new de minimis emissions threshold of 1,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per company annually would bring many additional smaller operators under the EU-ETS mandate. According to IBAC, some members of the European Parliament want to further lower the de minimis threshold for EU-ETS compliance to just 250 tonnes. The group said this would bring around 1,000 more operators under the requirements of the legislation. The EC also wants the scheme to apply to all flights from the European Economic Area to third-country destinations within a 5,000-kilometer (2,700-nm) radius of Frankfurt, Germany. IBAC says this will significantly increasing the number of flights from outside the European Union that would be subject to requirements. As part of its rebuttal of the proposed changes, EBAA has also protested that they will subject business aviation to broader carbon-pricing obligations than airlines by being denied access to sustainable aviation fuel allowances and to the use of book-and-claim options. The group has also complained that the new structure would take no account of other passenger and carbon taxes levied by individual European Union member states, such as France, Portugal, Italy and the Netherlands. IBAC director general Kurt Edwards has accused the EC of “sectoral bigotry” in consciously discriminating against business aircraft operators, which he said will be harmful to the viability of some companies. Edwards said excluding the industry from book-and-claim accounting for emissions is especially unreasonable since its companies commonly fly to airports where SAF is not available. “In their supporting text, the European Commission said that business aircraft operators have the means and the resources to buy SAF without providing evidence of that,” he told AIN. “Why strip away the benefit of taking advantage of [SAF] technology?” In what IBAC said would be a further divergence from the ICAO-backed CORSIA approach to achieving net-zero emissions for air transport by 2050, the EC intends to reduce the mtow threshold for EU-ETS from 5,700 kilograms (12,540 pounds) to 2,500 kilograms. Edwards said this will mean turboprop aircraft such as the Pilatus PC-12 and Daher TBM 980 would be covered by the scheme and its high cost of compliance and administration. At the EBAA Week event in Brussels this week, IBAC representatives will introduce a new vehicle-tonne-kilometer metric that they are proposing for business aviation. According to Bruce Parry, senior advisor for industry affairs with Bombardier Aerospace, this would be a fairer way to calculate the sector’s emissions than the passenger-kilometer metric devised with airlines in mind. Edwards said the EC’s allegedly discriminatory efforts to make EU-ETS compliance harder for business aviation companies are also unnecessary since the industry is strongly committed to decarbonization. “Part of the reasoning for excluding our operators from SAF allowances is that they believe we are more likely to electrify [aircraft] sooner, but this simply isn’t the incentive they think it is,” he concluded. Ultimately, if the EC presses ahead with the proposed changes, IBAC has indicated that the industry may be forced to take legal action to challenge the new rules on grounds of discrimination. In June, lawyers acting for Dassault Aviation, with EBAA support, successfully challenged the process by which the European Commission had excluded business aviation from its “taxonomy” definition of environmentally sustainable activity. The European Union General Court in Luxembourg ruled that the industry had been excluded in an unfair and discriminatory way.

artigo.texto: Expansão dos data centers deve diminuir após resultado das midterms Democratas no Congresso ameaçam impor moratória sobre novos data centers de IA; medida pode impactar mercado e demais setores de tecnologia A rápida expansão dos data centers de inteligência artificial se tornou uma das questões centrais nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos. Campanhas populares surgiram em diversas comunidades ao longo do país, levantando preocupações sobre os impactos locais desses grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos. Durante o programa "Resenha do Dinheiro", os apresentadores destacaram que os democratas se posicionam contrariamente à expansão acelerada dos data centers. Entre as principais preocupações levantadas estão o elevado consumo de energia, o encarecimento das tarifas energéticas para a população local, a poluição sonora e a desvalorização imobiliária nas regiões onde essas estruturas são instaladas. Alguns governadores chegaram a sinalizar a intenção de limitar o número de novas instalações por meio de moratórias. Elizabeth Warren, senadora dos Estados Unidos, declarou que pretende implementar uma moratória sobre os data centers como medida prioritária. Essa postura foi interpretada pelo mercado financeiro como um sinal negativo para as empresas de tecnologia e de IA. "É um baque e isso terá uma forte queda nos resultados da Nasdaq", ressalta Bernardo Pascowitch, apresentador do Resenha do Dinheiro. Impactos para mercado O cenário gerado pelas eleições também trouxe reflexões sobre os efeitos no câmbio. Thiago Godoy, educador financeiro, aponta que, caso os juros nos Estados Unidos recuem, a atratividade do dólar como investimento diminuiria, o que poderia representar um fator positivo para o Brasil, com a valorização do real. "Porém, esse movimento depende somente da condução política fiscal americana, de como o Fed vai reagir nas próximas reuniões", pondera Godoy. Além disso, a desaceleração dos investimentos em data centers e IA pode representar o início da bolha no setor. Marilia Fontes, sócia-fundadora da Nord Investimentos avalia que esse processo já havia sido iniciado com o aumento da taxa de juros nos Estados Unidos e que a renda fixa americana, com taxas próximas a 5% no longo prazo, se torna um investimento extremamente atrativo em comparação com ações de tecnologia. "Com o cenário de atratividade um pouco menor por conta do capex em investimentos em data centers, a renda fixa passa a ser um baita investimento. Os EUA estão na vanguarda do crescimento da tecnologia, com o PIB resiliente mas a taxa de juros e os treasuries estão ganhando cada vez mais atratividade", afirma Fontes. Resenha do Dinheiro O programa é apresentado por Marilia Fontes, sócia-fundadora da Nord Investimentos, Bernardo Pascowitch, fundador e CEO do Yubb e Thiago Godoy, o “Papai Financeiro”; e propõe uma abordagem leve, direta e descomplicada sobre temas ligados à educação financeira e investimentos. A atração aborda semanalmente os principais temas da economia com a informalidade de uma conversa entre amigos — sem abrir mão da análise. O Resenha do Dinheiro vai ao ar todas as sextas-feiras, às 19h, no canal do CNN Money no YouTube e aos domingos, às 15h, na CNN Brasil.

artigo.texto: Trending SNOQUALMIE, Wash. -- In the race to meet the nation's growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new "battery farms" that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it's projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger -- along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers -- could threaten an industry that's becoming integral to the nation's energy future. 'Meteoric growth' Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion -- a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. "The meteoric growth is continuing," said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. "For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential." Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours -- but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it's needed, instead of firing up more costly "peaker" gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. "As we're dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we've already paid for," Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry's growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. "It's basically a no-regret path," Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. "Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there's battery storage." Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they've met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. "They're making us collateral damage," said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. "We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we're going to do in our backyard." The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. Indust

The U.S. is tightening restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips by closing a loophole that lets Chinese firms obtain computing power through overseas data centers, shifting controls from the physical movement of chips to remote access to their computing capacity. [para. 1][para. 4] 2. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule on Monday requiring licenses for shipments of advanced AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they provide large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China or other restricted jurisdictions. The rule also imposes new licensing requirements specifically on exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil, which the U.S. views as having a higher-than-normal risk of chip diversion. [para. 2][para. 3] 3. Under the new framework, exporters must seek U.S. approval if they know covered chips or servers are destined for a data center providing more than 12 million in aggregate total processing performance (TPP) to China-linked companies. This threshold applies to an individual facility or a group of linked data centers, regardless of the data center's location, and covers computing provided directly or indirectly to companies headquartered in China. [para. 5][para. 8] 4. Based on Nvidia product specifications and industry estimates, the 12 million TPP threshold is roughly equivalent to about 750 Nvidia H200 chips. While this is small compared with the tens of thousands of chips typically needed to train the most advanced AI models, it could still support substantial inference workloads that require less concentrated computing capacity. [para. 6][para. 7] 5. Data-center operators face new obligations after chips are delivered. If an overseas facility begins providing computing capacity above the threshold to covered Chinese entities, the owner, operator, or another involved party must obtain a license. Existing data centers already providing such services have 90 days from the rule's effective date to seek approval if they wish to continue, or they risk future U.S. export restrictions. Commercial recommendation systems, such as those used by online retailers, are exempt. [para. 9][para. 10][para. 11] 6. The separate licensing requirement for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil could have a particularly large impact on Southeast Asia, which has become a major destination for AI data-center investment. Advanced chips shipped to these five countries will generally require U.S. approval, though companies headquartered in the U.S. or owned by U.S. parents can qualify for an exemption if they meet reporting requirements. Washington cited elevated risks of diversion to restricted users in these markets. [para. 12][para. 13][para. 14][para. 15] 7. Southeast Asia has grown rapidly as a computing hub as Chinese tech companies expand overseas and seek AI infrastructure. Singapore had more than 1.4 gigawatts (GW) of computing-infrastructure capacity in 2025, while Malaysia had about 1.06 GW, Indonesia 900 megawatts, and Thailand 620 megawatts. Regional capacity is expected to exceed 10 GW by 2030, up from more than 4.4 GW in 2025. [para. 16][para. 17] 8. Chinese technology companies including ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have leased data-center capacity in Southeast Asia. Of roughly 1.5 GW of data-center projects approved in Thailand, as much as 60% to 70% are backed by Chinese investors or primarily serve major Chinese tech companies. In response, Malaysia plans legislation requiring data centers to disclose information such as operators, cloud customers, locations, electricity consumption, and GPU imports. Singapore said it is studying the new U.S. rules and engaging with affected companies and U.S. authorities. [para. 18][para. 19][para. 20][para. 21] 9. The rule also tightens requirements for semiconductor foundries and chip-packaging companies. Certain advanced chips designed by companies outside the U.S. and designated allied jurisdictions will be presumed to fall under U.S. export controls and to be intended for data-center use unless manufacturers or packaging companies can demonstrate otherwise. This builds on earlier restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese chip designers from using overseas foundries for advanced processors. [para. 22][para. 23][para. 24] 10. artigo.texto: BW ESS has partnered with French battery storage developer Wattmen to develop a battery energy storage system (BESS) portfolio of approximately 500 MW in France over the next three years. The partnership aims to expand BW ESS’ presence in the French energy storage market by developing large-scale, standalone battery storage projects connected to the transmission network. The collaboration will combine Wattmen’s local project origination and development expertise with BW ESS’ international experience in energy storage investment, project design and procurement. The companies will jointly work on advancing projects from the initial greenfield stage to ready-to-build status. This will include securing land rights, grid connections and the necessary regulatory authorisations required to move projects towards construction. The partnership will primarily focus on projects with connection capacities of at least 100 MW. The companies will priorities strategically located sites near grid connection points, with sufficient land availability to accommodate battery systems offering a minimum storage duration of four hours. This development strategy is intended to create a portfolio of large-scale energy storage assets capable of supporting the changing requirements of France’s electricity system. Under the partnership, Wattmen will lead local development activities, including identifying suitable project sites, negotiating land agreements, managing permitting processes and coordinating grid connections. The company will also work closely with landowners, local authorities and communities to facilitate project development. BW ESS will contribute its international energy storage experience, particularly in project design, investment and procurement strategy. The company operates across seven markets and brings experience in developing and managing battery storage projects at scale. Hazel Starmer-Jones, Development Director at BW ESS, said the partnership represents an important step in strengthening the company’s presence in France. She highlighted Wattmen’s technical capabilities and local market knowledge as important factors in selecting the development partner. Both companies aim to develop high-quality energy storage projects that can deliver long-term value while improving the flexibility and resilience of the French electricity system. Jean-Marc Guenée, CEO and Co-Founder of Wattmen, said the partnership combines complementary capabilities and a shared ambition to develop high-quality battery storage infrastructure. He noted that the collaboration would help advance strategically located projects and support the development of flexible energy infrastructure required for the energy transition. The agreement reflects BW ESS’ strategy of partnering with specialized local developers when entering and expanding in new markets. By combining local development capabilities with international investment and operational experience, the company aims to build a strong pipeline of energy storage projects. The latest partnership builds on BW ESS’ recent entry into France through the acquisition of two battery energy storage projects, each with a capacity of 100 MW and 400 MWh. These acquisitions, together with the new 500 MW development partnership, strengthen the company’s project pipeline and establish a foundation for further expansion in the French battery storage market.
