artigo.texto: Stars could disappear from the night sky because of space data centers – scientists warn of a threat Kyiv • UNN Tens of thousands of space data centers could change the appearance of the night sky and make astronomers’ work more difficult. Scientists also warn of collisions and orbital debris. The mass deployment of artificial intelligence data centers in Earth's orbit could radically change the appearance of the night sky. Scientists warn that satellites could become more visible than stars and create serious problems for astronomical observations. Axios reports this, citing a new scientific study, writes UNN. Details According to researchers' estimates, the deployment of tens of thousands of orbital data centers could result in artificial satellites becoming the brightest objects in the night sky across most regions of the world. In addition to light pollution, scientists warn of the risk of collisions between spacecraft traveling at about 27,000 km/h and an increase in the amount of orbital debris. Companies plan to launch tens of thousands of satellites According to Quilty Space, investment in space data centers increased from $197 million in 2025 to $1.11 billion in 2026. SpaceX has applied to create a network of 1 million satellites. Meanwhile, the Starcloud and Blue Origin projects envisage the potential deployment of 88,000 and 51,600 spacecraft, respectively. However, experts emphasize that the announced figures do not mean that all the satellites will actually be launched. The study's lead author, David Sandalow, urged companies to act cautiously, as the consequences of the mass deployment of data centers in space have yet to be sufficiently studied.

artigo.texto: Data centers são apenas um dos dez pilares para o Brasil disputar a liderança global em IA Monica Miglio Pedrosa Para se destacar globalmente na transformação pela inteligência artificial, o Brasil precisa desenvolver capacidade própria de produzir conhecimento e tecnologia. O Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) pode atrair investimentos para ampliar a infraestrutura necessária a essa ambição. Mas os data centers por si só não garantem autonomia sobre os modelos de IA que vão transformar os negócios e participar de decisões estratégicas nas empresas. O alerta é de André Luís da Fonseca, coordenador do Centro de Estudos em Estratégia e Inovação (CEEI) do COPPEAD/UFRJ. Segundo o pesquisador, os data centers podem ampliar a capacidade de processamento no país, mas manter os dados e a estratégia em tecnologias contratadas por empresas privadas estrangeiras. Além disso, de acordo com o periódico Technological Forecasting & Social Change, a infraestrutura é apenas um dos dez elementos para construir um ecossistema completo. Os demais são cultura, demanda, financiamento, instituições formais, intermediários, conhecimento, liderança, redes e talento. “A pergunta que o país precisa fazer não é apenas onde os servidores vão ficar, mas quem vai ser dono do conhecimento que roda neles. Capacidade de processamento sem capacidade de orquestrar a IA é aluguel de infraestrutura, não soberania”, afirma. Confira, a seguir, a entrevista exclusiva para a [EXP]. [EXP] O que a instalação de data centers representa para a participação do Brasil na indústria de inteligência artificial? [André Luís da Fonseca] A indústria da IA funciona sobre uma pilha de elementos. No nível mais básico estão o espaço onde fica o data center, a licença da prefeitura, a água usada para refrigerar os servidores e a energia elétrica que eles consomem. É uma camada sem a qual o restante não existiria, mas de menor valor agregado. Quando isso é feito por uma organização de fora, é quase como se estivéssemos exportando sol, água, uso da terra e autorização ambiental. Não tem muita diferença, para todos os fins práticos, de exportar soja. É quase como se tivéssemos um monocultivo agrícola, só que computacional. Isso contribui para o PIB, traz riqueza que de outra forma não viria e, portanto, é recomendável. A questão é passar a sensação de que estamos tendo uma participação na cadeia produtiva maior do que essa atividade de fato representa. Estamos pegando um pedaço da receita da indústria por meio do fornecimento desses recursos. Isso, por si só, não está diminuindo a dependência. Como avalia as contrapartidas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento previstas no Redata? Existem efeitos negativos associados ao uso do solo, da água e dos demais recursos de determinado lugar, assim como alguém poderia argumentar que uma plantação de soja tem efeitos ambientais negativos. Então, você exige uma compensação adicional. O Redata faz isso direcionando 2% da aquisição de hardware para investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. Esse investimento contribui para o ecossistema de desenvolvimento local, o que é uma coisa boa. E a oferta de 10% da capacidade ser oferecida ao mercado interno? O que ela representa? É preciso entender que estamos falando de vender uma parte da capacidade, não de dar. É como convidar alguém para montar um negócio no seu prédio e dizer que ele terá a chance de vender também para os moradores. Não sei se podemos atribuir tanta importância a esses 10%. Para o governo brasileiro, que tem a questão de manter o processamento dos dados públicos aqui, isso garante a possibilidade de comprar esse espaço. Garante que haverá capacidade disponível para rodar no Brasil o processamento de IA associado aos serviços do governo. Mas essa oferta não é exclusiva para o governo, já que a iniciativa privada no país também pode comprar e usar. Há outros benefícios econômicos que merecem ser considerados? No caso específico do Nordeste, há a possibilidade de aproveitar energia elétrica renovável que está sendo desperdiçada. Você leva o data center para perto da turbina eólica ou da usina solar e deixa de depender de linhas de transmissão para consumir aquela energia. Ela passa a ser monetizada, vendida na forma de computação, o que também é positivo. Não estou dizendo que isso não deva ser feito. Estou dizendo que tem muito mais a ver com PIB e geração de receita do que com diminuição da dependência. O problema é achar que estamos atingindo um resultado maior do que de fato estamos. Por que manter os dados no Brasil não resolve a dependência tecnológica? Estamos vivendo um aumento muito grande da dependência. Nossas atividades individuais e profissionais estão sendo estruturadas sobre uma cognição computacional que não controlamos. A empresa não controla e o país não controla. A simples possibilidade de um modelo deixar de estar disponível já é um problema. A questão é que estamos estruturando nosso trabalho e nossa pesquisa acadêmica cada vez mais em parceria com sistemas computacionais que não controlamos. Não é o fato de os dados estarem aqui que vai nos proteger disso. A tomada de decisão dos brasileiros está sendo feita em parceria com esses sistemas, e isso é uma fonte adicional de dependência. O dado pode estar aqui e continuar não sendo seu, continuar sem o seu controle. Não estamos falando de uma refinaria de petróleo que você pode expropriar e dizer que agora é sua. É uma máquina administrada por pessoas que estão em outro lugar e que tomam decisões com base em agendas que, eventualmente, não são as nossas. Que mudanças nas condições de uso desses sistemas podem afetar quem depende deles? Pode mudar o preço, a regra, as categorias sociais representadas naquele software. Podem mudar as políticas de tratamento dos dados que fornecemos o tempo inteiro. E a regulação, por si só, não resolve isso. O que resolve é ter alternativa. A própria maneira de tomar a decisão está sendo dividida com sistemas que não

artigo.texto: Hyperscale data centers’ energy consumption, carbon emissions newly estimated by researchers New research reveals the electricity consumption and carbon emissions behind America’s hyperscale data centers rivals that of some U.S. states For immediate release: November 16, 2026 Boston, MA—Over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers (HDCs)—the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since the rise of AI. The study was published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability. “Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now. But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics. “Our study helps fill that gap.” “Our goal is to give the public, policymakers, investors, and developers a much more concrete, up-to-date picture than was available before,” added corresponding author Francesca Dominici, Clarence James Gamble Professor of Biostatistics, Population, and Data Science and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative. “Decisions about where data centers go and how they’re powered are critical environmental and public health decisions, and they should be made with good data.” While data centers are known to require significant electricity to run, few studies have examined this topic facility by facility, estimating not just how much electricity each HDC uses, but what fuels generated this electricity. For this study, the researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 HDCs across the U.S. and estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid. The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. During the study period, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption, and was associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2—an amount two to three times higher than an earlier estimate for 2018. Today, electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely much higher than they were during the study period, the researchers say. “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Guidi said. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” The study also found that roughly 54% of the electricity powering the HDCs was generated by fossil fuels—mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%)—and about a quarter of the electricity was in grid regions dirtier than average. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more heavily on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is generated heavily by coal-fired power plants. The researchers also noted that just four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied. The study had limitations, including that there wasn’t enough available data to study all HDCs in the U.S., and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose versus AI-specialized operations at each HDC. The researchers also noted that the study didn’t directly measure the health effects associated with HDCs, but that is a subject they plan to pursue in future research. “Quantifying health impacts is an important next step,” said Dominici. “First, carbon dioxide drives climate change, which affects health through heat waves, wildfire smoke, flooding, and other pathways. Second, the fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. So when data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself.” Article information “Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers,” Gianluca Guidi, Francesca Dominici, Tiziano Squartini, Callaway Sprinkle, Jonathan Gilmour, Kevin Butler, Eric Bell, Scott Delaney, Falco J. Bargagli-Stoffi, Nature Sustainability, November 16, 2026, doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 The study was supported by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences–Harvard Center Pilot Project (P30ES000002), the National Institute on Aging (R01AG066793), and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (R01ES034373). artigo.texto: Mettler-Toledo Leading in lab-grade OCV testers According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Open Circuit Voltage Graders market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) Graders market is entering a transformative phase as battery manufacturing scales up to meet electric vehicle and energy storage demand. OCV graders, which measure resting voltage to sort cells for consistency and safety, have become indispensable in gigafactory quality control. The market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 6.8% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 192 (2025=100). Growth is driven by capacity additions in lithium-ion battery production, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America, and by tightening quality standards that demand 100% cell grading. However, cyclical oversupply in battery manufacturing and high capital costs pose restraints. This report provides a data-driven outlook on market size, segmentation, competitive landscape, and regional dynamics, equipping stakeholders with actionable insights for strategic planning through 2035. The baseline scenario for the Open Circuit Voltage Graders market anticipates steady expansion over 2026-2035, underpinned by global battery manufacturing capacity growth. As gigafactories ramp up production, the need for precise cell grading intensifies to ensure pack performance and safety. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 6.8%, with demand peaking in the late 2020s as new plants come online. Technological shifts toward higher-throughput automated graders and integration with manufacturing execution systems will shape product demand. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest market, while North America and Europe show accelerated growth due to local battery supply chain investments. Restraints include potential delays in gigafactory construction and price pressure from battery makers. Overall, the outlook remains positive, with the market index reaching 192 by 2035. Lithium-ion battery manufacturing is the dominant end-use sector for OCV graders, accounting for over half of global demand. As gigafactories scale production for electric vehicles and energy storage, the need for 100% cell grading becomes critical to ensure safety and performance. OCV graders measure resting voltage after formation and aging, sorting cells into precise bins for pack assembly. The shift toward higher nickel chemistries and larger cell formats increases sensitivity to voltage variations, driving demand for more accurate and faster graders. Through 2035, as global battery capacity multiplies, this segment will remain the primary growth engine, with demand-side indicators such as EV production volumes and battery plant utilization rates directly influencing grader sales. Current trend: Growing rapidly. Major trends: Ramp-up of gigafactory capacity worldwide, Increasing cell size and capacity, Integration with automated production lines, and Adoption of smart grading software. Representative participants: Arbin Instruments, Maccor, Bitrode, Digatron, and Chroma ATE. In solar panel production, OCV graders are used to test photovoltaic modules for voltage output and consistency, ensuring performance guarantees. As solar installations accelerate globally, manufacturers require reliable grading to minimize mismatch losses in modules. The trend toward larger wafers and higher-efficiency cells increases the importance of precise voltage measurement. Demand is supported by capacity expansions in Asia-Pacific and the United States, though growth is tempered by overcapacity in module manufacturing. Through 2035, demand will be driven by technological upgrades and quality standards, with indicators such as solar capacity additions and module efficiency targets shaping the market. Current trend: Moderate growth. Major trends: Shift to larger wafer sizes, Growth in bifacial module production, Automation of module testing, and Stringent performance warranties. Representative participants: Hioki, Keysight Technologies, Chroma ATE, and National Instruments. Electronics component quality control utilizes OCV graders for testing capacitors, sensors, and other components where voltage characteristics are critical. As electronics become more complex and miniaturized, the need for precise voltage grading in production increases. This sector benefits from the ongoing digitalization and IoT device proliferation, which drive demand for reliable components. OCV graders in this segment are often benchtop or automated systems integrated into production lines. Through 2035, growth will be steady, supported by trends in consumer electronics and automotive electronics, with demand indicators including semiconductor production volumes and quality failure rates. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Miniaturization of electronic components, Growth in automotive electronics, Increasing automation in QC, and Adoption of Industry 4.0 practices. Representative participants: Keysight Technologies, National Instruments, Ametek, and Hioki. Battery recycling and second-life assessment is a fast-growing end-use sector for OCV graders. As the first wave of EV batteries reaches end-of-life, the need to rapidly assess state-of-health and residual value becomes paramount. OCV grading provides a quick, non-destructive method to sort cells for reuse or recycling. The sector is supported by regulatory pressures for battery recycling and the economic value of recovered materials. Through 2035, demand will surge as recycling infrastructure expands, particularly in Europe and North America. Key indicators include EV battery retirement volumes and recycling capacity investments. artigo.texto: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is seeking a stronger foothold in Southeast Asia’s emerging carbon markets, with Aboitiz Foundation joining a regional framework as an Observer in a move that could open up opportunities for climate financing, carbon trading and investments in nature-based projects. Representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, Aboitiz Foundation has joined the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) as an Observer, marking a step toward greater Philippine participation in regional carbon market development. The engagement coincided with the signing of the framework’s Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, and the renewal of the agreement for another two years. The move provides Philippine stakeholders an avenue to contribute to discussions on carbon market standards, financing mechanisms and regional cooperation as Southeast Asian economies work toward more interconnected and credible carbon markets. “ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz chief reputation and sustainability officer and president of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines’ participation comes as the country works to strengthen its carbon market ecosystem through private-sector collaboration, knowledge-sharing and capacity-building initiatives. One such initiative is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together industry stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Together with the NbS Group, the coalition is also advancing a long-term initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection and community development, alongside the development of recommended governance frameworks. These efforts aim to position the Philippines to develop nature-based carbon projects that can attract climate financing while creating economic opportunities for communities involved in conservation and restoration. The country has significant potential given its extensive natural resources, but turning this natural capital into viable carbon assets will require credible project standards, transparent governance and mechanisms to ensure measurable environmental and social benefits. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, along with the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to coordinate regional initiatives and promote high-integrity carbon market development. Under its 2026-2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure and technical cooperation to facilitate credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. The inclusion of Philippine private-sector stakeholders as Observers provides an opportunity to exchange expertise with established regional initiatives while bringing local experience in conservation, restoration and sustainable investment into the discussions. For the Philippines, the engagement could help bridge the gap between its natural capital and emerging financing opportunities in regional carbon markets. As ASEAN moves toward greater market connectivity, the challenge will be to ensure that carbon trading delivers more than emissions offsets by supporting investable climate solutions that protect ecosystems, strengthen local livelihoods and build long-term environmental resilience.

artigo.texto: The Lansing Town Board is set to decide whether to ban data centers on Wednesday, following a public hearing held on Tuesday. The vote comes after multiple lawsuits and months of review of the Lake Hawkeye data center slated to be built on the banks of Cayuga Lake at the former Cayuga power plant, located in Lansing. Lake Hawk Eye LLC, a subsidiary of data center developer TeraWulf, signed an 80-year lease for the property in August 2025. The ban was proposed at the end of a special meeting on Sep. 29, called by the Lansing Town Board to evaluate the impact of the data center moratorium signed by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) in July. The moratorium prevents hyperscale data center proposals from receiving environmental permitting, a required step in the approval process, for one year. This was the first statewide data center moratorium signed in the United States. The proposed data center has been met with opposition by community members concerned about the potential noise, strain on the power grid produced by the project and the cost of litigation in the event that TeraWulf violated legal agreements with the town. Others have expressed agreement with the project, citing the potential for economic development as the data center would bring in jobs and millions of dollars in tax revenue. The question to build or ban the Lansing data center comes amid national debates on artificial intelligence and data center development regulation in the wake of the midterm elections. Voters across the country supported 41 ballot measures to restrict data center development on election night – only voters in North Dakota rejected adding industrial review to the data center approval process. Data centers manage, store and process information to support artificial intelligence and online platforms. TeraWulf plans to develop the physical campus with cooling and electrical systems and then will rent the site to a tenant such as an artificial intelligence company. In a Nov. 3 lawsuit, TeraWulf alleged the Lansing town supervisor failed to produce “legally sufficient” responses for two Freedom of Information Law requests. TeraWulf took legal action through its subsidiary, Lake Hawkeye LLC, filing an Article 78 petition with the Tompkins County Supreme Court. FOIL requests cost the town more than $200,000 from October 2025 through mid-June, a surge that can be largely attributed to transparency around the controversial Lake Hawkeye Data Center, according to town supervisor Ruth Groff. An earlier hearing held at the end of September heard over 30 comments, all of which opposed the project – except Pace Ralli, vice president of project development at TeraWulf. Following the comment period, the Town Board discussed worries that even with regulation, the town cannot afford to enforce their rules due to the cost of litigation. This is not the first legal action taken against the town board. In July, a member of the Lansing Zoning Advisory Committee, Laura Baker, alleged town board member Joe Wetmore misused his authority to block projects. Baker, represented by a legal firm that works with TeraWulf, filed the petition in June, accusing Wetmore of “manipulating” government processes to block projects he does not personally agree with, among other complaints. Wetmore is “not commenting on ongoing lawsuits,” he wrote in an email to The Sun. Two environmental advocacy groups, FLX Strong and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Network, filed an Article 78 petition against the Lansing Town Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf project developers in January. They allege the ZBA overstepped its authority by “allow[ing] the project to bypass rigorous environmental review,” according to the Ithaca Times. Almost 23,000 people have signed the No Data Center FLX petition that calls for the rejection of the data center development. The organization is set to hold a press conference before the public hearing at Lansing Middle School on Tuesday. The data center development involves construction through wetlands, potentially contaminating Cayuga Lake and increasing strain on the electrical grid, according to No Data Center FLX. “These people are not the enemy,” said Joe Scaglione III, an Ithaca resident, referencing TeraWulf. In an interview with The Sun, Scaglione said he met with five TeraWulf representatives, including Ralli, to tour the site and “ask them some hard questions.” He is concerned about property tax increases and said the data center will bring in $8.5 million in annual tax revenue and 150 permanent jobs that would replace the 150 positions terminated when the Cayuga Power Plant shut down in 2019. TeraWulf plans to prioritize hiring those who used to work at the plant, according to Scaglione. Beyond Tompkins One of the foremost issues during the midterm elections were “data centers and the price of gas and affordability and corruption,” according to Prof. Dan Lamb, public policy. He added that “allowing the Wild West with data centers is not serving the public well, and communities are getting exploited.” On the federal level, President Donald Trump signed an executive order in July to accelerate data center permits by expediting environment reviews to 10 days and providing financial support to development companies. The administration also proposed that the Environmental Protection Agency no longer require towns to solicit public feedback on applications for air pollution permits, including data centers, and allow the projections to begin development before procuring proper permits. New York State has home rule power, meaning municipalities have complete control over zoning law. This creates uneven data center and artificial intelligence regulation, according to Lamb. As a result, large development companies “weave around the difficult municipalities” and may even exploit communities — especially those with loose regulations, Lamb explained. artigo.texto: Publicidade O veículo de aquisição de data centers recém-listado da Blackstone adquiriu uma participação majoritária em duas joint ventures com a Amazon Web Services (AWS) em uma transação avaliada em cerca de US$ 5 bilhões. Em seu primeiro investimento, o Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Inc. (BXDC) passará a deter 13 estruturas energizadas recém-construídas em dois campi de data centers da AWS localizados no norte de Indiana e no Mississippi, segundo Nick Pell, diretor-presidente do fundo. O BXDC ficará com uma participação de 75% nos ativos, enquanto a AWS manterá os 25% restantes. A divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon arrendará todo o portfólio por um prazo inicial de 12 anos, com possibilidade de extensão para até 32 anos, de acordo com comunicado divulgado nesta segunda-feira. “Este acordo direto com a Amazon cria um roteiro para realizarmos mais operações desse tipo com hyperscalers ou desenvolvedores”, afirmou Pell em entrevista. Segundo ele, a joint venture assumirá dívida equivalente a 50% do valor da aquisição no fechamento da operação, prevista para ser concluída ainda este ano. As ações do BXDC avançavam quase 7% às 9h30 em Nova York. O fundo imobiliário reflete a ambição da Blackstone de se tornar uma das maiores financiadoras de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial do mundo, além de ampliar seu alcance entre investidores individuais. A gestora de ativos alternativos, que administra quase US$ 1,4 trilhão, construiu um portfólio de data centers avaliado em US$ 200 bilhões, que inclui a QTS Realty Trust, uma das principais empresas de construção e operação desse tipo de instalação. Continua depois da publicidade “Somente em 2027, estamos acompanhando mais de US$ 300 bilhões em novos data centers pertencentes a desenvolvedores e hyperscalers cuja entrega é esperada nos Estados Unidos”, disse Pell durante teleconferência com analistas. “Vemos ainda mais projetos surgindo em 2028 e nos anos seguintes.” Ele acrescentou que mais da metade dos novos data centers está planejada para polos emergentes, incluindo Richmond, na Virgínia, e San Antonio, no Texas, o que demonstra a expansão da demanda. Lançado em maio, o BXDC foi criado para adquirir data centers já estabilizados, avaliados entre US$ 250 milhões e US$ 1,5 bilhão, com contratos de locação de longo prazo assinados com hyperscalers. O fundo estima que esse mercado potencial alcance US$ 1 trilhão nos próximos cinco anos. Continua depois da publicidade “À medida que as restrições de oferta aumentam diante de uma demanda que continua muito forte, ativos já estabilizados, que já existem, já possuem energia disponível e já contam com um inquilino, tornam-se mais valiosos”, afirmou o diretor de investimentos do BXDC, Mike Forman. “Há muitos desenvolvedores e fundos fechados buscando vender ativos e reciclar capital. Estamos oferecendo uma alternativa para eles por meio do capital dos investidores públicos do BXDC”, acrescentou Pell. A vitória ampla do Partido Democrata nas eleições legislativas dos Estados Unidos tende a impulsionar iniciativas para estabelecer limites regulatórios ao crescimento dos data centers. A expansão dessas instalações tem enfrentado resistência organizada de comunidades locais, além da escassez de equipamentos, fatores que criam gargalos para novos projetos. Continua depois da publicidade Segundo relatório divulgado pelo JPMorgan Chase em maio, mais de 60% da capacidade de data centers prevista para ser concluída em 2027 ainda nem iniciou sua construção. Apesar disso, a demanda por infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial segue em expansão. A carteira de pedidos da AWS, indicador que mede contratos de computação em nuvem ainda não executados, alcança US$ 578 bilhões, afirmou o CEO da Amazon, Andy Jassy, após a divulgação dos resultados do terceiro trimestre em outubro. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.

artigo.texto: AmpereHour Energy has announced its role as the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) integration partner for IndiGrid’s recently commissioned 250 MW / 500 MWh standalone battery storage project in Rajasthan. Located in western Rajasthan, the project is connected to the 765 kV Bhadla-III pooling substation and represents another step towards expanding India’s utility-scale energy storage infrastructure. The project has a power capacity of 250 MW and an energy storage capacity of 500 MWh, enabling it to deliver electricity at its rated output for up to two hours. The facility is designed to store electricity when it is available and supply it during periods of higher demand. This capability is expected to support peak demand management, improve grid flexibility and facilitate the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. AmpereHour Energy was responsible for engineering and integrating the project’s AC-coupled BESS. The system comprises modular 40 MWh / 20 MVA blocks and a centralized Power Plant Controller (PPC). The PPC coordinates plant operations and supports various grid applications, including peak shifting and frequency support. The entire facility is managed through AmpereHour Energy’s proprietary ELINA Energy Management System (EMS). The platform supports battery operations and coordinates system activities with state and regional load dispatch centres. This technology is designed to help manage energy storage operations while ensuring the facility responds to grid requirements. Commenting on the development, Rahul Shelke, Managing Director and Co-Founder of AmpereHour Energy, said that large-scale battery storage plays an important role in making electricity available when the grid requires it. He highlighted that projects of this scale are essential for developing a power system capable of accommodating higher renewable energy generation while responding to changing electricity demand. Shelke also expressed appreciation for the partnership with IndiGrid, noting that AmpereHour Energy contributed its BESS integration expertise and proprietary energy management technology to support the deployment. Harsh Shah, Managing Director of IndiGrid, stated that battery storage is becoming an important component of India’s long-term power planning as renewable energy accounts for a growing share of the country’s electricity mix. He noted that energy storage can support renewable energy integration while maintaining grid stability. Shah further described the commissioning of the 250 MW / 500 MWh facility as an important milestone for IndiGrid and its third BESS project. He also acknowledged AmpereHour Energy’s partnership and support in bringing the project into operation. The commissioning reflects India’s increasing focus on standalone battery energy storage infrastructure. As solar and wind power capacity expands, large-scale storage facilities are expected to play a greater role in balancing electricity supply and demand, managing peak loads and improving the reliability of renewable-powered electricity networks. artigo.texto: Spartanburg County Council approves three data center agreements, advances three more Spartanburg County Council has approved three proposed data center development agreements on third and final reading. The agreement for Valara Holdings LLC passed in a 3-2 vote, with Councilmen Monier Abusaft and Grant DeShields voting against it. The proposed 457-megawatt data center is planned for about 300 acres along South Pine Street. The project represents an anticipated investment of roughly $2.8 billion and is expected to create 27 full-time jobs. The agreements for AIB CLT1 LLC and 300 Jones Road Associates LLC both passed unanimously. AIB plans to replace its existing Bitcoin mining operation at Tyger River Industrial Park in Moore with a permanent data center building. The 50-megawatt project represents an anticipated $1.2 billion investment and is expected to create 28 jobs. The Jones Road project would redevelop about 137 acres of the former R.R. Donnelley property into a data center with up to 65 megawatts of capacity. The company anticipates investing $1.5 billion and creating 25 jobs. Council also gave initial approval to three additional data center development agreements proposed by AIB for the Tyger River Industrial Park in Moore. AIB CLT2, CLT3 and CLT4 all passed unanimously on first reading. Those proposals will need additional readings before receiving final approval. Monday's meeting drew a large crowd, with council chambers filled with residents speaking both for and against the proposed developments. Opponents raised concerns about potential noise and pollution, while supporters pointed to the economic benefits and additional revenue the projects could bring to the county.

artigo.texto: The Broken Arrow City Council voted Monday to extend its moratorium on new applications for data centers and to hire a consulting firm to help write permanent rules. The city wants rules in place before any data center company can apply to build in Broken Arrow. What the council approved Council members approved two things Monday: - A contract with Westwood Professional Services Inc. to study data centers and help write permanent zoning standards. - An extension of the moratorium through June 30, 2027, so the city can finish those rules before it accepts any applications. The study will focus on three things: where data centers could be allowed, protecting the city’s water and other infrastructure, and the long-term impact. Work since June In June, the City Council passed a six-month moratorium on data center applications that was set to expire Dec. 31. Since then, the city formed a data center study committee and met with Public Service Company of Oklahoma about how to power large data centers and plan for the infrastructure. The city also reviewed data center rules adopted by other cities, including Oklahoma City. City Attorney Trevor Dennis said the goal is to bring the council “a set of regulations and recommendations” for amending the zoning ordinance for data centers. Support for police chief during public comment One person also spoke during public comment in support of Police Chief Lance Arnold, who has been on paid administrative leave since Oct. 14 while the city conducts an internal investigation. Action on Arnold’s employment was not on the agenda Monday because the chief reports to the city manager, not the council. Data center moratorium timeline - April 30, 2026: The city publicly discloses a developer’s interest in building a data center in east Broken Arrow. - June 10, 2026: The prospective company walks away from its letter of intent to buy privately owned land in east Broken Arrow. - June 15, 2026: The council passes Ordinance No. 3929, a six-month moratorium on data center applications through Dec. 31. - Aug. 18, 2026: The city announces the formation of a Data Center Study Committee. - Oct. 20, 2026: City staff briefs the council on their regulatory study. - Nov. 16, 2026: The council approves a consulting contract with Westwood Professional Services and extends the moratorium up to six months through June 30, 2027.

artigo.texto: Beijing, 14 nov (Xinhua) — A China acelerará o desenvolvimento de novos tipos de armazenamento de energia durante o período do 15º Plano Quinquenal (2026-2030) para apoiar a construção de um novo sistema de energia elétrica, de acordo com um plano divulgado na sexta-feira. O plano, emitido pela Comissão Nacional de Desenvolvimento e Reforma e pela Administração Nacional de Energia (ANE), estabelece uma meta de 300 milhões de quilowatts de novos tipos instalados de armazenamento de energia até 2030, com duração média de armazenamento de cerca de três horas. Também visa transformar o setor de uma expansão em larga escala para um crescimento impulsionado pelo mercado. Novos tipos de armazenamento de energia referem-se a tecnologias de armazenamento de energia além da hidrelétrica por bombeamento, incluindo principalmente armazenamento por eletroquímica, ar comprimido e gravidade. O plano pede que os novos tipos de armazenamento de energia participem de forma justa nos mercados de eletricidade e incentiva as megabases de energia renovável equipadas com armazenamento a integrarem os mercados de energia transprovinciais como uma única entidade. Também pede um mecanismo de precificação refinado que reflita o valor da energia armazenada, com preços de carregamento e descarga determinados por meio de negociação justa no mercado. A ênfase nos mecanismos de mercado surge à medida que o mercado de energia da China amadurece. O investimento em novos tipos de armazenamento de energia foi inicialmente impulsionado por políticas, dependendo principalmente de regras de implantação obrigatória e subsídios, mas o setor agora está migrando para mecanismos baseados no mercado, disse a Huayuan Securities em um relatório de pesquisa. Xu Dongjie, vice-engenheiro-chefe do Instituto de Planejamento e Engenharia de Energia Elétrica da China, chamou a meta de 300 milhões de quilowatts de uma meta mínima prudente e baseada em ciência, que atende às necessidades do sistema e apoia um aumento razoável na utilização, ao mesmo tempo que dá confiança à indústria e evita ciclos de expansão e contração impulsionados pelo investimento. A China lidera o mundo em novos tipos de armazenamento de energia, com capacidade instalada representando cerca de 40% do total global. Até o final de 2025, a China havia construído e colocado em operação 136 milhões de quilowatts de novos tipos de armazenamento de energia, com duração média de armazenamento atingindo 2,58 horas, 0,3 hora a mais do que no final de 2024, segundo a ANE. artigo.texto: Ireland’s Data-Center Lawsuit Puts Energy Policy Under Scrutiny (Bloomberg) -- With its temperate climate, sparse population and pro-business government, Ireland seemed for years like a perfect location for building data centers. Now, the country is becoming a test bed for legal opposition to those centers on climate grounds. This week, Ireland’s energy and water regulator faces a case in the High Court over its rules for new data centers. The case, brought by environmental law charity ClientEarth and Irish environmental groups, argues that the regulator’s latest policy for connecting large energy users to the electricity grid fails to comply with Irish and European law and risks locking Ireland into years of fossil-fuel use, undermining its ability to meet legally binding emissions targets. It’s part of a recent wave of action against data centers on climate grounds in Ireland — one of Europe’s largest data hubs — and around the world. Concern and anger about the energy and land demanded by the buildout is already high, but with global energy use by these centers expected to almost quadruple by 2035, according to BloombergNEF, the potential impact on emissions and man-made climate change is huge. The Irish case is significant because it targets overall policy rather than an individual development. It could also have implications for data-center construction in Europe more broadly. While European laws won’t change off the back of a domestic case, its outcome may guide decision-making in any similar challenges that come up in other EU states. “Ireland has a really robust legal framework when it comes to its climate targets,” said Eoin Jackson, a researcher at the London School of Economics whose work identifies Ireland as a hotspot for litigation against data centers on climate change grounds. Its data-center boom was also early, so “there were already a lot of challenges underway to data centers that kind of precede the concerns driven by AI.” As a result, he said, “Ireland has become a little bit of a canary in the coal mine when it comes to data-center litigation taken on climate grounds.” Obvious Choice In recent decades, tech companies including Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms Inc. and TikTok have all established their European headquarters in Ireland, attracted by a favorable tax regime and highly educated, English-speaking workforce. Corporation taxes paid by US multinationals are of huge economic importance to the country, allowing it to run a budget surplus. Ireland was also the obvious choice for many of the tech giants’ data centers, at least to begin with. It now hosts approximately 89 data centers — about 10 times more than the European per-capita average — most of which are in industrial areas surrounding the capital, Dublin, and along the east coast. In 2025, data centers accounted for 23% of metered electricity use in Ireland, more than all urban households and up from just 5% a decade ago. In a recent report, a United Nations academic body warned that Ireland offers a “cautionary example” of grid stress from concentrated digital infrastructure. Concerns about grid capacity and blackouts brought new construction to a halt in 2021. That November, the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) implemented a de facto ban on connecting new centers to the grid by introducing strict criteria around the location of data centers and their ability to provide on-site energy generation or energy storage. While the process didn’t amount to an outright ban, securing new connections became close to impossible. Industry groups argued that Ireland was missing out on the global capital pouring into AI infrastructure. However, the freeze was celebrated by environmentalists and Irish residents worried about energy costs alike. Ireland is far behind on meeting its legally binding climate targets. Its EU target is to reduce emissions by 42% by 2030 compared with 2005 levels; it is currently on track to achieve 13%, according to estimates by Ireland’s Environmental Protection Agency. The country got 47% of its electricity from gas-fired generation in 2025 and is heavily reliant on gas imports, mostly from the UK. It has ambitions to tap its significant offshore wind resources, but for now, it’s relying on smaller renewable inputs from onshore wind, solar power and batteries. Those may not be enough to keep up with the demand from hyperscalers. In December — at a time when various countries had or were considering pauses on data-center development — the CRU published a new policy on grid connections, bringing the de facto moratorium on grid connections to an end. Under the regulator’s new policy, any data center seeking a grid connection must install on-site generation or battery systems capable of meeting its full electricity demand, as well as providing power back to the national grid when needed. The CRU rules also allow for data centers to run on non-renewable energy for six years, after which point their energy supply must be 80% renewable. However, the renewable calculation does not take into account back-up generation. Innovative Case In their legal case, ClientEarth, Friends of the Irish Environment and Friends of the Earth Ireland argue the new policy is likely to trap Ireland into increased greenhouse gas emissions for decades, despite its legal obligations domestically and in the EU. “Both Ireland and countries across Europe are grappling with the energy demands of rapidly expanding data centers in the global race to scale AI,” said ClientEarth lead lawyer Natascha Hospedales in a statement. “That’s exactly why regulators like the CRU must ensure their approach to the infrastructure boom is responsible and aligns with legally binding climate commitments.” The CRU declined to comment. artigo.texto: EUA incluem Brasil em lista de países com restrições para comprar chips de data centers Foto: Joyce N. Boghosian/Casa Branca O governo de Donald Trump anunciou nesta segunda-feira (16) uma norma que impõe novas restrições à exportação de chips avançados de inteligência artificial para data centers instalados fora dos Estados Unidos. A medida busca impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem data centers em outros países para acessar esses componentes e treinar seus próprios modelos de IA. Além do Brasil, a norma exigirá uma licença do governo Trump para a exportação de chips avançados de IA a operadoras de data centers com sede na Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia, países que apresentam um risco de contrabando acima do normal, afirmou o governo dos EUA. “A norma foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em terceiros países”, aponta o departamento em comunicado divulgado nesta segunda-feira. A medida busca impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA tenham acesso a capacidade computacional localizada no exterior que utiliza processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. E foi tomada na esteira do escândalo da Nvidia, cujo ex-CEO, Jesen Huang, reununciou na semana passada após vir à tona que ele tinha um caso amoroso com uma executiva chinesa suspeita de espionagem. A norma busca fechar uma brecha que, na visão de muitos em Washington, tem permitido à China contornar uma proibição do Departamento de Comércio que impede empresas chinesas de comprar os chips de IA mais avançados fabricados por companhias como a Nvidia. A nova regulamentação estabelece restrições para data centers no exterior que forneçam “volumes significativos de capacidade computacional” a empresas com sede em um pequeno grupo de países considerados de alto risco, lista que inclui China, Rússia e Irã. Os data centers também serão obrigados a realizar verificações rigorosas sobre seus clientes. A medida, que entrará em vigor em 90 dias, deverá “prejudicar” a capacidade de empresas desses países de utilizar chips americanos para treinar modelos avançados de IA, segundo o comunicado. As ações de fabricantes de chips despencaram na manhã desta segunda-feira. Os papéis da Nvidia caíram mais de 2%. As ações da Intel recuaram mais de 6%, e as da Micron, mais de 7%. Os índices que acompanham esses papéis também registraram quedas: o Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recuou mais de 5%, enquanto o Nasdaq, índice mais amplo e fortemente concentrado em empresas de tecnologia, também abriu em baixa.

artigo.texto: SAN JOSE IS CONSIDERING a temporary pause on data center projects before development standards to guide limits on water use and other environmental impacts are finalized in December. Mayor Matt Mahan and Councilmembers Pamela Campos, David Cohen, Peter Ortiz and Domingo Candelas on Thursday announced a proposal to halt land use approvals for data centers, putting a pause on any related projects before the City Council votes on uniform standards on Dec. 8. This move comes after San José Spotlight reported that Google’s data center in Alviso could be approved ahead of the standards. The project located at 5087 Disk Drive would require 250 megawatts — enough to power 250,000 households. “After many months of community engagement and research, we are preparing to vote on the strictest proposed regulations for data centers in the country, which include requirements for 100% clean energy, closed loop water systems, union labor, monitoring and enforcement of noise restrictions, and bans on NDAs and any public subsidy,” Mahan told San José Spotlight. “But none of that matters if we allow projects to slip through just before these standards are adopted. The action we’re proposing is about holding every project to the same high bar — short of that would be an unacceptable betrayal of public trust.” In the proposed standards, data center developers will be encouraged to enroll with San Jose Clean Energy, which supplies renewable power. Diesel backup generators must follow the strictest federal emission standards, and can only run when there are power outages. The San Jose Planning Commission will consider the latest version of the proposed standards on Nov. 18. For months, residents have been demanding the city implement a moratorium on data centers before standards get put in place. But advocates such as Linda Hutchins-Knowles, co-founder of environmental nonprofit Mothers Out Front Silicon Valley, said the proposed pause still falls short. “After many months of community engagement and research, we are preparing to vote on the strictest proposed regulations for data centers in the country. … But none of that matters if we allow projects to slip through just before these standards are adopted.” Mayor Matt Mahan “I definitely appreciate there being a pause put now to stop any more getting through, but I still think that needs to be extended beyond their current timeline,” Hutchins-Knowles told San José Spotlight. “We believe that it would also be a betrayal of trust to not impose an actual moratorium in order to ensure that the standards are truly robust and that the community is on board. (The) city’s community engagement process was rushed and insufficient.” San Jose began the process of drafting the development standards in June. When officials presented the draft proposal last month, residents decried how the standards fell short of covering the heat island effect and studying how low-frequency infrasound will affect the community. What impact will new projects have? Advocates have asked city officials to consult with state and county agencies to study the cumulative effects of bringing on the 16 data center projects in San Jose’s development pipeline. They have noted that the city’s efforts to become the world’s artificial intelligence capital is in conflict with developing standards to regulate the industry it wants to attract. “The moratorium should be long enough to allow the city to conduct studies of the long-term cumulative impacts of the massive scale of data center development contemplated by the city, which are anticipated to triple our energy use,” a joint statement from eight environmental and advocate groups, including Green Foothills, the Sierra Club Loma Prieta Chapter and Alviso in Action, reads. The People Over Data Centers San Jose Coalition, a group comprised of neighbors and community organizations, has organized meetings and town halls in every council district to educate residents on data centers. The city has also conducted its own outreach and incorporated some of the feedback it has received from residents, including prohibiting open loop cooling systems that use drinkable water and can consume millions of gallons of water a year. Instead, the city will require data centers to use recycled water or a closed loop system that circulates water through pipes to absorb heat from the electronics. “The city must strike a balance between securing economic development and ensuring that growth is responsibly built,” a Nov. 6 memo from Planning Director Chris Burton said. “While the proposed standards do not address every concern raised through the community engagement process, they represent that balance.” Ortiz, who oversees District 5 in East San Jose, said the city is seeing unprecedented interest from developers for data center projects, and San Jose has a responsibility to ensure growth will benefit residents. “This proposed pause is not about stopping development. It’s about establishing responsible standards, protecting our communities and ensuring that industries benefiting from our city’s resources also contribute to addressing challenges like affordability,” Ortiz told San José Spotlight. “Economic growth should not come at the expense of our residents. It should improve their quality of life.” Contact Joyce Chu at [email protected] or @joyce_speaks on X. This story originally appeared in San Jose Spotlight.

artigo.texto: Deye’s 125 kW Hybrid Inverter: Advancing Flexible Energy Storage for C&I Applications Deye introduces the SUN-125K-SG02HP3-EU-GM10, a three-phase, high-voltage hybrid inverter designed to integrate solar generation, battery storage and AC power management within a single platform. November 17, 2026. By News Bureau As commercial and industrial (C&I) facilities increasingly adopt renewable energy and battery storage, the demand for flexible, efficient and scalable power solutions continues to grow. Addressing these requirements, Deye introduces the SUN-125K-SG02HP3-EU-GM10, a three-phase, high-voltage hybrid inverter designed to integrate solar generation, battery storage and AC power management within a single platform. High-Voltage Battery Integration The inverter supports high-voltage lithium-ion batteries with a voltage range of 160–1000 V and a maximum charging and discharging current of 200 A. Its battery management system (BMS) self-adaptation supports communication with compatible battery systems, enabling coordinated battery operation. With six programmable time periods for battery charging and discharging, the inverter allows users to configure energy management according to site requirements and solar generation patterns. This flexibility can help commercial facilities optimise battery utilisation based on their electricity consumption profiles and tariff structures. Efficient Solar Power Conversion The SUN-125K-SG02HP3-EU-GM10 delivers a rated AC active power of 125 kW and it offers a maximum efficiency of 98.70 percent. The inverter supports a maximum PV input power of 200 kW, with ten maximum power point trackers (MPPTs). These features provide flexibility in configuring solar arrays for suitable new installations and solar-plus-storage projects. Additionally, its 100 percent unbalanced output capability supports applications with uneven loads across three phases. The inverter can deliver up to 1.5 times its rated power for 10 seconds in off-grid operation, helping accommodate short-duration power demands, subject to system design and load characteristics. Flexible Retrofit and Scalable Design For facilities with existing solar installations, the inverter supports AC coupling, enabling battery storage integration while retaining suitable existing solar equipment. This provides an option for businesses looking to expand their energy storage capabilities without necessarily replacing their existing solar inverters. The system supports parallel operation of up to ten units in both on-grid and off-grid applications. It also supports multiple batteries in parallel, subject to equipment compatibility and appropriate system design. In addition, the inverter can store energy from a diesel generator, providing another option for installations incorporating generator-based power supply. Built for Reliable Operation The inverter features an IP65 protection rating and intelligent air cooling, with a specified operating temperature range of -40°C to +60°C. Integrated protection functions include DC reverse-polarity protection, AC overcurrent protection, thermal protection, anti-islanding protection, insulation monitoring and Type II AC/DC surge protection. Arc-fault circuit interruption is available as an option. Monitoring and communication options include RS485, RS232 and CAN, alongside optional Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G, LAN and GPRS connectivity. By combining high-voltage battery integration, AC-coupling flexibility, configurable energy management and scalable parallel operation, Deye’s 125 kW hybrid inverter offers a versatile platform for commercial and industrial solar-plus-storage applications. - Deye New Energy If you want to cooperate with us and would like to reuse some of our content, please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: A CPFL não esconde o entusiasmo com os primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) para sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, que deverão acontecer nos dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. “Nós estamos nos preparando há mais de dois anos, lembrando que foi um leilão que já foi anunciado há uns anos. (…) Nós temos uma expectativa importante”, disse o diretor vice-presidente de Operações de Mercado da CPFL, Vitor Fagali. “Acho que o Capex vai ser o principal driver de competitividade e a gente está trabalhando aqui bastante com fornecedores [para] que eles possam nacionalizar”, complementou o executivo, que acredita que a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) liberará nesta terça-feira, 17 de novembro, a lista dos projetos habilitados para o leilão. Segundo Fagali, a maior competitividade da CPFL deve ser no leilão com conteúdo nacional, previsto para o dia 2 de dezembro. Este também deve ser o certame com maior oferta de contratação. “Mas também estamos nos preparando para o leilão do dia 4, que vai ser para equipamentos importados, caso tenha”, garantiu. Fagali ainda comentou sobre o preço-teto dos editais, que ficou em R$ 1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para o leilão de sistemas com conteúdo nacional, e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para o certame de 4 de dezembro, aberto a equipamentos importados. “É um preço razoável, dá margem para todos os players poderem trabalhar e terem projetos aqui competitivos”, declarou. Além do leilão de baterias, a CPFL avalia como oportunidades de crescimento os leilões de transmissão, disse o presidente da companhia, Gustavo Estrella. A CPFL tem como controladora a estatal chinesa State Grid, que detém 83,71% do capital da CPFL. Consumo de data centers aumenta 42% em um ano Durante teleconferência sobre os resultados do terceiro trimestre nesta segunda-feira, 16 de novembro, a CPFL informou que o consumo de data centers em sua área de concessão aumentou 41,7% em comparação com o mesmo período de 2025, alcançando 329 GWh. “A expectativa é que vamos seguir com aumentos expressivos do consumo de data center, basicamente com os pedidos já feitos e aceitos pela companhia. Isso é importante, dada a restrição de conexão que a gente tem em diversos pontos de conexão na área de concessão, mas ainda assim com uma perspectiva importante e positiva de crescimento no consumo dos data centers”, avaliou Estrella. Considerando todos os grupos de consumidores, a demanda na área da CPFL aumentou 3,6% no ano, chegando a 19.194 GWh. Com exceção da classe rural, todas as classes apresentaram aumento no consumo. De acordo com a empresa, além do consumo dos data centers, colaborou para a maior demanda a média mais alta de temperatura. Por outro lado, a CPFL se preocupa com o aumento na inadimplência. A empresa enfrentou um gargalo atípico no trimestre, com implantação de um novo sistema de gestão (SAP), que impossibilitou a execução de cortes de energia durante o mês de julho. Mesmo assim, a companhia avalia que o cenário de juros altos e endividamento das famílias pressiona os consumidores, e pode se refletir na inadimplência. A Provisão para Devedores Duvidosos (PDD) apresentou um aumento de 33,8% em relação ao 3T25, chegando a R$ 97,5 milhões. O índice de PDD/Receita bruta de fornecimento foi de 1,16% no trimestre, contra 0,91% há um ano. Em distribuição, a diretoria da CPFL também destacou a renovação das concessões. CPFL reconhece R$ 38 mi em ressarcimentos de curtailment No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a CPFL teve níveis mais altos de curtailment, na comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Entre julho e setembro deste ano, a empresa teve cortes na ordem de 290 MW médios, que representaram 47,7% da geração potencial. Há um ano, o curtailment foi de 276 MW médios, ou 39,4% da geração potencial. Além disso, o período teve ventos mais fracos na comparação anual. Assim, a geração eólica da CPFL foi de 355 MW médios, com queda de 23,8% em um ano. A empresa também reconheceu reembolsos de R$ 38 milhões no resultado do terceiro trimestre de 2026 referentes à compensação financeira por cortes de geração eólica e solar ocorridos entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025, no âmbito da Lei 15.269/2025 e regulamentado pela Portaria Normativa 140/2026 do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), que prevê o ressarcimento de cortes classificados como restrições por confiabilidade elétrica e indisponibilidade externa. Apesar do reconhecimento no resultado deste trimestre, ainda não há entrada no caixa da companhia, já que o recebimento dos valores depende de assinatura do termo de compromisso com a União e a revisão e validação dos montantes. Resultados A CPFL registrou, no terceiro trimestre de 2026, lucro líquido de R$ 1,3 bilhão, com queda de 6,4% em um ano. O Ebitda (lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização, na sigla em inglês) foi de R$ 3 bilhões, com queda de 3,1% frente ao 3T25. A empresa justifica as reduções a um efeito contábil relacionado à renovação das concessões da CPFL Paulista, CPFL Piratininga e CPFL RGE. “O ativo financeiro da concessão foi reclassificado para o intangível, e sua atualização monetária deixou de transitar pelo resultado”, explica a companhia no comunicado de resultados. A geração de energia da CPFL no trimestre, considerando todas as fontes, foi de 4.205 GWh, com leve aumento de 0,2% em um ano. O lucro líquido da divisão foi de R$ 580 milhões, com avanço de 14,8% em um ano. Em transmissão, a CPFL reportou lucro líquido de R$ 107 milhões, com crescimento de 55,1% frente ao 3T25. Na divisão de serviços, o lucro líquido foi de R$ 28 milhões, com queda de 53,3% em um ano.

artigo.texto: Bloomington to consider extending data center moratorium, seek feedback on revised regulations BLOOMINGTON (25News Now) - Monday is likely not to be the final chance for the public to sound off on data centers in Bloomington as city officials want more time to consider regulations. Bloomington’s planning commission is being asked to recommend the city council extend the moratorium another six months as staff revises rules first proposed on Oct. 9. Changes contained in planning commission documents include requirements for air quality and noise control. Developers would be banned from entering into non-disclosure agreements for any size data centers, when the initial proposal said it would apply to only hyperscale facilities. Also, higher fines would be imposed for developers who violate city regulations. The city council’s six-month moratorium on data centers is set to expire at the end of this month. A second half-year pause would run until May. The planning commission’s second public hearing is scheduled for Monday at 4 p.m. at the Bloomington Center for Performing Arts. Another hearing would follow after staff reviews public testimony and prepares an ordinance for final city council approval. artigo.texto: Turkmenistan’s long-delayed TAPI gas pipeline… Nvidia’s leadership scandal and mounting… PJM Interconnection, the biggest grid operator in the United States, has proposed to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to streamline the processes related to new power generation capacity commissioning and large consumer connections in a bid to speed it all up. PJM, which operates in 13 states, has been struggling to cope with the sharp demand rise resulting from the proliferation of data centers, which has created a supply shortfall of some 6.8 GW, according to a Reuters report. Unless PJM secures generation capacity to cover that, the grid in those 13 states could become less reliable. The shortfall was revealed in PJM’s June 2028/2029 electricity procurement auction, organized earlier this year. The amount of capacity is what PJM needs to find before that year to make sure there is enough generation during demand spike periods. “Neither generation nor transmission is coming online quickly enough to keep pace with new demand growth driven mainly by large loads like data centers,” company spokesman Jeff Shields said. "The factor that PJM planning can influence is how quickly these new resources are studied for reliability." Last month, PJM had to issue a Maximum Generation Alert as a warm front moving across its area of operation met planned generation capacity maintenance, leading to a supply squeeze as some 62 GW in capacity were offline for maintenance. The unfavorable combination of circumstances prompted electricity prices to shoot up to over $1,000 per megawatt-hour. To tackle these challenges, PJM has proposed to FERC to reduce the time now required for the study of connecting new demand sources to the grid, from two years to 12 months. By streamlining its processes, the grid operator would also be able to identify the places for the most urgent grid upgrades related to the connection of new data centers. By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com More Top Reads From Oilprice.com

artigo.texto: A Astella iniciou no último dia 11, a operação de um data center no centro de Curitiba (PR), com capacidade inicial de aproximadamente 3,5 megawatts (MW). A unidade poderá chegar a 5 MW conforme a demanda dos clientes, a contratação de energia e a instalação de novos equipamentos. O empreendimento marca o início de um plano de expansão da empresa, que prevê R$ 300 milhões em investimentos entre 2027 e 2028 para implantar novas estruturas em seis localidades brasileiras. A operação está instalada em um edifício de 8.800 metros quadrados e 16 pavimentos, que já recebeu estruturas de data centers de grandes operadoras de telecomunicações. A empresa pretende aproveitar a infraestrutura existente e investir na modernização tecnológica do ambiente. Para 2026, estão previstos mais de R$ 30 milhões em investimentos destinados à atualização do data center. A unidade foi projetada para atender também à crescente demanda por processamento de inteligência artificial. Entre os recursos previstos estão sistemas de refrigeração líquida e soluções para racks de alta densidade, capazes de suportar equipamentos que exigem maior capacidade energética e controle térmico. Curitiba será o primeiro ponto de uma rede nacional que deverá combinar data centers, estruturas de edge computing, serviços de nuvem e infraestrutura voltada à inteligência artificial. A proposta é distribuir a capacidade de processamento e armazenamento pelo país, aproximando os recursos tecnológicos dos locais onde os dados são produzidos e utilizados. Segundo a empresa, esse modelo pode reduzir a latência, melhorar o desempenho das aplicações e otimizar custos operacionais. A expansão será realizada de forma gradual, acompanhando a contratação de clientes e a evolução da demanda. A infraestrutura deverá atender aplicações de computação de alto desempenho, inteligência artificial, processamento com GPUs, backup, recuperação de desastres e continuidade operacional. Outro ponto da estratégia é a soberania dos dados, tema que ganhou relevância com o aumento da dependência de serviços digitais e da computação em nuvem. A Astella pretende oferecer alternativas como colocation, nuvem privada, cloud híbrida, conexão com provedores de nuvem pública e edge computing. A escolha entre os modelos dependerá das necessidades de segurança, desempenho, custo e localização das informações de cada cliente. A empresa também pretende ampliar o controle sobre o fornecimento de energia utilizado em suas operações. O grupo ABL está incorporando uma usina solar de aproximadamente 2,7 megawatts-pico (MWp), já conectada à rede elétrica, como parte de uma estratégia para aumentar gradualmente a participação de geração própria renovável. A proposta é combinar essa produção com o fornecimento da distribuidora, mantendo a redundância necessária para evitar interrupções em operações críticas. Com capital próprio e nacional, a companhia também está em processo de credenciamento junto à Defesa Nacional. A iniciativa está relacionada à atuação em segmentos que exigem maior controle sobre armazenamento, processamento e proteção de informações. O data center terá como público empresas privadas, órgãos públicos, instituições financeiras, universidades, provedores de internet e operadoras de telecomunicações. “Estamos transformando quase três décadas de experiência em tecnologia, conectividade e infraestrutura crítica em uma plataforma preparada para uma nova demanda do mercado. A inteligência artificial está mudando a escala e a localização da capacidade computacional, e nossa estratégia é construir uma infraestrutura nacional capaz de acompanhar essa transformação com segurança, conectividade e eficiência”, afirma Agnaldo Lopes, presidente do Grupo ABL. *Foto: Alissom Zelak / Agnaldo Lopes, Presidente do Grupo ABL.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI secures 16-GWh US battery supply deal with Jupiter Power Summary Samsung SDI America has signed a deal to supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate batteries to Jupiter Power in the United States, with deliveries scheduled over three years starting in 2029. The batteries will be made at Samsung SDI’s Indiana plant for Jupiter Power’s large-scale energy storage projects. Including an earlier contract, Samsung SDI’s orders from Jupiter Power total about 27 gigawatt-hours. The agreement follows the start of mass production of lithium iron phosphate batteries at the Indiana facility. Key Facts - The contract is estimated to be worth several trillion won. - Jupiter Power has 19,700 megawatt-hours of projects operating, under construction or committed, and another 110,000 megawatt-hours in development across the United States. - Jupiter Power is backed by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock. - Samsung SDI said it is the only non-Chinese manufacturer of prismatic batteries for battery energy storage system applications in North America. - Samsung SDI is reinforcing its lithium iron phosphate supply chain through material supply agreements with Korean companies, including POSCO Future M and L&F. Samsung SDI said Monday that its U.S. subsidiary has signed a deal to supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate batteries to Jupiter Power, a U.S. energy storage developer and operator, in a contract estimated to be worth several trillion won. Under the agreement, Samsung SDI America will supply the batteries over three years starting in 2029 for Jupiter Power's large-scale battery energy storage system projects in the United States. Including a previous contract, Samsung SDI's total orders from Jupiter Power now amount to approximately 27 gigawatt-hours, the company said. Jupiter Power, backed by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock, has a portfolio of 19,700 megawatt-hours of projects that are operating, under construction or committed, with another 110,000 megawatt-hours in development across the United States. The batteries will be manufactured at Samsung SDI's plant in Indiana. The deal comes shortly after the company began mass production of lithium iron phosphate batteries at the facility, underscoring the competitiveness of its technology as it expands its presence in the U.S. energy storage market. Samsung SDI is the only non-Chinese manufacturer of prismatic batteries for battery energy storage system applications in North America. It has also secured non-Chinese sources for key battery materials, strengthening its supply chain and appeal to U.S. energy companies seeking alternatives to Chinese suppliers. The company has recently won a series of orders as it expands its battery energy storage system portfolio beyond nickel-cobalt-aluminum-based batteries to include lithium iron phosphate products. It is also reinforcing its lithium iron phosphate supply chain through material supply agreements with Korean companies, including POSCO Future M and L&F. "This agreement reflects the competitiveness and supply capabilities of our locally produced prismatic lithium iron phosphate batteries in the U.S.," said Fabrice Hudry, president of energy storage systems at Samsung SDI America. "Building on our differentiated prismatic battery technology and stable supply chain, we will continue to expand our presence in the global battery energy storage system market." Jupiter Power CEO Andy Bowman said securing reliable, domestically manufactured equipment was central to the company's plans to reduce risks in its project development. "Samsung SDI's lithium iron phosphate batteries, produced here in the U.S., strengthen our supply chain as we continue to deliver reliable power and capacity when and where the grid needs it most," he said.
