artigo.texto: Originals mapeia LiDAR e IA para medir carbono florestal Sensores a laser e visão computacional ganham espaço no monitoramento de projetos de reflorestamento como ferramentas complementares aos inventários de campo; Paulo Zidane, do Future Climate Group, analisa o potencial de maior rigor técnico e acurácia na medição da biomassa e explica por que a tecnologia está no radar da Originals Nos projetos de florestamento, reflorestamento e revegetação (ARR, na sigla em inglês), a medição de carbono tem como referência o inventário florestal, no qual equipes medem diâmetro e altura das árvores em parcelas amostrais e estimam a biomassa por equações estatísticas. A essa base começa a se somar o monitoramento, relato e verificação digital (dMRV), que reúne sensoriamento remoto, sensores LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging, ou detecção e medição por luz) e inteligência artificial (IA) para reconstruir a vegetação em três dimensões e acompanhar seu desenvolvimento com maior frequência. A tendência foi mapeada pela Originals, plataforma de restauração florestal e remoção de carbono do Future Climate Group, estruturada com a norte-americana Pachama. A empresa já utiliza inventários de campo no monitoramento de suas áreas e identifica no LiDAR associado à IA uma oportunidade de complementar esse trabalho. De acordo com a companhia, a Originals inicia operações com cerca de 12 mil hectares em sete regiões do Brasil e do México, potencial para o plantio de mais de 10 milhões de árvores e capacidade estimada de remover aproximadamente 5 milhões de toneladas de carbono ao longo do ciclo dos projetos, com meta de chegar a 25 mil hectares até 2035. O que os sensores acrescentam ao inventário No método de campo, técnicos aplicam modelos alométricos (fórmulas que relacionam diâmetro e altura do tronco à massa da planta) a uma amostra de árvores e extrapolam o resultado para toda a área. Uma pesquisa de 2022, publicada na revista Ecological Solutions and Evidence, com escaneamento a laser terrestre de uma floresta temperada no Reino Unido, encontrou biomassa acima do solo 1,77 vez superior à estimada pelos modelos alométricos usuais. Segundo os autores, metade da biomassa daquela floresta estava em menos de 7% das árvores, todas maiores do que as empregadas na calibração das fórmulas. "O inventário de campo continua sendo a base da medição, porque é nele que se confirmam espécie, diâmetro e altura das árvores. O LiDAR tem potencial para acrescentar uma leitura tridimensional da estrutura de cada copa, o que tende a elevar o rigor técnico e a acurácia das estimativas de biomassa quando os dois métodos são combinados", avalia Paulo Zidane, da área de geotecnologia do Future Climate Group. Como funciona o monitoramento digital Instalado em aeronaves, drones ou tripés, o LiDAR dispara pulsos de laser e registra o tempo de retorno de cada um após tocar folhas, galhos e solo. O resultado é uma nuvem de pontos que descreve altura, densidade e arquitetura do dossel. Com base nesse modelo, algoritmos estimam o volume de madeira e, com dados de densidade das espécies, convertem o valor em biomassa e em toneladas de carbono. Imagens de satélite completam o processo ao apontar mudanças de cobertura entre uma campanha de campo e outra. Nos primeiros anos após o plantio, a visão computacional aplicada a imagens de alta resolução pode identificar mudas e copas, estimar taxas de sobrevivência por espécie e medir o ritmo de crescimento por talhão. Esse tipo de leitura permite antecipar falhas de pegamento e programar replantios antes que a perda afete a curva de remoção prevista. Os padrões de certificação já incorporam parte dessa lógica: a metodologia VM0047, da Verra, voltada a projetos ARR, combina sensoriamento remoto e amostragem em parcelas como base para quantificar as remoções de carbono. Verificação e transparência O Banco Mundial aponta, em relatório técnico sobre o tema, que tecnologias digitais simplificam a coleta, o processamento e o controle de qualidade dos dados de monitoramento. Em outra publicação, a instituição pondera que esses sistemas ainda são complexos e caros de implantar, mas tendem a baixar o custo de geração dos créditos no longo prazo, com ganhos de transparência e segurança. "A combinação entre inventário em campo e sensoriamento remoto pode oferecer ao auditor e ao comprador uma visão mais contínua do que acontece na área, sem depender apenas do relatório periódico. Para a Originals, acompanhar a maturidade dessas tecnologias faz parte da preparação para um mercado que exige cada vez mais rastreabilidade", afirma Zidane. A demanda por evidências também parte dos compradores. Em maio de 2024, Google, Meta, Microsoft e Salesforce lançaram a Coalizão Symbiosis, compromisso de contratar até 20 milhões de toneladas em créditos de remoção baseados na natureza até 2030, com foco inicial em projetos ARR. Entre os pilares de qualidade definidos estão contabilidade conservadora, durabilidade, integridade ecológica e transparência. No Brasil, a Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE) e criou o Certificado de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVE), ativo que representa uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente reduzida ou removida segundo metodologia credenciada. Nesse cenário regulatório e comercial, enfatiza o executivo, a integração entre medições de campo e modelagem tridimensional da floresta tende a influenciar a forma como os créditos de remoção são calculados, auditados e negociados. "Em projetos de ciclo longo, ampliar a base de evidências para investidores, certificadores e compradores passa a ser um ponto de atenção durante toda a vida útil das áreas", conclui o porta-voz do Future Climate Group. Para mais informações, basta acessar: https://futureclimate.com/

artigo.texto: Weekend - Blackstone’s QTS cuts AI data center debt sale 60% as investors push back on pricing Summary - Blackstone-backed data center operator QTS cut a planned private debt sale to about $300 million from roughly $800 million after weak demand, refusing to pay higher yields. The pullback hints at limits to investor appetite for AI-related debt. For credit markets, the QTS cutback is an early sign that the price of financing AI infrastructure is starting to matter. Investors are putting limits on how much they will hold of repeat issuers and on concentrated exposure to the sector. If that spreads, data center and AI-linked borrowers could face wider spreads or smaller deals, pushing more issuance into private credit and project finance at higher cost. For equities, any rise in funding costs feeds into the capex economics behind the AI trade. That is a sensitive point for sentiment this week, with Nvidia due to report on Tuesday. The deal is small, so it is not a credit event, but it is a signal worth tracking in future AI debt deals. --- Big week for AI ahead: --- The AI build-out has had seemingly unlimited access to capital, but QTS’s shrunken deal shows that even a Blackstone-backed borrower now has to choose between paying up and settling for less. Summary: - QTS, a Blackstone-backed data center operator, cut a planned private debt sale by about 60%. - It is raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. - Some investors objected to pricing, while others were limited by QTS’s repeated use of the private placement market. - QTS has raised billions through at least two private placements in 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade sale last year. - Blackstone resisted higher yields because wider pricing could become a costlier benchmark for its other debt. - AI companies are tapping every part of the capital markets to fund investment that could reach the trillions of dollars. QTS, the data center operator backed by Blackstone, has scaled back a planned private debt sale by around 60% after struggling to find enough investor demand, and after declining to pay the much higher yields some buyers wanted, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the transaction. The company is now raising about $300 million, down from an initial target of roughly $800 million. Some investors objected to the pricing on offer, while others were constrained because QTS has already tapped the private placement market several times, according to the people. QTS has been a heavy user of that market. It has raised billions of dollars through at least two private placement deals over the past 18 months, including a $1.65 billion high-grade bond sale last year and a separate $800 million financing. Blackstone’s reluctance to sweeten terms reflects a wider concern. Because the firm borrows frequently across many markets and through many issuers, wider pricing on the QTS deal could set a more expensive benchmark for investors weighing other Blackstone-related debt. The episode matters well beyond one borrower. Artificial intelligence companies are reaching into every corner of capital markets, from investment-grade bonds to project finance, to fund build-outs that could cost trillions of dollars over the coming years. The QTS deal suggests that appetite is not unlimited, particularly in narrower pools such as private placements, where a small group of buyers can quickly hit internal limits on exposure to a single name or sector. That leaves borrowers with an uncomfortable choice: accept higher funding costs, shrink deals or spread issuance across more markets. Each option raises the cost or complexity of financing the AI infrastructure boom. For now, the decision to cut the deal’s size rather than pay up shows that well-backed issuers can still walk away. But it is a sign that the market is starting to discriminate on price. The next test will be how other data center and AI-related borrowers do in upcoming deals, and whether investors start demanding a premium for concentrated exposure to the sector. artigo.texto: Global energy storage owner-operator, BW ESS, has entered into a partnership with French battery storage developer, Wattmen, to develop a portfolio of approximately 500 MW of battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in France over the next three years. The partnership establishes a platform for originating and progressing standalone, transmission-connected projects, supporting BW ESS’ continued growth in the French market. The collaboration brings together Wattmen’s local project origination and development capabilities with BW ESS’ international experience in energy storage investment, project design, and procurement across seven markets. The partners will work together to advance projects from greenfield to ready-to-build status, securing the land rights, grid connections, and authorisations required for construction. The partnership will focus on projects with connection capacities of at least 100 MW, prioritising sites close to grid connection points and with sufficient space to accommodate battery systems offering at least four hours of storage duration. This approach is designed to create a portfolio of large scale assets with the flexibility to respond to the evolving needs of the French electricity system. Hazel Starmer-Jones, Development Director at BW ESS, commented: “Partnering with Wattmen is an important step in building our presence in France. We take a highly considered approach to development partnerships in new markets, and Wattmen have shown a depth of technical and local expertise that makes them an ideal partner in originating and developing high-quality energy storage projects. Together, we aim to build a portfolio that delivers lasting value and helps strengthen the flexibility and resilience of the French electricity system.” Wattmen will lead local development activities, including site identification, land agreements, permitting, and grid connection co-ordination, working closely with landowners, authorities, and communities. BW ESS will contribute its international energy storage expertise, supporting project design and procurement strategy. Jean-Marc Guenée, CEO and Co-Founder of Wattmen, noted: “This partnership brings together complementary strengths and a shared ambition to develop high-quality battery storage projects in France. By combining our local knowledge and development capabilities with BW ESS’ international experience, we can progress strategically located projects and help deliver the flexible infrastructure needed for the energy transition.” The partnership reflects BW ESS’ approach of working selectively with specialist local developers to build energy storage portfolios, combining local knowledge with the capabilities of a global owner-operator. It builds on BW ESS’ recent entry into the French market through the acquisition of two 100 MW/400 MWh BESS projects. Together, these investments have created a pipeline encompassing both greenfield and advanced projects, strengthening the company’s presence in France and establishing a foundation for continued growth. artigo.texto: COP31 draft decision calls for review of UN carbon market rules — Climate Home News At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, dozens of countries called for an assessment of the environmental integrity rules of the new UN carbon market. As Climate Home News reports, these demands are reflected in the first draft decision on the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism. According to the publication’s sources, concerns were raised in closed discussions by the Like-Minded Group of Developing Countries, which includes Saudi Arabia, India and China, as well as least developed countries and landlocked states. They believe that the combination of requirements for project developers introduced under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement could hinder their implementation. What the draft decision proposes The document proposes that the mechanism’s Supervisory Body assess how conservative assumptions in its rules collectively affect the number of carbon credits issued, costs and prices. The text states that this should prevent an “excessive accumulation of conservative adjustments.” The mechanism’s rules provide for a more cautious approach to issuing credits when there is uncertainty about emissions reductions. Industry representatives argue that this approach could lead to a systematic understatement of the number of credits and make projects financially unviable. Singapore and some Latin American countries, according to the publication, also stressed the need to preserve projects’ financial viability, while South Korea called for proportionate requirements. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Dispute over clean cookstoves One of the key subjects of dispute was the methodologies for projects distributing cleaner cookstoves. A 2024 Nature Sustainability study cited by Climate Home News stated that such projects may have been awarded approximately ten times more credits than they were actually justified in receiving. In October, the Supervisory Body required developers of such projects to set aside some credits in a buffer pool in case forests that the projects claim to help preserve later burn down or are cut down. The body rejected a request for an exemption from this rule submitted by developers, corporate buyers, some environmental organizations and the UN Environment Programme. Environmental organizations and researchers oppose weakening the standards. Erika Lennon, a senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law, said that loosening the rules is not climate ambition but a “license to pollute.” At the same time, the EU, Switzerland and Senegal, according to the publication’s sources, oppose assessing project profitability and lowering standards. The draft decision will still be discussed during the final days of the COP31 summit.

artigo.texto: OS DATA CENTERS PODEM PREJUDICAR O PARTIDO DE TRUMP NAS ELEIÇÕES DOS EUA? O repórter do Estadão, Daniel Gateno, fala sobre o documentário “Estadão na América”, que estreia nesta semana, e o medo dos americanos com o futuro dos Estados. Gerando resumo De acordo com uma nova pesquisa, publicada nesta segunda-feira, 16, pela revista Nature Sustainability, os maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos são responsáveis por 25,7 milhões de toneladas de emissões de dióxido de carbono anualmente — quase tanto quanto países inteiros como a Bolívia ou a Dinamarca. O estudo apresenta as primeiras estimativas revisadas por pares das emissões de dióxido de carbono dos maiores data centers dos EUA desde o início do boom da inteligência artificial. Seus autores, uma equipe liderada por pesquisadores da Universidade de Harvard, examinaram o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de carbono de 403 data centers entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. No total, essas operações consumiram quase 2% da eletricidade dos EUA, mais do que Nova York e Los Angeles juntas, e representaram cerca de 0,5% das emissões de dióxido de carbono dos EUA. O dióxido de carbono é o principal gás de efeito estufa responsável pelo aquecimento global. Os data centers em apenas três Estados, Virgínia, Iowa e Ohio, foram responsáveis por cerca de metade das emissões estimadas no estudo. Em Estados como o Oregon, os data centers são responsáveis por emitir menos dióxido de carbono por unidade de eletricidade consumida, porque uma parcela maior de sua energia é gerada sem combustíveis fósseis, constatou o estudo. Em todas as 403 instalações, 54% da eletricidade provinha da queima de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás natural e carvão. Um trabalho de detetive Grande parte da análise do estudo se resumiu a trabalho de detetive, ressaltando o sigilo sob o qual as empresas de IA têm permissão para operar. Sem uma lista pública de data centers para trabalhar, os pesquisadores começaram consultando um conjunto de dados comerciais cujas regras de licenciamento os impediam — e ao The New York Times — de publicar os endereços, nomes e proprietários das instalações. Os pesquisadores passaram horas estudando as plantas dos edifícios e imagens de satélite para confirmar a localização e o tamanho dos data centers, estimaram quanta eletricidade eles poderiam usar e, em seguida, calcularam suas emissões com base na matriz energética de cada rede elétrica regional. “O fato de termos que passar por um processo de reconstrução tão extenso apenas para entender onde a infraestrutura está localizada e qual a sua dimensão revela muito sobre a falta de transparência no próprio setor”, afirmou Gianluca Guidi, cientista de Harvard que liderou a equipe de pesquisa. Michael Thomas, que dirige a empresa de dados energéticos Cleanview e não participou do estudo, traçou um contraste entre data centers e usinas de energia, obrigadas a divulgar publicamente todos os tipos de detalhes sobre os impactos ambientais de suas operações. Coletar os detalhes das operações de um data centers, por outro lado, exige vasculhar milhões de documentos espalhados por bancos de dados municipais, estaduais e federais. “Talvez uns seis senadores tenham entrado em contato conosco. Eles perguntam coisas como: ‘Quantos data centers existem? Estamos tentando elaborar um projeto de lei’”, disse Thomas. “Por que o Senado está entrando em contato comigo e não a EIA ou a FERC?”, acrescentou, usando as siglas da Administração de Informação Energética dos EUA e da Comissão Federal de Regulamentação de Energia. Embora Estados como Virgínia e Ohio tenham começado a adotar uma supervisão mais rigorosa, Guidi afirmou que o governo federal deveria exigir que os operadores de grandes data centers divulgassem publicamente seu consumo de eletricidade e suas emissões. “As comunidades não deveriam precisar de uma equipe de pesquisadores de Harvard para analisar imagens de satélite a fim de compreender seu impacto ambiental”, disse ele. Os desenvolvedores de data centers dispõem de diversas ferramentas para ocultar os impactos de carbono e energia de seus projetos. Essas camadas de sigilo emergiram como um dos principais pontos de preocupação na crescente resistência a projetos de data centers em todo o país. Os eleitores optaram por limitar ou impedir o desenvolvimento de data centers em 40 das 41 iniciativas locais relevantes nas eleições de meio de mandato deste mês. “Acordos de confidencialidade, usuários finais ocultos e negociações a portas fechadas moldam as narrativas da oposição de forma mais consistente do que qualquer outra preocupação”, segundo um relatório recente da Relae, uma consultoria de clima e energia. Entre março de 2024 e o início de novembro de 2026, a oposição local bloqueou ou atrasou pelo menos 70 projetos de data centers para IA em 25 Estados, representando um investimento estimado em US$ 271 bilhões, de acordo com a pesquisa da Relae. Quatorze desses projetos estavam na Virgínia, o epicentro do boom dos data centers. Os data centers da Virgínia foram responsáveis por mais de um quarto das emissões estimadas no estudo. Na PJM Interconnection, a operadora da rede elétrica regional que atende a Virgínia, cerca de 60% da eletricidade que alimenta os data centers é produzida por combustíveis fósseis. Os números do estudo provavelmente subestimam todas as emissões de data centers dos EUA, porque a lista de instalações analisadas não representa um inventário completo. Ela exclui centenas de possíveis data centers que os pesquisadores não conseguiram verificar suficientemente, bem como instalações que não utilizam a rede elétrica, obtendo energia de geradores no local. É também um retrato de uma indústria que cresce a um ritmo vertiginoso. A instalação média no estudo tinha uma capacidade elétrica de cerca de 40 megawatts, enquanto projetos futuros, como o campus Hyperion de 5 gigawatts da Meta na Louisiana, terão mais de 100 vezes essa capacidade. artigo.texto: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks. The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws. This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September. BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. But Gov. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. While Beshear can’t stop the data center from happening, Anozie said, local governments can still make it difficult for projects to operate once they are built. “Where the states might have a way of regulating what is going on is using state environmental laws to challenge and to say, ‘Well, you didn't get the permit for this,’” he said. “But they cannot outrightly veto or zone out that area for a data center.” Amentum And DC Blox In South Carolina The Savannah River Site was one of 16 sites identified by the DOE in April 2025 to support the construction of data centers and the power infrastructure they require. The site was used to produce plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons in the 1950s, Spectrum News reported. Efforts at the site have centered on environmental cleanup and managing nuclear materials, as well as research and development. artigo.texto: U.S. construction economists continue to marvel at the historic strength of the data-center market, with unprecedented growth in project value and industry domination never before experienced. Experts assembled for the Construction Economy Outlook Fall 2026, presented by ConstructConnect on Nov. 12, spoke in superlatives throughout the webinar. Even threats such as growing public resistance and the uncertainty of financing may only cool the pace of data-center growth, not arrest it, they suggested. “We continue to see just amazing, unprecedented growth in data centers,” said ConstructConnect chief economist Michael Guckes. “Even though we’ve seen some political pushback on data centers, I think it’s too late. I think the train has left the station. “Once you have a technology with this kind of power, and other countries are competing in this realm for it, there’s no going backwards with this.” Guckes reported in 2022, the first $1-billion data center broke ground; in 2024, the U.S. had the first project that surpassed $3 billion; the next year saw the first $10-billion project; and now, he said, “Amazingly enough, we saw more starts in just January than we did in all of 2024. This is also the first time where we’re seeing these campuses of $50 billion and greater breaking ground.” Guckes added, “So this industry is not only huge for construction, but it has completely transformed within its own ranks. “If you go back to pre-COVID, you were seeing about 10 to 12 per cent of all non-residential construction dollars heading into megaprojects and now it’s more than one out of every $4.” Guckes was joined by Ken Simonson, chief economist, Associated General Contractors of America; Richard Branch, chief economist, American Institute of Architects (AIA); and Kristy O’Brien, director of content acquisition, ConstructConnect. Paul Hart, vice-president of economic content with ConstructConnect, served as the moderator. 2027 looks brighter Overall, U.S. construction spending is expected to remain slow, Branch said. Non-residential building construction spending is forecast to decline 0.3 per cent in 2026 before increasing three per cent in 2027, he said. Commercial construction is expected to grow 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 5.8 per cent in 2027, while industrial construction is expected to decline 11.6 per cent in 2026 and 0.6 per cent in 2027. Institutional construction is forecast to rise 2.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent, respectively. The Fed is expected to raise rates in the next year. “We’re probably looking at another 50 basis points of rate hikes between now and at this point next year,” said Branch. “I do think, though, if we start to see oil prices come down, that we’ll start to see inflation peel back, and as inflation peels back, particularly if it gets closer to their two-per-cent target, I think we will start to see they’re loosening rates.” Strong commercial numbers are largely because of data centers, Branch said. Traditional office construction is expected to decline five per cent and four per cent this year and next, respectively, while warehouse spending is forecast to decline 1.7 per cent in 2026 before increasing 1.4 per cent in 2027. Guckes reported ConstructConnect’s October 2026 economic forecast projects U.S. GDP growth of 2.1 per cent in 2026, rising to 2.4 per cent in 2027 and 2.7 per cent each of the next three years. Guckes identified various headwinds facing the construction sector: Higher interest rates make it harder to build profitably, while slow labour growth restrains the economy’s expansion. Inflation hurts consumers and spending, casting a shadow over the construction economy. Costs, rates squeeze margins O’Brien reported higher costs and rates are squeezing margins even as demand holds. She said tariffs and trade disruption continues to buffet the U.S. construction sector. Steel and aluminum imports have faced 50 per cent tariffs since June 2025, while overall construction material prices are up 11.0 per cent year-over-year, the fastest spike since May 2022. Tax cuts and business-investment incentives in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act continue to support demand, O’Brien stated. Bid prices are up 5.4 per cent. According to Simonson, tariffs, immigration enforcement, federal deficits and interest rates are the four major risks to construction. The concern is tighter immigration enforcement will worsen labour shortages. The webinar wrapped up with further roundtable discussion of the topic of the day. Branch said, “I think where that moratorium issue comes more is in 2028 spending data. There again, I don’t see a decline. I don’t see a collapse. I see more of a flat market in 2028 rather than a slowdown.” O’Brien noted Texas is leading in data-center construction, followed by Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas and the Midwest states. The sheer scale of the explosion, she said, brings constraints: power and water availability, public response and the cost of capital. Guckes said public pushback can be addressed in part through engineering. “Some of the solutions you talk about, noise, water, pollution of other types, a lot of those have engineering solutions…Those things generally just take money, and so far the data centers have access to a lot of it.”

artigo.texto: Publicidade Washington — Semanas depois de os eleitores demonstrarem forte insatisfação com os data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato, o Congresso debate uma ampla reformulação das regras federais de licenciamento que poderia ajudar as empresas de tecnologia a construir essas instalações mais rapidamente. O projeto de lei aceleraria as análises ambientais federais de vários projetos de energia, incluindo linhas de transmissão e gasodutos, facilitando para os desenvolvedores a obtenção da energia necessária para operar os data centers. Mas essa ajuda vem com uma enorme contrapartida: os data centers também teriam de pagar muito mais pela eletricidade, segundo uma disposição do projeto que cobraria das instalações uma tarifa adicional pelo acesso à rede elétrica. A medida alteraria décadas de regras federais do setor elétrico e poderia gerar uma economia de bilhões de dólares na próxima década para as famílias e outros consumidores. Leia mais: Boom de data centers de IA enfrenta reação negativa nas urnas dos EUA Leia mais: A SpaceX planeja investir US$ 74 bi na construção de data centers no Texas e Arizona A iniciativa de impor custos mais altos aos data centers evidencia como a política em torno da inteligência artificial se tornou complexa em Washington. Data centers gigantescos e ávidos por energia estão se espalhando rapidamente pelo país, pressionando as redes elétricas e provocando indignação em muitas comunidades. Neste mês, os eleitores aprovaram pelo menos 40 iniciativas locais para restringir essas instalações. Continua depois da publicidade Prós e contras Alguns ambientalistas que se opõem ao projeto de licenciamento o classificaram como um benefício para as empresas de tecnologia, argumentando que a legislação poderia acelerar o desenvolvimento de data centers abastecidos por gás natural. O projeto reduziria o alcance de leis ambientais federais para acelerar a construção de diversos tipos de empreendimentos, incluindo gasodutos, projetos eólicos e solares, linhas de transmissão de alta tensão, estradas, transporte público e moradias. Em contraste, os defensores apresentaram o projeto como uma oportunidade de endurecer as regras para as empresas de IA. “O período em que os data centers não pagavam sua parte termina quando este projeto for aprovado”, disse o senador Sheldon Whitehouse, democrata de Rhode Island e um dos autores do projeto. “A partir de agora, os data centers terão de pagar pelos custos adicionais que impõem à rede quando entram em operação. Eles não poderão transferir todos esses custos adicionais para a base tarifária da concessionária e fazer com que sejam arcados pelos demais consumidores.” Continua depois da publicidade O setor de data centers, por sua vez, permaneceu relativamente calado. Embora diversos grupos empresariais, sindicatos e algumas empresas do Vale do Silício tenham apoiado o projeto, uma das principais entidades representativas do setor ainda não o fez. A Data Center Coalition, cujos membros incluem Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft, afirmou que ainda está analisando a legislação. “Continuamos avaliando suas implicações com nossos membros, que estão fazendo sua parte para promover a acessibilidade e o crescimento econômico ao investir centenas de bilhões de dólares nos Estados Unidos todos os anos”, disse Jon Hukill, porta-voz da coalizão. Muitos data centers desenvolvidos para treinar e operar modelos de IA de ponta podem consumir tanta eletricidade quanto pequenas cidades, o que provocou debates sobre quem deve pagar pelos bilhões de dólares necessários para construir as usinas e linhas de transmissão de que precisam. Continua depois da publicidade Historicamente, as concessionárias distribuíram o custo das melhorias na rede elétrica entre todos os seus clientes. Mas, à medida que a insatisfação com os data centers aumentou, o presidente Donald Trump e vários governadores pressionaram as gigantes da tecnologia a assumir a conta e não repassar esses custos às famílias. A maioria das empresas de IA prometeu fazer isso, embora esses compromissos de proteção aos consumidores possam ser difíceis de fiscalizar. Inseridas nas 494 páginas do projeto de lei de licenciamento estão várias disposições destinadas a dar mais força a essas promessas. Cobranças extras Uma das medidas determinaria que a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, a agência federal americana responsável pela regulação do setor de energia, emitisse novas regras em até 90 dias. Essas regras cobrariam dos data centers tanto os custos de eventuais melhorias na rede necessárias para atendê-los quanto os custos de utilização da rede elétrica existente. Continua depois da publicidade Isso derrubaria princípios regulatórios antigos, em vigor desde 1994, que proíbem as concessionárias de cobrar duas vezes dos clientes pela mesma capacidade da rede. Na prática, o projeto afirma que os grandes data centers são diferentes e deveriam pagar potencialmente o dobro do que pagam atualmente. “É uma grande mudança em relação à forma como temos administrado a rede até agora, na qual os benefícios são amplamente compartilhados e socializamos os custos”, disse Robin Millican, diretor de programas de pesquisa e parcerias estratégicas do Center on Global Energy Policy, da Universidade Columbia. Outras disposições dariam aos reguladores estaduais mais liberdade para cobrar dos data centers valores adicionais pelas usinas de energia de que precisam e utilizar o dinheiro para conceder créditos nas contas das famílias. Pela primeira vez, o governo federal também seria obrigado a monitorar o consumo de energia dos data centers. Os políticos têm colocado os data centers no centro das discussões em parte porque a dimensão do boom da IA ameaça sobrecarregar as redes elétricas. As gigantes da tecnologia também priorizam a velocidade e frequentemente estão dispostas a pagar mais para obter energia mais rapidamente. The global battery circuit breakers market is entering a phase of sustained expansion as electrification reshapes transportation, power generation, and industrial infrastructure. Valued for their ability to safely interrupt high direct current in battery-powered systems, these specialized protective devices are indispensable in electric vehicles, stationary energy storage, and renewable energy installations. Between 2026 and 2035, demand is forecast to rise at a robust pace, supported by policy-driven decarbonization targets, falling battery costs, and the proliferation of DC-coupled architectures. Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing region, underpinned by China's dominance in EV and battery production, while North America and Europe accelerate investments in grid-scale storage and charging infrastructure. Technological shifts toward solid-state and hybrid breakers are expected to unlock higher voltage classes and faster response times, intensifying competition among established electrical majors and specialized innovators. Supply chains face pressure from copper price volatility and certification bottlenecks, but the overall outlook remains firmly positive. As automotive manufacturers transition from 400V to 800V architectures to enable faster charging and greater efficiency, the demand for high-speed DC breakers with higher interruption ratings intensifies. These breakers protect the battery pack, inverters, and onboard chargers from overloads and short circuits, which is critical for preventing thermal runaway. The shift toward solid-state and hybrid breakers is particularly pronounced in this segment, as they offer faster response times and lower power losses. Demand-side indicators include global EV production volumes, average battery pack voltage, and the penetration of fast-charging infrastructure. Through 2035, the segment is expected to maintain strong growth, although the pace may moderate as major markets mature. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow at a robust pace, with particular strength in regions with ambitious renewable targets. artigo.texto: Com tecnologia da chinesa CATL, a expansão industrial em Belo Jardim permitirá fornecer sistemas de armazenamento com capacidade superior a 8 GWh, preparando a fabricante brasileira para atender aos grandes projetos do setor elétrico a partir de 2028. A Moura vai investir R$ 200 milhões em Pernambuco para ampliar sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, instalada em Belo Jardim, no Agreste do estado. O projeto inclui uma nova linha industrial, transferência de tecnologia da chinesa CATL e previsão de mais de 200 contratações, com início da produção ampliada esperado para 2027. Conhecida nacionalmente pelas baterias automotivas, a empresa agora pretende disputar espaço em um mercado que ganha importância com a expansão das usinas solares e eólicas: o armazenamento de eletricidade em equipamentos de grande porte. O investimento já está em execução. Segundo reportagem da Exame, publicada em 14 de novembro de 2026, a companhia prepara seu complexo industrial para atender aos projetos que disputarão o primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento de energia em baterias. - Em apenas 81 minutos, leilões de energia movimentam R$ 14,25 bilhões, garantem eletricidade para os próximos anos e levantam uma pergunta incômoda sobre a conta de luz - Quem paga conta de luz no Nordeste pode ter alta de 9,58% em 2027, enquanto o Sul terá queda de 7,59%: a Thymos Energia projeta tarifa 2% menor na média do país - Montadores de subestação no Rio Grande do Norte esperam 2.299 vagas no Lote 7 da Axia, que tem 42 meses de obra e negocia até R$ 680 milhões com o BID para 3 compensadores síncronos em Açu e João Câmara - Operadores da Termocabo, em Pernambuco, vão trocar 250 toneladas diárias de óleo combustível por gás natural nos 3 motores da usina, convertidos pela Wärtsilä para um contrato de 10 anos A capacidade de fornecimento anunciada supera 8 gigawatts-hora (GWh), colocando a nova operação em uma escala industrial voltada ao atendimento de grandes empreendimentos do setor elétrico. Fábrica da Moura em Pernambuco receberá nova linha de produção e tecnologia chinesa A ampliação ocorre no complexo industrial de Belo Jardim, onde a Moura mantém uma de suas principais operações produtivas. O prédio destinado à expansão já está pronto, enquanto a nova linha industrial foi adquirida na China. A expectativa é iniciar a produção dos equipamentos no fim do primeiro semestre de 2027. A parceria com a CATL, uma das maiores fabricantes mundiais de baterias, divide responsabilidades entre as duas companhias. A chinesa fornece tecnologia de armazenamento e participa da comercialização dos sistemas. A Moura ficará responsável pela industrialização, montagem e integração dos equipamentos no Brasil. O processo envolve receber módulos de baterias e integrá-los em sistemas completos, instalados em contêineres industriais de aproximadamente 20 pés, equipados com refrigeração e proteção contra incêndios. De acordo com informações publicadas pelo Jornal do Commercio, a fabricação nacional também está relacionada às condições de financiamento do BNDES, que podem exigir índices de conteúdo local entre 50% e 60%. A produção em Pernambuco permitirá concentrar no Brasil atividades de engenharia, integração, testes e assistência técnica, fortalecendo a cadeia industrial brasileira de armazenamento de energia. Moura prepara mais de 200 contratações para ampliar produção de baterias em Pernambuco A ampliação da fábrica em Belo Jardim deve impulsionar a geração de empregos no Agreste pernambucano. A Moura prevê contratar e capacitar mais de 200 profissionais para atender à nova linha de produção de sistemas de armazenamento de energia, desenvolvida em parceria com a chinesa CATL. Atualmente, o grupo possui aproximadamente 7.400 funcionários, dos quais cerca de 3.500 trabalham no complexo fabril de Belo Jardim. As novas contratações acompanharão a expansão das atividades industriais, com demandas relacionadas à montagem, integração e operação de sistemas de baterias de grande porte. Com investimento de R$ 200 milhões e início da produção previsto para 2027, a expansão fortalecerá a estrutura industrial da Moura em Pernambuco, ampliará sua capacidade de fornecimento e criará novas oportunidades profissionais em um segmento estratégico para o setor elétrico brasileiro. Sistemas de armazenamento poderão alcançar mais de 8 GWh e atender grandes projetos elétricos O principal produto da expansão será o BESS (Battery Energy Storage System), sistema capaz de armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizá-la posteriormente, conforme a necessidade da rede. Esses equipamentos ganham relevância com o aumento da participação de fontes renováveis na matriz elétrica. Usinas solares concentram sua geração durante o dia, enquanto parques eólicos produzem de acordo com as condições de vento. O armazenamento permite aproveitar a energia gerada nesses períodos e disponibilizá-la em horários de maior demanda. As baterias contribuem para aumentar a flexibilidade operacional do sistema elétrico e favorecer a integração das fontes renováveis. A Moura desenvolve soluções de armazenamento desde meados da década passada e apresentou seu Moura BESS em 2019. Atualmente, a companhia acumula mais de 40 projetos instalados no Brasil, atendendo segmentos como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e infraestrutura elétrica. A nova etapa representa uma mudança de escala. A empresa já trabalha com equipamentos de aproximadamente 30 MWh, enquanto a expansão foi planejada para atender projetos a partir de 120 MWh. Para dimensionar a diferença, um único sistema de 120 MWh pode reunir aproximadamente 20 contêineres de 20 pés com baterias, na configuração descrita pela companhia. artigo.texto: Ministry of Heavy Industries Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh ACC Battery Manufacturing Capacity The tender covers 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity for grid-scale stationary storage applications under India's ₹18,100 crore PLI scheme. The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) manufacturing capacity under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for ACC battery storage. The capacity has been earmarked for grid-scale stationary storage (GSSS) applications and forms part of India's broader target to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The bids were submitted through a global tender floated on the Central Public Procurement (CPP) Portal to select companies for setting up giga-scale ACC manufacturing facilities in India. Technical bids were opened on November 11, 2026, at the Ministry of Heavy Industries in the presence of the participating bidders. The selection process is being conducted through a two-stage Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism. The 22 bidders include ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Avaada Electro, Exide Energy Solutions, Fujiyama Power Systems, GK Energy, Godawari New Energy, JPM Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy, Lineage Power, Mahendra Sponge and Power, and Megha Engineering and Infrastructures. Other companies that submitted bids include Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Reliance Industries, Renew Photovoltaics, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Sun Drops Energia, Utex New Energy, Vikram Solar, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions and Zetsol Energy. PLI Scheme Targets 50 GWh of ACC Manufacturing Capacity The tender is part of the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage, approved by the Union Cabinet in May 2021 with a budgetary allocation of ₹18,100 crore. The programme aims to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity and encourage domestic and international companies to set up manufacturing facilities in India. The 10 GWh allocation for grid-scale stationary storage is intended to address energy-storage requirements arising from the expansion of renewable energy capacity. The programme also seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and develop the local value chain for ACC technologies. The Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued on July 15, 2026, followed by a pre-bid conference on July 29. The deadline for submitting bids was November 10, with technical bids opened the following day. artigo.texto: On November 16, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule (IFR), “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors” (RIN 0694-AK50). The IFR closes what the government sees as a gap in existing chip controls: companies in China and other countries of concern can rent US-designed computing power from data centers in third countries rather than import the chips themselves. BIS says the IFR aligns the treatment of remote access with existing controls on physical shipments. It also adds new license requirements for five countries viewed as diversion risks—Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil—tightens the rules for chip foundries and packagers, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. Consistent with Executive Order 14434, the rule uses “Super Intelligence” (SI) in place of “artificial intelligence.” The changes reach chipmakers, server makers, distributors, cloud and data center operators, and their customers, both in the US and abroad. BIS has indicated that the IFR is expected to be formally published and go into effect on November 19. Key changes - New data center end-use control (new §744.24). A license is now required to export, re-export, or transfer (in-country) advanced chips and servers (ECCNs 3A090 (other than 3A090.c), 4A090, and related .z items, software, and technology) if the exporter, re-exporter, or transferor has “knowledge” at the time of the shipment transaction that the item is destined to a data center anywhere in the world that provides or will provide access to more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” (total processing performance) to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, China, another destination specified in Country Group D:5, or Macau. The threshold counts capacity at a single facility or across “linked data centers.” The new defined term “linked data center” includes digitally linked infrastructure, not just physically linked infrastructure. “For” such a company also captures instances where there is “knowledge” that a data center is providing remote access to a non-D:5 customer that in turn trains or provides SI models to a D:5 company. License applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. - Heightened diligence expectations. BIS points out that “to satisfy the requirement that you do not have knowledge” for purposes of §744.24(a)(1), companies will be expected to obtain and be able to provide sufficient information from the foreign data center regarding that data center’s “know your customer” due diligence checks. Such diligence checks will include diligence on whether any data center customers are subject to direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located in, headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide that information is a red flag that presumptively gives the exporter “knowledge” unless resolved. - No de minimis. Companies outside the US should note that the prohibitions under §744.24(a)(1) still apply when a US-origin item covered by paragraph (a) is incorporated into or commingled with a foreign-made item. Re-exporters and transferors cannot rely on the de minimis provisions if, at any point during the “development,” “production,” or “use” of the foreign-made item containing a US-origin item specified in paragraph (a), they have “knowledge” that the foreign-made item will be used for an end use prohibited under §744.24(a)(1). - Downstream notice and change-of-use authorization. Anyone who ships covered items without a license on or after the Federal Register publication date of this rule—expected on November 19—must notify the recipient in writing that a BIS authorization is required. Authorization is required if the item will be used to provide access to more than 12 million “aggregate TPP,” at a single data center or “through linked data centers” to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, Macau or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. Changing an item’s end use from a permitted use to one prohibited under §744.24(a) is considered an in-country transfer and requires an Export Administration Regulations (EAR) authorization under §744.24. New recordkeeping obligations apply. - Narrow “commercial recommender system” carve-out. The new prohibition does not apply to a “commercial recommender system”—which BIS defines as an SI tool “exclusively designed and exclusively used to rank, filter, or suggest commercial products, services, or content to users based on user behavior, transaction history, or item attributes.” BIS explains that this term does not include any SI system designed or used to generate novel text, image, audio, video, software, or other content in response to user inputs, or any system that incorporates such model, regardless of whether the system also performs recommendation functions. Relying on the carve-out triggers a specific submission to BIS, which requires a description of the due diligence performed to ensure the computing power access is exclusively being provided for a commercial recommender system and additional data points. When this alert was published, the link that BIS included in the IFR for this submission was not yet functional. - 90-day deadline to obtain a license for existing arrangements. Data centers that already provide significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered, or with an ultimate parent headquartered, in Macau or Country Group D:5 and wish to continue providing these services must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date of this rule or they may be subject to future export restrictions. - New license requirement for five diversion-risk countries. A license is now required for advanced SI items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil

artigo.texto: Batteries are great for many applications, but they can’t do everything. For example, they aren’t ideal when you need fast and large bursts of electrical current (like regenerative braking in your car). They also don’t have very long life-spans (usually between 1,000 and 10,000 cycles) or work very well in cold temperatures. Fortunately, batteries can be paired with (and perhaps one day even be replaced by) an energy storage device that brings its own unique set of strengths. Enter the supercapacitor. What is a supercapacitor? “Supercapacitors are energy storage devices that work in a fundamentally different way than batteries. They store charge physically, not through chemical reactions,” explained Materials Science and Engineering Professor David Estrada. “Supercapacitors have a long life of a million cycles and they are very useful in high power applications, such as backup power that bridges short outages, wearable electronics and sensors, and in aerospace and defense applications for pulsed loads, actuators and emergency power systems.” And at Boise State, a team led by alum Fereshteh Rajabi Kouchi (PhD, materials science and engineering, 2025) under the supervision of Estrada, are expanding the future of supercapacitors through the invention of a new 2D metal alloy ink. Printing with nanomaterial inks for energy devices Supercapacitors for various flexible applications can be printed using 2D printing technologies and energy material inks. However, the material properties of the inks ultimately shape the end product’s abilities. “In the grand scheme of things, materials are the heart of any electronic system,” Estrada said, “whether it’s a micro-fabricated transistor or a printed energy storage device. Without understanding the materials properties, and how they are affected by a fabrication process, it’s near impossible to get repeatable and reliable results to translate research from the lab to the fab.” For Kouchi, the goal was to widen the range of possible inks for supercapacitors by using special alloys (a mixture of two or more metals). And to do that, she set about inventing a completely new type of alloy ink. “In our lab, I used an aerosol jet printer that transforms these inks into a fine mist and deposits them onto a surface in precise patterns,” Kouchi said. “The exciting part of my research is that by combining different elements at the atomic level, we can create new materials with improved properties and use them to develop better-performing energy storage devices.” Kouchi blended niobium, tantalum and sulfur in a novel 2-dimensional (2D) material ink, within the 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) family of materials. 2D TMDs are materials that are three atoms thick where the metal layer is sandwiched between two layers of chalcogens atoms such as sulfur. What she and her team discovered was an alloy ink capable of being printed in patterns as small as 50 micrometers (about the diameter of a human hair), and that supercapacitors made from these inks could store far more charge than TMDs made from either metal alone. Importantly, the ink dried uniformly and met the material requirements to be printed on flexible substrates (like those used in wearable skin-based electronics). “Making a printable ink from a brand-new alloy meant solving several problems at once: keeping the nanosheets stable, preventing oxidation, and controlling how the droplets dry,” said Kouchi. “Seeing the alloy outperform both of its parent materials shows how the composition of 2-dimensional system can be used as a design tool for energy storage.” The research was supported by NASA EPSCoR, the National Science Foundation’s Center for Atomically Thin Multifunctional Coatings (ATOMIC), and the Penn State Two-Dimensional Crystal Consortium Materials Innovation Platform. Collaborators included The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Illinois Chicago, Tulane University, and Southern Methodist University. “This work shows that alloy engineering and additive manufacturing work well together,” said Estrada. “Fereshteh has created a general approach for taking newly discovered layered materials and turning them into printable inks, which brings flexible, miniaturized power sources for the Internet of Things closer to reality.” Kouchi’s discovery builds on Boise State’s decade-long history of stable, aerosol-jet-printable ink innovation. She previously reported a similar study on 2D transition metal carbides, known as MXenes, which showed excellent energy density – but lower power density than the alloy inks reported here. This research was conducted by Micron School of Materials Science and Engineering faculty and staff Fereshteh Rajabi Kouchi, Hailey Burgoyne, Tony Valayil Varghese, Ajay Pratap, Attila Rektor, Olivia Maryon, Mike Hurley and David Estrada with support from NASA EPSCoR, the National Science Foundation’s Center for Atomically Thin Multifunctional Coatings (ATOMIC), and the Penn State Two-Dimensional Crystal Consortium Materials Innovation Platform. Collaborators included The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Illinois Chicago, Tulane University and Southern Methodist University.

artigo.texto: Form Energy has appointed Lori Goler, former Chief People Officer at Meta, and Jon McNeill, a former senior executive at Tesla and Lyft, to its Board of Directors as the energy storage company prepares to expand manufacturing and commercial deployments of its iron-air battery technology. The appointments bring experience in organizational development, operations, sales, and scaling high-growth businesses. Goler currently serves as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, while McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of venture firm DVx Ventures. The appointments follow a significant period of financial and operational expansion for Form Energy, which is developing long-duration energy storage systems designed to improve electricity grid reliability and affordability. The company closed a $750 million Series G financing round in August 2026 and secured a $270 million credit facility in September to support manufacturing expansion and working capital requirements. The financing is supporting continued development of Form Factory 1, the company’s manufacturing facility in Weirton, West Virginia. Form Energy also expanded its executive leadership team with the appointments of Navneet Govil as Chief Financial Officer and Wes Sloan as Chief Operating Officer. Lori Goler Brings Experience Scaling Global Organizations Goler has served as President of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative since 2025, overseeing its work across science and education. Previously, she spent 16 years at Meta, serving as Chief People Officer from 2008 through 2024. During that period, she led the company’s global workforce strategy and organizational operations through substantial growth and transformation. Earlier in her career, Goler served as General Manager of eBay Stores and led consumer marketing at eBay. She was also a founding executive at online retailer eStyle. She previously served on the board of Stanford Health Care from 2013 to 2022. Goler holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, an MBA from Harvard Business School, and a Master of Public Policy from Harvard Kennedy School. Form Energy expects her experience developing organizational structures and managing workforce expansion to support its growing manufacturing and commercial operations. Jon McNeill Brings Tesla And Lyft Operating Experience McNeill is Co-Founder and CEO of DVx Ventures, a venture firm focused on creating and scaling companies addressing large market opportunities. Previously, he served as Chief Operating Officer at Lyft between 2018 and 2019 and as President of Global Sales, Delivery and Service at Tesla from 2015 through 2018. Before joining Tesla, McNeill was CEO and chairman of the board at software company Enservio, where he served from 2006 to 2015. Throughout his career, he has founded and scaled six companies, many of which were subsequently acquired by publicly traded businesses. McNeill has served on the boards of Lululemon Athletica, CrossFit, and Asurion. He also previously served on the board of General Motors from 2022 through 2026. His additional board experience includes Cruise, Stash, Tekion, TIER Mobility, and TrueMotion. McNeill graduated from Northwestern University. Expanding Long-Duration Energy Storage Form Energy is developing iron-air battery systems designed to provide approximately 100 hours of energy storage. The technology uses iron, water, and air, materials the company describes as among the most abundant and affordable resources available. The batteries are designed to store electricity and discharge it over extended periods, providing a potential solution for balancing renewable energy generation and electricity demand. Long-duration storage could help utilities manage periods when wind and solar generation are limited, while improving the resilience of electricity networks. Form Energy is manufacturing its systems at Form Factory 1 in West Virginia as it prepares to serve customers across the United States and internationally. The addition of Goler and McNeill comes as the company moves from technology development toward broader commercial production and deployment. KEY QUOTE: “Lori and Jon have each led organizations through critical periods of rapid growth and I am pleased to welcome them to the Board. Lori spent 16 years at Meta building a global workforce and culture, and as our team grows, that experience will be invaluable. Jon has scaled operations, sales, and delivery at Tesla and Lyft, which is just what we need as we continue to ramp production and deploy iron-air batteries to customers across the United States and internationally. Their perspectives will guide how we grow, and I’m looking forward to working closely with both.” Mateo Jaramillo, Co-Founder And CEO Of Form Energy

artigo.texto: Siga A Crítica de Campo Grande no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga A Crítica de Campo Grande no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Veja o resumo da notícia - Data centers dos EUA emitiram 25,7 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, volume similar ao de Dinamarca e Bolívia. - Estudo liderado por Harvard analisou 403 grandes instalações, que consumiram quase 2% da eletricidade usada no país no período. - Combustíveis fósseis, sobretudo gás natural e carvão, originaram 54% da energia associada ao funcionamento dessas estruturas. - Virgínia, Iowa e Ohio concentraram cerca de metade das emissões, enquanto o Oregon teve menor intensidade de carbono. - Pesquisadores usaram imagens de satélite e plantas de edifícios, o que expôs a falta de transparência das empresas do setor. - Oposição de comunidades bloqueou ou atrasou 70 projetos em 25 estados, que somam investimentos estimados em US$ 271 bilhões. - Especialistas defendem que grandes operadores divulguem consumo de eletricidade e emissões para permitir maior fiscalização. Os maiores data centers dos Estados Unidos responderam por emissões estimadas em 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. O volume é comparável às emissões anuais de países como Dinamarca e Bolívia, segundo estudo publicado nesta segunda-feira (16) na revista científica Nature Sustainability. A pesquisa, conduzida por uma equipe liderada pela Universidade Harvard, analisou 403 grandes centros de processamento de dados. Juntas, essas instalações consumiram quase 2% de toda a eletricidade utilizada nos Estados Unidos durante o período. Além disso, os pesquisadores identificaram que 54% da energia associada ao funcionamento dessas estruturas teve origem em combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás natural e carvão. Dessa forma, a expansão da inteligência artificial amplia o debate sobre o consumo energético e os impactos ambientais da infraestrutura digital. Consumo de energia varia conforme a localização O levantamento mostrou que a localização dos data centers influencia diretamente suas emissões de carbono. Isso ocorre porque cada região americana utiliza diferentes fontes para produzir eletricidade. Na Virgínia, em Iowa e em Ohio, por exemplo, as instalações concentraram aproximadamente metade das emissões estimadas no estudo. Por outro lado, centros de dados localizados no Oregon apresentaram menor intensidade de carbono, devido à maior participação de fontes de energia sem combustíveis fósseis. Para chegar aos resultados, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite, plantas de edifícios e informações sobre a capacidade elétrica das instalações. Em seguida, calcularam o consumo estimado e relacionaram os dados à composição da matriz energética regional. Entretanto, o trabalho também revelou dificuldades para acessar informações sobre o setor. Segundo Gianluca Guidi, pesquisador de Harvard que liderou o estudo, a necessidade de reconstruir dados sobre as instalações demonstra a falta de transparência das empresas. Além disso, os números podem estar abaixo do impacto real da atividade. Isso porque o levantamento não inclui todos os centros de dados existentes nos Estados Unidos nem instalações que utilizam exclusivamente sistemas próprios de geração de energia. Expansão da IA aumenta pressão por transparência O crescimento acelerado da inteligência artificial impulsiona a construção de novos data centers, estruturas responsáveis pelo armazenamento e processamento de grandes volumes de informações. Entretanto, a expansão também enfrenta resistência de comunidades preocupadas com o consumo de energia e os impactos ambientais. Entre março de 2024 e o início de novembro de 2026, movimentos de oposição conseguiram bloquear ou atrasar pelo menos 70 projetos em 25 estados americanos, segundo levantamento da consultoria Relae. Esses empreendimentos representam investimentos estimados em US$ 271 bilhões. Além disso, parte das críticas envolve a falta de informações públicas sobre o funcionamento das instalações e seus efeitos nas regiões onde pretendem operar. Diante desse cenário, pesquisadores defendem regras mais rigorosas de transparência. A proposta é exigir que grandes operadores divulguem informações sobre consumo de eletricidade e emissões de carbono, permitindo maior fiscalização. O estudo também retrata um setor em rápida transformação. Desde o encerramento do período analisado, pelo menos 250 novos data centers entraram em operação nos Estados Unidos, conforme dados da empresa Cleanview. Assim, os resultados reforçam a necessidade de acompanhar os efeitos ambientais da expansão tecnológica. Embora a inteligência artificial ofereça novas possibilidades econômicas e produtivas, seu crescimento também exige investimentos em fontes de energia menos poluentes e maior transparência sobre o consumo de recursos.

artigo.texto: Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company (Masdar), a global clean energy leader, has celebrated the completion of the $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California, marking another major milestone in the company’s growing US renewable energy portfolio. The Lockhart complex was developed by Terra-Gen, which is jointly owned by Masdar and Igneo Infrastructure Partners. The project includes more than 925,000 solar modules and 248 battery enclosures. Its 365 megawatts (MW) of solar generation and 173.7 MW of battery storage generate enough electricity to meet the annual needs of approximately 350,000 homes and businesses. Khaleefa Almheiri, President and CEO of Masdar Americas, said: "The completion of Lockhart demonstrates the scale of Masdar’s ambitions in the United States and our commitment to supporting America’s growing energy needs. By bringing together Masdar’s global expertise, investment capabilities and track record of delivering major renewable energy projects with Terra-Gen’s strong local presence, we are delivering reliable, affordable power, creating skilled jobs and supporting economic growth. As electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI, advanced manufacturing and wider economic growth, Masdar is proud to be a long-term partner in powering America’s future." The milestone was commemorated with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Hinkley facility, bringing together company employees, local officials, commercial lenders, project partners and customers. "Today is about recognising the people and partnerships that brought Lockhart to life and celebrating what this project means for the region," said John O’Connor, Chief Executive Officer at Terra-Gen. "Solar is one of the most economical sources of new electricity, and storage extends its value by making that energy available when it’s needed most. At the scale of our Lockhart facility, that combination can make a meaningful difference for California’s growing electricity needs." Engineering and construction of the solar and storage complex created more than 1,000 on-site jobs with 880,000 hours worked over four years. -TradeArabia News Service Copyright 2026 Al Hilal Publishing and Marketing Group Provided by SyndiGate Media Inc. artigo.texto: Combining wind power with solar and battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reduce the cost of delivering reliable renewable electricity by nearly one-fifth, according to a new analysis by energy think tank Ember. The report, titled 'Harnessing the Winds', finds that adding wind to solar and battery-based systems reduces the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105/MWh to $86/MWh. The analysis highlights the growing importance of combining different renewable energy sources rather than relying on solar or wind independently. While solar power provides electricity during daylight hours, wind generation often follows different daily and seasonal patterns. This allows wind to compensate for periods of lower solar generation, potentially reducing the amount of battery storage required to maintain a stable electricity supply. Wind Integration Brings Down Battery Storage Requirements Across Major Markets One of the key findings of the analysis is that wind power can reduce the duration of battery storage required to maintain electricity supply during periods of low renewable generation. Ember's modelling shows that the battery requirement for achieving 90% power supply reliability falls from 24 hours of load to 10 hours in Canada. In the US and Europe, the requirement declines from 20 hours to 12 hours, while China sees a reduction from 18 hours to 12 hours. However, the impact varies by geography. In India, the modelled battery requirement remains at 14 hours even after wind is added to the solar and battery combination. The difference is linked to regional weather patterns and the availability of wind resources. Wind generation tends to be stronger during periods when solar output is relatively low, particularly in regions with significant seasonal variations. Solar and Wind Coincide Only Once Every Four Years The report also examines the frequency of simultaneous low-generation periods for solar and wind, an important consideration for renewable energy reliability. Based on historical weather data, Ember finds that solar experiences a week-long period of generation below half its average output approximately four times a year globally. Similar low-generation periods for wind occur around eight times annually. However, periods when both solar and wind experience such conditions simultaneously occur only once every four years on average. This difference makes a combination of the two sources more resilient to weather-related generation fluctuations. When solar generation declines, wind can help compensate for the shortfall, reducing the need for conventional backup generation. Ember further estimates that adding wind allows regions accounting for three-quarters of global electricity demand to achieve 90% renewable power uptime at less than $100/MWh. Without wind, only around half of global electricity demand falls within this cost range. 706 GW of Planned Coal and Gas Capacity Could Face Renewable Competition Globally, around 845 GW of coal and gas power capacity is currently in the development pipeline. Ember estimates that firm solar and wind power, supported by batteries and limited backup generation, could offer a lower-cost alternative for approximately 706 GW of this planned capacity. Without wind, the comparable capacity falls to 520 GW. The report also estimates that global wind potential is at least 19 times the world's electricity demand under its conservative assumptions. Looking ahead, Ember projects that the cost of firm solar and wind power could decline from $89/MWh to $52/MWh by 2050, based on its modelled cost trajectories. The findings underline the importance of integrating solar, wind and battery storage into power systems as renewable energy penetration increases. Rather than depending on a single generation source, combining different technologies could help address intermittency, reduce storage requirements and improve the economics of delivering reliable renewable electricity.
